en: The Śrī Āpastamba Śulbasūtra, together with the commentary of Kapardin;
the sacrifices have been described.

The fire-places for these [fires] have fixed dimensions and fixed locations. Desiring to state their length and breadth, he says: "The dwellings and the yogas"—we shall explain the dwellings and the yogas. (ĀpŚus 1.1)
The *vihāras* are those in which the fires are established, namely the *prāgvaṃśa* and so forth, as well as the *gārhapatya* and so forth.
That by which something is joined is a *yoga*, which here refers to a particular kind of rope. The *vihārayoga* is the joining of the *vihāras*.
Alternatively, "vihāra" means dwelling itself;
the "yoga of those" is "vihārayoga.
The meaning is the complete exposition of that.
The plural form "yogān" (the yogas) is used to show that they are demonstrated in many ways; and this demonstration is for the purpose of establishing their importance.

Just as chariots and the like, which have fixed parts and measurements, do not move properly if even a single part is deficient by even a small measure, so too the fire-altars and other such structures do not attain the status of being effective means (*sādhana*) if they are deficient by even a small measure. Therefore, they must be accomplished with great effort. Because of the citation of the *Śruti* texts stating, "It is understood everywhere," the dimensions and so forth must be correctly accomplished in every respect through these very methods.
And in the event of a failure regarding the *āyatanas*, there must be an expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
To demonstrate this very point, the terms "atha" and "ataḥ" are employed in another *Śulba* [text]: "Now, therefore, the applications of the sacrificial sites (*vihāra-yoga*).
First of all, the determination of the directions (*diś*) ought to be stated; however, it has not been mentioned by this Ācārya.
It should be taken from within that cord:
"Indeed, these Kṛttikās do not deviate from the eastern direction;
one should measure by the sight of them"—this is one [view].
"One should measure by means of the Śroṇādarśana," says one [tradition];
"by means of the interval between Citrā and Svātī," says another.
Thus was it stated by the venerable Bodhāyana concerning the measurement of the *prāgvaṃśa*.

The direction in which the Kṛttikās and other stars set is the eastern direction (*prācī*). This is to be determined by placing water between the constellations Citrā and Svātī and observing its reflection. Alternatively, having leveled the ground where the sacrificial site (*devayajana*) is located with clay and water, one should drive a peg (*śaṅku*) into the center. Then, using a cord equal in length to the peg, one should draw a circle. In the forenoon, where the tip of the shadow of the peg touches the circumference of the circle, one should drive another peg; and likewise at the time of sunset in the afternoon. Those two [points] are the east and west.

Desiring precision, on the following day in the forenoon, having made a mark precisely along the line of the tip of the gnomon’s shadow, one should move the gnomon—which stands toward the west between the two marks of the gnomon—back toward the starting point.
*Āpastamba-Śulba-Sūtra-Vyākhyā Karavindīyā*:
"Om"—I praise this single-syllabled name, which transcends speech and nose (smell).
May that eternal lotus-eyed light of Viṣṇu— the supreme abode which the seers behold, accompanied by Lakṣmī and possessing the luster of an atasī flower— be ever present within my heart.
Salutations to the sage Āpastamba, the ground of the meaning of the Vedas,
upon whose sūtras the young maidens of the sacrificial scriptures stand supported;
this commentary on his sūtras and śulba-sūtras is intended to bring about the understanding of the literal meaning of the syllables.
Today, the commentary on the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya is being composed by Karavindādhipa.
By the venerable Āpastamba, who undertook the promise to explain sacrifice, the *haviḥ-yajñas*, *soma-yajñas*, and *pāka-yajñas* were both promised for exposition and subsequently explained.

In that regard, first of all, specific locations of fixed dimensions have been described in various contexts—ranging from the Gārhapatya hearth to the piled bricks (city-iṣṭakā)—for the rites pertaining to the Āhavanīya, Soma, Animal Sacrifice, and Wood-offering, whether they be symmetrical or asymmetrical, circular, square, triangular, or of various other forms. These too must be measured; thus, concerning their measurement, the nature of the means such as cords and so forth—which serve as the instruments for that measurement—is defined merely by their essential character: "this much cord is the measuring-line (karaṇī) for this much area."

Since it is impossible to know [the nature of yoga] and one must see that its exposition is necessary, the explanation of the yoga of *vihāra* is presented immediately after the explanation of sacrifice (*yajña*):
*vihāra* means wandering;
*yoga* is the means for that.
The "applications of the dwellings" (vihārayoga) are the applications belonging to the dwellings; these we shall explain, that is, we shall set forth.
The root *hṛ* preceded by the prefix *vi-* [is used here].
The term *vihāra* has many meanings, such as play, blazing, binding, wandering, and celestial palaces (*vimāna*).
It is designated as "vihāra" in various senses—such as place and so forth—precisely because of its connection with those specific actions.
However, in this context, it denotes a celestial palace (*vimāna*).
And *yuj* is of two kinds: that which signifies meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and that which signifies connection (*saṃbandha*).
Here, however, it signifies meditative absorption.
Samādhi is the correct establishment of the altar-ground (*vedī*) and so forth; this will be explained in the passage beginning with "That is *samādhi*.
They are called *yogas* because one is joined by means of them; they are the ropes and other tools that serve as the means for the ritual layout (*viharaṇa*).

Ritual layout (*viharaṇa*) is the demarcation for the various constructions of the hips and shoulders of the field to be measured, such as the altar-ground, according to the rule beginning with "At the ends of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line," and so forth.
The methods of practice (*vihārayoga*) consist of the cords (*rajjū*) and other tools that serve as the means for achieving that [practice]; these we shall now explain.
Explanation (*vyākhyāna*) is defined as providing a detailed exposition by establishing a point through a powerful reason when doubt exists—for example:
"They are equal and square because the word has no qualifying suffix; and because, among the meanings of measurement, the meaning of the word is subject to one's own preference," and so forth.

Now, one might ask: how can *vihāra* denote a state (*bhāva*), or how can it be a synonym for *vimāna* (measurement)? How is there a connection between the act of moving (*viharaṇa*) and the measuring cord (*vedī*) and so forth? How can ropes and the like function as instruments (*karaṇa*) therein? And how can the root *yuj* signify meditative absorption (*samādhi*), or how is the term *yoga* applied to the cords and other such things? It is replied: because of the indication of an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) in the statements "the act of moving has been stated" and "the act of moving has been explained," the word *vihāra* denotes a state (*bhāva*).

Furthermore, in the passages "that single-corded movement" (*tadekaravjā viharaṇam*) and "having measured with the cord" (*ravjā vā vimāya*), the terms *vimāna* and *viharaṇa* refer here to the function of the cord.
From the observation of both, there is their synonymy.
By the statement, "There are so many altar-constructions (*vediviharaṇa*)," the connection of the construction with the altar and so forth is established.

Because of the designation of the rope as "rope" (*rajjū*) in various places—such as in "the incoming fourth [side] is the diagonal rope" (*āgantucaturthamāyāmaśvākṣṇayārajjuḥ*) and "the measuring rope" (*pramāṇamātrī rajjuṃ*)—and because of the feminine gender used in those respective instances such as "the side-measuring [rope]" (*pārśvamānī*), "the cross-measuring [rope]" (*tiryaṅbhānī*), and "the eighteen-fold measuring [rope]" (*aṣṭādaśakaraṇī*), as well as the hearing of the instrumental case in the word "rope" (*rajjvā*), [it is understood that these terms refer to the rope].
Because it is the means for the stretching of cords, for this very reason they call this work *śulba*.
The teachers will refer to this entire collection of texts as "That is *samādhi*" and "Now another *yoga*";
by this it is known that the root *yuj* signifies *samādhi*.

Since the object of application (*yujer-artha*), which is meditative concentration (*samādhi*), is to be accomplished through movement (*viharaṇa*), the means for such movement are also the means for yoga; thus, ropes and other such items are called "yogas. The conventional usage of the term "yoga" with respect to the instruments of movement is intended to indicate one's dedication to the practice of moving [in meditation].
For what purpose is the inclusion of the word *yoga*? It has been stated that it is for the purpose of indicating its status as a means (*sādhana*).

If that is so, then in such statements as "We shall explain the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices," it is understood immediately after the promise (*pratijñā*) that the means themselves are what are to be explained.
If this is the case, then the inclusion of the word *yoga* is for the purpose of demonstrating the preeminence of mental means (*mānasa-sādhana*).

What is that preeminence? Although there exist mental means such as the *pada* and *veṇu*, nevertheless, by means of those, the accomplishment of the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) on the site of the altar (*vedi*) and so forth within the sacrificial hall (*vimāna*) is achieved with great effort; whereas by means of the *pajjusīra* and other [measuring tools], that same accomplishment in the sacrificial hall is easily performed—this is what constitutes preeminence here.

[Objection: But surely the fact that cords and the like are the means for the measurement (*viharaṇa*) will be established even from common worldly experience; for what purpose is it said, "we shall explain the applications of measurement"? [Reply: It is true that it would be established. Nevertheless...

Since place (*deśa*), like time (*kāla*), is also an auxiliary factor (*aṅga*) [of the ritual], the Teacher—considering that if the aforementioned measure of the place deviates by even as little as a sesame seed, either being less or more, there would be a deficiency in the auxiliary (*aṅgavaiguṇya*)—speaks this in order to demonstrate for himself the unambiguous and easily performed status of the rope and other tools as means (*upāya*).

Therefore, since the avoidance of deficiency or excess is required, if an error should arise through negligence or incapacity, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must necessarily be performed; it is for this purpose that he says: "We shall explain the applications of the layout (*vihārayoga*)."
Alternatively, "vihāras" are those things by which one moves about (*vihriyante*);
and the "yogas" are the means for accomplishing them, namely the ropes and so forth.

In this context, some [authorities] define direction first in order to make known the specific directions, because it is impossible for persons who do not know the distinctions of direction to perform the moving about of the sacrificial ground and other sites, which possess fixed spatial conjunctions and the like.

As the Blessed Kātyāyana said: "Having fixed a gnomon (śaṅku) in level ground and having drawn a circle with a cord equal in length to the gnomon, the shadow of the tip of the gnomon falls where it touches the two lines; that is the east.

Having fixed a gnomon there and subsequently doubling the cord and making loops at both ends, one should fasten the loops to the two gnomons and, using a marker, pull [the cord] southward from the middle gnomon; likewise toward the north—this is the north."

The meaning of this is as follows: Now, when one intends to perform a sacrifice to the gods in a pure place, having leveled that place with water and driven a peg (śaṅku) into the center, one should prepare a cord of equal length to the peg with a loop at one end; having fastened it to the peg and circumscribed a circle with it, one should make a mark at the point where the shadow of the tip of the peg falls upon the line of the circle in the forenoon—those two marks, the eastern and western, constitute the east-west direction. That [line] is the eastern direction.

Having driven a peg into each of two marks and having made a cord twice the distance between them with loops at both ends, one should make a mark in the middle. Having fastened the two loops onto the pegs and pulled [the cord] southward by means of the mark, one should drive a peg into the mark; likewise to the north, having pulled [the cord] by means of the mark, one should drive a peg.
Those two pegs, being south and north, constitute the northern direction.
Thus it is stated in the *Jyotirjñāna*:

"By means of the intersection of two circles drawn from the tips of the shadows of a gnomon situated in the center of a desired mandala, the directions south and north are to be known by means of a fish-figure [formed by the intersecting lines].
Thus, the determination of the directions has been described in various ways in many places by other authorities as well.
Because it is already well-known, the Teacher has not stated it here.

Since the status of the side-measures (pārśvamāna) and so forth as means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is established through the etymological derivation "that by which something is measured" (pramīyate 'nena), they are designated by the technical term "means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa).
The *Sundararājīyā*, a commentary on the *Āpastamba-Śulbasūtra*:

Having examined the entire meaning of this profound treatise known as the *Śulba* which was composed by the venerable Āpastamba, as explained in the commentaries (*bhāṣya*) and other works; [this work is now presented].
Now Sundara, the son of Mādhavārya—the sacrificer who is a treasure of the Kuśika lineage—composes this commentary on the *Śulbapradīpa* for the sake of concise understanding.
*Vihāra* means the act of laying out; it refers to the construction of the ground in a square or other such shapes.
Its *yogās* are the methods or means for doing so. — *Kapardibhāṣya*.
The measurement is according to its length. ĀpŚus_1.2a.
"Yāvadāyāmam" is an avyayībhāva compound.
Regarding the rule "yāvad-avadhāraṇe" (yāvat used in the sense of restriction), what is restricted here? It is the length.
It is not the case that length alone is the measurement; there are also crosswise and diagonal cords, for by those two as well, the covering is possible.
The purpose of the designation "measurement" is for the sake of clearly identifying the length, as in the rule: "one should increase the measurement by one-third."
In Karavindīyā Vyākhyā,
the word *yāvat* denotes measure (*parimāṇa*), while the word *āyāma* denotes that which is the counterpart to width (*vistāra*).

The compound is formed with the sense of "as far as" (*yāvad-avadhāraṇe*). Whatever the length (*āyāma*) is, that much is the measure (*pramāṇa*). What is determined here? That the very measurement of length is the measure.
Therefore, in this case, because it is twice the length of the [measured] line, the measure is that of the rope or other material which serves as its substrate;
its purpose regarding the transverse measurements and so forth is stated in the *Kapardibhāṣya*.
Having practiced that half-measure on the other [side], he makes a mark at one-sixth on the third [side]. ĀpŚus 1.2b.
The word "that" refers to the measurement.
Having added half of that— that is, having projected it— above the measurement, at a third point minus one-sixth, he makes a mark.
Having made two loops at both ends with the measuring cord accompanied by its extension, one makes a transverse mark on the third part of the other side;
one should make a mark at the sixth part of the length.
Having fixed the two ends on the two ends of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line by means of a mark, he draws it southward and makes a mark. (ĀpŚS 1.2c)
The *pṛṣṭhyā* is that which pertains to the back.

Having driven stakes at its two ends and having fastened loops to them, one pulls it toward the south by means of a mark and makes a sign; having extended it by means of a mark so that the transverse cord (*tiryaṅbhānī*) is reduced by one-sixth, one shifts [the cord] in such a way that the remaining diagonal cord (*akṣṇayā rajju*) is thus displaced.
One should drive in a sign.
Karavinda’s Commentary:
It makes half of that.
Now, since the sacrificial altars for the iṣṭi, soma, and paśubandha sacrifices are generally long quadrilaterals, the method of measuring (viharaṇa) corresponding to them is stated.
By the word "pramāṇam" (the measure), the length that has been established as the measure is referred to.

"Tadardham" means half of that. "Abhyasanam" means adding on. "Aparasmin" refers to the subsequent part that follows. "Tṛtīye" means together with the third [part], which consists of the measure and its half. "Ṣaḍbhāgone"—a sixth part is a "ṣaḍbhāga"; when that part is subtracted from that same third [part], one makes a "lakṣaṇam"—that by which something is marked—a mark, which serves as the means for fully understanding the corners of the field to be measured.
One should perform [the following]: at the two ends of the *pṛṣṭhyā*—the middle of the field to be measured is the "back" (*pṛṣṭha*). How is this understood?

Because its constituent parts are designated as the hips (*śroṇi*), shoulders (*aṃsa*), and sides (*pārśva*); just as the middle of the regions of the hips, shoulders, and sides is the "back," so too is this [field]. The line situated there is the *pṛṣṭhyā*.

Having driven stakes into its two ends and having made loops at the two ends of the cord, having fixed them and attached them, one should pull the cord toward the south by means of a mark or sign—that is, drawing the cord toward the south—and there one should set up a stake as a marker, which serves as the cause for knowing the corner of the field.
The commentary of Kapardin is thus: "When it is reversed from the north to the other side, that is the *samādhi*. (ĀpŚus 1.2d)

Having thus moved the cord northward, one should act as before. Having reversed it on the other side, one should release the loop from the eastern peg and fasten it to the western peg; having released the loop from the western peg, one should fasten it to the eastern peg.
That is the inversion.
Having performed that, one shifts the right shoulder toward the north by means of that very same characteristic mark—reduced by a sixth part—from the other [left] shoulder; this is the *samādhi*.
Since the lateral sides and so forth have been brought about by the specific path described, it is called *samādhi*.
Karavinda’s Commentary:

In the same way, one should also pull the cord from the north and establish a mark. There is a reversal of the two ends of the cord: having placed the loop at the western peg that was previously [at the east], and the [other] end at the eastern [peg that was previously at the west], one should pull the cord from the other side—that is, from a location different from where the mark was made—and establish marks to the south and to the north.

This is what is meant: having projected this measurement onto the cord and divided the projected length into six parts, one should mark two points at the ends of the fifth part from the end. Having fixed stakes at the two ends of the back-line and fastened the cord to them, one should pull it southward along the mark and fix a stake; likewise, pulling it northward, one should fix a stake. Then, reversing the ends of the cord, one should fix two stakes in the other direction as well. But surely—

One might ask: "Why should the mention of 'the subsequent' not be for the purpose of excluding [the definition] from the first third? For even there, it would not apply simply because of the lack of contradiction.

If you say, "In that case, it will be for the purpose of explaining the middle third and indicating the preceding and following ones," this is not so. If this had been intended, he would have stated it more clearly as "in the middle third"; however, he did not say it in that way.

Now, if you think: "When it is stated that [the rope] for that purpose is other than the *abhaya*, another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is understood through the force of repetition; therefore, let there be a definition for that third [case]," this too is not tenable—because he will state that this repetition refers to the *āgantv* (additional) part, which is a remainder of the diagonal cord (*akṣṇayārajju*).

In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśikā*, regarding the eighteen-fold *upaśama* and so forth, he will state that the arrangement of the hips and shoulders is performed by means of the fifteen-fold [measurement] itself after having extended it; therefore, it is understood that in that case, the "other" [measurement] is indeed an additional one consisting of six parts, and that the *nirañjana* is [located] when six parts have been subtracted.

Now, if the word "other" (*apara*) refers to an additional [measurement], then the statement "the characteristic is when six parts are subtracted" would suffice; for what purpose [is the rest stated]?

Regarding the word "third" (*tṛtīya*): we do not see any purpose for it. It is said in reply: there certainly is a purpose for it; what is that? It is for the sake of making known that the procedure being taught here is the subject of all practice. How so? In this case, it is not fitting that even a single syllable uttered by the Teacher—who is omniscient and acts for the benefit of all—should be meaningless, let alone an entire word.
Therefore, it must be explained in such a way that the word possesses meaning according to its primary function (*mukhyayā vṛttyā*).

For this very reason, this word is explained as follows: by means of the "three-ness" denoted by the component word *tri* within the third word *āgantusamānādhikaraṇībhūta*, there is indicated the number of parts that can possibly exist in the repeated measure (*sābhyāsasya pramāṇasya*) according to the adventitious limit (*āgantuparimita*). Likewise, by means of the "six-ness" denoted by the component word *ṣaṭ* within the word *ṣaḍbhāga*, there is indicated the number of parts which is double the number indicated by the "three-ness," in order to correspond with that [measure].
By this, the following meaning is established:

In all instances of practice, having made the adventitious portion twice as large as however many parts of the measure—including the practiced portion—are produced, the marking is performed when that [adventitious portion] is reduced by one part.

For example: first, regarding half-proportion (*ardhābhyāsa*), one part is the half; the measure (*pramāṇa*) consists of two parts equal to that; for the measure with its proportion, there are three parts equal to the added portion (*āgantuka*); when the added portion is divided into twice that [measure], it has six parts, and the characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*) is made by subtracting one part from those. Likewise, regarding length-proportion (*āyāmābhyāsa*), the length is one part, and there is one part similar to that; thus, for the measure with its proportion, there are two parts, and when the proportion is divided into twice that [measure], there are four parts;
the characteristic mark is made by subtracting four parts from those.

Likewise—in the case of a third repetition, one part is the repetition, three parts equal to that are the measurement, and when the divisor is doubled, there are eight parts; the definition is to be seen as being [marked] by subtracting eight parts. In this very same way, for a fourth and subsequent repetitions, the calculation of parts is made by the force of the repetition itself for the measurement, while for the additional [repetition], the calculation of parts is made by a number double that; and the definition is to be seen as being [marked] by subtracting those parts.

Now, in a case where an equal degree of repetition is not possible for the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how can there be the postulation of a portion (*bhāga*) in both the primary means and the adventitious one, as well as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), such as cutting when the repetition is excessive and [replenishing] when it is deficient?

It is said: even in that case, this same method applies; however, having made the denominator of the *pramāṇa* (the standard) together with its numerator have a common divisor, and having made the denominator of the *āgantu* (the additive) also have a divisor by a number twice that [of the former], one should perform the subtraction (*nihañjana*) when the practice (*abhyāsa*) is deficient by as many parts as one part becomes deficient [in the result]. When the practice is excessive, that is, twice as much, then one part is the practice, and the *pramāṇa* is for the sake of the parts; in that case, when there is a common divisor with the half [of the *pramāṇa*] along with the practice.

In the case of two measures, there are half-units of division; when the divisions are doubled according to that number, there are six half-units of division therein. Since one part is subtracted by means of two [of those], the definition would apply to that deficiency.

In the case of a threefold repetition, the repetition constitutes one part, while the measure itself is a third part; thus, in the repetition, there are three such thirds. Consequently, the measure together with its repetition consists of four thirds. When the divisions are doubled for that, there are eight thirds in the additive portion; therein, the definition applies when it is deficient by three parts.

Thus, having calculated the portions in the practice of fourfold [divisions], one should establish the characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*) accordingly for the *āgantu* [measure]. Likewise, in the practice of three-quarters (*tripādābhyāsa*), one part is the practice (*abhyāsa*), one part similar to that is the measure (*pramāṇa*), and a third part is the *tṛtīyāṃśa*. When there is a division involving such parts, in the *sābhyāsapramāṇa*, there are seven thirds; the characteristic mark is established there when it is diminished by those three.
In this same way, the calculation of parts and the establishment of the characteristic mark should be understood for other divisions involving parts as well.

This too must not be forgotten: in all practices (*abhyāsa*), there is a single adventitious portion (*āgantubhāgaikya*), and by virtue of that, there is a unity of parts in the measure (*pramāṇa*), as well as a multiplicity of parts and a state of being merely a hundred [parts]. In this way, it should be understood that this method of spreading out (*viharaṇa*) pertains to the domain of all practices.

If this is established, how is it known that this rule has been accepted? It is said: because of the statement, "the diagonal cord (akṣṇayārajju) is the fourth of the transverse side," which demonstrates that the repetition of the length (āyāma-abhyāsa) is a specific type of diagonal cord for the fourth repetition; and because of the presentation of unequal repetitions in such cases as "the diagonal cord of the fifteen-unit and eight-unit [squares] is the seventeen-unit [cord]," it is known that this rule has been accepted. This is sufficient for the purpose, and it is also for the sake of distinguishing the diagonal cord from the transverse measurement (tiryaṅbhāni).
What is the purpose of mentioning "south" and "north"? It is for the sake of illustration regarding the crosswise [line]; otherwise, there would be a contradiction in the *sadas* and other areas.
Regarding the completion of this distribution at its end, he states the following for the laying down of another: "That is the concentration. This consists of two words.

By the word *tat*, "dwelling" (*viharaṇa*) is expressed; the masculine gender is used with reference to *samādhi*. The prefix *sam-* has the sense of "correctly" (*samyak*) or the sense of the word *sama* ("equal"); *āṅ* signifies "on all sides" (*samantato-bhāva*); and the root *dhā* means "to do" (*karoti*) or the sense of the word *sama*. Thus, *samādhi* is that which brings about a field (*kṣetra*) that is correctly neither deficient nor excessive on all sides. Alternatively, *samādhi* is the "possession" (*ādhi*) of those things that are "equal" (*samāna*).

The two side-measures (*pārśvamānya*), the two cross-measures (*tiryaṅbhānya*), and the diagonal cord (*akṣṇayārajju*) bring about mutual equality among one another; this is the "attainment" (*samādhi*), meaning that it renders the field equal in all four directions. This is the sense.

The "equipoise" (*samādhi*) is the state of the being-measured field remaining without deficiency or excess; and that is the fruit of the "movement" (*viharaṇa*), which is the correct means, because movement is its cause. By metaphorically treating cause and effect as non-different, that very movement is called "equipoise" and also "yoga. For what purpose is this stated? It is for the sake of encouraging the listeners' practice: when this aforementioned movement is equipoise, it brings about the straightness of the shoulders and hips; therefore, one should move with this without doubt.
The commentary of Kapardin states:
"A decrease or an increase [in the measure] is caused by that. (ĀpŚus 1.2e)

"Sign" (nimitta), "instrument" (karaṇa), and "primordial nature" (prakṛti) are synonyms. That for which this very [nature] is the object of purification is "caused by that" (tannimitta). "Diminution" (nirhrāsa) refers to the state of being born as an animal.
Or rather, there is an increase by means of the transverse lines themselves.
What is meant? It means that by the method already stated, they have been made to extend eastward, extended transversely, equal, and square.
This is the explanation according to Karavinda.

(Taking that as the cause: "That" refers to the meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which is the cause; "dwelling" (*viharaṇa*) is stated [as the effect]. "Cause," "reason" (*nimitta*), and "cause" (*hetu*) are synonyms. "Diminution" (*nirhrāsa*) is reduction (*apacaya*); "increase" (*vivṛddhi*) is augmentation (*upacaya*). These two would have that [concentration] as their cause. This is stated for the sake of brevity: when a large square has been laid out, one who wishes to produce a smaller square that is a portion of it, should drive stakes into the desired locations—such as the hips and shoulders of the large square—and, having tied a cord to the stakes...

Having extended [the cord] as far as desired, one should produce a small square with those [measures]. In the case of an increase, having tied long cords as desired according to the side-measures (*pārśvamānī*) and so forth of the square, and having extended them in accordance with the pegs (*śaṅku*) situated at its corners, one should drive a peg into the intended locations and take the distance between them; likewise, having driven pegs into the intended locations on the *karaṇīs* along the spine-line (*pṛṣṭhyā*), and having made other corresponding marks, one should extend the cord and effect either the reduction or the expansion of the field—this is the meaning.
The examples of reduction are the great altar (*mahāvedi*), the northern altar (*uttaravedi*), the sacrificial hearths (*dhiṣṇya*), and so forth;
the examples of increase are the great altar and others.
— *Sundararājīyā* [Commentary].
(Having measured that: A cord equal in length to the desired extent of the field is the measuring tool;
in all measurements, it has loops at both ends and is oriented toward the east.
That [line] remains fixed between the two pegs at the east and west ends;

because it lies along the back, it is also designated as the *pṛṣṭhyā*. Then, on another cord of the same length as that [line], one should add half of it, form a loop at the top, and make two loops at the two ends.
In that regard, there are three half-measures.
Having divided the third half-measure on the opposite side into six parts, one should make a mark at the fifth division starting from the cord.
Having fixed the two ends of this cord at the ends of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line, one extends [the cord] southward along the mark made and fixes a peg.
In the same way, having reversed the two cords in the north, one should likewise fix a peg at the eastern end;
that is the meditative absorption (samādhi), and that is the single yoga of the dwelling.
An illustration of this is as follows:

"In the eighteenth [chapter] of the *Ṣaṭtriṃśikā*," and so forth. When this has been done, if a decrease or increase is desired by means of a transverse line, that too must be performed using those very markers— the southern and northern pegs— which serve as the causal signs.
An example of reduction is: "Then, by half [of the measure] decreased by one from fifteen," and so forth.
However, in all cases, the eastern direction (prācī) should be understood as that which is [geographically] eastward.
Regarding this, Bodhāyana says: "Indeed, these Kṛttikās never leave the east."

"One should measure by the appearance of those [stars]—this is one view; one should measure by the appearance of Śroṇā—this is another; one should measure by the interval between Citrā and Svāti—this is yet another."

These characteristics are restricted to specific regions; Kātyāyana states the characteristic common to all regions: "Having fixed a peg in level ground and having drawn a circle with a cord equal in length to the peg, the point where the shadow of the tip of the peg falls upon the two lines is the east.
Regarding the phrase "upon the two lines," it means upon the eastern and western portions of the circular line.

Having practiced the lengthening according to the commentary of Kapardin, the fourth [measurement] is the addition; the diagonal cord is the length, and the remainder is the crosswise cord. The method of measurement has been explained. (ĀpŚus 1.3a)

Alternatively, having practiced the measurement and cast a cord of the length of the span into the span, one should join a fourth part of the incoming cord—which has been practiced as a fourth—to the span, and having made a mark, the diagonal cord (akṣṇayā rajju) is one and a quarter spans;
the remainder is three-quarters of a span. That is the cross-measuring cord (tiryaṅbhānī).
The dwelling has been explained;
the procedure for its expansion has been stated, but there is this distinction: the two shoulders should first be measured out, and the hips should be measured symmetrically in the opposite manner.

The purpose of this distinction in verbal formulation is for the sake of summarizing such statements as: "Having practiced [the measurement] three parts of the length, the characteristic mark is at the eighth part in the preceding fourth," and so forth.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"The mark made here by means of half of the non-traversed portion, and the portions he makes therein..."
Surely he will remain motionless for as long as it takes for one [digit] to be subtracted from the incoming [period].

Since the method of construction has already been established by the rules for the alternative options, why was it stated that "the tracing has been explained"? It was stated in order to demonstrate that the tracing mentioned in other *Śulbasūtras*—such as those concerning the seventh circle and so forth—is more cumbersome, and thus to show that this very tracing is the simpler one.
Karavinda’s commentary states the following regarding the measurement of the diagonal of this same tracing, to provide a preliminary view of it: "(The length—remainder)."
What must be done with the entire length of the *abhaya* [staff]? The intention is that one should perform the marking (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth according to the previously mentioned method.
This is the meaning: having multiplied the length by four, one should make a mark at the second [point], which is one-fourth of the whole.
When this is done, the fourth part added to the fourth part added shall be the diagonal cord (*akṣṇayā-rajju*) for the measurement of the length.

*Akṣṇayā* is an indeclinable (*nipāta*) resembling a case ending; it denotes a corner. A rope situated at a corner is an *akṣṇayārajju*, meaning a "working rope" (*karmarajju*). The "remainder" (*śeṣaḥ*) refers to the three other segments besides the part that has become the diagonal rope.
That by which something is measured crosswise is the *tiryaṅbhānī*, a rope stretched across.
The feminine gender is used with reference to the rope (*rajju*).
The word "or" (*vā*) is intended to include other types of practice;
it serves as a designation for specific varieties of practice, such as [measuring] twice the length, or three times, or a third, or a fourth part, and so forth.

This is the meaning: whatever length of rope is used as the measurement—whether shorter than that, longer than that, or equal to it—if one practices with it, then in each case, having formed squares of that respective size according to the previously mentioned method, and having made a mark one part less [than the full length], one should proceed by the method beginning with "having fixed the ends on both sides of the *pṛṣṭhyā*," and so forth.
Examples of these will be shown in the subsequent sūtra.

Now, indeed, for the purpose of defining the cause, when the rope has been removed, there is the state of being a diagonal rope for one part immediately following the measurement that preceded the definition, while for the other parts, the remaining [parts] are horizontal and diagonal ropes.

It is said: [If] it is intended that for the practice of the first stage there is only this much—that is, one hundred thousand [repetitions] reduced by a sixth part—then for what purpose is that half-reduced portion? Is the practice diminished from the root or from the end? Furthermore, for what purpose are the other portions, and from where do they come? This is not known because there is no restrictive rule regarding them.

There would either be no application [of the measurement] or an uncertainty here; for the fourth [side], the āyāma (length) is the diagonal cord (akṣṇayārajju), while the remainder is the transverse side (tiryaṅbhānī). Therefore, that one part is from the root of the repetition (abhyāsa); as for the others, since they constitute the diagonal cord and the other parts constitute the transverse sides, why has the opposite been stated when a separate repetition should have been mentioned? It is said: the opposite was done in order to reinforce, by means of the components of the sūtra, the rule regarding the scope of repetition—that half of the repetition constitutes half of the length (āyāma)—within the context of repetition.

Furthermore, here, in both the sixfold and fourfold divisions of the practice (*abhyāsa*), one portion attains the state of a diagonal cord (*akṣṇayārajju*), while all the other portions attain the state of transverse cords (*tiryaṅbhāni*). Regarding the phrase "the method of laying out has been explained" (*viharaṇaṃ vyākhyātam*), the meaning is that the method of laying out has indeed been explained; there is no other method of laying out. Even though the additional [measurements] (*āgantuka*) and the deficient [measurements] (*nyūna*) pertain to various subjects, the method of laying out remains exactly as previously stated—there is no other method of laying out. On this point, there are these verses:

As many as are the portions of the equalized [arc] corresponding to the arc of the ascensional difference, twice that number shall be the degrees of the oblique ascensions; when one is subtracted from that, it is the defining characteristic here. 1.1.
If those [divisors] of the common divisor are themselves composite, one should divide by the product of those composite numbers doubled; in this very case, the result will be one hundred thousand.

If there is a deficiency or a surplus in the adventitious [elements], how could there be a distribution of the portions when they are being equalized? Or how could there be the state of being stainless? 3.3.
There may be equality, deficiency, or excess, yet there is always oneness;
by virtue of that, in the measurement, there would be hundreds of parts within the unity of the portions. 4.
When the additive is greater, the quotient shall always have a fractional part;
when it is less, there shall be both a unity and a plurality of parts, whether the result is fractional or whole.

When [the remainder] is less than three-quarters, there is a fractional part; when it is half, it is nirañjana (stainless); when it is equal [to one], it is simply the unity of the parts—such is the calculation of the parts.
Having made a division into parts that are similar to the parts themselves, with equal practice;
then, having made a division into parts that are double the number of those previous divisions, even for a future [calculation].
By as many degrees as it is deficient here [in the native's ascendant], by that many degrees less than a full sign shall the definition of the incoming [ascendant] be determined. 8.

The practice is that by which a certain portion is diminished in order to complete a given number; that portion is defined by its characteristic, and twice that amount constitutes the completion of the portion. 9.
By employing the mention of "the third," the Sage intends here that when there is a doubling of the [first] two, the parts to be sung along with the practice are those accompanied by a sixth part.
Having stated that practice constitutes the third part by means of dividing the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) into three, it is considered to consist of six parts. 11.
Having accepted that, he established the defining characteristic in one part of it;
thus, by means of that, this [number] has an equal number of parts through repeated practice.
One should divide by two to eliminate the adventitious; when there is a remainder, it becomes *nirañjana*.
Immediately after that, regarding the number three, he spoke of the number six. 13.
The number associated with the "partaking of similarity" (sābhyāsamānabhāgīya) is intended to be doubled for a newcomer;
for the two [numbers] mentioned as the third and sixth parts pertain to the scope of that which involves repetition. 14.
They state that from the number with the repetition, one should subtract twice the number of repetitions;
or else, [the remainder] is joined with the number situated in the deficient portion, which is associated with a single count.

That which involves the calculation of shares for a guest in double the amount of what is held, or that which consists of a share similar to half of the practice, is "equal to the practice" (abhyāsamānaka). 16.
Having made [the calculation] according to that number, one should cut off one less than that as the characteristic here;
this principle is established by the force of the word "third. 17.
Furthermore, the very statement beginning with "of the fifteen-fold and the eight-fold" refers to that which is the measure of similarity between the fifteen-fold and the eight-fold. 18.
Alternatively, it is as follows: [the mandala] consists of twelve and thirty-five [squares], or else it is joined with three times the outer part and two-thirds of that preceding part. 19.

That which is joined with the other two [elements] by means of the fifth, or that which is endowed with the five qualities—these are for the purpose of movement within the sphere of the practice of *āyāma*. (20)
Since those two [the self and the object] would not exist for you, they must be based on the method of repeated practice;
likewise, in the case of half-practice, they mutually lead to exhaustion rather than to the cessation of exertion.
Likewise, the injunction regarding the constituent parts (aṅga) which involves mutual dependence is the basis for this principle;
it applies even when the guest element is diverse, as is the case with its corresponding portion.
Why is the rule for the stainless [altar] excluded by one part?
However, when the practice is halved, the characteristic mark is that which pertains to the third part.
Having set that aside, those who practice this [method] partake in its fruit;
[they obtain] one part of the separation [produced by] a cord laid diagonally across the three transverse parts.
Relying on this determination, he states that the definition here is lacking by one [element];
enough with excessive detail.
Sundararājīyā (on the measurement or the drawing):
Now he states another method.

In the *Śulba-sūtra*, regarding the measurement alone: having divided that rope, which is equal to the measurement itself, into four parts, one should make a mark between the third and fourth parts; having fastened the two loops at the front and back, the fourth part serves as the length (*āyāma*). At the time of the ritual layout (*viharaṇa*), it should be used as the diagonal rope (*akṣṇayā-rajju*). The remainder, being three-quarters of the length, takes the place of the transverse rope (*tiryaṅbhānī*). This is what is meant: having doubled the length, one should make a mark on one half at the fourth part.
Just as one would perform the ritual by making a mark at three *aratnis*— namely, at four *aratnis* and at four *aratnis* less— from the site of the *gārhapatya* altar;
this has been explained by the passage beginning with "the two ends of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line" and so forth.
In this regard, there are these two verses for the purpose of laying out [the altar] with a cord of the desired length:
"Upon the desired *pṛṣṭhyā* line, one should lay down the desired additional cord;
as many parts as there are in the total length, including the addition, they are equal to half of that [additional] length. (1)
First, having multiplied the practice by two and subtracted one, the resulting mark here shall be as follows:
one part is the length (sāyāma), and the remainder, when divided by three, shall be the hypotenuse (karṇa). // 2 //
The *Kapardibhāṣya* states:
"The diagonal cord of the long [altar] performs both that which the side-measuring cord and the cross-measuring cord perform when they are separate. (ĀpŚS 1.4a)
This means "of a long quadrangle";
because a regular circle lacks side-measures and so forth, and because it differs from an irregular quadrangle, the dimensions are taken [from the latter].

Because of the instruction, "Make the side-measure and the cross-measure," and because of the singular designation "the diagonal cord" (*akṣṇayā-rajju*), that which is taken as the single side-measure and the single cross-measure of a square—namely, whatever area is produced by the side-measure and whatever area is produced by the cross-measure when the square has been made—that both [areas] the diagonal cord produces; the meaning is that it produces both the area of the side-measure and the area of the cross-measure.
And he will state this with the words, "Of the triad and the tetrad," and so forth.
The square of the triad is nine (3² = 9).
A group of four multiplied by sixteen is twenty-five (4 × 4 = 16;
Twenty-five groups of five are likewise twenty-five (5 × 5 = 25); thus it should be understood everywhere.
The separate mention [of the word *pṛthak*] is for the purpose that there should be no sense of mere conjunction (*saṃsarga*).
For what purpose is the mention of the word *bhūta*? If it were simply said "they separate" (*pṛthakkurutaḥ*), there might still be a specific kind of conjunction;
when the word *bhūta* is included, this fault does not occur.
The manner of moving about has been explained by those [verses] concerning what is to be known. ĀpŚus 1.4b.

The "wandering" (viharaṇa) spoken of by those three who have been mentioned is to be understood as that which can be known— namely, that which is mentally constructed. The meaning is that one should wander according to the path thus described.
This sūtra has been stated here as well because it will be useful for the purpose of fully understanding the construction of the *prauga* and other such altars.
Karavinda’s commentary states:
"This method of spreading out [the altar] is called 'attainment' (*samādhi*) because it effects the perfecting of the sacrificial field."

Showing that this is the cause for this meditative absorption (*samādhi*), he says: "(The measuring of the long). "Of the long" means of the long square; by implication, "of the equal" is also understood. This will be explained right here: the diagonal cord and the cross-measure (*tiryaṅmānī*) have been mentioned. That by which the side is measured is the side-measure (*pārśvamānī*). When these two—being separate—that is, distinct—accomplish it, meaning they bring about it; both of them, being the measure of two fields, produce—that is, accomplish—one field. Of the long square, the side-measure itself [is the side-measure]. The side-measure itself [is the side-measure].

Having become both a side-measuring cord and a crosswise-measuring cord, whatever field one constructs, the diagonal cord itself, having become both a side-measuring cord and a crosswise-measuring cord, constructs a field equal in measure to those two fields combined. The method of measurement (*viharaṇa*) is said to be "knowable by means of those"—that is, by means of such side-measuring, crosswise-measuring, and diagonal cords which are thus characterized. These are called "knowable" because they can be known; that is, by knowing the measurement of either one of the aforementioned side-measuring, crosswise-measuring, or diagonal cords, the others can be known. Thus, they are "knowable."

How is that? Just as when it is known that "this is the side-measure" (*pārśvamānī*) and "this is the cross-measure" (*tiryaṅmānī*), it is understood that the diagonal cord (*akṣṇayārajju*) is the measure for the area of both those boards; so too, when it is known that "this is the side-measure" and "this is the diagonal cord," then, having subtracted from the area produced by the diagonal cord the area produced by the side-measure, it is understood that the measure of the remaining area is the cross-measure. Likewise, [it is understood] when it is known that "this is the cross-measure" and "this is the diagonal cord."

When the diagonal cord (*akṣṇayārajjū*) has been understood, and the transverse measuring cord (*tiryaṅmānī*), which constitutes the area of the result, has been subtracted from the area of the resulting field that constitutes the diagonal cord, it is possible to know that the square root (*karaṇī*) of the remaining area is the side-measuring cord (*pārśvamānī*).

These [cords] are thus to be known; by these "to-be-known" [cords], the aforementioned method of spreading out [the altar] (*viharaṇa*) is to be performed—the meaning is that the spreading out which was taught is to be done by means of those things that are to be known, not by those that are not to be known. The intention is that one should understand that this taught method of spreading out is the cause for meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Alternatively, the previously mentioned spreading out should be performed with those [cords] that are fit to be conceived in the mind as "to-be-known."

The meaning is as follows: having ascertained the measurements of the side-measuring cord (*pārśvamānī*), the cross-measuring cord (*tiryaṅmānī*), and the diagonal cord (*akṣṇayārajju*), one should measure a single cord equal to the combined length of both the cross-measuring and diagonal cords; then, having made a mark at the end of the cross-measuring cord, the previously described method of measurement (*viharaṇa*) should be performed by means of that [cord].

Here, some examples of the previously mentioned methods, such as the "half-increment" (*ardhābhyāsa*) and others, are stated. Regarding the half-increment: when a measurement of twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) is increased by half, it becomes eighteen finger-breadths.
In that case, when the measurement has been determined by means of an additional six-finger span, there are three parts of the six-fingers belonging to the measurement with its practice.
Of those three parts, when the additional six-finger span is divided into six by doubling those three parts, each single part constitutes one finger.
In that case, when the measurement has been reduced by one-sixth, the length increased by one part is thirteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*); this is the diagonal cord (*akṣṇayārajju*).

The remaining five parts are the cross-measure (*tiryaṅmānī*), which is five finger-breadths; therein, the measurement is twelve finger-breadths. It thus produces forty-four hundred finger-breadths of square areas.
Likewise, with a diagonal cord of thirteen finger-breadths, those two together produce one hundred and sixty-nine finger-breadths of square areas.

Regarding the length and the extension, as follows: the length is twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), and the additional portion (*āgantu*) is likewise the same. Together with the extension, two parts of the measurement are equal to the measure of the additional portion.

When the incoming [side] is cut according to double that number, there are four incoming parts of three finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) each. Therein, the diagonal cord (*akṣṇayārajju*) of the incoming fourth part is fifteen finger-breadths in length; the remaining transverse measuring cord (*tiryaṅmānī*) is nine finger-breadths. Therein, the nine-finger-breadth cord produces eighty-one finger-breadth squares; the length remains as before. The fifteen-finger-breadth diagonal cord—both of these together—produce one hundred and twenty-five finger-breadth squares.

Regarding the case where the width is double the length—for example, if the length is twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), the double is twenty-four finger-breadths; when the measurement is determined by means of that doubling, the doubling constitutes one part and the measurement is half of that. When one [unit] is determined by means of a half, there are three halves, which are the divisions for that double. Therein, each single half is four finger-breadths, and two halves are eight finger-breadths, which is one part; the mark is placed at its end, and the measurement joined with that is twenty finger-breadths as the diagonal cord (*akṣṇayārajju*).

In that case, for the incoming [line], the four sides are four *aṅgulas* each, making sixteen *aṅgulas* in total; that transverse measurement there, being sixteen *aṅgulas*, produces two hundred and fifty-six *aṅgula*-squares. The length is twelve *aṅgulas*, which makes four hundred and forty-four [squares]; both together, the diagonal cord (*ākṣṇayā-rajju*) produces four hundred and twenty *aṅgula*-squares. Or, where one part is the measure (*pramāṇa*), its half is in one part; when doubled, they become two numbers, and when the halves are doubled, they become two.

In that case, one number [is added] to the three numbers; when twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) have been subtracted from the incoming [measurement], each part of it is eight finger-breadths. The measurement, including that one [part], is "the diagonal cord (akṣṇayā-rajju) is twenty finger-breadths," which is exactly as stated previously.

Regarding the third repetition (*abhyāsa*), it is as follows: the measure (*pramāṇa*) is twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). Its third part is eight finger-breadths. When those twenty-four finger-breadths are added to that [original] twenty-four finger-breadths, the measure including the repetition (*sābhyāsa*) becomes thirty-two finger-breadths. In that case, there are four parts of the measure including the repetition, including the addition (*āgantuka*); when divided into twice that [number], the addition consists of eight parts. Among those, one part is one finger-breadth; thus, the measure is increased by that one part.
The diagonal cord (*akṣṇayārajju*) is twenty-five *aṅgulas*; the crosswise cord (*tiryaṅbhānī*) is seven *aṅgulas*, which makes forty-nine.
The measuring cord (*pramāṇa*) is twenty-four *aṅgulas*, which makes seventy-six and six hundred [units]. This same principle should be understood to apply to other variations as well.
With the words "of the three and four," etc., he himself will provide some examples later on.
Enough with this digression; [this concludes] the *Sundararājīyā* commentary on the long eye.
Now he describes dwelling in various ways with its underlying cause:

when a long rectangle is made into a square by means of its side-measure (*pārśvamānī*), whatever area is produced, and that which is produced by its cross-measure (*tiryaṅbhānī*), both together become the area when it is made into a square by means of the diagonal cord (*akṣṇayārajju*).
"Of the three and the four," and so forth, is an illustration.

And thus, when two of these are known, the third can be determined. Just as when the side-measure (*pārśvamānī*) and the cross-measure (*tiryaṅbhānī*) are known, those two are squared separately, added together, and the square root of that sum is the diagonal-measure (*akṣṇayārajju*); likewise, when the side-measure and the diagonal-measure are known, the square of the side-measure is subtracted from the square of the diagonal-measure, and the square root of the remainder is the cross-measure.
In this manner, having excluded the diagonal side-measure (*tiryaṅbhānīvarga*), the side-measure (*pārśvamānī*) is established;
thus, by means of these known quantities, the previously mentioned method of drawing the layout (*viharaṇa*) is to be understood.
The examples beginning with "of the three and four" (*trikacatuṣkayoḥ*) and so forth are precisely such illustrations.
The previous accounts as well are merely elaborations of this very same point.
The commentary of Kapardin states:
"The diagonal cord of a square makes a ground twice as large; it is the double-maker of that which is to be combined. (ĀpŚus 1.5)
One should increase the measurement by one-third; that [increase] is with distinction by means of the fourth [part], which is less than thirty-four parts of itself. ĀpŚus 1.6.
Having combined [the two], it is the diagonal cord (*akṣṇayārajju*) of a double-sided square; having combined [them], one makes double the area of whatever a square field is.

If it is asked, "For what purpose is the mention of 'having combined'?"—if you say it is for the purpose of excluding the long [rectangle], that is not so, because the meaning has already been stated.
Because there is no diagonal cord (*akṣṇayārajju*), a circle would not follow;
as for the claim that it is for the purpose of performing the measurement as equal in its entirety, that too is irrelevant,
because of the use of the singular number in the term "diagonal cord" (*akṣṇayārajju*).
One should increase the measure by one-third;
that is, one should add a third part to the measure.
"That" refers back to the measure to which the third part has been added.

The remainder [of the rule] is that one should multiply the third by its own fourth. By the phrase "by this minus one's thirty-fourth"—this is a qualification of the fourth; the meaning is: having divided that fourth into thirty-four parts and set aside one part, [one should proceed] with what remains.
"With a remainder" (*saviśeṣa*) is its designation.
Thus, because it exists together with a remainder for that which has been thus contracted, the designation is etymologically appropriate.
Having divided twelve by four, and one of those four by thirty-four, and setting aside one part, it becomes seventeen finger-breadths less a sesame seed (*tilona*).

The square of the number of sesame seeds in a twelve-finger span is one hundred sixty-six thousand four hundred sixty-four (166,464). The square of the number of sesame seeds in a seventeen-finger span less one sesame seed is three million three hundred twenty-nine thousand two hundred twenty-nine (3,329,229). Here, because there is no remainder for the two groups of threes, when the bamboo is taken with its specific [fractional] part, ten fields of sesame seeds are in excess.
Therefore, even a measure of half a *nīvāra* awn is in excess.
Therefore, having considered that the term "particular" (viśeṣa) will serve merely for the sake of conventional usage, the Teacher has applied this designation.
Now, another [rite]. ĀpŚus_1.7a.
The remainder [of the sentence] is "we shall describe the vihāra. He makes a cord of the exact measurement with loops at both ends. (ĀpŚus 1.7b)

Having made a cord of the same length as the square he wishes to construct, with loops at both ends, he should mark it in the middle and at the two halves. Having stretched the cord along the *pṛṣṭhyā* line, he drives stakes into the ground at the loops and the marks. Having fastened the two loops to the two stakes nearest the end, he pulls [the cord] southward by means of the middle mark and makes a mark for a stake. Having fastened the two loops to the middle [stake], he should pull the southern shoulder over the mark by means of the middle mark.
Having unfastened it from the front and fastened it at the back, he should stretch the southern hip by means of the middle mark; in the same way, the northern hip and shoulder.
The first section:
"In the middle" refers to the middle between the two characteristics (lakṣaṇa), namely the two [ends] consisting of the noose (pāśa). This is the meaning.

He states another method for the two-fold construction: one should increase the length of the square by its third part—that is, cause it to grow by that third—and that third part [should be increased] by its own fourth part; the meaning is "by a fourth part of the third.
By the word *ātman*, the fourth part is referred to. Thus, it is increased by one thirty-fourth of itself.
"One should increase"—this alone is the "viśeṣa" (distinction); its designation is "viśeṣa.
That by which the measurement is increased, starting from the third [unit] onwards, receives the name "viśeṣa.

For example: one should increase a measurement of twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) by four finger-breadths; that four finger-breadths should be increased by one finger-breadth less a sesame seed (*tilona*).

Those who know the measurements maintain that twenty-four sesame seeds joined closely together constitute one finger-breadth (*aṅguli*). He will say: "Having added half of that specific increment, one should take [the measurement] by means of the two external specific increments," and so forth. How so? Having fixed the middle [finger] with its specific increment, [one proceeds] with the fourth and the fourth with its specific increment, and so on.

In this context, that which exists together with a distinction (*viśeṣa*) is called *saviśeṣa*. It should be understood that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) itself, when accompanied by a distinction, is *saviśeṣa*.

For what purpose is this grand designation used? It is so that the term may be meaningful according to its etymology (*anvartha*). How so? Because the prefix *vi-* preceding the root *śiṣ* denotes excellence (*atiśaya*), as taught in the rule: "The root *śiṣ* [meaning] 'to leave' [is used] in the sense of taking everything, while preceded by *vi-*, it denotes excellence."
The term *viśeṣa* means that something is distinguished from or exceeds a portion of the measuring cord (*dvikaraṇī*) which has been laid diagonally; that is, it is left over.
Alternatively, *viśeṣa* refers to the time of measurement when it distinguishes—that is, exceeds—a certain area [of the ground].
For it has been stated that thirty-four sesame seeds constitute a finger-breadth (*aṅguli*).
The square of twelve finger-breadths is one million, six hundred and six thousand four hundred and twenty-four.
The square of seventeen finger-breadths less one sesame-seed is three million, three hundred and two thousand nine hundred and twenty-nine square plots measured by sesame-seeds;
here, one sesame-seed exceeds the double of the square plot.

Therefore, the term *viśeṣa* (the specific) is applied to it. When the fire-altar is being measured with the *veṇu* (measuring rod) together with the *viśeṣa*, and the self [the sacrificer] is being measured, whatever area remains in excess—even if it is only as much as the awn of a wild grain (*nīvāra*)—it is in no way considered an excess; rather, that which is less than that is "insufficient" (*nyūna*). Thus, the usage of the term *saviśeṣa* occurs in the context of performing the two-fold measurement (*dvikaraṇī*). Having now explained this one incidental method of drawing the lines (*viharaṇa*), he describes another method of drawing the lines:

Now, as for the other method of wandering [around the site]—the word "we shall explain" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Taking a cord of the measure of a *pramāṇa* (the length of a man's arms extended), with loops at both ends—that is, equipped with loops at the beginning and the end—and having made two marks by applying ointment in the middle, specifically in the middle of the first half and the middle of the second half, one should stretch the cord along the *pṛṣṭhyā* (the central line on the ground to be measured). Having extended it, one should fasten the two loops to five stakes at the marks.

Having drawn the cord southward from the center by means of the *nirañjana* (the stainless point), he makes a mark—a sign—for the purpose of indicating the direction. Having fastened two loops to the middle peg, and having drawn the cord further upward from above that mark, closer to its top, he fixes a peg at its end. Then, having released the two loops from the middle peg, he fastens one loop to the southern peg and the other loop to the eastern peg; thus, by means of the *nirañjana*, he should draw a line toward the southern shoulder.
One should stretch the cord so that it reaches the right shoulder;
in this very manner one should stretch [the cord] to the right hip, and so forth—having thus released [the cord], the subsequent sūtras beginning with "from the eastern [peg]" follow.
This application involving five pegs pertains to the case of a square of equal sides.

Thus, the diagonal cord (*ākṣṇayārajjū*) of a twelve-*aṅgula* square is seventeen *aṅgulas* minus one sesame seed. Likewise, the diagonal cord of a forty-eight-*aṅgula* square is sixty-eight *aṅgulas* minus four sesame seeds, and so forth.

Having driven a peg at the two ends of the square measurement, and having driven another peg between them, one should mark the "speciality of that half"—meaning the specific measure of that half—by the rule of increasing the measurement by a third; then one should bring it back and add it.

Having made loops at the two ends and having fastened the loop with the speciality upon the middle peg, and having fastened the other loop upon the eastern peg, one should drive a peg after moving westward along the mark;
that is the southern shoulder (dakṣiṇāṃsa).

Having fastened the cord from the eastern peg to the western peg, one should mark the southern hip with that same mark; having moved it northward by the same distance, one marks the northern hip; and reversing the process, one marks the northern shoulder.
This pair of yogas is perfectly symmetrical for the square.
Karavinda’s Commentary:
Now follows another [method for laying out the altar], beginning with "a cord of the measure of the hips and shoulders.

The third *karaṇī* is explained by this [same method]. When the three *karaṇīs* are explained, the third *karaṇī* is also explained.

To explain the understanding of the third *karaṇī*, he says:

Regarding the understanding of the third *karaṇī*, this is the distinction:
The field must be divided into nine parts. Of which field? Of a field of known dimension (*pramāṇakṣetra*) or of a field of three sides (*trikaraṇīkṣetra*).

This is the meaning: having divided that field for which the third side (*tṛtīyakaraṇī*) is to be established into nine parts, one makes the side-measure (*pārśvamānī*) and the cross-measure (*tiryaṅmānī*) of one part, and having made the diagonal cord (*akṣṇayārajju*) of that same part the side-measure, when a square is formed by those two and that square is divided into nine parts, the diagonal of one of those parts becomes the third side of a square whose dimension is the original side-measure (*karaṇī*).
And that division is the demonstration that it is one-third of the field of measurement.
By this, the same applies to the four-karaṇī, the fourth-karaṇī, and so forth.
For instance: if the measurement is four karaṇīs in length across, its diagonal cord (akṣṇayārajju) is five karaṇīs.

In the same way, it should be understood that the diagonal cord (*akṣṇayārajju*) of a square measuring five *karaṇīs* across is six *karaṇīs* long; likewise, the diagonal cord of a square measuring two *karaṇīs* across and three *karaṇīs* long is five *karaṇīs*;
and the diagonal cord of a square measuring ten *karaṇīs* across and [ten] *karaṇīs* long is fifteen *karaṇīs*, and so forth—all of which should be understood accordingly.

Likewise, the fourth [side] is transverse; the diagonal cord of that which has a length of three *karas* is the fourth-measuring cord (*turīyakaraṇī*). Similarly, the fifth [side] is transverse; the diagonal cord of that which has a length of four *karas* is the fifth-measuring cord (*pañcamakaraṇī*), and so on should be understood.
The third-measuring cord (*trikaraṇī*) and the fourth-measuring cord (*turīyakaraṇī*) are employed in the Sautrāmaṇī and other such rites.
[Objection: But surely, by the statement "the diagonal cord of the long [side]," the *trikaraṇī*, the third *karaṇī*, and so forth are already established.

[Response: It is said: *Karaṇīs* are of two kinds—those with pure roots and those with impure roots.
Those whose roots are pure are "pure-rooted" (*śuddhamūlā*).

Regarding those [series] to be described later—such as the "four-maker" (*catuṣkaraṇī*) and "nine-maker" (*navakaraṇī*), where four are produced from two and nine from three—it is stated here in order to demonstrate that they are always designated as "two-maker," "three-maker," "five-maker," and so forth. That which makes two is a "two-maker" (*dvikaraṇī*); that which makes three is a "three-maker" (*trikaraṇī*); that which makes four is a "four-maker" (*catuṣkaraṇī*); and that which makes five is a "five-maker" (*pañcakaraṇī*).
Furthermore, by the general statement "the cord of the diagonal of the long [side]," there is no direct comprehension of the *trikaraṇī* and so forth;

Therefore, the commencement of the specific rules for the *karaṇīs*, such as the *dvikaraṇī* and others, is indeed appropriate.
Now Sundararāja states the rule for the *trikaraṇī* (the side of a triangle):

Just as the transverse side is twelve finger-breadths and the side-measure is two times that (twenty-four) minus six finger-breadths and one-sixth (eighteen and one-sixth), so when a long rectangle is thus formed, its diagonal cord is twenty finger-breadths and one-sixth of a tila. That [diagonal] is the triple-maker; it makes the area measured by the standard threefold.

By means of the side-measure (*karaṇī*) of a shorter or smaller field, one should mark out a longer or larger one; that is to say, one should delineate a long rectangle such that the side-measure of the smaller [field] serves as the transverse dimension (*tiryaṅbhānī*) and the side-measure of the larger [field] serves as the longitudinal dimension (*pārśvamānī*). The combination (*samāsa*) of two squares of different dimensions—that is, of two squares with unequal measurements—is called "making" (*karaṇī*). By means of the side-measure (*karaṇī*) of the smaller square (*alpīyas*), one should mark a point of increase (*vṛddha*)—that is, a specific location—on the larger square (*barṣīyas*). The diagonal cord (*akṣṇayārajju*) of that increased [square] combines—that is, unifies—the two squares of different dimensions. This is what is meant: having combined the two squares of different dimensions, one should delimit the larger square along one of its transverse sides by means of the side-measure of the smaller square.
From that point, one should draw an upward line in such a way that it falls at the same distance as the transverse side-line on the opposite side.
The measure of the side of the smaller square divided by the lines is the transverse side.
Of what? Of the diagonal cord of a large oblong whose sides are equal to the measures of the [two] sides of the squares; these two squares of different dimensions are thus combined.

While "quadrangular" (*caturaśra*) is already understood from the context, the repetition of the term "quadrangular" is intended to indicate that even for the two circles, the composition is easily accomplished only by first making them quadrangular.

In that case, for the purpose of discarding one man’s space, one should mark out a diagonal line (*vṛdhra*) measuring one man's length, and then move the northern side-line southward and the other side-line eastward.

And there, in that [space] measuring two *puruṣas*—that is, measuring two hundred and forty fingers—one should cut off five sesame seeds [from each side]. When the square has been made by means of the remaining *karṇī*, the *puruṣa* is excluded. (Kātyāyana Śulba Sūtra, Kapardibhāṣya)
As he himself demonstrates:
"The rope, when its strands have been withdrawn, is four-cubit long; when it is cut, both the one part and the other part together perform whatever those two separate parts perform. (ĀpŚS 2.6a)
The side-measuring cord was previously brought together;

now, by means of the diagonal cord, that [diagonal] which makes four [squares], when cut from two men’s lengths, serves as the side-measuring cord for one and the crosswise-measuring cord for the other. That which they produce separately, both of those [together] it produces.
He asks "How? and replies:
"The *tiryaṅmānī* [cord] measures the person; the *śeṣa* [cord] measures three [persons]. (ĀpŚS 2.6c)
The cord running crosswise [to the length] makes the man;
the remaining two cords run diagonally.
Thus, those two together constitute its diagonal cord; in this way, he makes three.
Thus it has been said: ĀpŚus_2.6d.
And that too has been stated.
Karavinda’s commentary,
seeking to clarify this method by way of an illustration, says:
"It approaches that which is stated as being joined with the chest."
Taking as his subject matter a square measuring two persons on each side, that is, four persons in total, he provides an illustration:

regarding a long rectangle that constitutes a part of one such square, the diagonal side-measure that has been brought together is declared to be a "four-maker," meaning it produces a square of four persons;
and its cross-measure is declared to be a "one-person-maker."

It is not known how many cubits the severed side-measure (*pārśvamānī*) of this long rectangle should be; that very measure must be understood here. In this case, it is logically understood that the diagonal cord (*akṣṇayārajju*)—which is produced by the separate transverse measure (*tiryaṅbhānī*) and the separate severed side-measure—is the maker of both those areas. Therein, from the four-man square which is the result of the diagonal cord, when one man’s measure is removed from the result of the transverse measure, three men remain; therefore, it should be understood that it is the maker of a three-man [area].
Therefore, this has been stated: "The transverse line makes [the altar] a man; the remaining side-measure is cut off.
The masculine designation in the phrase "three men" (*trīn puruṣān*) is intended to refer to the *puruṣa* (man/measure).

Furthermore, the mention of the *puruṣa* in the context of the fire-altar serves as an illustration for the measurement by the *puruṣa*, the reduction by the *puruṣa*, and the contraction through the *samāsa* (combination) and *nirhāra* (removal).

The meaning is as follows: Desiring to make a square measuring three *puruṣas* by removing one *puruṣa* from a square that measures two *puruṣas* on each side and consists of four *puruṣas*, one should divide that square in the middle with a cord of the measure of one *puruṣa* to make it two parts. Then, having brought one of those half-sides diagonally toward the other side, one should cut off the side-measure where they meet, discard the remainder, and [proceed] with the remaining side-measure.
When it has been made into a perfect square, that square becomes a square measuring three puruṣas.

Likewise, having removed four *puruṣas* from all sides of a square measuring four *puruṣas*, one who wishes to make it a perfect square of twelve *puruṣas* should divide the perfect square by means of a transverse line measuring two *puruṣas*. Then, having brought one side-measure (*pārśvamānī*) to meet the other half, and having cut off the side-measure situated at their point of intersection and discarded that cut portion, when the remaining side-measure is used to form a square, that field becomes a perfect square of twelve *puruṣas*. The meaning is that the remaining side-measure which was cut off becomes the diagonal-measure (*karaṇī*) for that [new] square.
In this manner, having removed the third *dvikaraṇī* from the field of measurement, it becomes the third *karaṇī*.
In exactly the same way, the fourth *karaṇī* and all subsequent *karaṇīs*, up to the fourth *catuṣkaraṇī*, are to be understood everywhere.
This is stated [in the Śulbasūtra] by the words: "The cord for the long side."
Its application is found in the works of Droṇa and others; the commentary by Sundararāja illustrates that very point—
thus it has been stated.

The rope which is drawn diagonally and made into one is four cubits long; it is cut short by two persons' lengths. Its side-measure (pārśvamānī) is cut short by five barley-corns and measures two hundred and eighty fingers. The other—the cross-measure (tiryaṅbhānī)—is merely one person's length. Whatever those two do when separate, that both accomplish together because they function as the diagonal rope (karṇarajju). Among them, the cross-measure clearly makes [the area] exactly one person's length.
By the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it can be understood that the side-measure (*pārśvamānī*) makes three *puruṣas*.
This has been stated [in the sūtra] beginning with: "The cord across the length of the long [altar]," and so forth.
— *Kapardibhāṣya*
One who wishes to make a long quadrangle into a square should cut off a portion along the cross-measure, divide the remainder, and lay it down on both sides.

Desiring to make a long square into a regular square, one should cut off a portion transversely according to the measure of the transverse cord, divide the remainder into two parts, and place them on both sides—both at the front and along the sides—one should deposit them; the missing section should be filled with an additional piece. (ĀpŚS 2.7b)
One should fill the fragment with an additional amount that has come forth;
having filled it, one should discard that excess.
The removal of that [excess] has been explained. (ĀpŚS 2.7c)
The procedure for its relinquishment has been stated.
Thus ends the second section;
this is the Karavindīyā commentary.
