The method for making a long quadrangle without reduction has been stated.

Regarding the term "long": a square is one that has equal dimensions on all sides; a long quadrangle is one that is greater in length in one direction. To make it a square, one should cut off a portion from the middle extending south to north along a line measured by a cord equal to the cross-measure (*tiryaṅbhānī*). Having thus set aside the remaining eastern portion, one should divide that middle section vertically into two parts. Keeping the western part exactly as it was, one should place the eastern part to the north of the first [western] part, extending towards the east.
Having filled the empty northeastern portion with an additional segment and thereby making it a perfect square, one should then remove—that is, set aside—the excess additional segment.
Its removal has been described as: "desiring to remove a square from a square. Its utility is found in the construction of chariot wheels and the like.
Thus ends the second section;
the method for transforming a long quadrangle has been explained according to the commentary of Sundararāja.

Having cut off the side-measure by means of the transverse measure, one should make it a square; then, having divided the remainder, one should lay it down in the front and on the north, so that there will be an additional square fragment in the northeast corner. Its removal has been stated [in the rule]: "From a square, a square."
Thus ends the second section. According to the *Kapardibhāṣya*:
One who wishes to make a square or a rectangle should, having made the side-measure as long as he intends it to be, place whatever remains in excess according to the requirements. (ĀpŚus 3.1)

Desiring to make a square that is equal on all sides into one that is rectangular, one should mark a side with whatever length is required for the rectangle; then, one should add the excess area in such a way that it fits appropriately so that the field is covered.
Having divided the square, this application is used for both types of *prauga* altars and for the animal sacrifice of an *avakīrṇin*.
(Karavindīyā Vyākhyā)
Thinking that by dividing a square into two equal parts and placing one part on top of the other, a rectangle is formed, he describes its method:
"One should place [the second] square upon [the first] equally.
This means that having cut off a transverse portion, one should divide the remainder.

If one desires to make a square equal on all sides (samacaturaśra) into a rectangle (dīrghacaturaśra), and wishes to make the transverse dimension (tiryak-pramāṇa) of that square equal to any one part—such as one-third, one-half, or one-quarter—of the original square, he should cut off from one side of the original square a portion equal to that transverse dimension, thereby making it a rectangle. Then, having made the side-measure (pārśvamānī) of the remaining portion equal to the diagonal-measure (karṇī) of that original square, and having made it a square by means of that aforementioned transverse dimension, he should divide the remainder therein and place whatever is excessive in the appropriate manner.

Just as when a larger area is divided, each individual part—whether taken separately or all combined—is placed upon another portion so that, covering its width and joined together, they produce its length; in the same way, having divided [the space], one should place the entire remainder upon the other portion.

The meaning is as follows: one who desires to transform a square into a rectangle should first cut off one side of the square using a transverse line equal in measure to the desired width of the intended rectangle; then, having made the side-measure (*pārśvamānī*) of the remainder equal to that same measure, he should divide it into one or more parts; and so that all these parts together produce a rectangle, he should place the entire remainder successively on top of the other parts.
In this context, although the word *śeṣa* (remainder) under discussion denotes the object (*karman*), its sense of the genitive case is also understood due to proximity and contextual force.

Since the phrase beginning with "to that extent" (*tāvatīm*) is consistent when connected to the "remainder," the expression "as much as one wishes to do" (*yāvaccikīrṣet*) must also refer to length and breadth.
The same principle should be understood to apply to the long [measure] as well in the rule concerning long [measures].
Regarding this, there are verses:
Having divided a square into two equal parts,
and having placed another part upon [the first] part, that shall become a long rectangle when the other part is added.

Having divided the remaining portion so that the sides are equal in width to the length intended to be made, the construction of that [structure] should indeed be carried out according to the requirements.
The lateral measurements of the remainder shall likewise be equal to the straight-line portion,
extending across as far as the length intended for the structure to be constructed is desired.

*Sundararājīyā*: (One should lay down a square. This is the method here: having extended the two eastern side-measures as much as desired, one should stretch the diagonal cord from the north-east corner. Where that [cord] falls upon the cross-measure of the square situated in the middle of the long rectangle, one should discard the northern portion and make the southern portion the cross-measure; thus it becomes a long rectangle.
Even when the long vowel is long, this same method applies.
According to the commentary of Kapardin:
one desiring to make a square mandala should drop [the cord] from the center to the corner. (ĀpŚus 3.2a)
If one wishes to make a square mandala, its application is in the construction of the chariot-wheel-shaped altar (*rathacakra*) and so forth.
One should drop a cord from the center to the corner—having fastened the loop to the central peg, one should pull it toward the corner; one should pull it along the diagonal.
Having removed [the cord] from there and made a mark, one should draw the mandala by dragging it along the side together with a third part of the excess. ĀpŚus 3.2b.
By that same measurement, one should draw [the line] from the side.
That which lies beyond the square once it has been drawn is the *atiśaya* (excess).
Together with a third part of that *atiśaya*, and with half of the square, one should delineate the circle—drawing it on all sides.
That [altar] is eternal; it is the maṇḍala. ĀpŚus_3.2c.
The impermanent one forms a mandala;
the impermanent one is coarse.
As long as it is being poured, so long does it come. ĀpŚus_3.2d.
As long as [the cord] is laid down along the *straktis*, it does not go to the side.
And this statement is for the purpose of making known its closer proximity.
(Karavindīyā Vyākhyā)
(One should come to the square mandala.

Desiring to make—that is, wishing to construct—a square mandala, one should measure a cord with a loop on one end that is slightly longer than half the diagonal measurement of that square. Having fastened that loop to the middle peg of the square and having laid the cord diagonally across to the corner, one should make a mark there. Then, dividing the space between the side-mark and the excess mark into three parts, and omitting two of those parts at the end, [one should proceed] together with the single remaining part.
One should draw [the design] all around on every side with a cord of half the measure of the square, in such a way that the ground becomes a mandala.
When this is done, that *nityā* becomes the mandala—the field of the square and the field of the sesame seed.
"That *nityā*" means that ground is eternal; the meaning is that as long as the ground is a square, it remains so even within the mandala.

Regarding this, he states the reason: "As much as is diminished, so much is adventitious"—to whatever extent a field is seen to be diminished within the four squares (*caturaśrabhakti*), to that same extent it is seen as adventitious on the sides of the mandala; therefore, [the remainder] is eternal.

[Objection: But surely, by the principle that "the half of the circumference is obtained by multiplying the half of the diameter," the area of the earth is not perfectly equal [to the square of its radius]; so how can it be said to be constant? [Reply: It is said: although it is indeed inconstant, nevertheless, because other methods are far too crude, and because this method is close [to the truth], and because a truly correct method would require great effort and is thus impractical, the intention of the Teacher in speaking thus is that this very method is the most effective.
For as much as is lost here, so much is gained;
since the discrepancy between those two is slight, it is simply "that much."
There is no fault [in this], for although it is impermanent, it is said to be permanent for the purpose of encouraging engagement (*pravṛtti*).
Alternatively, just as the word "rope" refers to the rope that forms a circle, that term also intends the rope itself.
This is the *Sundararājīyā* commentary.
(To construct a circular mandala from a square:

Having driven a peg into the center of the square and having fastened a cord to it, one should drop it diagonally to the corner and make a mark; then, having drawn a line along the side and another along the adjacent side, one should make a mark there. Dividing the interval between the two marks into three parts, one should draw the circle using the half-diagonal of the square plus one of those parts. That cord, which forms the circle, is not fixed; as much as is subtracted from the corners, that same measure appears on the sides.

One who wishes to construct a square mandala according to the commentary of Kapardin should divide the diameter into fifteen parts and set aside two; thirteen remain. That is the standard square. (ĀpŚus 3.3)
Desiring to make a square mandala, one should divide the diameter (vyāsa) of the mandala into fifteen parts and discard two parts;
thirteen parts remain.
A cord measured by those thirteen parts will produce a square field of that same extent.
And that [measurement] is impermanent and much coarser.
The statement "thirteen remain" is intended to demonstrate that the measurement mentioned in another *śulba* [text] is superior even to that.
Its application is in the *Tīvrasutasoma*.
There, the first set of eleven [stakes] is to be measured.
There, a section of the altar measuring one span (prādeśa) should be taken by means of a finger-breadth (aṅgula).

If the *uparavas* are twelve finger-breadths wide, then having driven a stake six finger-breadths to the south of the mark at half a span, the eastern altar—measuring thirty-four steps in length and having that same width—is to be measured.
The field of ten [units] is,
according to the instruction of the author of the Sūtra, five hundred and forty finger-breadths;
half of that is taken as one finger-breadth.
Therefore, when the Vedic altar is being reduced in size,
the consecration of the eastern half is not performed;
thus, the excess area is eliminated.
In the Vedas, there is indeed a break in the sequence—
Karavindīya’s Commentary:
[one who desires to make a square out of a circle].
The width of the mandala is its diameter.
Having divided that into fifteen parts, one should subtract two parts.
The remaining thirteen parts constitute the side-measure (karaṇī) of the square.
In this case as well, the argument beginning with "that [nature] is eternal" and so forth is the same; those very same objections and refutations apply. This is the *Sundararājīyā* commentary.
Desiring to make a square mandala, one who makes it from a [pre-existing] square uses thirteen parts as the side-measure; thus he makes the square variable.
The variability of these two is understood from the contradiction with calculation and from their mutual contradiction.

To explain: the area of the fire-altar built in the shape of a chariot wheel (*rathacakra*), which measures seven *aratnis* and one *prādeśa*, is one hundred thousand and eight thousand finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). When this area is made into a square, its side-measure (*karaṇī*) is three hundred and twenty-eight finger-breadths, plus twenty-two sixteenths of a finger-breadth (tilas).
When a circle is drawn upon that [square] according to the stated method, its diameter (*viṣkambha*) becomes three hundred and seventy-four finger-breadths.
Its circumference (*pariṇāha*) is one thousand and seventy-five hundred finger-breadths.
As they have said:
"The circumference of the circle, which has a diameter of two ayutas, is one hundred and four thousand, eight hundred and sixty-two."
Thus:

the measurement of the fruit of this mandala is seen to be one hundred thousand, nine thousand, eight hundred and sixty finger-breadths (aṅgulas). And it has been said: "Half of the circumference, multiplied by half the diameter, is indeed the area of a circle."
Thus,

when a mandala such as the fire-altar (agnikṣetra), the chariot-wheel altar (rathacakracit), and so forth, has been constructed, eight hundred and sixty-one thousand finger-breadths (aṅgulas) remain in excess;
and in that case, there would be a mutual contradiction.

The diameter of a fire-altar (*agni*) that has been made circular with a side-measure (*karaṇī*) of three hundred and twenty-eight fingers plus one and a half sesame seeds is stated to be three hundred and seventy-four fingers. When that same circle is converted into a square by the prescribed method, it becomes three [times the side]; thus, four fingers and eighteen sesame seeds are subtracted from the previously mentioned side-measure.

Therefore, for one desiring precision when converting a square into a circle, one must discard one eighteenth part of the radius—calculated as half the diameter plus one-third of the excess—as prescribed in the Sūtra.
When it has been done in this way, with the chariot-wheel-shaped altar (citā), the diameter (viṣkambha) becomes three hundred and sixty-nine fingers less six barley-corns (ṣaḍ-tila),
and the circumference (pariṇāha) is one hundred and sixty-five thousand fingers.
By means of the previously mentioned calculation beginning with "of that circle having an equal circumference," the resulting area (phala) comes to be one hundred and eight thousand [square fingers].
In the case of making the mandala square, as stated in the Sūtra, one should add thirty-three hundredths to its own threefold diameter.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
"In the construction of a square mandala, an eighteen-hundredth part is to be discarded."
This is the diameter of the mandala, derived from the diameter stated in the Sūtra. //1//
Alternatively, having added one-thirtieth of the side of a square to itself, one should further apply one-eighth [of that result]; this is the diameter of the circle. //2//
In the construction of the square mandala, one should apply the measurement indicated by the cord to the diameter;
this [measurement] of the mandala is thirty-three times its own [diameter], increased by a third. //3//
Having set aside one three-hundred-and-twentieth part from the diameter of the mandala, one should discard the ninth part of the remainder; this is the diameter of the square. //4//

For when this is done, even though the circumference of the fire-altar consists of one hundred and one [units], that specific difference of two sesame seeds does not occur, nor is there any mutual contradiction. //5//
The commentary of Kapardin establishes authority by means of authority. ĀpŚus 3.4.
The term *pramāṇa* refers to that by which a square field is measured, such as a *prakrama* (step) and so forth.
Where the injunction is made by means of a specific measurement, it should be understood that the square shape is prescribed by that very measurement.
Furthermore, in passages such as "the right wing [is] one man," the number is intended to be significant.
The Karavindīyā commentary states that the *karaṇīs* beginning with the "double-measure" (*dvikaraṇī*) have been mentioned; in order to understand their results, it says: "By the measure...
(*pramāṇena*). (By the measure, the measure is prescribed.)
Where the measurement is by a single unit, there the result is a square measured on all sides by that same unit, as in the passage beginning, "A man [is placed] on the right wing," and so forth;
thus the *Sundararājīyā* commentary states the area of the squares:
"A measure is prescribed by means of a measure.
By means of a staff that is one *pramāṇa* in length, a field measuring one *pramāṇa* is prescribed—that is, it is measured.
— *Kapardibhāṣya*.
Anything other than a square is by command. ĀpŚus_3.5.
"Ādeśa" means that which instructs; it is an injunction (*vidhi*).

Something other than the injunction occurs—where something is enjoined, something else also occurs by that very same authority—as seen in the cases of the *gārhapatya* altar, the *citi*, the *uparava* pits, and so forth.
This is the explanation according to Karavinda.
"Other than the square" (*caturaśramādeśād anyat*):
"instruction" (*ādeśa*) means that which instructs (*ādiśati*), i.e., an *upadeśa*.
By this, it is understood that other than the square, there is the nature of being the fruit of the [directions] beginning with the east.
Alternatively, "ādeśa" means that which instructs—namely, the science of mathematics (*gaṇitaśāstra*). From that, the results for irregular figures and so forth are to be understood.

And it is said therein: "Having extended the side-area of all fields, [it is found] in their product"; the meaning of this is: having extended—that is, having produced—the two sides, namely the longitudinal and transverse side-measures, of all irregular fields.
Regarding their practice: the result should be understood as occurring at the time when one has the qualities of the other.
Having cut the triangle in two ways, one should apply the cutting of the one to the other;
therein, it becomes a long square.

They declare that [the area] is thus determined by the following principle: the determination of the area is achieved by multiplying the length of the side-measure of a long rectangle by its transverse measure; for a circle, by multiplying half the circumference by half the diameter; and for a bow-shaped figure (dhanus), by multiplying the measure of half the arrow (śara) by half the bow, and so forth—this is to be understood from the science of mathematics (gaṇita-śāstra).
Let us return to the subject at hand.
According to Sundararāja’s commentary (*Sundararājīyā*),
except for the instruction regarding the square, a square is constructed everywhere; it is precisely because of that rule that the circle and other shapes are formed.
According to the commentary of Kapardin, four [verses] result from two [sections]. ĀpŚus 3.6a.
When a square is made by two steps, there are four units of the measure of a man (*puruṣa*). The method for making squares from circles has been stated;
however, this method for making circles from squares—namely, that "by a cord of such length, a field of such extent is produced"—has not been stated.
Therefore, this is said: "Nine [stotras] with three [verses each]. (ĀpŚus 3.6b)
When a square is made by means of three steps, there are nine man-lengths of ground;
this should be visualized by drawing it on the ground.
(Karavindīyā Vyākhyā)
(Non-decrease by two):

Where there is a double measure by means of two [sides], and the vimāna is square with a measurement of two on all sides, the result consists of four squares each measuring two units. In a square measuring three units, the result consists of nine squares each measuring three units.
In Sundararāja’s commentary (*Sundararājīyā Vyākhyā*),
it is stated: "By means of a measuring-stick (*daṇḍa*) of two units, there are four measurement-fields (*pramāṇakṣetra*)."
According to the commentary of Kapardin:
as many units of measurement as the cord has, it forms that many squares. (ĀpŚus 3.8a)
"Of whatever measure"—meaning, of whatever length the rope is, it makes that many squares—it forms rows; it forms as many rows as there are units in the measure.
For five measures, it forms squares numbering five.
This should be applied everywhere in the same manner.
Likewise is the perception:
having drawn [a mark] on the ground, when it is inspected, it is perceived exactly as it was;
when made by two people, four horns appear when drawn on both sides; when made by five, they appear fivefold, and when drawn on both sides, twenty-five horns appear.
Thus it should be understood in all cases.
[The measurement] is according to the dimensions as they are found; this is the Karavindīya commentary.
Whatever the number of units of measurement a rope possesses, that rope produces that many squares—each equal in measure to those units—multiplied by that same number.
In the treatises on mathematics, the term "square" (*varga*) refers to an even quadrangle (*samacaturaśra*).
Thus, for example, a rope of four units produces sixteen squares when multiplied by four.

One should observe that when multiplied by five, the five groups [of letters] amount to twenty-five; with six measures (*pramāṇa*), forty-nine; with eight measures, sixty-four; with nine measures, eighty-one; with ten measures, one hundred; with eleven measures, one hundred and twenty-one; and with twelve measures, one hundred and forty-four, and so forth. Regarding the measure, he says: "Perception (*upalabdhi*) likewise"—that is, it is perceived in such a manner.
The meaning is that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the matters already mentioned.
Likewise, by cutting a square measuring two units in both directions in half, four [squares] are obtained;
by cutting one measuring three units in three ways, nine; by cutting one measuring four units in four ways, sixteen; and so on for those measuring five units and so forth.
Similarly, in cases such as "the diagonal cord of a long [rectangle]," they are obtained accordingly.
By practicing one [method] with two [factors], two fruits are obtained;
by practicing two with three, six;
by practicing two with four, eight.

For instance: having cut in two a [rectangle] with a side-measure of two units and a cross-measure of one unit, two [squares] are obtained. Having cut in two from the east and in three from the north a [rectangle] with a side-measure of two units and a cross-measure of three units, six [squares] are obtained.

In this way, for other cases as well, the understanding of the result is achieved by making the division from the north according to the number of the side-measure units, and the division from the east according to the number of the cross-measure units.
Sundararājīyā commentary:
"Four times sixteen, five times twenty-five," and so forth; [this refers to] the extent [of the measurement] as it is perceived.
The proof for this is:
"Because it is perceived as such.
— *Kapardibhāṣya*
A cord measuring one and a half puruṣas produces two [squares] at the beginning of the *sava*.

"One and a half" (*adhyardhā*) means that which has a half above; when made with that, it produces two squares at the beginning of the *sava* (1½² + 1½² = 9/4 + 9/4 = 18/4 = 4½). The square of one is one (1² = 1); before and beside it are two halves.
Together with the former, there are two; and the square made by the half is one-quarter at the corner.
By that [means], he forms two feet;
in this very same way, the subsequent sūtra is to be applied.
Three and a half men [measure] six and a quarter [cubits]. ĀpŚus 3.8b.
Now follows the section on the extreme limit. ĀpŚus_3.9a.
The rule is universal:
(5ñ2 n 5ñ2 u 6 1ñ4) as much as he draws with an excess [of cord], so much he places down on its two sides; and that by which a square is formed, that [he places] at the corner. (ĀpŚus_3.9b)
The measure of the foot is prescribed as half the measure [of the body].
To whatever extent it is necessary to mark an excess, one places it on the two sides and at the front;

that which makes it square is placed at the corner—thus, by means of what has been thus arranged, the square at the corner should be understood as being in correspondence with that very [measurement].
And in the filling of the mandala, one [unit] corresponds to one.
Someone might have the misconception that "half" means "half of half"; therefore, he says in response to them:
"By the measure of a half, the measure of a quarter is prescribed. By the measure of half of the [original] measure, the measure of a quarter is prescribed.
He states the reason for this very point: "Because of the completion of the quarter of that [verse] which has two measures. (ĀpŚus 3.10b)
By the third [verse], the ninth part [is completed]. ĀpŚus_3.10c.
The half [of the body] has a measure of two [padas], which is one *puruṣa* in length;
since it serves to complete the [total number of] quarters, it is said:
"By means of two, there are four."
"By the third, the ninth part (kalā) [is obtained]" means the ninth portion by the third measure; that is to say, the ninth part. This has also been stated as "nine by three.
Thus, in the *Kapardibhāṣya*, a commentary on the *Āpastamba-sūtra*.
The first chapter, third section, of the *Śulbākhyapraśna*: Karavindīya Commentary.
Now the measurement for cutting is stated: "one and a half" (*adhyardha*). (The ninth part is one and a half persons.
By practicing [the measurement] with the dimension of one and a half persons, one produces a result of two persons plus a quarter—that is, two persons together with a quarter.

"Two and a half men" (*ardhatṛtīyapuruṣā*) means those for whom two and a half is the measure; that [rope] which has such a measure is "two and a half men long. When it is used for practice, it produces a result of six and a quarter men. The measurement is likewise: for a square measuring one and a half men, there is a reduction by one-half and one [unit] to the east and to the north—one [unit], one [unit], two halves, and one quarter. Similarly, in other cases as well, when there is a reduction on both sides, it makes a middle rope of one and a quarter, which is one-sixteenth [of the whole].

Regarding the expansion of a square field, he explains the method for fully understanding the expanded field: "Antaḥsamīpa" means that which exists beyond that immediate vicinity; thus, "atyantaḥ" refers to a region that transcends the immediate area. That whose rule (*vidhi*) is such is "atyantapradeśaḥ"—meaning universal.
This concerns the subject of the regular square (*samacaturaśra*).
"Yāvatā" means by whatever measure; "yāvatādhikena" means by whatever measure in excess.
One occurrence of the word *yāvat* refers to the measure itself, while the other occurrence of the word *yāvat* refers to what is to be added (*āgantuka*).
The meaning is: "by whatever measure" or "by more than that much.

Regarding the tracing (*parilikhati*)—that which one traces for the purpose of making it square—one places (i.e., joins) that additional area, which is the square field of the root-measure, along the two sides, both eastward and northward.
And that which is made square by means of that same additional measure joins that field to the corner.

This is what is meant: in every case of increasing a square field, one should imagine a square of the original dimension in the south-western portion of the enlarged square; then, on its eastern and northern sides, one should imagine a field whose side-lengths are equal to those sides and whose transverse side-length is the measure of the increase. That field which is formed by that single measure—whether it produces a result of one, two, four, three, nine, and so forth—is to be imagined as having its corners oriented toward the east and north.
The meaning is that in all such cases, when expanding a square field, one should perform the calculation of the field in this manner.

Regarding "by half-measure" (*ardhapramāṇena*): by half of the measure, the "quarter-measure" (*pādapramāṇa*) is established; here, a "quarter" (*pāda*) refers to the fourth part. That measure is prescribed—that is, it is accomplished—such that a field measured by half [of the original] becomes the fourth part of the object to be measured. Why? Because the quarter is filled by two measures of the half; since the half consists of two measures, the fourth part of the ground is completed.

By the third [measure], the ninth part is filled—the ninth portion of the field is completed by the third measure. The perception is likewise: when a plot of land measuring one unit is halved by a cut toward the east and north, half a unit of land is produced; if that same [half-unit] is further halved by a cut toward the east and north, a plot of land measuring one-third of a unit is seen, which is the ninth part of the [original] one-unit land. Thus it is perceived.

Likewise, sixteen digits are filled by the fourth [part], twenty-five digits by the fifth, and thirty-six parts by the sixth. In this manner, the other results of the divisions should also be understood.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Śulbapradīpikā composed by the venerable Karavindasvāmin.
Now, the commentary of Sundararāja states the result of those [measurements] involving cuts: [The text continues with the technical details of the cuts.]
[The rule applies to] six [bricks] measuring one and a half puruṣas and a quarter [puruṣa],
and likewise twelve measuring three and a half puruṣas and a quarter [puruṣa], twenty measuring four and a half puruṣas and a quarter [puruṣa], and so forth.
It should be understood that [the same applies to] bricks measuring one puruṣa and a quarter, and one and a sixteenth [of a puruṣa], and so on.
This rule is universal: one who wishes to enlarge the entire square places [the excess] to the east and to the north by whatever measure he desires to enlarge it;
that square which is made with the additional measure is at the northeastern corner.
Now, he states the result of those cuts:
(Now, regarding the absolute area:
Since half of a rope measuring two units— namely, that which measures one unit— is for the purpose of completing the verse,
the area of a rope measuring two units is four.
"One part" (*pāda*) refers to one of its [four] parts; the meaning is that it completes [the whole].
(The ninth part in the third [section]):
The portion of the digit (*kalā*) of that which measures three units is not explicitly stated because it is understood from the fact that the ninth of the third is complete.
It should be observed that by the fourth there are sixteen, by the fifth twenty-five, and so forth.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Śulbapradīpa*, a commentary on the *Āpastamba-śulbasūtra* by Sundararāja.
[This is] the *Kapardibhāṣya*.
Previously, the measurement was stated without distinction, namely: "its length is this much, its width is this much, and it should be arranged in this manner.
For the purpose of prescribing the specific details, he says:
"In the sacrificial enclosure (vihāra) pertaining to the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), it is understood [as follows] between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires. (ĀpŚus 4.1a)

The mention of the *gārhapatya* and *āhavanīya* fires is for the purpose that the space should be between these two, and not between the *āhavanīya* and *dakṣiṇāgni*, nor between the *dakṣiṇāgni* and *gārhapatya*.
It is "known"—that is, it is heard;
the scriptural authority (*śruti*) is what is about to be stated.
A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fire at eight steps; a Rājanya at eleven; and a Vaiśya at twelve. ĀpŚus 4.1b.

It is heard in all [the texts] without distinction that it should be placed not too far from the twenty-four [finger-breadths], or from the immeasurable, or as far as one judges with the eye. (ĀpŚS 4.2)
He will state the measurement by means of the *prakrama*.
Having stepped eight *prakramas* beyond the *gārhapatya*, he establishes the *āhavanīya* fire.
In the same way, for a *rājanya*, it is eleven [steps].
For a Vaiśya, it is at twelve [steps],
or twenty-four, or as much as he judges by sight;
therefore, it is heard in the scripture that for all [classes] without distinction, it should not be placed too far away.
"Or as much as [possible]" means that for all [of these], the rule is optional. The reflection is that the perfection of the monastery is achieved within this interval.
The prohibition against excessive distance is for the purpose of avoiding interruptions.
If it is placed too far away, then dogs and other animals might pass between; thus, the general rules for the sacrificial enclosures have been stated. Karavindiya’s commentary has been explained.

Now, with the intention of explaining specific details regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices, the injunction for the sacrifice of the *vihāra* (the sacrificial ground) belonging to the *āgnyādheya*—which is the first [of such rites]—is stated.
That rite in which the fires (*agni*) are established (*adhīyante*) is called *āgnyādheya*;
that which pertains to it is *āgnyādheyika*.
"Vihāra" means that in which the fires are placed; it refers to the various sections of the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*).

With reference to that, [the text says] "in the interval between the Gārhapatya and the Āhavanīya. By the words "Gārhapatya" and "Āhavanīya," there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of their respective locations, because of the force of the scriptural mention of the "interval. Regarding the interval, having introduced the interval, it is understood—that is, it is heard—in the scripture.
Everywhere, this is precisely the meaning of the phrase "it is understood": because of the mention of the Gārhapatya and the Āhavanīya, it is specifically in the interval between those two.
The Śruti is recited thus:

"A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires at eight steps, a Rājanya at eleven, and a Vaiśya at twelve; or at twenty-four, or at an unlimited distance, or as far as one can see with the eye; therefore, it should not be established too far away."
It is heard [in the scriptures] that for all [of these], without distinction;
he will state the starting point as "two steps or three steps," while "eight steps" and so forth serve as specifications of the interval.

"At an interval of eight *prakramas*, and so forth. Regarding the number "immeasurable" (*aparimita*), Kātyāyana states that it refers to a quantity beyond twenty-four, because it follows immediately after that; or, it is "immeasurable" in terms of measurement, meaning it is greater than that. Alternatively, it means one measures by whatever extent one judges with the eye—that is, by the measure grasped by the eye—thinking, "this much is twenty-four *prakramas*"; such is measurement by the eye.

Although [the distance] is recited as being beyond twenty-four [steps], nevertheless, in accordance with the Taittirīyaka Śruti beginning with "in twelve strides" and "whom in twelve strides," all measures starting from eight strides and so forth must be accepted. Thus, it is possible [to say]: "this much is eight strides," "this much is nine," or "this much is twelve strides. Therefore, the fire-altar should not be placed at a distance too far from twenty-four [steps]. By this, the excessive distance resulting from the rule regarding "unmeasured" [space] is prohibited.
From this point, the yogas extending back to a very great distance are of twenty-four kinds.

The fourfold procedure beginning with the number twenty-four applies without distinction to all [castes], including the Brāhmaṇas and others. Furthermore, the rule regarding "twelve strides" is also obtained for all without distinction.
The commentary of Sundahabhājīya states: "A Vaiśya [is the officiant] for the establishment of the sacred fires (āgnāyādheya).
It is understood that these [distances] are measured in steps (prakrama) passed in front of the Gārhapatya fire; this is the Śruti of Sāvarṇika.
(It is heard with twenty-four [syllables].
"Immeasurable" means "having surpassed all measures"; this is another ritual manual (*kalpa*).
"He perceives with the eye" is a prohibition against measuring with a staff or other such instruments.

"Eight steps this far, eleven steps this far, twelve steps this far"—by means of his vision, he should place it not too far from that limit, in the vicinity of the boundary, over as much space as he judges.
All of this, which was stated at the time of the preparatory ritual (prayoga), is here restated.
— *Kapardibhāṣya*
To the south-east, at the third part from the front, closer to the Gārhapatya fire, the location of the Dakṣiṇāgni is known. (ĀpŚus 4.3)

"To the south-east"—in the region of the south-eastern corner, at the "third part" (vitṛtīyadeśa)—meaning slightly less than a third part—of what? Of the interval between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires; it means at the nearest third part from the side.
There, it is heard in the scripture, "the location of the Dakṣiṇāgni fire.
This is the Karavindīyā commentary.
(From the south; it is not explicitly known:

To the south, in front—that is, in the south-eastern corner—at a point closer to that Gārhapatya fire, specifically at one-third of its distance, the word *vi* being used in the sense of "slightly," the location for the Dakṣiṇāgni is heard to be within a space slightly less than one-third of the way [from the Gārhapatya].
The commentary of Sundararāja. He speaks for the purpose of prescribing the sacrificial ground with its southern edge facing east:
"(It is not known) to the south."
"At the third part" means at the deficient third part, that is, slightly less than the third part.
To the south and slightly to the east of the Gārhapatya fire, at its nearest third part, is the location for the Dakṣiṇa fire.
The Commentary of Kapardin:
How is that [measurement] to be taken?

Having divided the space between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires into five or six parts, and having added the sixth or seventh part as an increment, one divides the remainder into three equal parts. Having made a mark on the third part from the end, and having fixed the two ends at the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires, one draws a line toward the south using the mark as a guide and makes a reference point; that is the location for the Dakṣiṇā fire, according to the force of the scriptural injunction (śruti). (ĀpŚus 4.4)

The construction is: "having divided the space between the *gārhapatya* and *āhavanīya* fires into five parts, or having divided it into six parts. If it is divided into five, then the sixth part is an addition (*āgantuka*). Having added that sixth or seventh part to the [original] portion, one divides it equally into three parts.
If it is divided into six parts, then the seventh part is the *āgantu* (the additional space).
Having combined that and joined it [to the whole], one should divide it equally into three parts. The word "equally" (*samam*) is used so that there may be no inequality with the *āgantu*.

Having made a mark on the third [part] from the rear, and having fixed two loops by tying them to the ends of the *gārhapatya* and *āhavanīya* fires, one should pull [the cord] toward the south along the mark and drive in a peg.
The location for the *dakṣiṇāgni* is established by the force of the scriptural statement (*śruti*).

"Force" here refers to the denotative power (*abhidhāna-śakti*) of the scripture, which establishes that this specific meaning alone is intended. By this, the following [erroneous] views are refuted: that the space between the *gārhapatya* and *āhavanīya* fires consists of three squares, each with a width and length equal to one-third [of the total]; or that having constructed three such squares, the *gārhapatya* is placed on the northern hip of the western square, the site of the *dakṣiṇāgni* on its southern shoulder, and the *āhavanīya* on the northern shoulder of the eastern square, and so forth.
In all cases, the fire-places may be either square or circular.
However, in this context, they prescribe that the *gārhapatya* fire-place be circular, the *anvāhāryapacana* half-circular in shape, and the *āhavanīya* square;
the rules for the circular and square shapes have already been stated.
Now, the bow-shaped [altar] for the Dakṣiṇāgni fire is described: having made a square with two karaṇīs of a piśīla, one should construct a circle according to the previously stated procedure.

Having moved a quarter of the diameter of that circle northward from the stake previously driven in the east of the Dakṣiṇāgni, one should drive a stake there, fasten a cord to it, and, drawing a circle with half the diameter, one should discard the northern half.
Regarding this, there are two verses: [The verses follow.]
From the mark of the southern fire-altar, a northern mark should be made at ten finger-breadths minus eleven sesame-seeds; it will be equal to the bow of the work to be performed.
Having fixed the cord upon that [line], one should draw it extending twenty [units];
however, by reducing it by twenty-two *tilas*, one should discard half toward the north.
Thus [ends the section].
According to Karavinda’s commentary, [the placement] of the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires is determined by the force of the Vedic injunction.
He describes its measurement:

having divided the space between the *gārhapatya* and *āhavanīya* fires into eight or six parts—measuring eight *prakramas* or more—and having multiplied it [into those parts], one should add the sixth or seventh part as an increment. When multiplied fivefold, one adds the sixth part; when multiplied sixfold, one adds that part. Having added this increment, one should mark a point on the third [part] adjacent to the *gārhapatya*. Then, having fixed the two ends of the cord at the limits of the *gārhapatya* and *āhavanīya*, one should place the western loop of the cord upon the eastern peg of the *gārhapatya*.
Having first fastened the loop of the cord to the western peg of the Āhavanīya fire, one should make a mark at that point by drawing the cord southward along the measuring-line.
That mark is the center of the southern fire-altar, which is shaped like a bow; this is because no specific instruction to the contrary is heard.
According to some, the two ends of the cord should be fixed to the two middle pegs between the Gārhapatya and the Āhavanīya fires.
This is by the force of the scriptural authority (*śruti*),
meaning by the power of such scriptural passages as "to the south-east" (*dakṣiṇataḥ purastāt*).

Here, in the fivefold division, the western portion of the space between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires— measured from the midpoint of the site for the Dakṣiṇāgni fire along a line extending southward— is thirty-one finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and sixty-nine sixtieths of a finger-breadth (*tṛtīyalā*).
The front portion is twenty-eight finger-breadths and twenty-seven *tilas* plus one-third;
the hanging part (*lambaka*) is thirty-six finger-breadths and fifteen *tilas* less a quarter.
According to the sixfold division, the front portion is thirty-two finger-breadths and twenty-seven and a half *tilas*.
The hypotenuse (lambaka) measures thirty fingers and seventy *tilas*.

When the interval is measured at eight quarters (*pāda*), and when it is measured as eleven and so forth, the measure of the hypotenuse for those two parts should be inferred; we shall explain the method of such inference right here.

In this case as well, the *āyatanas* (sacrificial hearths) are merely symbolic forms; or rather, because the *prājahita* fire is also seen to be a *dhiṣṇya* (fire-place), and since the square and circular shapes of the *āyatanas* would otherwise be obtained without restriction, the *gārhapatya* hearth is specifically circular. This is because, in the sequence of that section of the text where it is praised as the earth—according to the passage "The three fires are indeed the triple knowledge"—the earth has that shape, and thus it is circular. The *dakṣiṇāgni* hearth is semi-circular or bow-shaped, because in that very same place it is praised as the intermediate space (*antarīkṣa*).

Furthermore, because the sky has that same shape, the Āhavanīya fire-altar is square; for in that very context, there is praise of the heavenly world, and it is seen in another scripture that "the square is the station of Indra. Therefore, the Sabhya and Āvasathya fires are also square, as they are modifications of that [Āhavanīya].

Regarding the *yoga* (the ritual preparation) here: having marked out a square measuring one *piśīla* at the site of the *Gārhapatya* fire, one should make it circular; for there is also a scriptural injunction regarding the *Dakṣiṇāgni*. Having marked out a square measuring two *viśīlas* and made it circular, one should determine the site of the *Dakṣiṇāgni* by means of a fourth part of the diameter of that circle. Having driven a peg (*śaṅku*) to the north of that [southern point] as a reference, and having fixed the middle of its diameter upon that peg and made the two ends equal, one should draw a circle. Then, having drawn an eastward line through the center of the circle, one should discard the northern half.

To the south of the site of the Gārhapatya fire, having left a space of eight steps or more in front, one should construct the Āhavanīya fire-altar as a square measuring one *piśīla*. Leaving a passage in front of it, one should construct the Sabhya fire-altar like the Āhavanīya, and in front of that, the Āvasathya fire-altar as well, likewise measuring one *piśīla*. A *piśīla* is two *prādeśas* in length.
Some say that a *piśīla* is a cubit (*aratni*) formed by the closed fist;
others say that a *piśīla* is the space between the two arms;
some maintain that the word *prakrama* also refers to a step (*pada*), as it is said "one proceeds" (*prakramyate*).

Nevertheless, it is obtained; this is the procedure for measuring here: having measured the two hearths of the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya, and the space between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya, and so forth, one should extend [the cord] toward the south, fix it, and make a mark. Using that very same reference point, one should reverse it to the north and make marks both to the south and to the north. Then, by means of a quarter of the diameter of a square circle divided into two parts (piśīla-dvikaraṇī-caturaśra-maṇḍalī-vaṣkambha-caturthāṃśa), one should drive a peg (śaṅku) between the two southern marks, in accordance with the two marks made to the north.

At the western peg of these two, having drawn a circle with a diameter equal to half the span of the *piśīla*-measuring cord, and having determined the east by means of the eastern peg, one should discard the northern half of the circle.
The southern half becomes the site for the Dakṣiṇāgni hearth.
This is the commentary of Sundararāja.
(Since there is no direct scriptural statement regarding the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires, by virtue of their functional capacity:

To the question of how that should be understood, he says: "All is equal" means that from the eastern peg of the Gārhapatya fire and the western peg of the Āhavanīya fire, the site for the Dakṣiṇāgni fire is to the south.
Others say that [the *āhavanīya*] is in the middle of those two locations;
according to that view, even for the *gārhapatya* and *āhavanīya*, only those in the middle are to be taken.
All *āgraya* locations are one *piśīla* in measure, and they may be either square or circular; however, because it is a *dhiṣṇiya*, the *gārhapatya* is circular.
The traditionalists say that the hearth of the Dakṣiṇāgni is a half-maṇḍala and that of the Āhavanīya is a square, and that all hearths are equal in terms of their area.

Regarding this, the rule for the maṇḍala has been stated: having laid out a square for the Āhavanīya using a diagonal cord and having made a circle according to the prescribed method, one should leave out the northern half; that is the hearth of the Dakṣiṇāgni.

The eastern side of the altar is one *kaparda* (a cowrie-shell) wide and as long as the sacrificer, or it may be of unlimited length, so that the sacrificial oblations may fit upon it; the crosswise side is raised toward the east. The two corners (*vedyaṃsau*) are directed forward; the two buttocks (*śroṇī*) are directed backward; it is narrower in front and broader behind, being more deeply curved in the middle—for "thus indeed is a woman," so it is known from the description of the altar for the New Moon sacrifice. (ĀpŚus 4.5)
The scriptural injunction regarding the sacrificial altar (*vedi*) for the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*) begins with "measured according to the sacrificer" (*yajamānamātrī*).
Karavinda’s commentary explains the meaning of this scriptural statement precisely through the rules for measurement.
Immediately after the performance of the *āyatanas*, the performance of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, which constitute the fundamental ritual, is described.
[Regarding the phrase "of the measure of the sacrificer" (*yajamānamātrī*)—it is understood as referring to the altar (*vedi*).
Thus, "of the measure of the sacrificer."
The eastern side is nine cubits long, measured at ninety-six finger-breadths; it is unmeasured [in width].

The northern side is longer than that, facing eastward; "saṃbhava" means pervasion. Just as the sacrificial oblations (havīṃṣi) are placed close together in mutual connection, so should the crosswise side (tiraśvī) be oriented transversely. The crosswise side at the rear is three parts less than the length.
Bodhāyana states: "The crosswise side in front is half of the length."

And it is likewise seen in the *Paśubandha* sacrifice: "Or [the altar] with four *aratnis* behind, six in front, and three at the east. In the modified sacrifices (*vikṛtis*) involving many oblations, the altar is wide; in those with few oblations, it is as in the archetype (*prakṛti*). He raises the two eastern corners of the altar (*vedyaṃsau*); by being oriented toward the east, he should make the two front corners extend beyond [the front edge]. He makes the two western corners (*śroṇī*) facing west; thus he should make the two hips distinct. It is narrower—slender—and wider—extensive—and more deeply curved, exceedingly thin; for such indeed is a woman.
The expression *evamiva hi* is a collection of particles used to denote what is well-known.
For example: "For just so is the animal; for just so is food eaten.
Indeed, this very likeness is her similarity [to food].

The fact that [the altar] is thin in the middle, broad at the shoulders, and even broader at the hips is also obtained from the wording of the mantra: "The four-crested young woman, well-formed. Although the altar of the *darśika* sacrifice is common to both the *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is called *darśika* because it is seen (*dṛśya*) on the day before the *darśa*.
Alternatively, the reference is made by applying the grammatical rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retaining only one term) to both the *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
The commentary of Sundararāja states:
"It is understood to be the measure of the sacrificer.
Being the measure of the sacrificer means it should be four or five *aratnis* in length, so that the sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) may fit and be contained within it.
Thus, *tiraścī* means transverse, having half the characteristic [of a line];
*unnayati* means it leads upward or extends lengthwise;

*pratīcī* refers to the westward direction, and its resemblance to a woman is known from the wording of the mantra, "four-crested" (*catuḥśikhaṇḍā*), pertaining to the *darśikī*—that is, the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice.

Having marked out a long square measuring one *kaparda* in breadth and one *kṣārya* in depth to the west of the Āhavanīya fire, and having stretched a cord of that same length, he makes a mark in the middle. Having fixed it between the two southern corners (the *śroṇi* and *aṃsa*), he draws it southward along the mark and makes a point. Having fixed the cord at that point and brought the two ends together, he should draw a line from the southern *śroṇi* to the southern *aṃsa*. He does the same on the north side. Having likewise doubled the transverse cord (*tiryaṅmānī*), he should mark off [the lines] behind and in front.
In the case of a square [shed], one should bring together the two side-measures at the front, by virtue of the force of the scriptural injunction. (ĀpŚus 4.6)
Thus ends the fourth section.

To the west of the Āhavanīya fire, having measured out and prepared a square area one rope-length or more in length, the side-measure (pārśvamānī) should be equal to the height of the sacrificer, so that the oblations placed there may fit together without touching one another; the cross-measure (tiryaṅmānī) should be such that it remains unconfined by the others.
Regarding this, it is established in another *Śulba* of Bodhāyana that the cross-measure may be one-third less than that [side-measure].

Having extended the cord to that same length and made loops at both ends, having fixed the two ends on the southern hip and shoulder and fastened the loops, having pulled it southward by means of a mark and driven in a peg as a marker, having tied the cord to that peg and unfastened the loops, and holding it with that hand, one should draw a line starting from the southern hip up to the southern shoulder.
In the same way, one should draw the northern side. This is the continuity of the altar.
One should also proceed in this manner for the cross-line (*tiryaṅbhānī*).

Having taken a cord equal in measure to the cross-line, having made a mark in the middle, having fastened loops at both ends, and having moved it from the side, one should drive a peg there; having tied the cord there and joined the two ends, one should draw [the line] starting from the southern hip as far as the northern hip.
One does the same in front as well.
In this way, the hips and shoulders are elevated;
for such is the form of a woman. The word "hi" (for) is used here to establish the well-known nature of her appearance.

The meaning is that the woman [the cord] has its head directed toward the east; "in this very way" means that when the measured [altar] has been made square, one should contract—that is, shorten—the two side-measures at the front.
This is by the force of the scriptural statement: "It is narrower in the front," according to the power of that Vedic injunction.
Otherwise, there would not even be a resemblance to a woman.
Thus ends the fourth section.
Karavinda’s commentary explains this by means of the following method of construction.
"To the west of the Āhavanīya fire" (and likewise to the north). Regarding the word "to the west": it means to the west of the Āhavanīya, that is, in its vicinity behind it.
Although there is a great distance between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires, the sacrificial altar (vedi) is nevertheless located in the vicinity of the Āhavanīya;
some desire it to be long, with its length being twice its width.

Having laid out the Āhavanīya fire-altar as a long quadrangle of the stated measurement behind [the Gārhapatya], having fixed stakes at the two corners (śroṇis) and the two shoulders (aṃsas), and having extended a cord equal to the length [of the altar] to make a cord twice the length of the span, one should make a mark in the middle by applying a dye. Having fastened the two ends to the southern corner and shoulder, and having pulled it southward along the mark, one should fix a stake; having looped the cord around that stake and joined the two loops together, one should draw a circle starting from the corner and ending at the shoulder. On the northern side, having pulled it northward, one should do exactly the same.
(One should draw the cross-line—making it double)—regarding the phrase "the cross-line":

having made the previous cross-line double as before, one should pull it forward and, starting from the southern shoulder, draw [a line] to the northern shoulder; one should do exactly the same with the western cross-line. Having pulled a cord equal to the eastward extent of the altar between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires according to the stated method, one should make a mark at the two-thirds point as before, having also made a mark to the north outside the altar for the sake of the northern part. From the altar...
Thereafter, one should likewise make a mark at the third point from the back. One should make the mark at the middle—the central space—between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires.

Regarding the phrase "in the vimitā" (vimitāyām): because the force of the scriptural statement does not explicitly prescribe it, one should—before drawing the lines—contract the two side-measures (pārśvamānyau) toward the front, that is, at the eastern end, once the ground has been made square (caturaśrīkṛta). One should thus narrow them.
Thus ends the fourth section.
This is the commentary by Sundararāja.
(The other [measurement] is due to the force of the scriptural statement.)

He describes its drawing out: having fixed and fastened a cord at a mark and in the middle of the cord, one should draw a line starting from the southern hip (dakṣiṇā śroṇi) up to the southern shoulder (dakṣiṇaṃ aṃsa).

Having made a mark in the middle of the two transverse lines as well, and having fixed the ends on the two hips and the two shoulders, one should pull [the cord] back and forth; this and so forth is to be understood.
This is precisely the raising of the hips and shoulders.

In the case of a *vimita* (shed) that has been made square, one should slightly contract [the dimensions] even before the bending, on the strength of the scriptural injunction: "It should be narrower in front.
Regarding this, Bodhāyana says:
"The eastern side is equal to the sacrificer's height; the cross-side in front is half of that; the cross-side behind is three parts less; [and] thirty paces."

The commentary of Kapardin states that the rear cross-line (tiraścī) consists of thirty paces or steps; it is known from the description of the Saumikī altar that it is thirty-six paces long toward the east and twenty-four paces across at the front. (ĀpŚus 5.1)

In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśikā*, having combined eighteen [units] from the other end, one fixes the two ends of the spine on the fifteenth and twelfth marks; having pulled southward with the fifteenth, one drives in a peg. Likewise to the north are the two hips (*śroṇī*). Having reversed [the process], one pulls with the fifteenth and drives in a peg on the twelfth; likewise to the north are those two shoulders (*aṃsau*). (ĀpŚus 5.2a)
"Steps" refers to our own Śruti:
"Thirty steps or paces [are measured] behind;
transversely," meaning it becomes oriented crosswise.
"The thirty-six [cubits] are the eastward spine, and twenty-four [cubits] are the crosswise base in front"—this is the scriptural injunction regarding the Soma-altar at the Soma sacrifice.

In the thirty-six-fold cord, having added eighteen [units] together and having made loops at both ends, one should make a mark at twelve [units] from the other end and a mark at fifteen [units], leaving a space between them. Having stepped three *prakramas* eastward from the middle of the *lālāṭika* line at the end of the *pṛṣṭhyā*, one should drive a peg into the ground. From that, having driven a peg into the ground at thirty-six *prakramas* to the east, one should fasten loops to those two. Then, having pulled [the cord] southward by fifteen [units], one should drive a peg into the ground;
that is the southern hip (*dakṣiṇā śroṇī*).
In this manner, having moved northward, one should drive in a peg;
that shall be the northern hip, and the shoulders shall be reversed.
Having approached with the fifteen-finger-breadth cord, one should drive in two stakes at the twelve-finger distance; in this same manner, the two shoulder-stakes are placed to the north.
Having unloosed the two loops from the central stake, one should fasten the eastern loop onto the western stake, and the western loop onto the eastern stake.
That is the reversal.
By means of that very reversed [measurement] made upon the rope, those two [points] are to be measured.
Having moved twelve [units] toward the south with that same unmarked [rope], one should drive a stake into the ground at the twelfth [point].
Having moved twelve [units] northward from that very point, a stake is fixed;
those two are the shoulders.
Why is this measurement of the great altar (mahāvedi) stated?

To what extent is this established? Some offer the following rebuttal: it was stated with the intention of expressing the dwelling of multiple cords (*rajjū*). Others maintain that, according to the alternative view beginning with "or the length" (*āyāmam vā*), the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) applies to twelve [units], while the "stainless" (*nirañjana*) applies to twenty-seven when the characteristic consists of fifteen; thus, it is for the purpose of demonstrating a multiplicity of characteristics.
The construction of squares and rectangles has been explained;
however, others say that here [the method applies] to long and irregular quadrilaterals. That is the construction by means of a single cord. (ĀpŚS 5.2b)
The diagonal cord for the two triads is fivefold. With those [cords] multiplied three times, the shoulders [are measured]; with them multiplied four times, the hips. (ĀpŚS 5.3)
In the case of a square whose transverse side is three units and whose lateral side is four units, its diagonal cord is five units.
The two shoulders are to be measured by those [units];
the three units, when repeated three times, become twelve.
The fourfold [measurement] consists of sixteen [units] in each pentad, making twenty.

Having driven a stake sixteen units behind the stake for the sacrificial post-hole (*yūpāvaṭīya*), one should fasten a pentad with its repetition upon it; having fastened a triple [unit] with its repetition upon the stake for the sacrificial post-hole, one should stretch the shoulder-line.
The two hips are marked by those [lines] repeated four times.
With those same [measuring cords] joined by four repetitions, the two hips (śroṇī) are to be measured.
Having fixed a peg at the twentieth [mark], one should fasten a fivefold cord with its repetition there, and having fastened a fifteenfold cord, one should mark out the two hips with them.
Karavindīyā Vyākhyā:
Following the measurement of the altar for the Darśapūrṇamāsa, the measurement of the altar for the Soma sacrifice is described in the archetype:
"The altar is known to be thirty paces or steps."
"Thirty," it is said.

The *Taittirīyaka-śruti* states, "Thirty paces behind, it becomes transverse (*tiraśvī*)," while another recension (*śākhāntarīyā*) says, "Thirty *prakramas*. Therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*). Even though the ritual instruction uses the word *prakrama*—in the passage, "From the middle of the *prāgvaṃśa*, three *prakramas* toward the east, at the level of the forehead"—nevertheless, the word *prakrama* is used there for the purpose of demonstrating that the two scriptural statements are optional alternatives.
In that context, the word *prakrama* is used because [the distance] is measured by steps (*prakramāyata*).
The western cross-line and the western transverse line are the eastward length; the eastern cross-line and the eastern transverse line are called the measurement.
(Thirty-six-shouldered) means "in the thirty-six-fold [system]."

A *ṣaṭtriṃśikā* is a cord measuring thirty-six [units]. Having combined eighteen [units] of it and joined them together, starting from the other end—the western extremity—one should mark a point at twelve [units] for the sake of the shoulders (*aṃsa*) and at fifteen [units] for the sake of the hips (*śroṇi*). Having passed three *prakramas* eastward from the middle of the *prāgvaṃśa* shed, one should then draw an eastern line measuring thirty-six [units]; that is the *pṛṣṭhyā* line. Having fixed stakes at its two ends and attached loops to them—

Having measured fifteen units toward the south, one drives in a peg; that is the southern hip. Likewise, having measured toward the north, a peg is driven in; that is the northern hip. The two shoulders are to be measured by reversing the positions [of the pegs].
Having measured fifteen units [from the center] toward [the east], a peg is driven in twelve units to the south and twelve units to the north; those are the two shoulders.

Now, one might ask: since this current method of laying out [the altar] is already established by the previous rule, "Having practiced that for the sake of this," why is it stated again here? To this, some respond: "It is for the purpose of introducing a preceding number. Others say: "It is because of the intention to express multiple cords (*rajju*). Still others maintain: "It is for the purpose of demonstrating the multiplicity of measurements—such as a measurement-mark at twelve units of length and practice, a measurement-mark at fifteen, and the removal of the *niraḍhañjana* at twenty-seven and so on. Furthermore, while the laying out of long quadrilaterals was taught there, others hold that it is for the purpose of [teaching] the laying out of an irregularly long quadrilateral here.
(The measurement with that same cord:
"That" refers to the aforementioned [cord].
And since this rope is one, it is "a single rope" (*ekarajju*); the laying out of the hips and shoulders is performed with that very same single rope.
He restates what was previously mentioned regarding the laying out by means of a method involving two pegs, three pegs, or five pegs, because he intends to describe the method using multiple ropes.
Regarding the "threefold" and "fourfold" [measures]— the diagonal cord for the pentad—
it is called "tri-ketī."
The *trikā* has three *prāṇas*, the *catuṣkā* has four *pramāṇas*, and the *pañcikā* has five *pramāṇas*.

Regarding the phrase "of the *trikā* and the *catuṣkā*," that which is obtained through the repetition of the length is restated; by means of that repetition, the hips and shoulders are prescribed, and so it is with the subsequent repetitions.
(With those [fingers] repeated three times each on the shoulders:

with those [fingers] repeated three times separately, and placed above three times—twelve from the triad repeated three times, sixteen from the tetrad repeated three times, twenty from the pentad repeated three times; with these, the two shoulders are to be measured.

(The two hips are measured by fourfold repetitions. From the *trika* [measuring rod] repeated four times, there are fifteen; from the *catuṣka*, twenty; from the *pañcaka*, twenty-five. By these, the two hips are to be measured. Having driven a peg sixteen units behind the peg at the pit for the sacrificial post (*yūpāvaṭīya*), one should fasten the *pañcaka* repeated three times and the *catuṣka* repeated four times to it; having fastened the *trika* repeated three times and the *catuṣka* repeated four times to the peg at the pit for the sacrificial post; and having fastened the *trika* repeated four times to the first-pinned peg—by those two, the two hips are measured. This is established through the multiplication of the length.
Or it may be established by doubling the length as the measurement.
The commentary of Sundararāja:
"It is known that thirty *padās* or *prakramas* constitute the altar (*vedi*).
And Bodhāyana has stated that there are two kinds of *pada*: "A small *pada* is ten *aṅgulas*; a [regular] *pada* is fifteen *aṅgulas*."
Kātyāyana says that [the measure] is twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). These three types of *pada* are optionally interchangeable with a worldly *pada*.
Thus he will say: "In the *pada*, the *yuga*, and the *aradna*, etc."
These same four types of paces, when doubled or tripled, constitute the *prakramas*.
These, moreover, are of seven kinds.

Among them, in the case of the *soma* sacrifice involving the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicityā*), measurement by paces is not obtained, because the area for the fire-altar (*agnikṣetra*) would be impossible [to construct].

Thus, the cessation at twenty finger-breadths has been explained regarding the sevenfold fire-altar; however, some maintain that in the case of the non-piling of the fire-altar (*anagnicitya*), there is an option (*vikalpa*) for all the steps (*prakrama*) according to one's preference.
Others, however, desire the following fixed rule: in the case of the non-piling of the fire-altar, the measurement is by means of four kinds of steps or by a step of twenty finger-breadths.

In the case of a single-altar fire (ekavidhāgni), it is twenty finger-breadths; for those from the two-altar up to the five-altar fires, it is twenty-four finger-breadths; for those from the six-altar up to the twelve-altar fires, it is twenty finger-breadths, or according to the worldly standard, two paces; and for those from the thirteen-altar upwards, it is thirty-six finger-breadths, and so forth.
In all these cases, however, the fires are possible with a step (prakrama) of forty-five finger-breadths.
In that regard, an increase in the Vedic measures must be made in accordance with the fire-altars.
In the *Yūpaikādaśinī*, this is the introductory section for the principle [of measurement], such as "one hundred and one kinds" and "eighty finger-breadths," and so forth.
Now, he describes the layout (*viharaṇa*) of this altar (*vedi*)—
[the section on] the layout in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśikā*:
This is an elaboration on the measurement that was stated as being "as long as the length.
Now, he describes the laying out of this very altar using multiple cords:
"(The two hips are [formed] by the three- and four-unit [cords])."

By means of these [measures] multiplied and laid out across the two lateral sides of the three-unit and four-unit [sections], as follows: the three-unit [section] multiplied three times is the twelve-unit [measure]; the four-unit [section] multiplied three times is the sixteen-unit [measure]; and the five-unit [section] multiplied three times is the twenty-unit [measure].
By these three multiplied measures, the two shoulders (aṃsau) are to be measured.
By these same [measures] multiplied four times—namely, the fifteen-unit and the twenty-unit—the two hips (śroṇī) are to be measured.
Even with these [measures] repeated twice, the two shoulders can be measured;
in all cases, the twelve-unit [span] applies to the shoulders,
while the fifteen-unit [span] applies to the cross-measure (tiryaṅbhānī).
The other two śroṇi-measures are on the spine as the lateral sides; thus is the measurement performed with six cords.
It is the same in the subsequent cases.
The commentary of Kapardin:
When the first peg has been struck, there is a triangle with an extension.
The diagonal cord for the twelve-unit and five-unit [sides] is thirteen units; with those doubled, the two shoulders are formed, and with them doubled, the two hips. (ĀpŚS 5.4)

Having driven a peg five [units] behind the peg at the pit for the sacrificial post (yūpāvaṭīya), one should fasten a thirteen-unit cord to it; then, having fastened a five-unit and a twelve-unit cord to the peg at the pit for the sacrificial post, the two shoulders (aṃsa) are to be measured by means of those [three cords].
The two hips (śroṇī) are to be measured by those same [three] cords doubled.

Having fastened a thirteen-unit cord with its repetition and a twelve-unit cord with its repetition to the peg at the pit for the sacrificial post, and a five-unit cord with its repetition to the first [peg] that was driven, the two hips are to be measured by means of those [four cords].
Karavindīyā Vyākhyā:
(The twelvefold cord.
This is for the sake of clarity.

(With those [measures]): having driven a peg fifteen [units] behind the peg of the sacrificial post-hole (*yūpāvaṭīya*), and having fastened a thirteen-unit cord to it, and having fastened a twelve-unit cord to the peg of the sacrificial post-hole, the two shoulders [are determined] by those two.

Likewise, having fastened a five-unit cord doubled to the first peg that was driven, and having fastened a thirteen-unit cord doubled to the peg of the sacrificial post-hole, the two hips are determined by those two.
This is attained through half-practice, or it is attained through fourfold practice of extension.
The commentary of Sundararāja:
(The hips are twelve digits wide); by means of those [lines] beginning with the twenty-six digit [line], which are repeated twice.
The side-measure is one and a quarter [parts].
The diagonal cord for the fifteen- and eight-part measures is seventeen parts; by means of these, the two hips are marked. (ĀpŚS 5.5a)
Having driven a peg eight [units] east of the first peg, one should fasten a seventeen-unit cord and an eight-unit cord to it, and a fifteen-unit cord to the first peg;
by means of these, the two hips [are determined].
The diagonal cord for the twelvefold and thirty-fivefold [measures] is the thirty-sevenfold. With these, the two shoulders are marked. (ĀpŚS 5.5b)

Having driven a peg in front of the first peg at a distance of one prakrama, and having fastened a cord of thirty-seven units and a cord of thirty-five units to it, as well as a cord of twelve units to the peg for the sacrificial post-hole—
one should measure the two shoulders with those [cords].
There are this many altars and altar-sites to be known. || ĀpŚus_5.6 ||
Only these many altar-sites with pure foundations can be known;
other pure foundations are impossible to construct.
Therefore, they are determined to be exactly this many.

Karavindīyā Vyākhyā: (The two hips are fifteen units long. At the first peg struck, there is a fifteen-unit cord; then, eight units further toward the east, there is a seventeen-unit cord; by means of these two, the two hips are formed.
This is either one-seventh of three times the length plus two, or one-seventh of two times the length plus three.
"(The two shoulders are the twelfth [finger-breadth]).
Regarding the term "the twelfth":
this too has its meaning already explained.

The twelve-unit cord is for the sacrificial post-hole (*yūpāvaṭīya*). Having driven a peg at a distance of one *prakrama* in front of the first driven peg, a thirty-seven-unit cord is fixed to it; these two [pegs] form the shoulders (*aṃsau*). This is obtained by doubling five and adding two, or by dividing seven by five and multiplying by five.
(There are this many); "there are this many" means this.
The determination that "only this many [measures] can be known because they have pure roots" is a restriction.

These many have been stated; others are also to be inferred. Indeed, the measurements for the altar (*vedi*) occur through the reduction and increase of ropes with cuts. Although this measurement has been explained by means of a single rope with two connections, nevertheless, one should measure accordingly even with three or five pegs through reduction and increase; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of assuming that the prescription of those [three or five pegs] serves a transcendental purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Therefore, this is an illustration for all measurements.
According to Sundararāja:
(there are fifteen [fingers]; there are this many [fingers] without cuts).
There are also many other [configurations] involving the cutting away [of corners], such as:
the diagonal cord (*akṣṇayārajju*) for a twelve-and-a-half [unit square] and a four-and-a-half [unit square] is thirteen-and-a-half [units]; by those [cords], the two shoulders (*aṃsau*) are formed.
For a fifteen [unit square] and an eleven-and-a-quarter [unit square], the diagonal cord is nineteen-minus-a-quarter [units]; by those, the two hips (*śroṇī*) are formed, and so forth.
The commentary of Kapardin:
the great altar consists of one thousand and twenty-eight quarters. ĀpŚus 5.7a.
There are nine hundred and seventy-two (972) steps, or units of *prakrama*, for the square dimensions of the great altar (*mahāvedi*).

For what purpose is the word "great" (*maha*) used? It is for the purpose of indicating that when the great altar is measured by *pada*s, the *sadas*, *havirdhāna*, and other structures are also measured by *pada*s; whereas when it is measured by *prakrama*s, the *sadas* is prescribed with a width of nine *aratni*s and a length of one *aratni*, measured specifically by *aratni*s and *prakrama*s.
Because of the prescription of a fixed measurement as "nine *aratni*s across," it is inferred that the measurement is indeed by means of *aratni*s.
Likewise, it is inferred that the *havirdhāna* has a width of three *aratnis* and a length of nine *aratnis*.
How, then, is the measurement of these two obtained by means of a *pada*? It is said because of the statement: "fifty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*) [plus] sixteen.

Behind the *sadas*, there are fifty-four finger-breadths; between the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna*, there are two hundred and sixteen finger-breadths; and the space for movement (*saṃcara*) between the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* is fifty-four finger-breadths.
The Havirdhāna shed measures two fathoms plus sixteen finger-breadths;

the remainder is eighteen finger-breadths. Therefore, since it is impossible for the Uttaravedi, the Sadas, and the Havirdhāna to all fit within the inner altar (antarvedi), an expansion must be arranged.
Or rather, a reduction from the *aratni* should be calculated;

both of those [options] would be unscripted (*acodita*). Therefore, it is established that for the purpose of measuring them, the *pāda* (foot) is to be taken as the unit by which the altar was measured.
Karavindīyā Vyākhyā:
(The Mahāvedī is twenty-eight less).
There are nine hundred and seventy-two areas measured by a *pada* for the Mahāvedī; it is the same even when measured by a *prakrama*.

For what purpose is the mention of "pada" (foot-step)? It is said: by the mention of "pada" and "mahā" (great), this is understood: when measuring with the *vedi* (altar), the *sadas* and *havirdhāna* sheds are also measured by the *pada*, not by *aratnis*; and the *uttaravedi* is only a *yuga* (measured by a yoke) in extent, not ten *padas* on all sides. This is because, if the *vedi* were measured by *prakramas*, it would be impossible for the *sadas* and *havirdhāna*—which are prescribed in *aratnis*—and the *uttaravedi*, which is ten *padas* on all sides, to exist [within that space]. Thus, it is established that the measurement of the *sadas* and *havirdhāna* is by the *pada* alone, and the *uttaravedi* is only a *yuga* in extent. The purpose of the enumeration [of measures] is seen in such passages as "he sacrifices in the third [part]" and so forth.
According to the *Sundararājīyā*:
the great altar (*mahāvedi*) is reduced by twenty-eight [units].
The mention of the "square" (*pada*) is also an elliptical indication for the "step" (*prakrama*).

One should draw a line from the right shoulder to the right hip, twelve units long; by reversing the cut, one should lay it down on the north side. This forms a long square; one should observe it as being thus constructed.
Starting from the right shoulder, one should distribute [the measurement] across the hips in twelve steps.
Three steps should be placed in the region of the hips; having reversed the direction, one should mentally fix [the remaining steps] upon the left shoulder.
When this is done, it becomes a long rectangle with a width of twenty-seven [units] and a length of thirty-six.
When that same-sized altar is multiplied by thirty-six, it becomes one thousand and twenty-eight deficient squares (28 less than 1,000).
It is known from the Sautrāmaṇī ritual that one should sacrifice on a third part of the Saumika altar. (ĀpŚus 5.8a)
