Regarding the rule "one should sacrifice on a third [of the ground]," since [the measurement] of the Dārśika and Pāśuka sacrifices is impossible [therein], that of the Saumika sacrifice is obtained;
therefore, it is said, "of the Saumika. Its *prakrama* becomes equivalent to the *dvikaraṇī* or the *trikaraṇī* of the *prakrama*. (ĀpŚS 5.8b)
The term *tṛtīyakaraṇī* refers to the position of the step (*prakrama*); the suffix *-cha* is applied optionally after a word ending in *sthāna*.

Having made the third part of the side the step, one should proceed according to the rule beginning with "in the thirty-sixth [square]," etc., or by means of the third part of the side according to the method that will be explained.
The two cross-measures are eight-fold and ten-fold; the spine is twelve-fold.
The *aṣṭikā* cord is laid out transversely from the east;
the *dvādaśikā* cord is the spine.

Having made a mark at the sixth [unit] by combining six [units] from the end of the western [cord], and having made a mark at the fourth [unit], one fixes the two ends on the two ends of the spine, stretches five [units] toward the south, and drives in a peg.
In this manner, the two hips [should be] toward the north; with the shoulders reversed,
one should pull [the cord] southward by five units and drive four stakes.
In this way, the two shoulders extend to the north;
the sacrificial altar for the Sautrāmaṇī consists of three hundred and twenty-four padas. || ĀpŚus_5.9 ||

Starting from the right shoulder, one should extend [the line] across the four [sections] down to the right hip; then, as before, one should transpose the remainder and so forth. It becomes twelve padas in width and twelve padas in length; thus one should instruct.
"It is known from the Aśvamedha that the sacrificial altar (vedi) is twice as large. (ĀpŚus 5.10)
To what does "twice as large" refer? To the Soma-altar, because it is the subject under discussion and because it serves as the archetype (prakṛti).
Thus ends the fifth section.
[This is] the Karavindīya commentary.
Regarding the statement that the mention of "the third" in the case of the field is not authoritative, as to how the mention of "the third" follows from the number, he says:
"From the southern shoulder—one should mark.
Starting from the southern shoulder of the altar, one should drop a line or a cord at twelve [units] toward the southern hip; having dropped it, one should cut outside of that.

Having reversed—that is, turned over—the cut portion that lies outside the line, one should place it on the other side; thus there arises an oblong quadrangular altar (*vedi*) twenty-seven units wide and thirty-six units long. One should calculate it as being joined and constituted in such a manner. By this, the method of calculation for irregular quadrangles is to be understood. In connection with the altar, its modifications are now stated:

It is known from the *Saumikī* [text]: "The *Sautrāmaṇī* has Sutrāman as its deity; one should sacrifice upon the third part of its altar (*veditṛtīya*). This is what is heard in the scripture. "The third part of the altar" means the third region of the altar (*veditṛtīyadeśa*). Of which [altar] is this? Of the *Saumikī*. It is like the expression: "rice-gruel measured by an *āḍhaka* of parched rice."

(Regarding the term *prakrama-pṛṣṭhayā*: The third *karaṇī* of the *prakrama* is explained as being equivalent to the *prakrama*. The suffix *cha* is applied in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*) by the rule beginning with "after a word ending in *sthāna*, optionally" (*sthānāntād vibhāṣā*).

Likewise, by the passage beginning with "In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśatikā*," etc., the altar (*vimāna*) and its three-fold measurement are described as in the *Kaumika*. In the case of the *Aṣṭikā* and *Daśikā*, the transverse line is twelve units; the transverse line at the back is ten units, and the length is twelve units. In the *Dvādaśikā*, having combined six [units], one marks the lines on four [rows] for the hips and on five [rows] for the shoulders. He states that the third part is from the field: "(Three hundred and twenty-four padas is the *sautrāmaṇikī* vedi)."
The altar for the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice measures three hundred and twenty-four [units].
From the right shoulder onwards, it is like that of the Soma sacrifice;
this is because of the observation that "one-third of a *prakrama* is the measuring unit. Here too, the *pada* and the *prakrama* are optional alternatives.

By beginning with the word *prakrama* and concluding with the word *pada*, it is indicated that even in other instances—such as "in eight *prakramas*" and so forth—the term *pada* also conveys the meaning of a measuring unit (*vimāna*). For it is known from the *Aśvamedha* sacrifice that "the altar (*vedi*) becomes twice as large [as the original]. Because of its being the subject under discussion and because it is the archetype (*prakṛti*), the altar at the *Aśvamedha* is indeed twice as large—that is, double—the size of the Soma-altar. Due to the connection with a multitude of sacrificial animals, the requirement for the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) to be spaced at intervals equal to the axle of a chariot—as obtained through the general rule (*codaka*)—is set aside by the direct injunction of the altar being twice as large.

Therefore, in this case, there are exactly twenty-one sacrificial posts (yūpas) at intervals that do not exceed the standard measure. Having measured three times the length [of the altar], the step-measurement is three paces;
in the case of the eleven posts (yūpaikādaśinī), the expansion of the altar occurs twice the length. Thus it is.
The commentary of Sundararāja.
He states the method for counting:
"One should look toward the right shoulder."
Starting from the right shoulder and extending to the end of the back on the right side, one should lay down a cord twelve units long.

Having mentally transformed that long triangular cut-out on the right into its reverse, one should place it on the northern side; this becomes a long rectangle measuring thirty-six units in length and twenty-seven units in width. One should calculate it as such:
when the product of twenty-seven and thirty-six is computed, it becomes nine hundred and seventy-two.

For a space of ten finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), the *trikaraṇī* is seventeen finger-breadths and eleven sesame seeds; [this is expressed as] aṃ 7 ti 11. For twelve finger-breadths, it is twenty finger-breadths and twenty-seven sesame seeds; [this is expressed as] aṃ 20 ti 27. For fifteen finger-breadths, it is twenty-six finger-breadths less one sesame seed. In this same manner, it should be understood for the *prakrama*s as well.
(The three [altars] are the Sautrāmaṇī altar.
This same [altar] belongs to the Kāṭhaka fires as well;

Thus ends the fifth section of the *Kapardibhāṣya*. The double-measure of the *prakrama* serves as the substitute for the *prakrama*. (ĀpŚus 6.1)
One should increase [the measurement] by one-third of the measure using the two karaṇīs; the procedure for laying out [the altar] is the same as that which has been increased by this method.
A *prakrama* consists of either two or three paces. Regarding the *prakrama*, one may act according to one's desire, because the meaning of the word is subject to interpretation. (ĀpŚus 6.2a)
Two feet are thirty finger-breadths;
three feet are forty-five finger-breadths;
for it is stated that one foot is fifteen finger-breadths.

*Kāma* means desire (*icchā*). *Yāthākāmī* means according to one's desire; one should take [the measurement] exactly as one wishes. In the case of *prakrama*, the terms *adhyardhaprakrama* (one and a half steps) and *viprakṛṣṭaprakrama* (extended step) are not names derived from their literal meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*).

Just as a derivative (*yaugika*) word denotes a meaning exceeding [the literal measure] of its constituent parts, so too does a two-word or three-word compound express such a meaning. For instance, *krama* means "that by which one strides" (*krāmatyanena*); when it is established as *prakṛṣṭaḥ kramaḥ* ("an excellent stride"), it is a conventionalized term (*nirūḍha*). Because it expresses a substance that is a conceptual object (*kalpanārthadravya*), it is called *padādhika-prakrama*. Since the meanings of words possess the quality of being "pervasive" (*viśayitva*)—meaning they denote even conceptualized objects—it follows that there is a multiplicity of denotative expressions. It belongs either to the sacrificer or to the Adhvaryu; for he is the performer of the ritual actions.
The footprint of the sacrificer (yajamāna) should be taken because of his ownership;
or rather, that of the Adhvaryu— the word "or" (vā) serves to set aside the previous position—
it is not that of the sacrificer.
Why the Adhvaryu alone? Because he is the performer of the activities. "Activities" (ceṣṭāḥ) refers to actions (karmāṇi), as they are that which cause movement.
Since he is the performer of those actions, the word "hi" indicates the reason.
Therefore, it belongs to the Adhvaryu alone, not to the sacrificer.
This is the Karavindīya commentary [on the rule]:
"It pertains to the *prakrama*."

On an altar twice the size [of the standard one] for the Aśvamedha sacrifice, there is a double-step (*dvikariṇī*) in place of the single step (*prakrama*); one should measure out [the altar] using this double-step as the unit of measurement. (The *prakrama* is so called because it is traversed.

One step (*pada*) is fifteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). Two steps are thirty finger-breadths. Three steps are forty-five finger-breadths. Since both two steps and three steps are used in common parlance as a *prakrama*, both are to be understood here.
Alternatively, "prakrama" denotes the act of taking a step; here, "steps" and so forth are understood as the means for measurement.
Therefore, there is no purpose served by mere stepping alone.

However, there is no need for any substance related to that [space]; rather, there is a requirement for something such as a rope measured by the interval between different locations, which is characterized by conjunction and disjunction resulting from the act of stepping. For every person walking casts one foot down after having stepped it out; in this regard, the Person (*puruṣa*) remains equal while moving without modification. He walks in such a way that the interval between the two feet—the one already placed and the one being set down—becomes measured by the length of a single step. Therefore, by means of the stepped foot, two steps [are traversed].

The two-word sequence is "vyāptam" (pervaded); since the word "sthitam" (established) also functions as a cooperative factor with that [first word], there is a pervasion of three words by those two, and thus it becomes a three-word [sequence].

Regarding the sequence, "yāthākāmī" means desire; "yathākāmam" is the non-transgression of that [desire]; its state is "yāthākāmyam"; "yāthākāmyam" itself is "yāthākāmī"—the meaning is "according to one's wish. "Viśaya" means he lies down in various ways; the meaning is that usage is observed in both senses.

Is it not the case that an irregularity in the sequence is also observed, as for instance in the passage: "He strides four Viṣṇu-strides, moving eastward, each subsequent one greater than the preceding"?

This is not a fault, because that statement is intended to enjoin that each subsequent stride be greater; its meaning is that when taking the strides, one should take either two feet or three feet, but one should not mix them. Since the irregularity of the sequence in the phrase "four Viṣṇu-strides" is based on a direct scriptural injunction (*vācanikatva*), there is no grounds for questioning that irregularity of sequence.

Therefore, in the case of a rule concerning a specific *prakrama*, one should employ either of the two *prakramas* consisting of two or three *padas* respectively, and should not mix them; this is the meaning.
Furthermore, as will be stated in the *Padādi-sūtra*, there is indeed an option between the two *prakramas* based on the variation of the *pada*.
(It belongs to the sacrificer).
The two *adhvaryu*s are those who are performing the ritual; the word "hi" indicates the reason. "Ceṣṭāḥ" means those who act, namely, the ritual actions (*karmāṇi*). This is the meaning:

the footprints and so forth are to be taken by the sacrificer because he is the owner; why? Because there is freedom of choice (*yāthākāmī*); that is, either by him [the sacrificer] or by the *adhvaryu*.
The word "vā" (or) has the sense of an option.

Since this Adhvaryu is the performer of the ritual actions (*ceṣṭā*), therefore his footprints and so forth are to be taken, because he is the one who performs the actions. This statement is for the purpose of obtaining [the merit] for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), whereas for the Adhvaryu it serves to set aside the obstructing [claim]; hence there is an option (*vikalpa*).
This is the *Sundararājīyā* commentary, [noting that the rule applies] because the *prakrama* is the subject matter.
Regarding the phrase "of the word-meaning"—that is, of the basis for the application of a word—it means "being the object" (viṣayitva), which is to say, "occurring in many instances.
The meaning is that this "optionality regarding the sequence" (yāthākāmya) mentioned here is stated because the word-meaning is the object [of multiple applications].
Bodhāyana states: "The sequence consists of two words."
"Three steps constitute a *prakrama*," says Kātyāyana;
it is understood that both views are approved by the Teacher [for either the sacrificer or the Adhvaryu].
The effort should be undertaken by means of the foot or the fingers, because of one's ownership [of the body].
He states the reason:
"For this indeed occurs."
It is measured by cowrie shells.
It is known from tradition that the altar for the Nirūḍhapaśubandha sacrifice is the size of a chariot.
"The sacrificial altar for one who has performed the animal sacrifice (Paśubandha) is the size of a chariot," so says the Śruti.

Indeed, its rear side is as long as a chariot axle, extending crosswise; it is oriented toward the east by means of the pole; and its front side is as wide as the yoke and the two side-pieces of the chariot. (ĀpŚS 6.3b)
The word *khalu* is used as an ornament.
In that regard, concerning that matter, those who know the dimensions of a chariot—the chariot-makers—said:
"To the west, it should be the measure of a chariot axle in width; to the east, [it should be] the measure of the crossbar and yoke; to the west, it should be the measure of a chariot axle in width."

The mention of "chariot" is for the purpose of excluding the cart. The *pṛṣṭhyā* line is as long as the pole. Regarding "with a cross-bar": that yoke by which the path is traversed is a "cross-bar yoke" (*vipathayuga*).
The *abyantara* is the interval between the two holes of the yoke;
its measure is the horizontal distance in front [of the axle], or as much as the external hole. ĀpŚus 6.3c.
To whatever extent there are two apertures on the outside of the yoke, to that same extent the crossbeam of the altar (vedi) extends horizontally in front.
This is the Karavindīyā commentary:
(the crossbeam is equal in measure to the chariot, with apertures on the outside).
The *rathamātrī*—meaning "measuring the size of a chariot"—is the altar for one who has performed the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), according to the Śruti.
He demonstrates what is stated in the Śruti by means of the statement of an authoritative teacher (*abhiyukta*).
The word *khalu* serves as a rhetorical ornament (*vākyālaṃkāra*) for the sentence.
Regarding this, the experts say: [the chariot] is as long as a chariot-axle (rathākṣa) in measure; it is behind [the axle], extending crosswise, and equal in length to the pole (īṣā), facing forward.
That by which the path is traversed is "vipatha," meaning a traveling chariot (cāraṇaratha). The yoke of such a vehicle is a "vipathayuga."

The transverse [measurement] at the front is equal to that; or else, it is as much as the external openings require—that is, the transverse measurement at the front is such that when taken, the two external openings are formed.
This is the Sundararājīya commentary.

"The outer holes [should be] the size of a chariot," so say the teachers: the crosswise beam at the back is the size of a chariot axle; the front beam is the size of a chariot pole; and the crosswise beam at the front is the size of a "vipathayuga" (a yoke from which the path has departed).
That yoke from which the path has departed is a *vipathayuga*.
The yoke is eighty-six finger-breadths long, including the external holes;
or rather, the distance between the two external holes is eighty finger-breadths.
(Kapardibhāṣya)
This has been stated in a single line: "With a fifteenfold [cord], using a half-eye and a half-yoke, one should mark out the hips and shoulders. (ĀpŚS 6.4)

Regarding the phrase "that same cord": is it the cord used for the Soma sacrifice that is taken, or rather the first [cord] used for the Soma sacrifice? This is because of the observation of the term "by the fifteen-fold" (*pañcadaśika*); for that characteristic applies there [in the case of the first], and not elsewhere.

Having divided the pole (*īṣā*) into thirty-six parts and taking one part as the step (*prakrama*), one should measure the width [of the altar] by stretching it out with the fifteen-fold [cord] as in the Soma sacrifice, and mark the two hips (*śroṇī*) with the half-axle (*ardhākṣa*).
Some say one should mark the distance between the two [shoulders] with the half-yoke (*ardhayuga*).
Others, however, take the first single cord.

If it were taken as belonging to the Soma sacrifice, the assumption of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) would follow; if it is asked how this can be so with "the fifteenfold [cord]," it is because by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), that which is fifteenfold within the thirty-sixfold [cord] is also indeed less than six parts.
Therefore, it is not possible to indicate "less than six parts" by means of the phrase "with the fifteenfold."
Therefore, there is no assumption of an unseen entity (*adṛṣṭa*).
But is there not figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) elsewhere as well? That indeed exists, but it is worldly; moreover, because of its commonality, that very same rope is what is common.
Therefore, that alone should be grasped.

The same should be applied in the subsequent cases as well. Having marked the center of the axle-hole (ardhākṣa) and the center of the yoke (ardhayuga), and having drawn a line six parts inward from there, the two hips (śroṇī) are at the center of the axle-hole, while the two shoulders (aṃsa) are at the center of the yoke.
Karavindīya Commentary:
(One should measure it out with a single cord.
This method of measurement has been explained by means of the "single-cord" measurement.

The term "single cord" (*ekarajju*) includes cords made of two, three, five, or more pegs; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of assuming that the prescriptions for the subsequent [cords] serve no visible purpose. This has been explained in the section on the *saumikī* [altar].
Likewise, by the phrase "with the fifteenfold [cord]," the cord marked with a specific measurement reduced by one-sixth is intended;
and that serves merely to demonstrate the absence of coloring (*nirañjana*).

"Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of [the action] having an invisible purpose (adṛṣṭārtha)," as stated in that very [text]. Since the measuring with multiple cords was mentioned there, and since there is no contradiction here either, it is certainly accepted here as well.
Having made a step (prakrama) equal to one-thirty-sixth of the length of the pole (īṣā), one should measure out [the altar] by that very [measure].
This is the commentary of Sundararāja.
"One should dwell with a single cord" (tadekarajjvā viharet).
By the passage beginning with "having combined eighteen [parts] out of thirty-six," the measurement for that single cord is stated.
One-thirty-sixth part of the pole (īṣā)—that is, five finger-breadths (aṅgula) and seven and a half sesame seeds (tila)—is to be understood as the measure of a step (prakrama).
Alternatively, by the term "single cord" (ekarajju), what is intended is the measurement of the full length.
In this view, the expression "by the fifteenth part" refers metaphorically to exactly two-thirds less one-sixth;
thus it is said, "In that [case], it became fifteen paces."

In the same way, in the subsequent cases as well, when the view is that the external space between the openings [is the measurement], the removal of the shoulder-piece is by half of that. Regarding this, they also cite the *Kapardibhāṣya*: "ĀpŚus 6.5a."
The word *atha* (then) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
Thus they cite as examples the chariot-makers' measurements for a chariot:

"The pole is one hundred and eighty-eight [units] across; the axle is four hundred; the yoke is eighty-six; such is the chariot called 'the traveler'. This is the measurement of the chariot. (ĀpŚus 6.5b)
Thus they cite and declare the measurement of the chariot from all sides;
and since it is established by implication, the finger-breadth (*aṅguli*) is understood.
The measurement of the chariot pole is one hundred and eighty-eight finger-breadths.
The word *tiryak* has the sense of "filling.
The measure of the axle is one hundred and four;
the measure of the yoke is eighty-six.
A chariot possessing such characteristics is a *cāraṇa*; it is called *cāraṇa* because one moves by means of it (*carati anena*). Alternatively, *cāraṇa* is simply *caraṇa*.
The inclusion of the term *cāraṇa* is for the purpose of excluding chariots used for play and other such purposes.

Alternatively, one should supply the word *yasya* in place of the word *asya* and apply it [to the verse]; or else, by means of a transposition of syllables. Or [the measurement may be]: four *aratnis* to the west, six to the east, and three in front. That which was described with a single cord using fifteen [units] should be drawn out by two [units] and one and a half [units] to mark the hips and shoulders. (ĀpŚS 6.6)
Or it should be measured with *aratnis*; this is the remainder [of the sense].
With four [aratnis] is the crosswise-measuring cord (*tiryaṅbhānī*) at the back; with six is the *pṛṣṭhyā* cord facing eastward.
The cross-spans are three [parts] in front;
this has already been explained by the "single cord" method and so forth—this is understood.

It is known from the *Paitṛkī* altar that it should be four-cornered and measured by the height of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). This has been described by the "single cord" method using exactly fifteen parts; having laid out half of that, one should then mark off the two hips and the two shoulders. (ĀpŚus 6.7)
Regarding the Vedic tradition concerning the altar for the ancestors (*paitṛkī vedī*): it should be measured so that its corners (*sraktayaḥ*) are positioned according to the directions.
"With a single cord" has already been explained.
This is the Karavindīya commentary.
Since the comprehension of the meaning of the Vedas depends upon many other branches of knowledge,
he cites a verse concerning the measurement of a chariot as stated by Gārgya, Agastya, and others in the science of carpentry— (and furthermore, this is the authoritative measure):
*athāpy u pramāṇam* (And yet, there is also this authoritative measure).

Furthermore, the two words *atha* and *api* are used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*). The sages cite [the following]: "one hundred and eighty-eight" (*aṣṭāśītiśatam*), "four hundred" (*catuḥśatam*), and "eighty-six" (*ṣaḍaśīti*). Having presented the manifold nature of the chariot through various classifications such as the *āyodhana*, *puṣpa*, *jaitra*, and *cāraṇa*, they stated "one hundred and eighty-eight," and so forth. The meaning of this is as follows: among these many types, that chariot whose pole (*īṣā*) measures one hundred and eighty-eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), whose axle (*akṣa*) measures one hundred and four, and whose yoke (*yuga*) measures eighty-six, is called a *cāraṇa* chariot.

Thus the sages describe the dimensions of the chariot. Now, while it has been stated that the axle is the transverse side, it is not known which of the two poles is the longitudinal and which is the transverse. It is said in reply: by the very rule that the axle is transverse, it is understood through implication that of the two poles, whichever is longer is the longitudinal (prācī) and whichever is shorter is the transverse (tiraśvī); thus they believe that the pole (īṣā) is the longitudinal side.
In the case of the alternative involving the openings and the intermediate spaces, the crosswise side is sixteen finger-breadths shorter at the front;
or (it may be measured) with cubits at the front.
(One should determine that by means of a single cord.)
This too has been explained;
here, the characteristic [measurement] is two aratnis less than a ratni.
One should carry it out with the length of the sacrificer.

"This is the altar of the ancestors"—that is, the great ancestral altar for the Mahāpitṛyajña. Although [the measurement] is already established by the general rule (*codaka*), it is stated again specifically for the sacrificer alone so that the same applies to its width as well.

(The length: The corners extend toward each direction; the intermediate directions [are formed by] the great cardinal and intermediate points, according to the scriptural observation that "all [directions] are indeed intermediate. Here is the practical application: leaving a small space for circulation in front of the *Anvāhāryapacana* fire, one should construct a square measuring one *yajamāna* (the height of the sacrificer) and two cubits in front of it. Then, having laid out the lines using the "fifteenth part" and so forth so that the corners fall at the midpoints of the cords, one proceeds with half of that [square], and then with half of that *yajamāna*-measure.

One should remove [the cord] from the hips and shoulders; this refers to the reduction or increase mentioned [in the rule]. On the Great Altar (mahāvedi), having drawn [the cord] by means of the *pada* alone, one should fix a peg at a distance of half the measure of the sacrificer; thus the altar is oriented toward the south-east.
The commentary of Sundararāja: (Now they also cite the measurement of a chariot:
the fingers are to be counted.
It will be stated that [the height] of a man with his arms raised is one two-hundredth part of a finger-breadth (*aṅguli*);
[namely], "A man is five *aratnis* long, and twenty-four finger-breadths make one *aratni*."
And that [unit] they call thirty-four *tilas*.
As stated by Bodhāyana:

"The measure of a finger (*aṅguli*) consists of fourteen *aṇus*; another [measure] consists of thirty-four broad, closely joined *tilas*. Because it is the subject at hand, "four hundred" (*caturadhikaṃ śatam*) refers to four hundred *yugas*, which is called a *vipathayuga*.

However, those learned in the science of carpentry (*takṣaśāstra*) maintain that a *yuga* is one hundred finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), whereas the venerable teachers (*ācāryapādīyāḥ*) hold it to be ninety-six finger-breadths.
As they have said: "A bow (*dhanus*) is four cubits (*hasta*), and a *dhanus* is a staff (*daṇḍa*), a *dhanvantara*, and a *yuga*."
Thus it is said: "A cubit consists of twenty-four finger-breadths," and also:
"Or [the front part] by aratnis."
Some say it is the altar for the animal sacrifice; one should carry it out with one [verse],
and the two hips with two [verses].
The shoulders are one and a half [aratnis] each;
it is known to be the measure of the sacrificer,
being five aratnis long.
"One should remove that single [line]";
here, *tataḥ* is the suffix *tasil* derived from a word in the genitive case;
the *pṛṣṭhyā* line runs toward the south-east.
The hips and shoulders are at the cardinal directions.
Regarding this, Kātyāyana states the concise method: "Having made a square measuring two persons on the father’s [line], stakes are placed at the centers of the sides; this is the solution."

Regarding the method there: having made a square with sides of one hundred and seventy fingers using a measuring cord (*karani*) of ten *tilas* less than two *puruṣas*, one should drive stakes into the centers of the measuring cords, fasten loops of two ropes of ten *aratnis* each to the eastern and western [stakes], fix them between those two on the south and north, and cut away any excess protruding outside.
Some also desire this to be four *aratnis* [in length];
in that case, it is not possible to set out the clarified butter and the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*).

The sacrificial ground for the *kapardibhāśaṣya* sacrifice is ten paces wide, as is known from the *Soma* ritual. This has been described using a single cord: one should measure out the two hips and the two shoulders by means of the fifteen-fold [cord] itself, after having laid it out across half [the space]. (ĀpŚus 6.8)
The mention of "padas" (steps) is for the purpose of illustration.
On the Mahāvedi that has been measured out, the Uttaravedi is ten padas on all sides; this is because of the statement, "By measurement, measurement is prescribed.
Or, it may be ten padas in terms of area.
Then, having made a long rectangle with a width of one *pada* and a length of three *padas*, one should take the diagonal cord of that [rectangle] and make a square.
In the case of a *prakrama* as well, having laid out a square with a width of one *prakrama* and a length of three *prakramas*, one should take the diagonal cord of that and make a square.
That which was stated regarding the single cord—"half of that"—means "of that" (*tasya*), where the suffix *tasil* is used in the sense of the genitive case.
Having measured that [space] for the sacrificer either by a yoke or by paces, he measures it around with a *śamyā*. ĀpŚus_6.9 ||
By means of the measurement stated by the Yaugas, or by the steps of the sacrificer;
because of the mention of the "sacrificer," it is not obtained for the Adhvaryu.
Some maintain that the mention of the sacrificer is for the purpose of illustration.
From that very statement, it is understood that the *uttaravedi* is to be four cubits (*yugamātrī*).

On the great altar (*mahāvedi*) of the *some* sacrifice, having measured out the *uttaravedi* by means of a yoke or by foot-steps according to the measurement of the cord (*śaulba*), the subsequent measurement with the *śamyā* staff must be performed for the sake of an unseen spiritual purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
It is thus stated that the injunction "he should measure with the *śamyā*" is for an unseen purpose and is not a rule regarding the actual dimensions.
Karavindīyā Vyākhyā: (It is understood from the *Daśapada*:

"Beyond the first peg struck on the Mahāvedi, having struck a peg at twenty-five [steps] to the east, and having struck a peg at ten [steps] further east of that, one should measure out [the area] by means of the fifteen-step [cord]," and so forth. One should perform the measurement according to this procedure.
"One should remove that by one [part]," meaning by half of five parts.

It is heard in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*: "On all sides it is ten parts. Since it is stated that "measure is prescribed by measure" and "it is a square," in the absence of a specific definition, it is ten parts on three sides.
Thus says Kātyāyana.
According to this view, having laid out a long square with a width of one pada and a length of three padas, the Uttaravedi is measured by the diagonal cord (akṣṇayārajju) of that [square].
In this view as well, the laying out of the hips and shoulders is performed using half of this [long square] as the side-measure (karaṇī).
(He measures it with a yoke):
he measures that northern altar (*uttaravedi*) by the measure of a yoke.
Regarding this, it has been said: "A yoke is eighty-six [finger-breadths]."
Having measured [the space] by the footprints of either that [animal] or the sacrificer, he measures all around with a wooden yoke-pin (*śamyā*) for an invisible purpose.

The measurement of the *śamyā* is stated in another Sūtra as "thirty-six [finger-breadths] is the *śamyā*. Since there is no other [means of measurement] available in the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), the prescription of the *śamyā* is solely for the purpose of measurement; this is also indicated by the grammatical mark (*liṅga*) in the phrase "this is its measure" (*mātraivāsyai seti*).
From this very statement, it follows that the *uttaravedi* of the Soma sacrifice may also be four cubits (*yugamātra*) in size.
Sundararājīyā commentary:
(One should remove ten squares.
"Ten squares" means on all sides.
In terms of the field, it consists of one hundred paces;
(one measures that with a *yuga*).
A *yuga* is likewise a means of measurement consisting of ten paces, just like a bamboo pole.
Some say that his [the sacrificer's] own manual (tantra) is the authority; this need not be examined by the learned.
The mention of the "sacrificer" is for the purpose of excluding the *adhvaryu*.
The measurement with a yoke-pin (*śamyā*) is for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

The measurement may be by cowrie-shells, kṣāṣyas, pada, yuga, aratni, or śamyā; in matters of measurement, one may act according to one's desire, because the meaning of the word is subject to such variation. (ĀpŚS 6.10)
Regarding words such as *pada* when they signify measurement, one may take [the meaning] according to one's desire—that is, one should accept it according to one's wish.
What is this saying?
Fourteen *aṇu*s make one *tila*;
thirty-four *tilas* make one *aṅgula* (another [definition] states they are joined side-by-side); twelve *aṅgulas* make one *prādeśa*.
A span (vitasti) is thirteen finger-breadths;
a foot (pada) is fifteen finger-breadths;
and a cubit (aratni) consists of twenty-four finger-breadths.
The knee is thirty-two finger-breadths;
the *śamyā* is thirty-six finger-breadths;
the yoke is eighty-six finger-breadths.
The measurements for the parts of the proportions— such as "four hundred akṣas" or "one hundred and twenty akṣas for a person," and so forth— as described in other Śulba-sūtras, should be taken here.
Having measured by means of a group of characteristics, one may proceed there according to one's desire, because the word and its meaning are subject to such application;
thus, the *pada* may also be fifteen finger-breadths,
and it is also the *pada* of the sacrificer.
In that context, "one or the other should be accepted" refers to the act of establishing [the measure].
"This much, namely twelve strides" means that one should adopt either one's own experience, the experience of others, worldly consensus, or the consensus of the treatises.
In the *vimita* [shed], one should bring together the side-measures at the front, according to the force of the scriptural injunction. (ĀpŚS 6.11)

When the square has been thus produced, one should contract the side-measures from the front, on account of the force of the scriptural statement: "The young maiden with four tufts. The force [of the argument] consists in the reference to her similarity to a young maiden.
Thus ends the sixth section. Karavindīya Commentary:
[The phrase] "because it is contained within the pair of footprints" [is used].
In the *Hiraṇyakeśi-Śulba* and the *Baudhāyana-Śulba*, it is stated: "In a *pada*, a *yuga*, an *aratni*, an *avi*, a *prādeśa*, a *prakrama*, and a *śamyā*.
Furthermore, regarding the measurement of a finger (*aṅguli*), another [tradition] says: "Fourteen *aṇus*, thirty-four *tilas* closely joined together.
Ten *aṅgulas* constitute a small *pada*.
The [chariot] is twelve spans long;
in the subsequent wider yoke, it is thirteen [spans], and in the stride, fifteen.
The pole is one hundred and eighty-eight [finger-breadths].
Eighty-six [finger-breadths] constitute a *yuga*;
thirty-two are a *jānu* (knee), and thirty-six are a *śamyā*. Two feet make a *bāhu* (forearm), which is at will; two *prādeśas* make an *aratni* (elbow).
Likewise, five *aratnis* make a *puruṣa*, or four *aratnis* make a *yāma*.

In that very context, the Teacher has already explained during the occasion of the Brāhmaṇa commentary—using measurements such as "knee-deep" and so forth—that one offers [the oblation] at this much distance, carries it at this much distance, takes up this much, performs this much, and it becomes this much, and so on.
In that regard, since the means (such as the footstep) have been specified by mental intention, the meaning is that one may act according to one's desire; that is, one should do as one wishes.
This is because the meaning of the word is subject to the scope of the speaker's intention; thus the point is established.

The meaning is this: one should take the *pada* and other units as they are conceived by a finger belonging to either the sacrificer or the *adhvaryu* priest—whether that finger be conceived as consisting of atoms (*aṇu*) or of sesame seeds (*tila*).
This is because the referent of the word *pada* and so forth is employed in both cases.
*Aṇavaḥ* (atoms) are a specific kind of grain.

Since the Teacher himself, in the context of the *nirūḍhapaśu* sacrifice, cited "one hundred and eighty-eight" as an example from the *Takṣa-śāstra* for the purpose of knowing the dimensions of the chariot, and since he used the word "measurement" (*klpti*) to refer to the conventions of those who know the rules—such as "the hawk [altar] is five cubits, the man is one [cubit]" and so forth—there is no obligation to adopt the term "finger-breadth" (*aṅguli*) and other measures accepted in other treatises.

Furthermore, regarding the discussion on the commencement [of the altar], because of the statement "two-footed or three-footed," referring either to the sacrificer or the Adhvaryu priest, the term "foot" (*pada*) and so on is not to be understood merely as a measure delimited by fingers measured according to specific body parts.
Having concluded the incidental discussion, he states the remainder of the topic at hand:
"It is measured by its capacity"—
this has already been explained in the *Dārṣikī*.

In this case, however, because of the force of the Vedic revelation—"O four-crested one, young maiden"—and because of the concluding statement, "Some say she is not inferior in front," an option regarding the instruction for the ritual action has been stated.
Sixth Section.
The Commentary by Sundararāja.
(Because it is the object of focus for the pair of feet.)
The fourfold division of the *pada* has been stated;
the twofold division of the *yuga* consists of eighty-six and ninety-six hundred *aṅgulas*.
The *aratni* is of two kinds: the twenty-four *aṅgula* and the *hasta*.
"By this much" is intended to mean a *prādeśa*.
That is of two kinds: twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) when the thumb and forefinger are extended;
and a *śamyā* is of three kinds—"A *śamyā* consists of four, eight, or thirty-two finger-breadths," says Kātyāyana.
"Thirty-six *śamyā*s," so says Baudhāyana; [in this case] the third [unit] is a common worldly measure.
Among these measurements, one may proceed according to preference, because the meaning of the word applies to more than one [measure].
(*This is because there is no capacity [to perform the rite] once the shed has been measured.*)
That "it is shorter in front" has already been stated previously to be optional.
The sixth section:
The commentary of Kapardin states that it is known from the Sadas [hall] that it is nine aratnis wide and twenty-seven [aratnis] long, extending toward the north. (ĀpŚus 7.1)
According to some, there are eighteen. (ĀpŚus 7.2)
Having stated that it is one rajju, one should determine the hips and shoulders by means of fifteen [units] and four and a half [units] respectively. ĀpŚus 7.3.

The Śruti concerning the *sadas* states that it should be understood as follows: nine *aratnis* long from east to west for the transverse measurement, and twenty-seven [cubits] northward for the side measurement.
It should be measured either by a *pada* or by a *prakrama*.
The method of measurement has been stated.

Having driven a peg (śaṅku) one *prakrama* to the south of the first peg that was driven, and having fastened a cord to it, one drives a peg to the south on the *pṛṣṭhyā* line at a distance of seven and a half [steps] to its east;
that is the central location for the Audumbarī post in the Sadas.

Having driven a peg (śaṅku) at a distance of seven and a half [units] to the east along the spine-line (pṛṣṭhyā) from the first peg, one should fasten a cord to it and, moving the pegs upward and upward toward the north, drive a peg at the fourteenth and a half or at the ninth [unit].

Having fastened the cord to that peg which is on the spine-line, one should move the cord for the site of the Audumbarī post upward and upward toward the south and drive a peg at the fifteenth and a half or at the tenth [unit];
this is the length of the Sadas.
Having practiced half of that measurement along the length (āyāma), one should mark it according to the sūtra.

Having practiced the twenty-seventh [measurement] as fourteen and a half, from the right shoulder, at eleven steps there is a marking-point (nirajjana); at the hip (śroṇyaṃsa) there is a characteristic mark (lakṣaṇa) of four and a half [units], or having added nine [units] to eighteen and a half, at eight and a half there is a marking-point; the hip-shoulder mark is at four and a half [units]. Having fixed the two ends of the length (āyāma) at the marking-point of four and a half, one moves back by that same amount and fixes a peg (śaṅku) at four and a half.
Having moved five and a half [steps] forward, a peg is driven in; these two are the hips. Having reversed the orientation of the *sadas*, the two shoulders are marked.

The measurement of the *prāgvaṃśa* hall and the *āgnīdhra* shed has not been stated by this teacher; therefore, that which is stated in another *Śulba-sūtra* should be adopted, as it constitutes a modification (*vaikṛta*).
One should measure out the *havirdhāna* shed three *prakramas* in front of the *sadas*, with a width of ten *prakramas* and a length of twelve *prakramas*.
Having fastened a loop to the middle southern peg of the Havirdhāna shed using a cord of one length with five pegs or three pegs, and having drawn it northward, a peg is fixed at twelve steps;
that is the location of the Āgnīdhra fire-shed. Having drawn that same cord southward, the Mārjālīya shed is established at twelve [steps].

On the *pṛṣṭhya* line, having fastened the loop to the eastern peg of the *sadas* and moved it northward, one should drive a peg at nine minus a quarter [spaces]; from that, one should drive another peg six [spaces] to the north.
From those two, one should drive a peg six *prakramas* to the east.
In this manner, one should measure out a regular square using five pegs.
One should measure out the *prāgvaṃśa* (front hall) with a width of eight *prakrama*s and a length of twelve;
others say it should have a width of twelve and a length of sixteen. This is the explanation according to the *Karaṇindīyā*.
(Navāra ekeṣām):
According to some, it is nine cubits wide in the east and twenty-seven cubits long in the north;
according to other teachers, it is eighteen cubits long.

(One should determine that alone): it has been stated that on a sacrificial altar (*vedi*) measured by *pada*s, the measurement of both the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* is also by means of the *pada* alone; however, when measuring by *prakrama*s, the measurement is indeed by *aratni*s. Regarding the *havirdhāna*, an instruction for the ritual is given as being "unmeasured" (*aparimita*). The measurement of the *sadas* beyond twenty-seven [steps] is called "unmeasured. Starting from ten *pada*s to the south of the transverse line (*tiraścī*) behind the great altar (*mahāvedi*), one should draw a line or lay down a cord as far as the transverse line in front; thus [is the measurement] along the *pṛṣṭhyā* line.

To the north as well, starting from the western end across eight steps, one should draw two lines between those same [two] points, extending from south to north; that becomes the *pṛṣṭhyā* of the assembly hall (*sadas*).

On the eighteen-finger [space], having made a mark at the ninth finger and at the four-and-a-half and seven-and-a-half fingers, and having spread it out according to the rule beginning with "at the ends of the *pṛṣṭhyā*," one should drive stakes into the four-and-a-half fingers; that becomes the *sadas*.
Although the dimensions of the *havirdhāna*, the *āgnīdhra*, and the *prāgvaṃśa* have not been taught here by the Teacher, they are to be accepted as taught in other *Śulbas*.
The *havirdhāna* is ten [units] in length and ten in width; the *āgnīdhra* is six in length and six in width; half of it is within the *antarvedi* and half is outside the *vedī*;
the *prāgvaṃśa* is sixteen in length and twelve in width.
It should be twelve *ayāmas* long and nine wide.

From the first driven stake, fifteen *śaṅkus* ahead, one should construct the *havirdhāna* shed—nine *ayāmas* long and wide, or ten *padas*—using any one of the stakes starting from that second stake.
The commentary of Sundahabhājīya [states]:
"In some cases,
it is simply 'oriented toward the north' (*udagāyatam*)."
The eastern [side] is exactly nine *aratnis*.
Therein, by a step (*prakrama*) of twenty or twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), it is eight *aratnis* on each side;
in the subsequent sacrifices (*kratu*), it is twenty-seven *aratnis*.
The location, however, has already been stated in the ritual procedure (*prayogakalpa*) itself, beginning with the words, "from the second joint," and so forth. (One should remove that one [brick]);
this refers to the northern *pṛṣṭhyā*.

It is known from the sacred tradition regarding the *uparavas* that they have openings of one span (*prādeśa*) and intervals of one span. Having marked out a square measuring one cubit (*aratni*), and having driven stakes into its corners, one should trace each [square] with an interval of half a span, according to the force of the scriptural injunction. (ĀpŚS 7.4)
The term *uparavamānam* is explained by its verbal root (*nigadavyākhyāta*).
The word *aratnī* has already been explained.
This is the Karavindīya commentary.

(The location is understood): at the time of pressing, because they are "possessing stones" (*rayavanta*) above them with the pressing-stones (*grāvan*), they are called *uparavas*. Alternatively, *uparas* are specific types of pressing-stones; thus, those [holes] possessing them are the *uparavas*, which are specific types of pits.

(At the distance of an *aratni* from the [northern] limit): having marked out a square measuring one *aratni* on the southern hip of the southern *havirdhāna* cart using any one of the [measuring tools] beginning with the two-pronged [gauge], and having driven stakes at the corners, one should draw lines around those stakes using either a wooden brace (*karkaṭa*) or a cord, with a span of half a *prādeśa*.
In this way, they become one *prādeśa* wide at the openings and separated by an interval of one *prādeśa* from one another.
In this way, this scriptural statement becomes meaningful:
"The altar is measured by the measure of a foot."

Now, the dimensions of the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) and the pavilion (*vimāna*) are described: having prepared a plot of land measuring fifty *pada*s eastward and thirty *pada*s north-south as suitable for the sacrifice, one should prepare a portion of that land in the middle, equal in length to that [plot], as suitable for the sacrificial ground. Having drawn an eastward line through the middle of that [portion] and stretched a cord along it, one should drive stakes at its two ends. Then, at the time of the ritual, one should construct the *prāgvaṃśa* hall and other structures accordingly; at the western end, the *prāgvaṃśa* shall be sixteen *pada*s in length.

Having constructed [the altar] twelve units in width and twelve units in length, or nine units in width, one should place three *lālāṭika* pegs to the east and so forth; starting from that very *śaṅku*, there is an outer *vedi* of three *padas*, at the end of which is a *śaṅku*. Then, extending from there toward the east, is the great *vedi* (*mahāvedi*), thirty-six *padas* long, thirty *padas* wide to the west, and twenty-four *padas* wide to the east. Having thus measured out the *mahāvedi*, there is a space of three *padas* for movement at its western end; to the east of that, measuring nine *padas* eastward and eighteen *padas* northward.

The *sadas* is eighteen steps in length from south to north; in its center, one step’s distance to the south of the *pṛṣṭhyā* cord is the location of the *audumbarī* pillar. In the eastern half of the *sadas*, leaving a space of half a step for a passage in front, the *hotrīya* and other *dhiṣṇya* hearths are situated behind that, along the *pṛṣṭhyā*, measuring either one cubit or one span. Between each of these, there is an irregularly arranged passage to the north; in front of the *sadas*, there is a passage three steps wide.

To the east of that is the Havirdhāna shed, nine *aratnis* in length and breadth; it is three *aratnis* wide and nine long, as seen from the rule: "The middle [shed] at the middle roof-beam, while the other two roof-beams are silent.
Bodhāyana states: "The Havirdhāna is ten *aratnis* in length and breadth.
There is a space of one step for passage behind the peg marking the sacrificial post-hole (*yūpāvaṭīya-śaṅku*).
Behind that, at a distance of one *yuga*, is the northern altar (*uttaravedi*). The space between the northern altar and the two *havirdhāna* sheds is the inner altar (*antarvedi*).

To the south of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line is the southern *havirdhāna*, and to the north is the northern *havirdhāna*. On the southern hip of the southern *havirdhāna* are the *uparava* pits. Behind the *havirdhāna* is the *āgnīdhra* shed; at the height of its arms, twelve *parājālīya* steps are measured to the south of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line.

In the same manner, from that very water-mark, twelve [steps] toward the Āgnīdhrīya fire-altar are measured; the sacrificial hearths (*dhiṣṇiya*) are each one *piśīla* in size. From the northern shoulder of the Sadas, pegs are driven at intervals of three-quarters of a *pada*, nine-quarters of a *pada*, and so on. These two [pegs] mark the hips of the Āgnīdhra shed.
Starting from the western end of the Havirdhāna shed, they are placed three *padas* to the east and to the north of the *pṛṣṭhyā* cord.
The two stakes are at eleven and one-quarter cubits and seventeen and three-quarters cubits [from the center]; these are the two shoulders of the Agnīdhra’s altar-pavement.
Behind the twenty-six-cubit cord and at the eastern end of the *pṛṣṭhyā* cord, half is within the altar and half is outside the altar.
"The sacrificial post-hole has a width of three steps and a circumference of three steps," says Bodhāyana.

From the northern shoulder of the altar, at a distance of one step toward the north, the *cātvāla* pit is measured out, equal in size to the *uttaravedi*. The center of the *cātvāla* is level with the edge of the altar.
Twelve steps west of the *cātvāla*, at its outer limit, is the *utkara* heap; between the corner of the altar and the *utkara*, sixteen steps to the north is the *śāmitra* hearth.
These are the measurements in *pada*s.

While proceeding, having passed three steps westward from behind the *sadas* and *havirdhāna*—measured by the span (*aratni*) of the *agni* or the *uttaravedi*—the *havirdhāna* is placed transversely at a distance of nine *aratnis*, and so on, up to the maximum possible width for the *sadas*.
The *dhiṣṇya* hearths are the size of a *piśīla*;

all measurements are made by means of the step (*prakrama*), which is limited to thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). The *uttaravedi*, however, is ten paces or the measure of a yoke (*yugamātra*); or, in its place, the *agni*.
Everything else is performed according to the standard procedure.

With reference to the set of eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*), one measures a cord that is ten *ratha-akṣas* long plus one additional part; then, by means of a twenty-fourth part of that cord, one measures out the altar (*vedi*).
It has been stated that in the case of the eleven-fold set [of posts] aligned toward the east, it serves as the substitute for the *prakrama*.

Regarding the option of eleven [post-holes] in the eastern direction, Baudhāyana says that one should cut off five and a half foot-measures for the shoulders from the front of the altar, including half of the sacrificial post; having cut off the shoulder, one should place it facing eastward in front of that.

Regarding the option of eleven [post-holes] in each of the directions, one should cut off five and a half foot-measures for the two shoulders, divide them into eleven parts, and beginning from the end and the start of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line, one should place one division facing east in the middle.
To the south and north of that, one should place five divisions each facing east.

When the fire-altar increases in size, the great altar-ground (mahāvedī) increases; the sacrificial hall (prāgvaṃśa) and its eastern extension increase as well when there is a multiplicity of intermediate spaces.
Enough with this excessive detail.
According to Sundararāja:
(due to the force of the specific location) the place has indeed already been indicated by the passage beginning with "of the southern *havirdhāna*," and so forth.
In all cases where the measurement is by *prakramas*, nine *aratnis* for the *sadas* are to be left remaining after three *prakramas* from the other edge of the altar site;
and nine *aratnis* for the *havirdhāna* shed are to be left remaining after three *prakramas* behind the *uttaravedi*.

However, when the measurement is by *padas*, since the previously stated dimensions for the *sadas*, *havirdhāna*, and *uttaravedi* would be impossible, a reduction must be made in accordance with the size of the altar site.
The *cātvāla* pit, however, is exactly one *śamyā* in measure everywhere, according to the statement of Bodhāyana: "The *cātvāla* is one *śamyā* in measure.
Regarding this, there are the following verses:
The sacrificial altar (saumikī vedi) is measured by steps (prakrama), each consisting of twenty fingers (aṅgula).
First, in three [sections], there are nine, two, one, one, two, five, and two [steps] respectively. (1)
In the spaces of one, two, two, and one cubits, there are fifteen stakes;
the measuring cord is thirty-six [cubits] long, and its mark is at the thirty-second [unit].
In the vimāna, twelve steps are prescribed between the two cords (pāśas);
the śroṇī is at the fifth minus one, and the sadas is at the fourth immediately following that.
Its corner [is formed] by five, nine, ten, and even eight [asterisms];
in the third [case], the asterisms are separated by two; their revolution occurs according to their respective extent.

When seventeen *śaṅkus* have been reduced by one-quarter in these Rudra-measures, the Āgnīdhra shed is located there; however, the two *dhiṣṇya* hearths are recorded as being at the fifth [mark] out of twelve.
In the sixth [space], there should be the placement of fifty-two in the fifth;
in the seventh, as before, the Āgnīdhra; and in the ninth, the Manu-utkara.
In the eleventh [section], having crossed the two cords of the Havirdhāna shed as before,
the Śāmitra fire-altar occurs in the twelfth [section] among those reduced by half of sixteen.
On the third [mark] from the northern end, however, the Uttaravedi of the Śaṅku should be at the thirteenth and fourteenth; for the two penultimate [marks], it is half a [mark] beyond them.
In the last [measurement], one's own shoulder [shoulder-line] and the *cātvāla* pit emerge from the north;
one should leave five steps in front and behind the *sadodhāna*. 9.
In the southern Havirdhāna shed, one should leave three steps behind;
on both sides, two steps each, increased by two finger-breadths.
The characteristic mark of the *uparava* pits in the center should be one *aratni* in measure;
likewise, the measurement may also be by means of four kinds of *pada* units.
The fifth step combined with the *pada* is desired as the width of the sacrificial fire-places (*dhiṣṇya*).
However, Bodhāyana has clearly stated that the *cātvāla* pit should be the measure of a *śamyā*;
otherwise, there would be a contradiction regarding the fire-altar, and no other measurement is known. 11.
It is made of cowrie shells and is six finger-breadths wide;
it is known from the Gārhapatya altar that it is of the measure of a fathom. (ĀpŚus 7.5)
"Square," say some; "circular," say others. (ĀpŚS 7.6)
The span of the cord is four *ratnis*. That is the measurement for the piling of the *gārhapatya* fire-altar.
According to the opinion of some followers of other recensions (*śākhins*), the *gārhapatya* piling is square.
"The piling of the Gārhapatya fire-altar is circular," so says the Śruti according to some.
One should cause the third width and the seventh length of the sacrificial ground to be measured out as the preparation for the ritual exertion. ĀpŚus 7.7.
The method for constructing a square is now stated:
the side-measure is one-third of the diagonal, and the cross-measure is one-seventh of the diagonal.
In this manner, one should cause the construction to be made.

Since it says "he should cause [it] to be made" (*kārayet*) instead of saying "he should make [it]" (*kuryāt*), it is understood that this is to be done by other skilled craftsmen such as carpenters, and not by the Adhvaryu priest himself. That which is used for making bricks is called a *karaṇa*, and it is made of wood;
there are twenty-one of them. (ĀpŚus 7.8)
By that measurement, twenty-one bricks are made; they are placed in that Gārhapatya altar—this is the remainder [of the sentence].
This is the Karavindīyā commentary. (It is understood from the practice.)
The vyāyāma is four aratnis.
(Regarding the square, for some) for some teachers both [the square and the circle] occur;
(they become the instruments).
That by which bricks are made is the *karaṇa* (instrument); it is made either of wood or of metal.
Its length is thirty-two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), its width is thirteen finger-breadths and twenty-four sesame seeds (*tila*), and its height is one-fifth of the knee.
"Twenty-one" expresses the attainment of the number;
[the term] "having five layers," and so forth, is for the purpose of understanding the number of the aggregate.
The commentary of Sundararāja. Now, regarding the piling of the fire-altar— (the ritual procedure is understood).
The span is four *ratnis*. Regarding that, for some it is four-cornered in length—
(They become the instruments: the third is thirty-two finger-breadths;
the seventh is fourteen finger-breadths less ten sesamum seeds.
There are twenty-one [bricks] in each layer;
in the first layer they are oriented eastward, and in the subsequent one they are oriented northward. (ĀpŚus 7.9)
Extending eastward—meaning extending toward the east—in the first layer; extending northward—meaning extending toward the north—in the second layer.
When it has been laid out in this manner, no division occurs.
By this it is known that in all cases, differentiation (*bheda*) is to be avoided.
This was stated by the Blessed One Bodhāyana himself: "In all cases, differentiation is to be avoided.
They teach that differentiation consists in the arrangement of the ribs in a lower and upper sequence.
This has been stated by this teacher: "One should pile [the altar] in reverse order.
This is the Karavindīya commentary on the first layer, which extends eastward.
While being laid down, they should have their lengths oriented toward the east; on the second [layer] to the west, however,
they should be oriented toward the north in order to avoid any break in continuity.
And it was said by Baudhāyana: "In all cases, one should avoid distinctions.
This is the explanation of the Sundahājīyas.
(The [verses] beginning with *prāgāyā* are the *gāyāmāḥ*.)
The bricks are to be laid down. According to the *Kapardibhāṣya*:
having formed a mound of clay in a circular shape, and having fixed a peg in the center, one should draw a circle with a radius equal to half the *vyāyāma*. ĀpŚus_7.10a ||
If the Gārhapatya altar is to be circular, then— [the word] *ha* being a particle used here in the sense of *atra* (in this case)—
having performed the excavation and having smoothed the surface of the clay body, one should drive a peg into its center and trace a circle with a radius equal to half the *vyāyāma*.
That circle becomes exactly one *vyāyāma* in measure.
Some here, hearing the word "together" (*saha*), describe it as being with the second [line].
However, this is not what the Teacher intended for the sake of equalizing the field; for he says, "by half the effort.
Had it been his intention, he would have simply said, "having made a mound of clay, one should make the mandala."
But it has been stated that [the measurement] is other than the instruction, and he will say "to that extent of ground.
How, then, is it said to be "together"? One who wishes to construct a mandala, having performed this, should mark out the circumference with half the length of a vyāyāma.
The particle *ha* is an expletive;
it should be applied by supplying [the word] "thus" (*evam*).
Alternatively, this very scripture is of such a nature.
One should fix a square upon that as far as it may extend; having divided it into nine parts, one should further divide each part into three. (ĀpŚS 7.10b)
The word "in that" refers to the mandala.
In that mandala, one should draw a square as large as it extends;
having divided its equal circumference into four parts and made marks at the intermediate directions, one should draw the square so that the corners fall exactly upon those marks.

In the four directions, [the lines] are four bow-lengths long. Having divided that square into nine parts, one should have a square construction made according to the measurement of one part. One should divide each of those three parts further into three.
It is called *pradhika* because it is prepared for movement;
and that is the side-bow (*pārśvadhanus*).
It is termed *pradhika* because it is a representation of that [movement].
Having divided each of the *pradhikas* into three parts, one should have the ritual instruments (*karaṇas*) fashioned.
The measurement for the square is eighty-four finger-breadths minus four sesame seeds.
In the center of that circle, one should have one *pradhika* instrument made with its middle part, using twenty-two and thirteen [finger-breadths] respectively.
One should have it planed to a length of thirty finger-breadths.

Just as the shape of a bow is such that there is a depression of one *tila* (sesame seed) and one *aṅgula* between the two ends of the string, so one should fashion three parts: one measuring thirteen *aṅgulas* less by two *tilas*, one measuring exactly one *aratni* (cubit), and one measuring twenty-seven *aṅgulas* less by eight *tilas*.
One should fashion the bricks in this manner, reversing the third part so that the two initial *aṅgulas* are situated in the middle between the two fire-ends.
During the laying, one should ensure that the corners meet at the intermediate points of the square.
At the time of laying the foundation, during the first layer, one should join the corners of the square to the intermediate points and the corner points.
In the square, half-bricks do not lie;
in the square, nine bricks lie.
In the twelve [verses] that are superior, there are twenty-one in both the nine and the twelve; this is in the other arrangement of the middle [section]. ĀpŚus_7.11b.

In the second layer, one should bring the middle bricks of the squares together toward the intermediate directions; one should pile them in an alternating manner for as many layers as one intends to construct. ĀpŚus 7.11c.
As many layers as one wishes to construct, so many should one pile in reverse order:
that which was first becomes third,
and that which was second becomes fourth.
"It is known from the Dhiṣṇya texts that they are merely of the size of a pestle. (ĀpŚus 7.12)
According to some, they are square; according to others, they are circular. (ĀpŚus 7.13)
Some say that the space between the two arms is a *piśīla*; others say that a cubit (*aratni*) measured by a clenched fist is a *piśīla*;
and still others say that a span (*prādeśa*) is a *piśīla*.
According to some, the *dhiṣṇya* hearths are square; according to others, they are circular.
Having fashioned bodies of clay and having divided the *Āgnīdhrīya* hearth into nine parts, one should place a stone in the place of one of them. (ĀpŚS 7.14)
Having drawn the other [lines] in their respective order, one should place them accordingly. (ĀpŚS 7.15)
The phrase "of clay bodies" is an illustration for [the rule] beginning with "in that case, a square," and so forth.

Although it is established that they consist of nine stones (*aśmanavamāḥ*), the specific mention of "in the place of one" is for the purpose of indicating that the material bricks (*dravyeṣṭakā*) are to be placed in the pits (*avaṭa*).
This has been clearly stated by Baudhāyana.
Substances that cause obstruction to the world should be placed in pits.

One should place them according to the requirements; as many hearths (dhiṣṇiya) as are prescribed in the Agnikalpa, having marked out that many [spots] and prepared the implements, one should place them according to the requirements, in whatever manner is appropriate.
Thus ends the seventh section.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Śulba-praśna of the commentary by Kapardisvāmin on the Āpastamba-sūtra.
Karavindīyā Vyākhyā:
Since the construction of the circular Gārhapatya altar is achievable only through great effort, he describes an alternative method for the production of the bricks:
"(One should draw a circle)."

On some clean ground, having fashioned an image out of well-prepared and thoroughly kneaded clay mixed with substances suitable for mixing, one should construct a circular mandala in its center with a square area of one *vyāyāma*. Having fixed a wooden peg (*śaṅku*) in the middle of that, one should draw a circle using a radius equal to half a *vyāyāma* plus an additional third part.

In that [space], one should draw as much of a square as can be made within that mandala. When this is done, there is one equal square in the center of the mandala, and on its sides there are four bow-shaped figures; these are called *pradhayas*.
A *pradhi* is a component part of a chariot wheel.
A *pradhi* is so called because one moves forward (*pradhīyate*) or runs forward (*pradhāvyate*) by means of it;
due to its similarity to that [wheel], the segments of the rim are also called *pradhis*.
One should divide that into nine parts;
one should divide that square into nine parts by drawing lines for three parts each, and having divided it into nine parts, one should divide each *pradhi* into three.
The square consists of nine bricks; there are four primary lines divided into three parts each, making twelve longitudinal lines, resulting in twenty-one bricks.
This is the procedure for constructing a square within a circle:

having established the east and north directions within the circle, one should divide the circumference of the circular line into four equal parts, mark signs at those divisions, and draw lines from sign to sign.
When this is done, a square is formed in the center of the mandala.
Therein, half the diameter—fourteen and a half finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and twenty-two sesame seeds (*tila*)—is the measure for constructing the central square.
Seventy-seven finger-breadths and eight sesame seeds constitute one-third of that [diameter].

One should construct the *karaṇas* consisting of twenty-five finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and twenty-five sesame seeds (*tila*). These are described as follows: one *karaṇa*, measuring twenty-five finger-breadths together with twenty-five sesame seeds, is for the *pradhīs*; there are three such *karaṇas*.
The middle of the *pradhīs* is formed by four [of these].
Its side measures fourteen finger-breadths and seven times seventeen sesame seeds;

its back is twenty-five finger-breadths together with twenty-five sesame seeds; and its face is twenty-nine finger-breadths (or twenty-seven and three-quarter finger-breadths). Having drawn this out using a cord of the measure of half the width or by means of a compass, one should plane it.
The two *pradhīs* (side-boards) and the back of the cloth are likewise [thirty-six finger-breadths].
The face, however, is thirty-six finger-breadths; the right side belongs to the southern [board], and the left side to the northern.
These indeed are the measurements for the four *pradhīs*.
In this way, the mandala-pile has four functions.
(In the laying out on the foundation):

At the time of laying out the mandala, during the first layer, one should join the corners, the ends, and the intermediate directions of the square toward the intermediate points. In the second layer, one should join the centers of the square toward the intermediate points.
In this way, there would be no "division" (*bheda*).

"Division" refers to the uniformity at the edges of the bricks following the pattern of the layout (*prastāra*); it is understood from explanatory statements found here and there that this must be avoided everywhere.
There is also a specific statement: "One should avoid divisions everywhere."
"One should pile [the bricks] in reverse order for as many layers (*prastāra*) as one intends to construct.
The meaning is "having reversed them, having reversed them. The layers (*prastāra*) are specific arrangements of bricks.

Regarding the injunction "one should pile [the fire-altar] in five layers," it is understood from this very restriction that as many [layers] as there may be, one should pile them by alternating [the order]. From this, it is known that the characteristics of the *agni*—such as the measurement of the height of the brick-receptacle and so forth—apply here. Among the layers (*prastāra*), the first, third, and fifth are equal;
the second and fourth are equal. Now, how is it obtained that [the altar] is "exceeded by a third"?

It is said: by the force of the word "together" (*saha*), and because it is prescribed that one-third of the side of the square remains as the radius for constructing the circle, the circle is constructed with one-third of the side together with half the diameter (*viṣkambha*).

Since this very *gārhapatya* altar is intended to have an area equal to that obtained when the square is transformed into a circle, the method for constructing a circle from a square must be followed.
Furthermore, it is observed that this construction of the circle is preceded by the square.
Therefore, that very [text] should be followed.
However, some treat "saha" as a separate word and connect it with "sārdhavyāyāmena"; we do not see any specific purpose for these two words in their hands.
Therefore, it is well said that [he] is together with more than three hundred.
(Regarding the term *piśīla*): *Piśīla* is understood as three feet; some say that a cubit closed into a fist is a *piśīla*;
Bodhāyana says that the space between the two arms is a *piśīla*.
The *dhiṣṇya* fires are so called because of the scriptural observation: "Or rather, the *dhiṣṇyas* are the fires. By that term, their respective altars (*āyatana*) are indicated.
The ground for the altars of the fires is one *piśīla* in measure.
In the absence of a specific exception, there is indeed equality of the site even when there is a difference in shape.
"According to some, it is square"—
this has been explained.
Here, he states a specific rule regarding this sacrifice involving the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicityā*).

(Making clay bodies: Having made clay bodies—that is, having fashioned images which are accumulations related to clay—one should, after marking out the *āgnīdhrīya* fire-pan in nine ways by dividing it three times from east to west and three times from north to south, place one stone upon the single central [cell] with a single [mantra].

Having delineated the other bodies of clay for the Hotrīya and the other hearths according to their respective measures—each according to its own number, whether twelve, sixteen, twenty-one, twenty-four, or otherwise—one should place each brick in its proper location, wherever that particular brick is required, as appropriate.

It is known from the tradition: "One places twelve, sixteen, twenty-one, or twenty-four [bricks] on the *hotrīya* hearth; eleven on the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsīya*; six on the *mārjālīya*; and eight each on the other *dhiṣṇiya* hearths.
The other *dhiṣṇyas* are those of the *praśāstṛ*, *potr̥*, *neṣṭṛ*, *acchāvāka*, the *cātvāla*, the *śāmitra*, and the *avabhṛtha*.
Alternatively, one may fashion the bricks after having performed the ritual formulas (*karaṇas*).

In the case of a square, the *hotrīya* hearth measures one *prādeśa* on all sides. In the case of a twelve-part [hearth], there are two *prādeśas* and two [sides] of nine finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). In the case of a sixteen-part [hearth], there are nine [finger-breadths] on all sides. In the case of a twenty-one-part [hearth], there are two [sides] of nine [finger-breadths] and two [sides] of seven finger-breadths plus seventy *tilas*. One of these [sides] has seven *tilas* and seven finger-breadths on all sides; here, having divided one side of the square fivefold, one should divide four parts by the first [method] into four, and one part by the second into five.
In the case of a twenty-four-part [hearth], these same [proportions serve as] the construction-measures.
There, having divided [the area] into five parts as before, one should divide four parts into five using a measure of seven *aṅgulas* and seventy *la*s;
the other [part] into four.

For the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin’s [shed], there are eight [measures] for the Hotṛ’s [shed], twelve for each of the others; three for the Āgnīdhrīya; and for the Mārjālīya, there are one *prādeśa* on one side and six and a half on the other.
For the others—the *potrīya* and so forth—there are six *āgnīdhrīya* bricks; on the *mārjālīya*, there are two.
In the case of the circular altar (*maṇḍala*), because it would entail a multiplicity of instruments, only the scraping is prescribed.
For the *āgnīdhrīya*, there is a threefold division toward the east and the north.
In the twelve-part division of the *hotṛ* share, there is a threefold division on one side and a fourfold division on the other.
In the sixteen-part division, it is fourfold on all sides.

However, in the twenty-one-part division, one should first divide it fivefold on one side, then divide four of those parts into four, then divide another four parts into five, and finally divide the remaining part into four.
In the case of eleven parts, one should divide one part into four, divide three [of those] into three, and divide the other [one] into two.
In the case of six parts, one should divide one part into three and divide the other [part] into two.
And in the case of eight parts, one should divide one part into three, divide two portions into three, and divide the other [portion] into two.
The Teacher considers this very method to be preferable because the *dhiṣṇya* hearths consist of a single layer (*ekacitīka*) and are thus easy to construct.
Regarding this, there is a verse:

In the case of a fire-altar built to the measure of a *vyāyāma*, the sacrificial implement should be made of wood; or, in the case of a melted (*laiha*) altar, it should be made of four wooden planks, as that is prescribed.
The fingers shall be thirty-two aṅgulas in length, thirteen in number,
and the width of the hand in the *karaṇa* position shall be twenty-four *tilas*.
Within that mandala-self, there should be a fourfold instrument:
one in the center and three in the periphery; these are described in their proper order.
The fingers consist of twenty-five [parts] each, including twenty-five sesame seeds;
however, there is one single construction on all sides, while in the middle, by means of this, is the shape of the brick.
There should be three [wooden pegs] on the rim-wheels; the rim-wheel is fastened by means of three [pieces].
The central part of the rim-wheel should be fastened by means of four planks.
The back is twenty-five finger-breadths, with five sesame seeds;
each side is fourteen finger-breadths, provided with seventeen sesame seeds.
The mouth of the instrument should be thirty-two and a half finger-breadths at its widest point in the middle, and likewise at both ends.
Regarding the back and the sides, the face there measures thirty-six finger-breadths; whichever side belongs to a particular [section], that [measurement] applies to it and not to the other.
Having drawn the openings of the instruments here according to the measurement of half the width,
one should plane them using a cord, or otherwise draw them with a compass.
The hearths (dhiṣṇiyas) are thirty-six finger-breadths in length and equal on all sides;
now, the instruments (karaṇas) for each of these are described according to their respective numbers.
Since it is one span on one side and eighteen finger-breadths on the other,
six bricks are placed by means of the Mārjālīya for the Dhiṣṇiya hearths.
Since it is a span (prādeśa) on all sides, those [measures] are made at the Āgnīdhrīya;
that which has twelve finger-breadths (aṅgula) in one place has nine finger-breadths in the other.
In the Hotrīya fire-altar, there are twelve additional bricks; those made by him are the twelve bricks.
The Hotrīya fire-altar should be nine finger-breadths on all sides; by that measure, it becomes sixteen [finger-breadths] in total.
Combined with five sesame seeds, there are seven finger-breadths on one side;
on the other side, it should be nine finger-breadths; such is the instrument for twenty-one [recitations].
The fingers on all sides are joined with seven [or five] *tilakas*;
this occurs here in the twenty-first [finger], and both of these also in the twenty-fourth.
In the first [section] there would be twenty-one; by the other [method], sixteen and five.
In the twenty-fourth [section] there are twenty by the second [method], while the rest are from the other.
Those [fingers] which are eight *prādeśas* and three finger-breadths (*aṅgulis*) long,
as well as those that are ten *prādeśas* long— these alone are used for the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* and the *dhiṣṇiya*.
The rule for the eight [bricks] is that six *prādośa* bricks, measuring one and a half *iṣṭakas*, are placed;
however, the placement of those beginning with the *potriya* is to be done on all sides as appropriate.
Since there is no room for a distinction among the hearths belonging to a single city,
the multiplicity of the instruments would arise solely from the disparity in their numbers.
Having drawn [the lines] according to their respective numbers, one should place the bricks here;
"according to what is appropriate"—thus the Teacher spoke regarding the mandala.
When the ground is multiplied by the hypotenuse and divided by twice the hypotenuse,
the square root of the resulting difference from the ground— whether that ground is diminished by the quotient or not— is [the desired value].
