When that square is subtracted from the square of this hypotenuse,
those who know it understand the square root of the remainder to be the perpendicular.
Having stretched the cord measured by the disputant eastward between the two points mentioned for the interval,
one should pull it south-north across the eastern and western halves of the altar.
The two [lines] should be known as extending from east to west, with the *utkara* mound to the north;
the middle portion of the fire-altar, however, lies between the eastern and western [lines].

By means of the characteristic, for the sake of the sign, it is removed in the second transformation; and in the latter [transformation], as well as in the subsequent one, the sign is likewise removed.
But having reversed the previous orientation of the north and south markers, one should establish the cross-beams; this shall be the characteristic for both as well.
One should stretch a cord or a line between those two marks toward the east;
taking the southern end of the line, one should discard it toward the north for the sake of the mandala.
When the circumference is divided by four, the resulting value is the side length; when sixfold, it is the curved mark.
A line drawn from corner to corner serves to establish the squareness of the quadrangle.
This square root of twice the square of half the diameter is the calculated *karaṇī* for constructing a square within a circle.
Alternatively, the square of the diagonal is produced by taking the square root of half the square of the base of the supporting pillar;
this applies to a square mandala as long as its possible dimensions allow.
Indeed,
they say that for a square, the diagonal cord extending as far as its possible extent constitutes the diameter of an equivalent circle.
When the square of the interval between the diameter is subtracted from the square of half the diameter,
the square root of the remainder shall be the characteristic of the side.
From the square of the half-chord of the arc intercepted by the diameter, subtract the square of the half-chord of the previous arc;
[the remainder is] from the square of the semi-diameter.
When [the square of the string] has been subtracted, the remainder is the square of the base of that bow;
the square of the string multiplied by six is equal to the square of the bow.
But when struck by an arrow, the bowstring is shattered; this is the fruit of the bow.

The width (viṣkambha) should be joined with twice its own measure, and that [width] with a twentieth part of itself; it receives the name "fifth" when joined with a twenty-fifth part. When those two are combined with their breadth, this is the calculation for the circumference.
The circumference should consist of two parts and eleven spokes; one part of that [circumference] is likewise divided into two.
The diameter consists of the vowel-parts (seven), and together with the circumference, these parts should be increased by a fourth and a seventh part.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Karavindīya-bhāṣya commentary on the Āpastamba-sūtra, in the section known as the Śulba-praśna.
This is the Sundahājīya commentary.
Since there is much to be said regarding the instruments for the mandala, he describes the method using bricks even without them:
"One should divide the body of the mandala; its height is six finger-breadths."
The particle *saha* is used as a syntactic filler (*vākyālaṃkāra*).
Alternatively, there is a division [of the compound] as *sa iti*.
Satyāṣāḍha states: "One should trace out the circle with half a *vyāyāma*."
One should mark out a square with a side measuring sixty-eight finger-breadths less three sesamum seeds—that is, by half the diameter plus a specific increment.
Having divided the square into nine parts, one should divide the *prathikas* into three.
A *prathika* is simply a *prathi*.
[The altar] extends as far as the outermost wheel.
Alternatively, one may construct the bricks using the measuring instruments (karaṇas) themselves.
There are three instruments: the square, the middle of the breadth, and the end of the breadth.

Here, the measurement for the side-measures of the middle-width is a square of twenty-two finger-breadths and one-twentieth of a finger-breadth; each side-board should be carved in the shape of a bow,
with a cross-measure of thirteen finger-breadths less three-twentieths of a finger-breadth.

Just as twelve finger-breadths and two *tilas* constitute the measure of an arrow, so too is the measurement of the *prathyanta*. Of that [altar], one side is like a square; another is thirteen finger-breadths less two *tilas*; and another is twenty-six finger-breadths less two *tilas*. One should plane it like a bow so that it becomes an arrow measuring twenty-seven finger-breadths and seven *tilas*.

One should desire to perform the placing [of the bricks] for both the circular and the square [altars]; this is common to both in order to avoid a division [of the ritual], and by this it is known that in all cases a division must be avoided.
And so says Bodhāyana:
One should avoid the defects of the lower and upper parts; they call the joining of the sides a "defect" (bheda), which does not exist at the beginning or end [of these parts].
Piśīla is understood as being of five kinds: the space between the two arms is the first, and a cubit measured with the fist clenched is the second.
The third is an aratni not made into a fist; the fourth is thirty-two aṅgulas; and the fifth is thirty-six aṅgulas.
The remainder of the instruction is that one should make these square.

The Āgnīdhra should place the other hearths (dhiṣṇiya), having scratched them out according to their respective numbers: twelve or sixteen and so forth in the Hotṛ’s hearth, eleven in the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin’s, six in the Mārjālīya, and eight each in the others.
Regarding these, some say that their divisions should be made as far as possible.

For the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths that are square, the bricks must be made square as well; for it is said that "other than what is specifically prescribed, [the shape] is square. For those *dhiṣṇiya* hearths whose diameter is one *aratni*, the bricks of the *Āgnīdhrīya* are eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) long.
In the center of the twelve-finger-long *Hotrīya* hearth, there are four bricks measuring four finger-breadths each.
On all sides, they are eight finger-breadths [wide].
In the sixteen-finger [square], all are six finger-breadths.
In the twenty-one-finger [square], there are nine in the center that are four finger-breadths, and twelve on the periphery that are six finger-breadths.
In the corners of the twenty-four [finger-breadth] [altar], there are eight finger-breadths; the remainder is twenty-four finger-breadths.
In the *vlāhnaṇācchaṃsīya*, there are seven [fingers] of six finger-breadths and four [fingers] of nine finger-breadths.
In the *mārjālīya*, there are five [fingers] of eight finger-breadths.
Others, however, say: because of the statement "the others according to their respective order," all bricks must indeed have equal areas.
Since it is impossible to construct only those that are perfect squares, even long quadrilaterals (rectangles) may be made;
in that view as well, the Āgnīdhrīya [altar] is as described before.
The bricks of the twelvefold *hotrīya* are eight *aṅgulas* in length and six *aṅgulas* in width;
those of the sixteenfold are exactly as before;
but for the twenty-one-fold, they are eight *aṅgulas* in length and seven *aratnis* in width.
The [hearths] for the Caturviṃśaka are six aṅgulas in length and four aṅgulas in width;
those of the Mārjālīya are one span (prādeśa) in length and eight aṅgulas in width; those of the Aṣṭakās are one span in length and six aṅgulas in width.
For the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsī, there are two tracks (saraṇa); one construction-measure is eighteen tilas long and six aṅgulas wide.
By that [calculation], there are three bricks with a width of six aṅgulas;
another has a length of nine aṅgulas less nine tilas;
by that [method], there are eight bricks.
In other cases where there are merely bricks, the bricks should be understood according to this same principle.

Now, having placed in the center of the Āgnīdhrīya fire-altar a circular stone with a diameter of thirty-six *aṅgulas*, one should fashion eight bricks around it. For these, the side-measure is twelve *aṅgulas*; one of the transverse planks is fourteen *aṅgulas* less eight sesame seeds (*tilas*). One should plane this like a bow so that the chord (*śara*) becomes one finger and twelve *tilas*. Another transverse plank is four *aṅgulas* and twenty *tilas*; one should plane this also like a bow, but with an inward curve so that the chord becomes fifteen *tilas*.
In this manner, there are three ways of preparing the bricks for the other *dhiṣṇiya* hearths. For all of them, however, there are two planks, each eighteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) long.

For the *hotrīya* hearth, which measures twelve [finger-breadths], the third plank is nine finger-breadths long plus eleven *tila*s; one should plane it so that it is shaped like a bow (*dhanus*), such that the arrow (*śara*) consists of twenty-one *tila*s. This same principle is to be observed for those measuring sixteen [finger-breadths] and so forth.

The third plank of the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* measures ten finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and fifteen sesame seeds (*tila*); one should plane it into the shape of a bow. Its arrow (*śara*) is twenty-five sesame seeds; according to some, it is seven sesame seeds. The third plank of the *mārjālīya* is eighteen finger-breadths; one should plane it into the shape of half a bow. Its arrow is two finger-breadths and fourteen sesame seeds. The third plank of the *aṣṭakas* is fourteen finger-breadths less eight sesame seeds; one should plane it into the shape of a bow. Its arrow is one finger-breadth and twelve sesame seeds.
And other villages should also be understood in accordance with this.
Thus ends the seventh section.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Śulbapradīpa*, a commentary on the *Āpastamba-Śulbasūtra* by Sundararāja. [This is] the explanation by Kapardin.

The distributions (*viharaṇa*) for the *haviḥyajñas* have been stated, as well as those pertaining to the *saumika* rites involving the piling of the fire-altar (*agniciti*). However, the measurement of the site for the fire-altar, the construction of the bricks, and the rules for their placement (*upadhāna*) have not yet been mentioned.
Desiring to explain these, he introduces the topic:

"It is indeed as if he becomes [the bird] who piles the fire," so it is known; for it is enjoined by way of its form that "this [fire-altar] is piled in the likeness of birds," or because it is directly prescribed [as such]. (ĀpŚus 8.1)
With a bamboo measuring rod as prescribed, he measures out the men within the square self. ĀpŚus 8.2a.
This scriptural statement merely provides an introductory context and does not establish a result,
because there is an absence of an injunctive verbal suffix;
it is like the eternal fire on the northern altar.

"Regarding the statement, 'The *uttaravedi* is for the *agniṣṭoma*; the fire-altar is for the subsequent sacrifices,' because this is a mandatory injunction (*nityavacana*), if the *prastāva* were accepted by this scriptural text [as applying to all], then the *prastāva* should not be performed prior to the *gārhapatya-citi*.
This is true."

The purpose of this introductory statement here is so that the rules (dharmas) to be described hereafter may apply specifically to the Mahāgni alone. What, then, are those rules? In Kātyāyana’s Śulba-sūtra, it is clearly stated: "The knee-deep [pits] and so forth belong to the Mahāgni alone"; thus, these rules are explicitly declared to pertain to the Mahāgni.
Furthermore, the reason for using this introduction is so that the rules enjoined by the word *agni* without any qualifying prefix should apply [here].
For example: "The sacrificer himself should pile that very [Agni]. Here, the sacrificer is the agent for the Great Fire (Mahāgni) alone, not for the Gārhapatya and other fires.
The Adhvaryu priest is the agent for the Gārhapatya and the Dhiṣṇiya hearths.
The purpose of prescribing the Dhiṣṇiyas earlier, when they were to be prescribed later, is as follows.

That which is white belongs to Agni; even though this scriptural statement is made because there are many enemies, it prescribes the form and essential nature of this fire—that it is to be piled in the likeness of birds, that is, of winged creatures. Thus, the injunction concerns its configuration and intrinsic character.
Bodhāyana has stated that the meaning is "by the shadow of those who are flying. The word *vai* expresses certainty.
This teacher will also say: "with a curved tail and outstretched wings."
Therefore, the Śyena-pile is indeed the first.
It is stated in another *Śulba* text: "The Śyena-pile is the first fire among all fires.
If the Śyena is obligatory (*nitya*), how can it be said that one performs it "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*)? It is like the material of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

Just as in the case of "the *khadira* wood for one desiring heaven," the *khadira* wood possesses both a mandatory (*nitya*) and an optional (*kāmya*) character; this is because it is directly enjoined by the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*). The word "or" (*vā*) serves to set aside the alternative position.
Therefore, even this objection—that the Śyena is the archetype—is not valid. Why? Because it is directly enjoined;
here, it is indeed directly enjoined.
Starting from the statement "it becomes winged," the measurement of the wings and the tail is also prescribed.

Therefore, because of this contradiction, [the claim] that "this is an injunction regarding shape" is not an injunction (*codanā*); nor is it a prescriptive rule (*vidhi*), because there is an absence of a prescriptive verbal suffix (*vidhivibhakti*).
It is indicated as "it is piled" (*cīyate*); it does not mean "one should pile" (*cinuyāt*) or "that which is to be piled" (*cetavyam*).
Furthermore, because it is a supplement to another injunction, we see that it is not itself injunctive.

Starting from the passage, "The exponents of Brahman say: 'Should the fire-altar be piled face down? Or face up? and continuing with, "He places the head of the Puruṣa facing eastward and face up," the placing of the Puruṣa's head is what is enjoined.
This [text] is supplementary to that [preceding injunction] and is not an independent prescriptive rule.

This statement—"The first of the fires is built in the shape of a hawk"—is made with reference to the *piṭhaka-śyena* (the hawk-shaped brick-altar), which is designated as a "hawk" because it has wings and a tail the size of a human being.
Therefore, there is no contradiction.
The similarity extends only as far as what is prescribed;
thus, having grasped the similarity consisting in the possession of wings and a tail like those of a bird, the word *vayaḥ* (bird) is applied.

Therefore, it is established that the fire-altar (*agni*) is merely a man-sized entity possessing wings and a tail, and that other specific forms, such as those with curved wings and so forth, are optional (*kāmya*) based on that very same archetype (*prakṛti*).

He will say, "The optional [altars] are modifications of the qualities. With a bamboo of the characteristics previously described, resembling fire, he measures four *puruṣas* on the self-altar—he measures it. He measures half of the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) according to the method to be described later; the self-altar is two *puruṣas* on all sides, because of the statement, "four [puruṣas] by two," and thus there are four *puruṣa*-fields on the self-altar:
one *puruṣa* on the right wing, one *puruṣa* on the tail, and one *puruṣa* on the left [wing]. (ĀpŚS 8.2b)

One *puruṣa* on the right wing, one *puruṣa* at the tail, and one *puruṣa* on the left—these three squares, each measuring one *puruṣa*, together with the body (*ātman*), constitute seven *puruṣa*-sized areas.
He extends the right wing by one cubit on the south; likewise, he extends the left wing on the north. ĀpŚus_8.2c.
By means of the measure of a cubit (aratni), he extends the right wing on the right side— making it long—
and likewise the left wing on the left side.
The tail at the back is one span or one palm in length.
The remainder [of the instruction] is that one should extend the tail by twelve or thirteen finger-breadths.
In this way, there are seven and a half *puruṣa*-measures of ground.
This is the Karavindīya commentary.
The sacrificial fires for the rites beginning with the *agnyādheya* and ending with the *soma* sacrifices have been described as consisting solely of the *vihāra* (the arrangement of the fires).

Now, with the desire to prescribe the specific *vihāra* for those sacrifices involving the piling of the fire-altar (*agni-citi*), the author recites the Vedic scripture that ordains the piling of the fire.
The word *bhavati* occurs [here] in the sense of prosperity (*samṛddhi*).
The expression *iva khalu vai* is a collection of particles used for the purpose of poetic ornamentation at the beginning of a sentence and so forth.
"It is indeed known: 'He who piles the fire-altar becomes like the essence (rasa); he who perfects the fire through piling becomes prosperous.'"
This is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) intended to glorify the injunction regarding the mantra;
the expression "he piles" (*cinute*) is a reference to the present tense.
Therefore, how can this be construed as a scriptural injunction (*śruti*) for the piling (*cayana*), which is a consecration of the fire?

True; because this very Śruti is primary in the Taittirīyaka, and because it is impossible for it to be a mere restatement (anuvāda) since its meaning is not already established, this Śruti is postulated as the injunction for the piling (cayana) itself.
Furthermore, because there is no connection with a specific desire, it is considered obligatory (nitya).
But is it not the case that, like the piling, the sense of "becoming" (bhavati) must also be enjoined?
It cannot be an injunction; why? Because since the piling (cayana) is a consecration of the fire, it is impossible for it to be a restatement of its own result.
"Vayasām adanā vayāṃsi" means birds—hawks and other such winged creatures.
"Pratimā" means a representation, a likeness, a resemblance, or a form. "Codanā" refers to the Vedic injunction that impels [one toward action].
The meaning is that this fire-altar is to be constructed in such a way that it takes the form of a hawk (*śyena*).

And in another *Śulba* [text], it is stated: "Of the fires piled as hawks, this is the first fire. Furthermore, referring to the hawk, it will later state: "It has curved wings and a spread-out tail."
Therefore, the hawk—distinguished by its wings and other features—is to be made the archetype for the fire-altar;
it is eternal.
Just as the *khadira* wood and other materials serve as the archetypes for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), so too shall this [hawk] serve the one who desires heaven.
The word "or" (*vā*) in this [sūtra] serves to exclude the alternative position: namely,
that the statement "he is measured out as a counterpart of birds" is an injunction for specific forms such as the hawk (*śyena*).
Why? Because it is directly prescribed.

Since by the sentence beginning with "he becomes a bird," the form of the fire is directly prescribed as having the shape of a bird with wings and a tail consisting merely of the sacrificial effort (*vyāyāma*); therefore, the statement "this is built in the likeness of birds" expresses only a similarity to birds. This cannot be an injunction regarding the form of a hawk.

Furthermore, because the word *cīyate* (is piled) indicates a present action and because this sentence is a supplementary part (*śeṣa*) of the injunction regarding the placing of human heads, it is not prescriptive.
As for what was stated in another *Śulba*—"it is said that the first of the fire-altars built in the shape of a hawk (*śyena*) is the [Agni] fire"—this is not a flaw;
for in that context, even a fire-altar with wings and a tail measuring only one fathom (*vyāyāma*) is called a "hawk."

Therefore, by means of the Vedic tradition (āmnāna), only that degree of similarity which is prescribed—namely, the possession of wings and a tail equal in measure to the person itself—must be accomplished.
Consequently, it is established that the fire-altar (agni) is of the nature of a person possessing wings and a tail, and it is eternal. He now states the essential form of this fire-altar:
With the bamboo—in the manner that will be described—he measures four persons within himself;

for "measuring" (avamāna) is indeed the same as "measuring" (vimāna), as seen in the scriptural statement: "Having measured you [the sacrificial post] with the thought, 'I shall be able [to perform the sacrifice] to this extent,' they sacrifice."
The self [altar] is two *puruṣas* on all sides; with those two, the self becomes four *puruṣa*-fields.
Likewise, there are three [fields] measuring one *puruṣa* each for the two wings and the tail.
Thus, there are seven *puruṣa*-fields. With a cubit (*aratni*), he extends the right wing to the right; that is, he should make it long toward the right.
In this manner, one should also make the northern wing longer toward the north. The tail at the rear should be one *prādeśa* or a *vitasti* in length.
A *prādeśa* is measured by the thumb and the index finger; a *vitasti* is measured by the thumb and the little finger. One should extend the tail westward using either of these two measures.
Thus, seven and a half *puruṣa*-measures constitute the area of the fire-altar (*agni*).
This is the explanation according to Sundararāja.
The construction of the altar for the Soma sacrifice is performed by steps of twelve finger-breadths each.
In the first three and the [next] seven, on the second, third, second, and fourth lunar days.
In the [first] three, two, one, and five [yugas], there are fifteen spikes;
[the height is] thirty-eight cubits less sixty-six tilas and six aratnis. 2.

The mark of the *vimānarajju* (the celestial cord) should be made; then, upon its seventeen [divisions], two loops (*pāśa*) are to be formed, and between them, twelve [divisions] are traditionally taught.
The cord for the vimāna may be thirty-six units long and possess eight characteristics;
the hip is fifteen units, while the hall (sadas) is in the first and the fourth [sections] immediately following. 4.
In the tenth and eighth [sections], those corners are three [aratnis] long;
the sacrificial hearths (dhiṣṇyas) have an interval of one span (prādeśa), while the Āgnīdhra hearth is in the fourth [section].
When seventeen Rudra-śaṅkus have been reduced by one-quarter here, the Mārjālīya and Āgnīdhra hearths are to be made at the fifth and sixth marks. 6.6.

In the seventh [space], as before, the placing of the grains occurs in the Āgnīdhra fire-altar; in the tenth peg, which measures four and a half [units], the heap of earth (utkara) is placed, following the sequence toward the north of the Manu-peg.
Furthermore, in the eleventh [section], there is the location for digging the *ūvathya* and *go* pits;
here, the *havirdhāna* is as before, with the addition of the transposition of the two *pāśas*. 8.
The *śāmitra* fire-altar should be located at the twelfth mark when sixteen marks are reduced by half;
the *uttaravedi* altar-ground should be at the two penultimate marks, one and a half [units] from each other.
In the final [sacrifice], the Cātvāla pit is twelve cubits from the shoulder;
it is determined that the Cātvāla belongs to the Paśubandha, and this applies to the Soma sacrifice as well.
Because it is stated that [the measurement] has been explained even without mentioning another measure, Bodhāyana clearly declared that it is to be one *śamyā* everywhere. 11.
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction regarding the fire, and no other authority is known;
the Āstāva is proclaimed to be on the northern shoulder of the Mahāvedi. 12.
In the southern *havirdhāna* shed, one should leave three steps behind;
on the side, at a distance of one and three-quarter *aratnis*, the *uparava* holes are prescribed.
Their rotation around the corner-śaṅkus is half a prādeśa;
having left three quarters of a prakrama from the front of the uparavas. 14.
The pathway, measuring one *śamyā* on each side and forming a square, is contiguous with the *khara*;
it lies in the middle of the *audumbara* shed, to the south of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line, in due order.
And there arises, as it were, an impulse from the reflection of the shadows of birds flying by;
and so too says Baudhāyana:
"The meaning is 'by the shadow of birds flying [overhead]';
by this, it is known that the Śyenaciti is obligatory."
And there are the words of the mantra, such as "Thou art Suparṇa, Garuḍa," and so forth;
and there are the indicative marks, such as "he draws the head from the tail" and "on the head [of the two] wings," and so forth;
for indeed, a square figure has no head.
Or rather, the shape is to be understood from the direct injunction that "it becomes winged on both sides, with wings and a tail each measuring one fathom," and so forth;
by this, the fire-altar is prescribed as being square.
And that is the archetype of all fires; he explains that very point first, as follows:
"up to the latter."
According to the traditional instruction, as it has been handed down, [the measurement] is for a person five *aratnis* in height, as will be described later.
Thus the measurement of the sevenfold fire-altar in its entirety has been stated; now he states another alternative:
"An *aratni* is a *vitasti*, which consists of twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*)."
As it was stated by Kātyāyana: "A man [is] five *aratnis*, ten spans (*vitasti*), or two hundred fingers."
Etymologists state that a *vitasti* consists of twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
The word *vitasti* is the explanation for the term *prādeśena*.

Since the meaning of the word *prādeśa* is that which is measured by it, it is the *vitasti* itself that is to be understood here by the word *prādeśa*, and not the thumb and forefinger extended [as in the common gesture]. This is the sense.
Alternatively, because it is stated in the Vājasaneyaka, "The tail [should be] one span (vitasti)," the word *vitasti* itself is explained by the more well-known word *prādeśa*.
The word *vā* ("or") is connected to the sense of the sentence;
by that, all of this is made optional.
For instance, the optional nature of the enlargement of the tail is understood because the *Taittirīyaka* does not mention such an increase.

And Kātyāyana makes this clear: after stating, "The two wings become longer by one cubit (*aratni*)," and having thus described their increased length, he concludes with, "The two wings and the tail are each the measure of a fathom (*vyāma*)," thereby concluding that [the size] is indeed merely that of a man.
This is evident.
And on this point, Bodhāyana says: "With a bamboo pole of man's height, or with a cubit, the two wings and the tail [are formed]; the wings become longer than the shoulders."

However, some, considering a *vitasti* to be thirteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and calculating it by means of a *prādeśa* of twelve finger-breadths, claim that the increase of the wings and tail by one *aratni* and so forth is permanent.
For them, [the rule] beginning with "having divided the remainder of those starting from the eightfold [altar] into seven parts" and "the seventh part-maker" and so on, does not cohere.
This is because, if a *vitasti* of thirteen finger-breadths were accepted, it would be impossible to lay down a surface area of exactly one hundred and twenty finger-breadths in the tail.
Regarding this, someone says: "Let it be filled with earth (*purīṣa*). The author of the Sūtras does not accept that, as he states:
"Because the earth constitutes a different half," and "That which would be diminished for those being baked.
Furthermore, if everything deficient were to be filled by means of earth, why is such great effort now being made in the extensive text regarding the measurement of half a brick?
Therefore, this claim that a *vitasti* consists of thirteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) is not correct.

Others hold the view that there is a difference in terminology between the *vitasti* and the *prādeśa*—both of which consist of twelve finger-breadths—due to a difference in ritual injunctions, just as there is between *āmikṣā* and *payaḥ*;
and that these two are mutually interchangeable.
For them as well, the aforementioned inconsistency is quite evident, as is the contradiction with the Brāhmaṇa;
for in the Taittirīyaka, the growth of the tail is not mentioned even as a possibility.

Therefore, we consider it more appropriate that the use of non-jeweled bricks (*aratniniprādeśa*) is merely optional. Furthermore, how does the fact that the fifth *karaṇa* (measure) of the eight-finger bricks serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in this context? For in that case, since the laying down (*upadhāna*) can be accomplished by means of the first and third *karaṇas* alone, the other three *karaṇas* exist for the purpose of avoiding fragmentation;
therein, the laying down is easily accomplished even without the fifth.
Regarding the increase of the autumnal equinox and other such occasions, the manner of that [observance] for the Nitya rite has been shown by the venerable Bodhāyana:
"In the sacrificial hall, on the eastern and western sides of the wings," and so forth.
And there is another method: first, ten bricks in the self (the body of the altar); fifteen extending toward the north;
and between the tips of the two wings, three each facing east.
On each of the two sides of the tail, there are five [bricks] each; at the two corners of the tip of the tail, there are two bricks measuring one span (prādeśa) each;
and by means of those two, there are two half-bricks (adhyardhāṣṭakā) facing north.
At each corner at the tip of the wings, there is one line of one and a half units extending northward;
at the two joints, there are five lines each according to the sūtra;
and in the middle of the tip of the tail, there are two lines facing east.
In the remainder, there are five rows.
This is the two-hundred-brick layout (*prastāra*).
On the other hand, on the wings and the flanks, there are six half-bricks each, oriented toward the north.
On the body (ātman), six lines run eastward on the south side and six on the north side;

at the hips and the shoulders, two lines each run northward, measuring one and a half [units]; at the junction with the tail (puccha), five lines run eastward, extending across the body and measuring one cubit (aratni).
In the remainder, there are five [sets] from the fifth;
having removed the middle one from the tips of the tails, two half-bricks are placed toward the north.
This is the two-hundred-brick arrangement.

Thus, when the arrangement is accomplished by means of these four methods, that which is the fifth method is for the purpose of completing the total of two hundred, even in the absence of the placement of gems, by avoiding any discrepancy.
All of this should be examined by the learned; therefore, I shall desist.

The fire consisting of one kind has the hair-tuft as its sacrificial seat; the second is of two kinds, and the third is of three kinds. In this very manner, they arise up to one hundred and one kinds. (ĀpŚus 8.3)

That which has one person (*puruṣa*) in it is "of one kind" (*ekavidha*). Because there is no reason to skip the first [option] when the rule states "one should pile [the fire-altar] with one person more than one," the first case is that of being "of one person. Thus, the "fire-field" (*agnikṣetra*) is so called because bricks of this one-person variety are prescribed therein. [The suffix] *iṅ* is applied by the rule *ātaścopasarge*.
This "one-fold" (*ekavidhā*) is what is to be observed.
They rise and go up to one hundred and one layers;
the prefix *ā* is used here in the sense of "inclusive limit.

However, one should indeed pile it in seven layers only. For the natural fire-altar consists of seven layers. It is known from tradition that from that point upward, the layers increase by one each time. (ĀpŚus 8.4)
The collection of particles [is used] for the exclusion of an alternative:
that "one kind" and so forth are not to be piled.
"Vā vā" is used for emphasis.
The natural fire is indeed sevenfold—meaning it is of the nature of *prakṛti*. The secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) is used here in its own primary sense.
Beyond the sevenfold [fire], there are those increasing by one each, according to the Śruti of the Vājasaneyins.

The first [set] consists of seven-and-a-half bricks; beginning with the rule "by means of the *puruṣa* alone," since the prescription of the seven-and-a-half is established, it is heard in the injunction for the placement (*upadhāna*) that one places them on the right wing.

Thereafter, "one more than the preceding" means exceeding the *puruṣa* by one; thus, in the second application it should be understood as eight-and-a-half, and in the third as nine-and-a-half, and so forth.
This is the Karavindīyā commentary.
It is understood as being of one kind (*ekavidha*).

Having raised the doubt that it might be the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the sevenfold [altar], he says this in order to demonstrate its nature as the material cause: "It is arranged (*vidhīyate*) and measured (*mīyate*)," thus *vidhā* refers to the measurement of the fire-altar. Since the areas of the person (*puruṣa-kṣetra*) are measured here one by one with a bamboo rod of the length of a person, the word *vidhā* denotes the area of a person. That fire-altar which has one such *vidhā* is "one-fold" (*ekavidha*).

Because there is no reason for skipping the first, the first is of one kind; that alone is the archetype (*prakṛti*), while the others are modifications (*vikṛti*). And these fires increase—that is, they become greater—by the addition of one person at a time, up to one hundred and one kinds.
The particle *ā* is used in the sense of inclusive limit.
How is it that the word *vidhā* is a synonym for *vimāna*? It is said: its meaning is "it arranges" (*vidadhāti*), which is to say, "it performs.
The root *kṛ* (to do/perform) is seen used in various instances with respect to *vimānas* in the sense of their functional operations;
therefore, *vidhā* and *vimāna* are synonyms.
Therefore, the first is of one kind;
that which is of one kind is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), while those of two kinds and so forth are its transformations (*vikāra*).
Therefore, one should indeed pile it in sevenfold—*tadu ha vai* is a collection of particles used here to set aside the alternative view;
this is not the case that "the first is single-fold. What then? One should pile that very first altar in sevenfold.
Why? Because the natural fire (*prākṛta-agni*) is indeed sevenfold.
The particle *vāva* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*), as seen in such passages as "He, indeed, is the king of all" (*eṣa vāva sarvato rājā*).
The word *prākṛta* is simply *prakṛti*; here the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is used in its own sense. Therefore, Agni is of exactly seven forms as the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Consequently, he is to be piled up first in exactly seven forms, not in a single form, because it is precisely in that [sevenfold form] that the limbs such as the wings and tail are taught; this is the intended meaning.
By "sevenfold," it is meant specifically the "half-eighth" (seven and a half).
Since it will be stated later that "the fire, measuring a *aratni* and a *prādeśa*, becomes sevenfold," the Śruti says:
"Beyond that—that is, beyond that sevenfold [fire]—one should build fires increasing by one each.
As for the statement "Agni is strength," this is from the Vājasaneyaka.

Therefore, in the second and subsequent offerings, one should pile only the sevenfold [altar]; this is the tenth [type]. Thus, the progression of increasing by one should be understood up to the hundred-and-first-fold [altar].
This is the commentary of Sundararāja.
"Single-fold" (*ekavidha*) means that which is established (*vidhīyate*) from non-establishment (*avidhāt*), thus it is a "fold" (*vidhā*); the field is merely the person (*puruṣamātra*).
In the first meal, it is single-fold.
In this way,
for the hundredfold [arrangement] and so forth, there is one hundred men in the hundredth meal;
that indeed is clearly understood.
He states another alternative: "The *prākṛta* is simply the *prakṛti*, with the suffix *aṇ* [applied] to *prajñā* and so forth.
Beyond the sevenfold [classification], there are many hundreds of varieties, each increasing by one.
In all cases, there is no increase in the number of *aradniprādeśas*, because the increase is stated to apply only to the *vidhās*."
This is also indicated by the scriptural mark (*liṅga*): "In the twenty-first [altar], there is no practice of *aratni*-measurements for the fire-altars.
This has been clearly stated by Baudhāyana: "The first fire-altar consists of seven and a half *puruṣas*; the second, eight and a half; the third, nine and a half," and so forth.

However, for one who takes up the measurements according to the sequence of single-fold and so on, there is an absence of *aratni*-measurements even in the seven-fold and subsequent altars, because there is no contradiction in the principle of increasing by one unit. Thus, when a seven-fold altar is taken up with *aratni*-measurements, the subsequent ones also do not have *aratni*-measurements.

Because the *Kapardikṣāṣya* and the *Vājasaneyika* prescribe alternative methods for the fire-altar (*agnivikalpavidhāna*), it is also obtained that one may build even the "seven-and-a-half" altar in the second *vihāra*.

For those [altars] beginning with the single-fold (*ekavidha*), there are no wings or tail, because they are supplementary to the statement regarding the seven-fold (*saptavidha*) altar and because of a contradiction with the direct Vedic text (*śrutivipratiṣedha*). (ĀpŚus 8.5)

From this as well, we see that only the seven-and-a-half-fold [altar] is to be piled. For what reason? Because for those [altars] beginning with the one-fold and ending with the six-fold, there are no wings or tail.
What is meant by this? Since they have no wings or tail, the meaning is that the bricks do not lie within them.
He asks "Why? and replies: "Sevenfold.
The meaning is that they are prescribed with reference to the sevenfold fire.
[The rules] such as "one places the Rathantara on the right wing" and "the Bṛhat on the left wing" are not separated [from the context].
Therefore, altars consisting of one kind and so forth are not to be piled;
rather, only that of seven kinds is to be piled.
To the question, "Why should wings and tails not be fashioned for those very [altars]? he says: "Because of the scripture."
There is a contradiction—a conflict.

If a division into the nature of wings and tail is made for that which is of a single form, then the state of being merely a fathom in length for those consisting of wings and tail is lost. On the other hand, if the state of being merely a fathom in length for those consisting of wings and tail were maintained so that this defect would not occur, then its being of a single form would be lost.

Therefore, there is a contradiction; and because of this contradiction, [the measurements] from one-fold up to six-fold must not be performed. To the question, "How then are the eight-fold and subsequent [measurements] to be measured?", he says:
Whatever [portion] remains from those beginning with the eightfold [division], one should divide that into seven parts and assign it to each person.

Regarding those [altars] beginning from eightfold up to one hundred and onefold: whatever else remains beyond the seven and the seven-and-a-half, that is divided sevenfold and seven-and-a-halfwise. As for that which was to be added beyond the seven-and-a-half, it is divided seven-and-a-halfwise; how is this obtained? Because of the statement "sevenfold," only the eighth part is taken, since the *aratni* and *prādeśa* are included within that. He will state later: "sevenfold."
One [part] of eight kinds is to be added; two [parts] to nine kinds;
three [parts] to ten kinds—in this manner it should be understood from the one hundred and one-fold person.
Having divided the person into seven and a half parts, one portion is to be added for each person.
In a man's [measurement] consisting of seven and a half *aratni*-spans, there are thirty-five fifteen-part units (*pañcadaśabhāgīyā*);
in half a man, there are fifteen.
Thus, in one man’s field, two hundred and twenty-five fifteen-part units lie.
These [lines] are to be inserted into the eightfold [field]:
thirty lines of fifteen parts each into one man-field (puruṣakṣetra).
When they have been inserted, it amounts to two hundred and fifty-five.
The group of sixteen [rods] consists of fifty-six [units].

According to the principle that "from a square, a square [is derived]," when one field consisting of fifteen parts is removed from a single [unit], the cord [remaining] stands in the place of a *puruṣa*;
its fifth part stands in the place of an *aratni*.
By that measurement, the entire field of the person becomes smeared;
the same should be understood for the ninefold [fire-altar] and others, since no modification of the shape has been prescribed. (ĀpŚus 8.6b)
"He measures with a man's length; he measures with a bamboo pole," so it is known. (ĀpŚS 8.7)
If the field of the person were cast into one place, its form would undergo transformation.
"Aśruti" means that for which there is no scriptural authority (śruti);
the meaning is that there is an absence of scriptural authority regarding any such modification of form.
"By means of a man" requires a substance; "by means of a bamboo" requires a measure. The connection between these two is like that of the lost horse and the burnt chariot.
He measures with a bamboo staff of human length;
he makes a hole in the middle of the staff at a height equal to the sacrificer with his arms raised, and a third [hole] in the center. (ĀpŚus 8.8)
Because of the mention of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), a bamboo of the Adhvaryu’s own measurement is not taken.
He makes the two holes such that the distance between them is exactly the measure of the sacrificer;
the remainder of the sentence is that he makes one hole in the middle of those two in the bamboo.

Another [assistant], having placed a bamboo pole along the spine at the location of the sacrificial post-hole, having driven stakes into its holes, and having released [the cord from the previous pegs], should trace around [the hole] toward the south-east with the other two [ends of the cord] until the edge. ĀpŚus 8.9.

Having placed the bamboo rod behind the *sañcara* along the spine (the *pṛṣṭhyā*) in such a way that it is aligned with it, and having driven a peg into each of the three holes, he should release [the cord] from the two rear pegs and trace a line to the south-east, reaching to the edge of the fire-site.
Having released it from the eastern peg and fastened it to the western one, he should trace a line to the south-west, reaching to the edge. ĀpŚus 8.10.
Having fixed [the cord] at the eastern peg and having fixed it at the western peg, one should draw a line toward the south-west up to the edge.
This is the eighth section; the Karavindīyā commentary.

It has been stated that the sevenfold fire is the primary form (*prakṛti*), while the other fires are modifications (*vikṛti*); regarding this, he states the distinction between the six types beginning with the single-fold: "for the single-fold and the others... they do not exist" (*na bhavanti*), meaning they would not come into being.
Why? Because there are seven types of supplementary statements (*vākyaśeṣa*) and because of a contradiction with the revealed scripture (*śruti*).

This is because the statement prescribing the tail—beginning with "it becomes the wing" (*pakṣībhavati*) and so forth—is understood to be supplementary to that [context] due to its recitation within the section on the sevenfold [altar]. Furthermore, if one were to create the division of wings and so forth for the "one-fold" altar, it would result in the loss of its being a mere laborious effort; and if one were to create the wings and so forth as a mere laborious effort, it would result in the loss of the "one-fold" nature. Thus, since there is a contradiction between the two scriptural passages (*śruti*) which prescribe the one-fold nature of the wings and the tail, the wings and other parts cannot belong to those altars starting from the one-fold.
Their construction, the placement of the altar-base (*upadhāna*), and so forth, will be explained in the section concerning those [altars] starting from the one-fold (*ekavidha*).

Now, regarding the view that there is an increase starting from the eight-fold (*aṣṭavidha*) and so on, it is said: "In the case of the increase and decrease of the number of parts (*vidhā*) among those with wings and tail, having made the seventh construction-line (*karaṇī*)—which stands in the place of the person (*puruṣa*)—the measure, one should perform the ritual.
This demonstrates a sevenfold division even in the case of decrease starting from the one-fold, for the purpose of determining the division of the wings and tail.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even in the case of diminution, the act of diminishing would lack a visible purpose.
Therefore, it is understood that [the rites] apply even to those of a single kind.
How then could it be said that they do not apply to them?

It is said: "The first fire-altar is of one kind," and "One should indeed build it as sevenfold"—since these two scriptural statements (śruti), which express contradictory meanings, cannot be combined, an option (vikalpa) alone is appropriate. Therefore, the first altar is either of one kind or of seven kinds.

In that regard, when the first is of one kind and serves as the archetype (prakṛti), then in the subsequent rites starting from the second day, those of two kinds and so forth—each increasing by one—must be employed.
In the single-fold [altar] which is the archetype (*prakṛti*), the wings and tail do not exist because they are not mentioned by name;
however, in the seven-fold [altar], they certainly do exist.
Likewise, in the eight-fold and subsequent [altars], they certainly exist as well, because those [altars] are modifications (*vikāra*) of that [archetype].

When the sevenfold [altar] is the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the others are its modifications (*vikāra*), then even those starting from the one-fold [altar] would likewise possess wings and a tail, just like the eightfold one; in this way, the division into seven types mentioned in the context of the reduction of forms will be meaningful. In that case, just as with the *Atirātra* sacrifice, the performance of the modification—even the one-fold one—may indeed occur first at times. Even under this view, the rule of increasing by one remains intact when the one-fold is the archetype.
At the first feeding, they are without wings or tails;
at the second and subsequent feedings, those of two types up to seven types remain without wings or tails,
while those of seven types and above possess both wings and tails.

When the first offering consists of a single part, whether it be the primary form (*prakṛti*) or a modification (*vikṛti*), then it includes both the wings and the tail. In the second and subsequent offerings, all those consisting of two parts and so forth likewise include the wings and the tail.

When the first offering consists of seven parts, whether it be the primary form or a modification, then from that point onward, those consisting of eight parts and so forth consist of exactly seven parts.
Therefore, for the six types beginning with the single-fold, both the state of having wings and tail and the state of having no wings or tail indeed exist; thus, everything is logically consistent.
As for those beginning with the eight-fold and increasing by one, how is there a division of the additional [parts]? To this he says:
"In the eight-fold... and so forth.

The meaning of this is as follows: from the eightfold and other [altars] up to the seven-and-a-half-fold, whatever additional [space] there may be that is adventitious, one should divide that into seven parts or seven-and-a-half parts and assign one part to each person—that is, for every person. Why? Because of the indicative mark (liṅga) stating, "In each half [of the altar], however much fire there is, that is the sevenfold [altar] measuring a cubit and a span," since no modification of the shape is heard of—that is, because there is an absence of scriptural statement (śruti), which means an absence of authoritative evidence.
In that regard, twenty-five hundred and fifteen parts (*bhāgīyā*) lie within the area of one *puruṣa*; of these, thirty-three fifteen-part units must be added to each *puruṣa*.

Fifteen [parts] are added to half [a *puruṣa*]. This is the meaning: having divided what is to be added into fifteen parts, two parts thereof are to be added; that which makes up the *puruṣa* for the sake of not altering the shape is to be taken as the measure (*karaṇī*) for that *puruṣa*.
The meaning is that the bamboo staff (*veṇu*) becomes exactly that much.
Now the celestial chariot (vimāna) is described:
this consists of two pairs of strings.
In this regard, one scriptural passage refers to the requirement of the substance, while the other refers to the requirement of the measure;
these two are joined together like the proverb of "the lost horse and the burnt chariot.
The meaning is that [the flute] is made by a man's height.

"To whatever extent"— meaning, one should make the interval between the two holes in the bamboo cane equal to the measurement of the sacrificer when his arms are raised, so that it corresponds to that dimension.
It will be stated later that "a man [is] five cubits (aratnis) long," and that statement is based on this very reason.

Leaving a passage behind the sacrificial post-hole (yūpāvaṭa), one should place a bamboo pole (veṇu) along the spine-line (pṛṣṭhyā). Having fixed pegs (śaṅku) into its holes, one should release the bamboo from the two rear pegs, insert a wedge (kīla) into another hole, and fasten it to the front peg. Starting from that very peg, beginning from the base of the rear peg, one should draw a line toward the southeast. The meaning is that one should draw the line with the bamboo starting from the edge of each direction until it faces the opposite direction.
Having unfastened [the cord] from the eastern peg and having fastened it to the western peg, one should draw a line toward the south and toward the west as before.
This is the Sundararājīyā commentary.
And [this applies to] the single-fold [fire-altar].
There is a contradiction with the Vedic scripture regarding the statement, "The two wings and the tail are each a fathom long," for this refers specifically to the square-shaped [altar].
However,
the *śyena-cit* and other such altars possess wings and a tail, because it is precisely that shape which is prescribed as the object of the injunction.
The eightfold [measure] that is in excess of the seven is fourteen thousand four hundred *puruṣakṣetrāṅgulas* (14,400).
One should multiply those by the [number of] *puruṣas* in excess of the seven, divide by seven, and add the quotient to the *puruṣakṣetrāṅgulas*.
These are to be known there as the finger-breadths of the human field (*puruṣakṣetrāṅguli*).

Just as in the eightfold [calculation], the finger-breadths of the human field are fourteen thousand four hundred and seven; having multiplied by one person in excess of seven, and divided by seven, the result is two thousand fifty-seven finger-breadths plus five sesame seeds.
These should be added to the human finger-breadths.

There, those finger-breadths of the human [unit] amount to sixteen thousand four hundred and fifty-seven finger-breadths plus five sesame seeds (16,457 + 5). Its square root is one hundred and twenty-eight finger-breadths plus ten sesame seeds (128 + 10). For this reason, it will be stated: "Having made the seventh part of the side the measure of the human [unit], one should proceed."
Thus, in the ninefold [system], one multiplies the *puruṣāṅgula*s (14,400) by two and divides by seven; the result is four thousand one hundred fourteen *aṅgula*s and ten *tila*s more.

When added to those *puruṣāṅgula*s, they become eighteen thousand five hundred fourteen *aṅgula*s and ten *tila*s more (18,514 ti 10). Its square root is one hundred thirty-six *aṅgula*s and two *tila*s (136 ti 2). Such is the measure of the *puruṣa* in the ninefold system.
It should be understood in the same way for the tenfold and other systems.

Another method: having multiplied the number of *puruṣas* in the fire by the number of *puruṣa*-fingers, and divided by seven, the quotient obtained is the *puruṣa*-fingers, which are exactly as previously stated: sixteen thousand four hundred fifty-seven and five sesame seeds (*tilas*), i.e., 16,457 5/7.
This applies likewise to the ninefold and other [measures].
In one *aṅguli*-field, there are one hundred eleven thousand five hundred and fifty-six sesame seeds (115,556).
In this way, for those fires that are devoid of the *aratni* and *prādeśa* measures and possess wings and a tail, there is the *puruṣa* and the *veṇu*.
Here, because the square fire was introduced first, it is stated that for single-fold fires which are square and lack wings and a tail, [the measure is] from the eight-fold onwards.

However, since the rule for building the hawk-shaped fire (*śyenacit*) and others is common [to all], and because their form is prescribed by the statement, "This is built as the image of birds," the single-fold and other fires take on the shape of hawks and so forth, possessing wings and a tail.

In that case, it should be understood that whatever is deficient from seven should be divided into seven parts and subtracted for each person; the method of division there is indeed evident. That being so, in the case of a single-layered Śyena altar, the number of human finger-breadths is two thousand, fifty-seven, and five sesame seeds (2057 5/6).
The root of that [measurement] is forty-five finger-breadths and twelve sesame seeds.
In the case of the two types of *puruṣa*, however, there are four thousand one hundred fourteen *puruṣa*-finger-breadths together with thirty sesame seeds.
A bamboo-staff of a *puruṣa* is sixty-four finger-breadths plus four sesame seeds.
The same should be understood regarding the threefold [fire-altar] and others.

Whichever person stands in place of the fire in a given case, there, for the purpose of arranging the bricks, one-twentieth of that person's measure is to be calculated as a finger-breadth (*aṅguli*),
and one thirty-fourth of that finger-breadth is a sesame seed (*tila*).
Regarding this, there are these verses:
From the number [of years] multiplied by one, seven, four, three, and one, divided by seven, the square root of that result shall be the *puruṣa*. (1)
For the square altar and the Śyena-altar, when they are respectively reduced by one *prādeśa* and one *aratni*,
a finger-breadth (*aṅguli*) must be proportionally calculated in each case based on one two-hundredth part [of the total measurement].
However, regarding the division for the altar with its *aratni* and *prādeśa*, the following distribution has been stated by Bodhāyana:

"Whatever remains other than the *prakṛti*, one should divide that into fifteen parts; having done so, one should combine two parts for each layer (*vidhā*), and with those [parts], numbering seven and a half, one should pile the fire-altar."
And so forth.

Regarding that, the method is as follows: having multiplied the number of *puruṣa*-finger-breadths by more than seven hundred and fifty *puruṣas*, and having divided the product by fourteen thousand four hundred, one should double the quotient and add it to the *puruṣa*-finger-breadths;
those are the *puruṣa*-finger-breadths in that context.

For example, when nine and a half *puruṣas* are multiplied by one [to find the number of *puruṣa*-finger-breadths] and divided by fifteen, the result is nine hundred and sixty finger-breadths. Doubling that and adding it to the *puruṣa*-finger-breadths, the total observed *puruṣa*-finger-breadths are sixteen thousand three hundred and twenty (16,320). The square root of that is the measure of a *puruṣa* there, which is two hundred and seventy-five finger-breadths minus a quarter (*pāda*).
Likewise, in nine and a half *puruṣas*, there are eighteen thousand two hundred and forty *puruṣa*-field-finger-breadths.
It should be understood that a *puruṣa* consists of three hundred and thirty-five fingers (*aṅgula*s), plus two sesame seeds (*tila*s), and so forth.

As for those [altars] such as the *prauga-cit* which lack wings and tails, whether they are joined with or separated from *aratni*s and *prādeśa*s, one should likewise bring in a *puruṣa*, calculate a finger to be the two-hundredth part of it, and perform the layout and the preparation of bricks.

For example, in the *prauga-cit*: in a single-form (*ekavidha*) altar, one thousand four hundred and forty-four fingers minus six sesame seeds constitute a *puruṣa*; its two-hundredth part is there the "finger," and so forth.
Regarding this, there are two verses:

"From the number of days, space, sky, hearing, and Vedas (5040), multiplied by twice the number of persons (2), one should divide by the lunar days (15); the square root of that result shall be the number of persons. (1)
For the square and the Śyena-altars, when measured in spans and cubits,
and likewise for the Prauga and other altars, this same method should be used for the calculation in human finger-breadths.

As for those who claim that the increase of a *aratni* and a *prādeśa* is constant, they would have to apply great effort to reconcile this with the meaning stated by Bodhāyana in this sūtra—namely, "from seven" and "seven and a half"—as well as "thus the sevenfold [altar] is the half-eighthfold," and likewise later, "the measuring cord of the seventh division.
Here, the entry of additional persons is mentioned for each person;
regarding that, he states the reason:
Because it possesses a specific form,
it is by nature distinct from any other form, as there is no scriptural authority for such a modification.
However, if additional persons were to be deposited in some single location— whether within the self or on one side— [it would be untenable].
For the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is modified into the form of fire;
it is extended by the person (*puruṣa*)—the meaning of the two scriptural passages being: "one should measure the fire with a bamboo as long as a person with upraised arms."
To the extent that this external aperture-appearance is brought forth for the sake of ease regarding the external, and for the two apertures in relation to the external object,
it is [perceived] by another from the perspective of the tame.
Leaving a space for the path of movement to the other side of the location of the sacrificial post-hole, he places the bamboo staff.

Having unfastened [the cord] from the eastern end—which is marked by the range of his vision at its limit—and having fastened it to the western end, he should draw a line toward the south and west until the edge.
This is the eighth section.

Having loosened the cord from the middle peg, having fixed the end of the bamboo against the hole of the last peg, and having placed the bamboo above and level with the line, one drives a peg into the hole of the last peg. Having fixed the middle hole of the bamboo against that peg and having established the other two [ends] at the ends of the line, one drives pegs into the two holes. (ĀpŚS 9.1a)

Having fastened one end of the bamboo to a stake on the south, and having placed the bamboo with its tip pointing south so that it rests upon the intersection of the upper lines, he drives a stake into the last hole.

Having fastened the middle hole of the bamboo to the two ends of that stake, and having positioned it so that it stands across the interval between the two lines, he drives stakes into the two holes at the very ends of those lines.
That square is a *puruṣa*. ĀpŚus_9.1b ||
And that person is four-cornered.
In this manner, he measures out four persons within himself, starting from the front and moving to the right.
In this manner, one should measure out the four fields of men (puruṣakṣetra) clockwise according to their respective positions within oneself:
a man on the right wing, a man at the tail, and a man on the left [wing]. ĀpŚus 9.2b.
On the right wing—that is, on the right side—having fastened the bamboo at the three middle [points], one proceeds with "the other two" and so forth as before; thus the square man is formed.
Likewise on the left wing—that is, on the left side—one fastens it at the same three middle points for the northern [wing].

Having fixed the middle hole of the bamboo rod against the western intermediate peg, laid the bamboo rod crosswise, and driven pegs into the two holes, one should release [the rod] from the northern pegs and draw a line counter-clockwise.
Releasing it from the southern peg, one should fix it against the northern peg at the height of a man's length and draw a line clockwise starting from the peg of the final hole.

Releasing the bamboo rod, fixing it against the middle peg, and placing the bamboo rod above the intersection of the lines behind, one should proceed as before with the final [hole] and so on; that is the tail.
"It is said: 'With the cubit, from the south, [he measures] the southern [side]'. (ĀpŚus 9.2c)

In this manner, one should extend the southern wing of the vimāna to the south and the northern wing to the north by one *aratni*; the transverse measurement (*tiryaṅbhānī*) of the two wings shall be one *aratni* plus one *puruṣa*, and the lateral measurement (*pārśvamānī*) shall be one *puruṣa*. Likewise, one should extend the tail to the rear by one *prādeśa* or a span (*vitasti*); its corresponding lateral measurement (*supārśvamānī*) shall be that *prādeśa* plus one *puruṣa*, and its transverse measurement (*tiryaṅbhānī*) shall be one *puruṣa*.

Alternatively, having laid a bamboo pole across a man’s height from the spine, with one end toward the east and the other toward the west, one should mark out the right shoulder from those two points; then, reversing the orientation, one marks out the two hips.
Having fixed another peg at a man’s length [from the previous one], he should move it southward along the southern hip and then lay out the northern hip;
as before, he should lay out the northern shoulder. (ĀpŚus 9.3b)
This has been explained. According to Karavinda’s commentary:
having released the bamboo from the other peg, having fixed another hole of the bamboo onto the middle peg, and having placed the bamboo directly above so that it is level with the upper line;
The *lekhāsamara* (meeting of the lines) is the intersection of the lines.

Having placed [the cord] close above that, one drives stakes into the final holes; having fixed the middle hole of the bamboo-cord (*veṇu*) upon that [middle stake], and having established the other two holes at the ends of the line, they drive stakes into the two holes. That becomes a square known as a *puruṣa*. In this manner, one should fashion four such *puruṣas* within oneself, proceeding clockwise.

In the west, having fixed a peg into the hole of the bamboo staff (*veṇu*) in this manner, and having placed the bamboo staff along the spine-line (*pṛṣṭhyā*) from behind, one should drive another peg into the two rear holes as well and construct a second *puruṣa* as before; likewise on the north side. Having marked the north-west and the north-east, he measures out two *puruṣas*. Leaving a passage behind the sacrificial post-hole (*yūpāvaṭa*), one should drive a peg into the spine-line, fix the hole of the bamboo staff into it, lay the bamboo staff along the spine-line, and [fix] two pegs into the two holes.
Having fixed the bamboo at the western peg into its hole and having laid it down along the *pṛṣṭhyā* line toward the west, one should fix two pegs.
Thus there are five pegs.
Having fixed the bamboo at the middle and eastern pegs and having marked [the ground] as before, one should make two *puruṣas*.

Having fixed the bamboo at the two penultimate pegs on the east, and having marked [the line], one should mark a man’s length on the southern wing; then, having fixed it at the two penultimate pegs on the north, one should mark a man’s length on the northern wing. But for the tail, having fixed the middle hole of the bamboo on the western peg and having placed the bamboo running north-south, one should drive a peg into the two holes, fix the bamboo across them, and having marked the west-north and west-south lines, one should make a man’s length.
Having done this, one extends the southern wing to the south by means of the cord.
On the northern side as well, he extends the tail toward the north by one span, a cubit, or even more, using a non-jeweled cord.
The word *vā* (or) has the sense of an alternative;
thus, here the measurement is by bamboo.
First of all, there are two bamboos.
Of those two, one is a man's length;
the other is equal to a diagonal cord of a man's length.
By means of these two, a passage for movement is left behind the sacrificial post and the pit for the foundation-stone.
A peg is fixed at the *pṛṣṭhyā* line;
then another peg is fixed the same distance behind it.

Having attached a bamboo rod of the measure of a diagonal (*akṣṇayāmātra*) to the middle peg, and having attached a rod of the measure of a man (*puruṣamātra*) to the front peg, one should draw out the southern shoulder-line from those two.

Having released [the cord] from the eastern peg at the distance of one *puruṣa* and fastened it to the western peg, one should drive pegs at the distance of half a *puruṣa* on both sides of the northern shoulder, as well as on both sides of the southern, northern, western, and central pegs; one should do the same for the tail and the hindquarters of the *puruṣa*.
Battle slays after unyoking— the encounter where the two lines fall into the gaps between the preceding and succeeding [parts],
and it is those very ends of the lines that he measures out.
On the *pṛṣṭhyā* line, the rear peg is at the western corner of the two eastern squares, and the eastern peg is at the eastern corner of the two western squares.
Having fixed a bamboo pole across the middle three of the five southern pegs, one proceeds with the phrase "by means of the two rear [pegs]," and so forth.
Having fastened [the cord] at the rear hole of the last two of the three western pegs, one should drive a stake into the middle hole.

In the same way for the two northern ones; then, having fastened a bamboo pole in the middle of the three middle holes of these five thus positioned, one should proceed with the northern ones, and so forth, as should be understood.
The *puruṣa* is in the north,
like the southern wing;
it is stated [to be] one *aratni*.
Having made a mark at the fifth *veṇu* from [the shoulder], one should extend the two wings by that measure; likewise, having made a mark at the tenth. He states another method for the tail:
"The *maṃsa* is the end of the *pṛṣṭhyā*; here there are two *veṇus* with apertures on both sides, measuring one *puruṣa* plus a fraction."

On the *pṛṣṭhyā* line, having driven three stakes at intervals of one *puruṣa*, and having fastened the cord with a special loop on the middle stake and the other end on the front stake, the point where the two ends meet at the outermost holes is the right shoulder (*dakṣiṇāṃsa*). Having reversed the process and fastened the cord at a distance of one *puruṣa* on the rear stake, the two hips (*śroṇī*) are marked as before; this is the left shoulder (*uttarāṃsa*). The same procedure applies to the wings and the tail.

The bamboo pole with its specific dimensions is one hundred and seventy fingers minus ten *tilas*. One should measure it either with a cord or with the bamboo pole itself, according to the method used for the *uttaravedi*. (ĀpŚus 9.4)

Or, having measured [the length] with one of the ropes as on the *uttaravedi*, he measures it behind with a bamboo for the sake of avoiding confusion. When there is an increase or decrease in the number of parts (*vidhā*) including the wings and tail, one should proceed by taking the seventh part of the measure as the representative unit of a man (*puruṣa*). (ĀpŚS 9.5)
When there is an increase in the number of parts, there are eight parts and so forth;
when there is a decrease in the number of parts, there are one part and so forth.
Among those, starting from one part up to seven parts, the bamboo by which one measures is such that its half-eighth part becomes the seventh constituent part.
That [space] stands in place of the person.
Having thus made it square and divided it as before, one should dwell [in the hall].
The mention of "with wings and tail" is for the purpose of establishing a single type [of hall].

When these [altars], such as the *śyena* and others, are being constructed, if they consist of one unit (*ekavidha*), one should divide that into fifteen parts, combine two portions to make a square, and then take the measurement using a bamboo rod of that size;
that serves as the substitute for a man (*puruṣa*).
This applies everywhere in the same manner.

Having made that field as many types [of units] as it possesses and having made it a perfect square, one should take its measure; for example, four thousand and eighty *tilas* (4080) constitute a *puruṣa*. The square of these is: one *koṭi*, sixty-six *niyutas*, four *ayutas*, six thousand, and four hundred (166,464,00). If it is of eight types, one should multiply by eight, add the first half, divide by fifteen, double the result, and take the square root;
that becomes the *puruṣa* of that [field].
In the case of diminution (*apacaya*), however, there is no conjunction with a half [of a foot],
because there is no such thing as a three-quarter foot.
Everything else is equal to accumulation (*upacaya*).
There is no fault if it is deficient or excessive by even half a sesame seed, because no specific distinction is observed.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
[The square root of] 4080, which is space (ākāśa), wind (vasu), sky (ambara), and Vedas (veda).
The sweet [number] increased by the lunar days (tithis) and divided by them;
the square root of the resulting increased value, when halved, is the measure of the Puruṣa during the period of increase, and that same value is the measure during the period of decrease.
It should always be present during both decline and growth...
Thus [it is said].
But has it not already been established that the *śyena* and other such sacrifices, consisting of one type [of brick] and so forth, must be constructed with curved wings and tails?

Therefore, what is the point of this great effort in demonstrating the reasons? This is true! It is on the basis of the premise that those consisting of one type and so forth must be constructed that, in certain cases, if those consisting of one type and so forth are to be constructed, they are then employed for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*).
Then, the hawks and others, being modifications of form and consisting of the nature of man, would rest upon those modified forms.

Just as hawks and others proceed by modifying the mere man-form into wings and tail according to the "seven-and-a-half-fold" rule, so too they would enter into the one-fold and other altars by modifying the man-form. In that case, when the one-fold and others possess wings and tail, this is the prescribed rule; thus, there is no fault even for the eight-fold and subsequent altars, as they are ordained through another method.
Because of the rule stating "in those with wings and tails," there are no single-fold and so forth in the *prauga* and other such altars;
some, however, maintain that there are eight-fold and so forth.
And it will be stated: "As much as the fire [is], so much is the *aratni* and *prādeśa*.
Others, however, explain that these do not exist in the one-fold and other [altars], nor in those involving reductions, because of the statement "as much as the *aratni* and *prādeśa*."
Karavinda’s Commentary: (He measures with a cord) means that,
having measured the fire-altar with a cord consisting of one or any other number of strands, he subsequently measures it with a bamboo for the sake of an invisible purpose.

According to the principle of the *uttaravedi*, just as the *uttaravedi* is measured by a yoke or by the steps of the sacrificer and then demarcated with a wooden pin (*śamyā*) for an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), so too here, after measuring with a cord, the measurement with a bamboo staff would be for an invisible purpose. Likewise, because the fire-altar (*agni*) is a modification of the *uttaravedi*, there should be a measurement with a bamboo staff and a wooden pin after measuring with a cord for an invisible purpose.

Regarding the *sapakṣa* (the symmetrical wings): in the case of fires other than the *prauga* and so forth—whether through addition (*abhyāsa*) starting from the eightfold fire, or through subtraction starting from the single-fold fire—the rule for the laying out of the *karas* (measuring rods) is stated as follows: "Having made the seventh *karas* of the sections (*vidhā*) the representative of the *puruṣa* (the man's measure), one should perform the layout.

Whichever [rod] makes the seventh of however many sections the fire has, that is the "seventh-of-the-sections *karas*" (*vidhāsaptamakaraṇī*). Having made that the representative of the *puruṣa*, one should perform the layout of the body, the wings, and the tail by means of it.

The meaning is as follows: if the fire-altar is of one kind, one should divide that single kind into fifteen parts, combine two of those parts, and having made them into a regular square, one should take its measurement and apply it in place of the *puruṣa*; with this [measurement], one should construct the body, wings, and tail.
One should proceed in exactly the same manner for those of two kinds and so forth.
Four thousand and eighty sesame seeds constitute a *puruṣa*.

One group of these [units] consists of one koṭi, six prayutas, six niyutas, four ayutas, six sahasras, and four hundred (16,646,400). If one multiplies this eightfold class of persons by eight, adds half of the original quantity, and divides that result by fifteen, the quotient is doubled and its square root is taken; that is the measure of the person.
However, in the case of decrease, because there is an absence of cubits and spans, there is no addition of half.
The other [type] possesses accumulation (*upacaya*).
Now, it was stated that for those consisting of a single type and so forth, there are no wings or tails; this is indeed correctly stated.
However, because they consist merely of the form of exertion (*vyāyāma*), this does not apply to those of a single type and so forth; it has been explained in that very context for this purpose.

And for the purpose of demonstrating that they possess a single-fold nature, there is therefore no absolute prohibition; even those [altars] consisting of a single-fold and so forth certainly have wings and tails.
Regarding this, they cite the following verse:
"The number [of breaths] consisting of ether, wind, sky, and the Vedas (400), increased by eight and divided by the lunar days (15)."
When that [affliction] has increased, one should seek its root through self-restraint; and when it is in decline or increasing, one should likewise investigate its cause.
Thus— according to the commentary of Sundararāja—
he measures with a cord.
In this view, the measurement of the bamboo is for an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), like the *śamyā* measure.
Now, he describes the ritual layout (*viharaṇa*) of those [altars] consisting of eight types and so forth, as well as those consisting of one type and so forth.
The fires are shaped like a winged bird with its tail, as well as square, shaped like a hawk, a heron, or a crane;
in these cases, there is a repetition of the various forms beginning with the eightfold one.
There is a reduction in the single-fold and subsequent types. The *vidhāsaptamakaraṇī* is the side-measure (*karaṇī*) of the seventh [fold] when all the folds are unified as one.
The side-measure of that portion of the fire-altar being built stands in the place of a *puruṣa*.
And that [measurement] has already been demonstrated in the very passage beginning with "of those starting from eightfold.
Here too, according to the view that the altar is reduced by one-third, it should be understood as "one-and-a-half times the eighth part of the side" (*vidhārdhāṣṭamakaraṇīm*).
The mention of reduction is for the sake of the *śyena-cit* (falcon-shaped altar) and others.

Because square altars (*caturaśra*) consisting of one type (*ekavidha*) and so forth lack wings and tails, the entry of the *puruṣa* was mentioned previously; now, its measurement (*viharaṇa*) is stated, and thus there is no redundancy.
Alternatively, the previous sūtra concerned the eightfold (*aṣṭavidha*) and other types as well as square altars.
There is a distinction, namely that [the altar] is common to both those consisting of a single brick and so forth, as well as to the Śyena and others.

By this it is understood that the Śyena-altar and the like, which are modifications by way of accessory qualities (guṇavikāra), occur even in altars of one brick and so forth, just as they do in those of seven bricks and so forth.
Furthermore, its status as belonging to another recensional branch (śākhāntarīyatva) has already been stated previously.

Precisely because that position must be accomplished with effort, the method of placing [the fire] in that very context will be stated: "As great as the fire is, including the *aratni* and the *prādeśa*," and so forth.
(Kapardibhāṣya on Āpastamba Śulbasūtra 9.6a): One should cause the eight ritual implements to be made by means of the fifth part of the person.
The remaining sense is: "We shall describe the making of the bricks.
One should have them made with a fifth part of a man's height (*aratni*).
Of those very [bricks], one side is one and a half [parts]; that is the second [type]. A fifth part of a man's height is one span (*prādeśa*) on one side; that is the third [type]. (ĀpŚus 9.6b)

Among those very bricks, some are one-and-a-half [units] on one side—that is, exceeding by half a unit. Their third *karaṇa* (instrumental measure) has a side-measure (*pārśvamānī*) of three *prādeśas* and a cross-measure (*tiryaṅbhānī*) of one *aratni*; this is the second *karaṇa*. For the third *karaṇa*, the side-measure is one *aratni* and the cross-measure is one *prādeśa*. This is that third *karaṇa*.
That fourth [measurement] is a span (prādeśa) on all sides; those fifteen-part bricks, being equal squares, constitute the fifth.

The bricks are eight finger-breadths [in size], and that is the fifth method. For what purpose is the inclusion of the term "perfectly square" here? It is for the sake of ensuring their inclusion even in those fires where the bricks are exclusively perfectly square.
