And he will state later: "The *aṇūka* bricks occupy the place of the fifteen-part bricks."
The *aṇūka* and the fifteen-part [brick] share the same subject matter.
[One should have the] instruments made; this is the Karavindīya commentary.

Now the measurements for making the bricks are stated: a standard *puruṣa* consists of five *aratnis*. By its fifth *aratni*—the word "fifth" being used in the singular to denote the class—is [the measurement taken].
The meaning is "by the fifth [finger]";
one should have it made by those skilled [craftsmen].
With four of those *aratnis*, the first [measure of] the hand is formed.
Of those—that is, of those very bricks made fivefold—those which on one side—in one part—are one and a half *aratnis* in length; their making is such that one should have them made as a second [set].
The phrase "of those very" is to be connected everywhere.
The third [construction] is that of those [boards] which have twenty-four finger-breadths on one side and twelve finger-breadths on the other; that is the third. This is the final [construction].
The construction of those [bricks] for which the measure is a span (prādeśa) on all sides is four-finger-breadths (caturtīrtha).
The inclusion of the term "on all sides" indicates that in some cases there is an inclusion of the term "span.
The fifth [brick] is equal.

Fifteen parts of a man are eight *aṅgulas*. The bricks measured by that [unit] are the *pañcadaśabhāgīyā* bricks; they are such that they are equal squares. The construction of these is the fifth [topic].
By the very mention of "equal squares," the *kāryā*, *ūkā*, and so forth, which are made from the *pañcadaśabhāgīyā*s, are already implied.
In that regard, it is understood that there is no requirement for the shape to be square in the east, north, or west.

For what purpose is the practice of numbering them as "second" and so forth? It is solely for the sake of an unseen spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭa*), as is observed in the case of the placement of bricks (*upadhāna*) and other such rites.
In the *Sundararājīyā* commentary, he now states the methods for making the bricks of the measured fire-altar:
"One should have the instruments made."
This single measuring instrument is one cubit (aratni) long, equal on all four sides.
Of these, the side-measure is thirty-six units, and the cross-measure is twenty-four units.
By means of this third part of the man’s measure, the half-bricks are thus formed.
On all sides, [the measurements] are eight finger-breadths. —
*Kapardibhāṣya*
The vertical measurement of the bricks should be made as five parts of the distance from one knee to the other. ĀpŚus 9.7a.
The height of the bricks should be one-fifth the height of the knees;
the knee measures thirty-two finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
One should construct [the height] with one-fifth of that, which is six finger-breadths plus thirteen sesame seeds.

This is indeed for the bricks of the Mahāgni; having prescribed the constituent parts of the Mahāgni according to their respective rules, [one proceeds] with half [the measure] of the Nākasads and the Pañcacūḍās. ĀpŚus_9.7b.

One should construct the height of the gods dwelling in heaven (nākasad) and those with five topknots (pañcacūḍa) as three and seven-sevenths of an aṅgula, using half of the measure consisting of five knee-units.
Whatever part of the bricks being baked should sink down due to the filling material (purīṣa), that one should fill up again, because the quantity of the filling material is not fixed. ĀpŚus 9.8.
As the bricks are being baked, there may be a reduction in both their height and their dimensions; one should fill that [gap] with *purīṣa* (clay-filler).
Why? He says: because the *purīṣa* has no fixed dimension—the bricks have a fixed dimension, whereas the *purīṣa* has no fixed dimension.
Since there is no rule stating "this much *purīṣa* must be thrown in," it is to be filled by that very material.
Ninth Section:
Karavindīya Commentary.
[Regarding the phrase] "upwards"—let it be so.
One should make the height—the elevation—of all bricks equal to five times the knee;
according to Bodhāyana, the knee measures thirty-two finger-breadths (*aṅguli*) in the context of finger-measurements.
Its fifth part is six finger-breadths, four and a half *tilas*, and one-half of a *tila*.
The height of the bricks shall be commensurate with that [measurement].

One building for the first time should build [the altar] knee-high; since there is a convergence of the two scriptural injunctions—"there are five layers" and "one should build it knee-high"—and because no specific rule is heard regarding the height, it should be equal [to the knee]; thus, the bricks should be knee-high, with the knees being the fifth [layer].
The navel is double the height of the knees.
The mouth is three times the size of the knee.
There are one thousand bricks reaching up to the knees; two thousand for those reaching up to the navel, arranged in two layers;
and three thousand for those reaching up to the mouth, arranged in three layers.
In all those cases, since no specific measurement is heard, the height of the bricks is intended to be exactly up to the knees.

Although the phrase "one should have [the altar] made of bricks" continues to apply here, the mention of "those two" again is for the purpose of ensuring that the bricks of the Gārhapatya hearth also reach up to the knees.
By half—of the *ṣaṣ* (six).
One should cause [the altar] to be made with five parts by half and [another] half;
these are the specific mantras for the placing of the *nākasat* bricks. They are to be placed with those [mantras].

The five *paḍhceṣṭakās* are to be made knee-high, as is seen from the statement, "He places the *uttarā nākasadbhyaḥ*," which indicates their relative position of upper and lower within a single layer (*prastāra*). Since the height of the altar is achieved by means of bricks alone— such as being knee-high— the *purīṣa* (filling soil) is placed upon them for the purpose of leveling the altar and for its further growth.

When a reduction—meaning a depletion—occurs due to the baking of the bricks that have been prepared for the purpose of cooking, one should fill that [space] with loose earth (purīṣa); by this, the bricks do not become defective, because such shrinkage is unavoidable, as indicated by the scriptural mark: "O Mitra, cook this! Furthermore, drying by means of wind and sun is indeed a form of baking.
For this very reason, when the brick has become deficient in both length and breadth due to the process of baking, one should fill it with loose soil (*purīṣa*) at the time of laying it down.
Why? Because the quantity of loose soil is unrestricted;
for there is no fixed rule that "only this much loose soil must be thrown in."
Therefore, for that which has been diminished due to baking, there must be filling with *purīṣa*.
Clay moistened with water is *purīṣa*;
with that, one should fill up the deficiency of the bricks.
In the *Sundararājīyā* commentary:
"One should cause [the knee] to be made upright;
'The knee is thirty finger-breadths [in height],' so says Āgniveśya."
Its fifth [section] is six finger-breadths wide; "It is six finger-breadths in height," so says Kātyāyana;
and by half [of that], it is three finger-breadths.
This is an illustration for all those [grains] that are ripening and drying;
Bodhāyana says: "That which diminishes through drying and ripening."
The ninth section:
Regarding the placement of the *kapardikṣāṣya* bricks, he places ten half-bricks on the front part of the body facing westward, and ten on the back part facing eastward. (ĀpŚus 10.1a)

In the front part of the body, one lays down ten half-bricks (*ardheṣṭakā*) extending westward, each thirty-six finger-breadths in length. In the very back part of the body, one lays down that same number of those same bricks extending eastward.
Five [half-bricks] are placed at each of the tips of the wings; at the junctions of the wings, there are *viśaya* bricks, which occupy half the space of a brick on the wings. (ĀpŚS 10.1b)
At the two tips of the wings, there are five [bricks] each extending southward and five extending northward;
and there are five *viśaya* bricks extending both northward and southward.

By the word "brick" (*iṣṭakā*), only those consisting of five parts (*pañcabhāgīyā*) are intended, and not the half-and-a-quarter bricks (*adhyardha*), because of the indicative mark [in the scripture]: "the points of union are even though reversed."
Five by five [bricks] are placed on the right and left sides, facing south and north respectively. (ĀpŚus 10.1c)
There should be five, five, and one and a half [bricks] extending southward and northward; they are to be laid down in such a way that only a space of about a *pradeśa* remains near [the center].
This is the Karavindīya commentary on the *upacīḥ*.
At the time of laying the foundation, one should lay down the bricks produced for the second layer on oneself at the eastern end;
they should run westward, that is, toward the west, and northward.
These same bricks [are then laid] from behind, running eastward on oneself at the western end; these are the very same ones.
The five [fingers] are those very same ones; the two eastern lines are the wings, and the objects of perception are at their junctions.
The dissolution of the wings (*pakṣāpyaya*): the roots of the wings (*pakṣamūla*) are the objects of dispute (*viṣayāḥ*), for they rest upon both the self and the wing.
He explains how much of these rests on the self and how much on the wing:
"Of these, at the end... (*tāsām antaḥ*).
Of those rows, those measuring half a brick are placed on the two wings;
"the self" (ātman) means by a space of one cubit (aratni), that is, the wing.
There are two rows facing east.

There are five on each side of the tail; five are directed northward and five southward, with the two eastern rows facing south and the two northern rows facing north. To ensure there is no division at the northern sūtra, it will be demonstrated that the region of the tip of the tail is not to be laid out separately. Therefore, these [bricks] are to be placed starting from the tip.
In the commentary of Sundararāja,
"pratyacīḥ" means extending toward the west;
"udīcaḥ" refers to [the lines] in the self (ātman) itself.
These [senses] are directed upward, for otherwise the five would be impossible;
they rest upon the side and within the self, thus they are called *viṣayas* (objects);
for they indeed measure a cubit (*aratni*) within the self.
Having left a space of one *prādeśa* at the front,
and having placed a *prādeśa* at the tail, one should cover the entire fire-altar with bricks measuring one-fifth of a side (*pañcamabhāgīyā*). (ĀpŚus 10.2)
One should complete the count with fifteen parts. ĀpŚus 10.3.

Having placed a span (prādeśa) at the tail [of the altar], whatever remains near the self [the body of the altar]—that remaining portion is a span; here, there are two half-bricks in the middle, and six spans on both sides. As for the question, "How can it be said that one should place a span when an increase by a cubit (vitasti) has been prescribed?"—it is replied: although an increase by a cubit was indeed prescribed, nevertheless, because another means of construction is enjoined, the area of a span alone is to be covered with bricks; therefore, that which was set aside as being merely a finger's breadth must be filled up with *puruṣa*-bricks. It is precisely to demonstrate this point that it is stated, "having placed a span."
"Everything is covered by fire-bricks"—meaning one should cover half of the altar with fifty-one bricks as prescribed in the Sūtra, two of which are half-sized.
One hundred and ten five-part bricks lie there;
together with the previous ones, they total one hundred and sixty-eight.
Regarding the term "fifteenfold" (*pañcadaśī*): nine fifteenfold bricks lie within a single fifth-part field.

Having divided four fifth-part bricks into nine parts, they are to be inserted anywhere among the fifteenfold bricks; however, for the sake of ease in placement according to the ritual formulas (*mantra*), the term "span" (*prādeśa*) is used.
In the second row of the body (*ātman*), there are eighteen, excluding two from the middle.
And in the eighth row there are eighteen;
thus, the arrangement consists of two hundred [squares].

Karavinda’s Commentary: One should place that area of one prādeśa which exceeds the puruṣa in the tail; having placed it there, one should cover the entire fire-altar with bricks measuring a fifth part.
This is the intention: when the altar is being covered starting from the front with bricks measuring five *vitastis* (finger-breadths), a space of one *prādeśa* remains at the tip.

Considering that many defects would arise in the tail (*puccha*) if it were filled with these *yogā* bricks, the Teacher [Āpastamba] has prescribed that one should cover it starting from the tip, beginning with the placement of a *prādeśa* in the tail.
Alternatively, the meaning is: "having placed a *prādeśa* in the tail"—that is, having joined it to the tail—having acted in such a way that the *prādeśa* does not protrude separately from the tail.
Alternatively, having placed a span (prādeśa) upon the tail—that is, having set it down and fixed it there—as in the phrase "having laid down six of those as the primary ones";
or alternatively, one should place the span that was at the tip at the root of the tail. One should lay them down on both sides by reversing the division.

The meaning of this is as follows: insofar as the mode of expression is intended to ensure that there is no difference whatsoever, its purport is that one should not treat the tip of the tail as being separate from the tail itself.
In all these positions, a *prādeśa*’s worth remains unattached in the middle of the tail;
one should place half-bricks measuring a *prādeśa* on both sides of that.

Furthermore, regarding the subsequent layer, because of the statement, "As the two wings were in the first layer, so is the tail," he will declare an inversion of the *adhyardha* bricks obtained by extension at the base of the tail: "The *apyayas* are also inverted.
This would be consistent only if the placement were done in this manner;
otherwise, it would result in a contradictory meaning and be purposeless.

Therefore, this alone must be accepted as the meaning of the passage: "having placed a span [of brick] on the tail. Now, one might ask: how can the entire fire-altar be covered with fifteen-part bricks? It is said in reply: here, when the altar is being covered with fifth-part bricks over its whole extent without displacing the bricks already laid down, it becomes impossible for those [fifteen-part bricks] to fit in certain parts. In such cases, the expressive power (*śakti*) of verbs—which convey their own meaning—is a necessary auxiliary; for even by a hundred statements, it is impossible to enjoin a meaning that cannot be conceived. This is because it is impossible to cover [the altar] with square [fifteen-part bricks] in those specific locations.
In accordance with all the words understood first, the term "pañcamabhāgīyā" (the fifth-part bricks), which is of secondary importance, must be explained as intending abundance.

Therefore, the inclusion of the *prādeśas* here is for the purpose of ensuring that the covering is accomplished even by those [bricks] belonging to this context that may arise along with their respective auxiliaries;
this principle is to be accepted there.
Even though those [bricks] located there are already attached, what is the purpose of covering [the gaps]? Are the half-bricks (*ardheṣṭakā*) produced by this rule not employed anywhere else?
By the force of the instruction alone, their application must be made here for filling the number and for covering, as appropriate.
Furthermore, he will state the general rule (*paribhāṣā*): "Whatever becomes square or triangular, one should cover it with half-bricks or quarter-bricks (*pādeṣṭakā*)."
Or rather, the laying out here should be as follows:
within this self [the altar], in the interval between the two joints, there are forty bricks of the fifth part; of these, ten are in front and ten are behind.
There are twenty on the two wings and ten in the tail.
These aforementioned one hundred and ten *pañcamabhāgīyā* bricks consist of fifty half-bricks, four half-bricks, and two *prādeśa*-lengths, totaling one hundred and sixty-six bricks.

By such statements as "One building [the altar] for the first time should build it with a thousand [bricks]," the numbers beginning with a thousand will be prescribed for each fire-altar (*agni*) brick.
Furthermore, it will be demonstrated in that very context that these numbers vary according to each construction (*citi*) and each layer (*prastāra*).
He explains how that number, one thousand, is to be accomplished here.
One should fill five rows with fifteen-part bricks measuring eight finger-breadths each.

What number is to be filled here? Is it the number pertaining to the whole collection, or that pertaining to the individual layers (*prastāra*), since there is no distinction made? It is not the number pertaining to the whole collection, because of the immediate sequence [of the instruction] and because of the rule of two hundred [bricks] for each layer. Therefore, it is determined by the force of this statement that the number to be filled pertains specifically to the layers; thus, for the purpose of filling the number, the removal or shifting of some of the covering bricks is appropriate as the case may require.
In this context, thirty-four [units] must be produced in order to achieve the completion of two hundred *prastāras*.
This is accomplished by removing some of the hidden [bricks] and replacing them with the laying down of *yogya* bricks.
In that regard, nine fifteen-part bricks lie within a single fifth-part field.

Regarding the lack of restriction on the location for each individual placement, once those [bricks] have been removed and their placement is to be performed, the rule for the restriction of the removal and placement locations is stated for the sake of facilitating the placement with mantras.
In that case, there are ten rows (rītis) on the stone; there, having removed two from the middle rows, one should deposit eighteen fifteen-part bricks (pañcadaśabhāgīyā) there.
Having removed them from the very ends of those same two rows, one should deposit eighteen [bricks].
There are four rows extending eastward in the tail; having removed the ends of the two middle [rows], one should lay down four half-bricks (*ardheṣṭakā*) facing north.

In this way, the layer (*prastāra*) of two hundred [bricks] is completed. Regarding this, some place ten *prādeśa*-length bricks at the tip of the tail and cover them with fifth-part bricks (*pañcamabhāgīyā*); however, because that would result in the pointlessness of the contrary statement and the occurrence of a flaw (*maita*), they should not be laid down in such a manner.

Furthermore—had the laying down of the *prādeśa*-bricks at the tip of the tail also been intended, then [the text] would have stated even more clearly, "fifteen *pāda*-bricks on the tips of the wings and fifteen at the tip of the tail," or simply "at the tip of the tail.
But it was not stated thus.
Therefore, it is established that the sequence of laying is exactly as previously described.
According to the commentary of Sundararāja:
one should lay down those bricks by which the remaining space of one span (*prādeśa*) from the tail can be filled without leaving any gaps.
In that regard, there are two bricks measuring one span each on the two sides, and in the middle, four half-bricks (*ardheṣṭakā*) oriented toward the north.
This indeed is the purpose of performing the proportional reduction (*prādeśakaraṇa*). Therefore, it is carried out by means of the absence of such reduction.
When the remaining fire-altar is covered with bricks measuring one-fifth of a side, there are one hundred and sixty-six bricks.
In a space devoid of the *aratni* and *prādeśa*, there are one hundred and fifty bricks.
Therein, in the northern part of the body, there are nine rows.
Among those, in the middle row of the body, having removed four central bricks, fifty-four are to be laid down.
In both cases, having removed two fifth-iṣṭakas from the tips of the tails, four half-iṣṭakas are to be laid down extending northward;
thus the layer consists of two hundred [iṣṭakas].

On the next layer, he places ten bricks of one-and-a-half units each on his own body, eight with their heads toward the east and extending northward on the right side, and ten on the left side extending southward. (ĀpŚus 10.4a)
In the body, he places ten bricks and a half on the right side, extending northward; in the body itself, on the left side, he places ten bricks and a half, extending southward.
As were the two wings in the first layer, so are the tail; as was the tail, so are the two wings, though reversed at the point of convergence.
At the tip of the tail, there are one and a half [squares] extending eastward;
on the right wing, there are five extending westward from the rear and five extending eastward from the front;
and six extend westward.

And on the northern side, there are likewise five [lines] extending eastward and five extending westward; at the junction of the tail, there are five extending eastward and five extending westward, each measuring one and a half [units].
At the end of the puccha, five bricks with an additional half-measure are laid out lengthwise;
their halves, measuring the size of a half-brick, are placed upon the body (ātman).
In the same way, they are also reversed at the end of the puccha.
In front of them, five half-iṣṭakās are placed facing north.
One should cover the entire fire-altar with iṣṭakās that constitute a fifth part.
One should complete the count with fifteen parts. ĀpŚus 10.6a.
This has been explained.
As before, there is a two-hundredfold array (*prastāra*).
[End of] Karavindīya-vyākhyā.
On the second layer, one should place ten bricks of the measure of one and a half [bricks] in the southern part of oneself and ten in the northern part.
Just as the two wings were laid out in the first layer, so too are they at the tail;
just as the tail was laid out, so too are they on the two wings.
This is what is meant: at the tip of the tail and at the joint of the tip of the tail, five [bricks] measuring one and a half [units] each are to be placed;
on the two sides of the wings, however, those measuring one and a half [units] are to be placed. Regarding this, he states a specific rule: "they are reversed at the junction."

Since it would follow—by virtue of the extension (atideśa) from the case of the tail-end—that those bricks measuring one and a half [aratnis] which were prescribed for the body would instead measure only one aratni at the tail, and those measuring half a brick would instead measure only one brick at the tail, he says:
"In this case, they should be reversed; that is to say, those measuring half a brick should be in the body, and those measuring one aratni should be in the tail.
And the purpose of this is the absence of division (bhedābhāva), as was stated in the previous arrangement (prastāra).
In this case, as everything from the front part onwards is being concealed within oneself, when one reaches the end of the tail, a span remains in front of the space occupied by the *puruṣa*-measure.

Since it is impossible to use bricks measuring a fifth part there, five half-sized bricks (*pañcārdheṣṭakā*) should be laid down facing north so that there may be no gap; the reason for their placement has been stated.

Here, within the self (ātman), in the middle, there are sixty-five fifth-parts (pañcamabhāgīyās) and five half-parts; on the two wings, twelve fifth-parts each; and on the tail, fifteen. Thus, these total one hundred and four fifth-parts, five half-parts, and fifty-four adhyardha-parts.
These [verses] are sixty-three and one hundred; here, the number thirty-seven is to be completed.
In this case, having removed five [bricks] from the self in both wings and four fifth-parts from the tail, one should lay down thirty fifteen-part bricks;
having removed five in the middle of the eastern row on the self, one should lay down ten half-ṣṭakās facing north; thus is the two-hundred-brick layering.
In the commentary of Sundararāja:
"Likewise, on the other side, there is the tail; here too, there are five and a half [units] for each of these two."

On the sides, there are five and a half [bricks] each; it should be understood that when the span (aratni) increases, there are six each. Those which are laid down at the junction of the tail (puccha) have the size of half-bricks (ardheṣṭakā) in the body (ātman), while in the tail they are of the measure of a span.
And this applies when there is an increase in the width;
otherwise, if the tail consisted only of half-bricks,
one would not fill the entire fire-altar.
As before, having removed four or six bricks from the middle of the *ātman*, there shall be nine or eight *aṅgulas* in the place of each one.
In the case of using a *aratni* and a *prādeśa*, five half-bricks (*ardheṣṭakā*) oriented northwards are to be placed prior to the points where the tail (*puccha*) and the *āpyaya* meet.
In the *ātman*, following the previous method, having removed the five middle ones, one should place ten half-bricks oriented northwards.
Thus, there are two hundred [bricks].
However, in the absence of the *aratni* and *prādeśa*, there are two hundred minus two, namely one hundred ninety-eight, by means of fifty-four bricks each divided into five parts.
Having removed one fifth-brick from each of the two sides of the tail, four half-bricks (*ardheṣṭakā*) are placed extending toward the east.
In this manner, there are two hundred [bricks]. According to the Kapardibhāṣya:
one should pile them in an alternating fashion for as many layers (prastāra) as one intends to construct.
This has been explained.
There are five layers (*citayaḥ*). "He piles on with five fillings (*purīṣa*)," [it is said]; thus, the layer ends with the filling, because the filling is a distinct entity. (ĀpŚus 10.7)
The loose soil (purīṣa) is for the purpose of joining the bricks;
therefore, the layering (citi) ends with that.
Because it serves that purpose, it is included by the mention of that [term].
One building the fire-altar for the first time should pile it knee-deep and consisting of a thousand bricks.
He who piles first should pile [the fire-altar] knee-high and numbering one thousand;
since this injunction refers specifically to the Mahāgni, the Śālāmukhīya and the Dhiṣṇiya hearths are not included within the count of one thousand,
nor do they possess the quality of being knee-high.
The second [altar] is two thousand [bricks] high, reaching up to the navel; the third is three thousand, reaching up to the mouth; each subsequent one is larger than the preceding. ĀpŚus 10.8b.
One piling the second [altar] to a height of two thousand [bricks], measuring the navel;
one piling the third, measuring the mouth;
the third is three thousand [bricks], each subsequent one being larger than the preceding.
Our own Śruti states: "One who piles the second [altar] with a height of two thousand [bricks] reaching up to the navel;
one who piles the third reaching up to the mouth;
and [one who piles it] reaching up to the neck with three thousand."
"It is known from scripture: 'One who desires heaven should pile it large, vast, and immeasurable. (Āpastamba Śulbasūtra 10.8c)
One should take progressively higher food;
it is superior by way of its method of practice and by its great elevation.
In terms of its extensive scale,
it is immeasurable compared to [texts] such as the *Sahasra*.
Because of the statement "one who desires heaven" in the *Āgnikalpa* and because of the mention of "the Vājasaneyika" [in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*], there is an option between them.
The commentary on the Karavimandīya has been completed.

Now, one might object: "In what is called 'alternation' (*vyatyāsa*), when a certain kind of piling has been performed in a particular layer (*prastāra*), in the layer immediately following it, a different kind is piled—namely, those same kinds [of bricks] but from another direction and with long sides.

And there is no purpose served by the absence of difference; since that [absence of difference] is already established here simply by the teacher's practice, why is it stated that 'one should pile with alternation'? It is replied: The statement regarding alternation is so that the doubt of those of dull intellect—that there might be no fixed rule for the layers above and above regarding the rule of alternating piling as taught by the author of the Sūtra in two other instances of layering—may not arise. Thus, the mention of alternation is made.

Furthermore, even after the mantras have been applied, if a displacement is observed through negligence, there arises—out of a desire to avoid that—the possibility of shifting those very items already placed, as occurs in common worldly practice. Since this is seen to lead to defects, as expressed in the passage, "That Indra pulled up the brick; they were indeed scattered," the statement regarding the transposition is intended for the purpose of avoiding such displacement by ensuring that the bricks remain in their fixed positions without obstruction, as determined at the time of laying them with the cord (*śulba*) by those skilled in the cord. This applies to the five-fold and six-fold [arrangements].
"Jalādrā pṛt" means "moist with water.
"Abhyūhana" means "smearing.
Having laid down each layer of the altar (citi), one should smear it with clay moistened with water.
By two statements, it should be understood that one *citi* (layer) extends up to the placement of the *purīṣa* (filling soil);
it does not mean [the layer] alone.
This is because the *purīṣa* has a different purpose; "purpose" (*artha*) here means the objective or function.
"Antarā" means "difference";
the meaning is that because the purposes are different.
The purpose of the layers (*citayaḥ*) is one thing, and the purpose of the loose earth-fillings (*purīṣas*) is another.
The purpose of the loose soil (purīṣa) is distinct from its function in making the layers (citīḥ) reach the height of the knees;
that purpose is the drying, baking, and filling of the gaps in the bricks, as well as their mutual adhesion.
For this very reason, the quantity of the loose soil is not fixed.
Furthermore, there is no authoritative basis for the claim that the avoidance of a reduction in size and mutual cohesion are achieved by these specific amounts of loose soil (*purīṣa*).
Therefore, the amount of loose soil is indefinite;
hence it is said that "the layer ends with the loose soil."
And thus it is heard in scripture: "He covers [it] with soil; therefore, the bone is covered by flesh.
The meaning of this is as follows: just as the bones, which constitute parts of the body, are capable of performing the functions of the body only when they are indeed covered by flesh.

Thus, the bricks, which constitute the constituent parts, are capable of performing the function of the fire-altar (*agnikārya*) only when covered on all sides with loose soil (*purīṣa*). Therefore, the layering (*citi*) extends up to the final covering of soil.
Furthermore, if the application of loose soil were for its own sake (and not for the sake of the altar), then the fire-altar would exceed the prescribed measurements such as being knee-deep.
Therefore, the very purpose has already been stated.

By this observation of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "they become ten" and "they become twelve," it is established that they have a single purpose, so that no suspicion of the *cit* and the *purīṣa* having different purposes may arise. This is understood.
In this context, there are three scriptural injunctions prescribing the height [of the altar], beginning with: "One building for the first time should build it knee-high";
likewise, there are three scriptural injunctions prescribing the number of bricks for the fire-altar, beginning with: "One should build it with a thousand [bricks]".
"Knee-high" means measuring up to the knees; "navel-high" means measuring up to the navel; "mouth-high" means measuring up to the mouth.
A *sāhasra* is measured by the number one thousand; a *dvisāhasra* is measured by two thousands;
a *trisāhasra* is measured by three thousands.
The rules concerning dimensions depend on their accomplishment;
the rules concerning numbers depend on their substratum.
These have been recited in sequence by being combined through mutual dependence, like the proverb of the lost horse and the burnt chariot.

"Greater" (jyāyāṃsam) means by way of superior methods such as crushing (mardana) and other excellent treatments; "excellent" (utkṛṣṭaiḥ) refers to those things which are to be administered (saṃsarjanīyaiḥ). "Great" (mahāntam) is in terms of height (utsedhataḥ); "vast" (bṛhantam) is in terms of dimension (parimāṇataḥ); "immeasurable" (aparimitam) is said in terms of number. Regarding number and so forth, it is immeasurable because it exceeds the limited measure; Kātyāyana states that for the measurement [of the body], a treatise of a thousand [verses] is the authority.
However, this is especially so for one who desires heaven.
However, for one who has no desire [for specific results], it is indeed obligatory.

Since it is stated, "for one desiring heaven," and because of the statement in the *Agnikalpa*, "this is according to the Vājasaneyins," there is an option regarding the two-thousand-brick altar and the others.
Furthermore, in the Taittirīyaka, it is heard in the scripture: "as high as the neck."
Both [expressions] have exactly the same meaning,
because there is no injunction for an interval between the height of the bricks and the construction [of the altar],
and also because of the Brāhmaṇa statement: "For the head and neck are the same."
Moreover, because "neck" (*grīvā*) and "mouth" (*āsya*) are seen to be synonyms;
furthermore, the synonymy of "neck" and "mouth" is observed in common usage—as in *daśāsya* and *daśagrīva*.
Therefore, the two words have the same meaning.
In the commentary of Sundararāja,

it is stated that the bricks for the sacrificial mound (sthāṇḍila) are made of earth free from impurities, while the filling soil (purīṣa) is intended for the purpose of joining those [bricks] together.
Therefore, because their purposes are distinct, it does not fall under a different category of number.
[The term] *jānudaghnīm* means "knee-deep"; *ajyāyāṃsam* means "not greater"; *sāhasram* means "having a measure of one thousand.
In the cases of *dvisāhasram* and *trisāhasram*, the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs according to the rule *pūrvapadāt*.
"Successively higher" refers to the fourth [dhyāna] and above.
Regarding this, he cites a Brāhmaṇa as authority:
"The Great One is not fully known."
"Great" by means of the practice of [multiplying] the height;
"immeasurable" and "vast" by means of the measure of the thigh.
On this point, Bodhāyana says: "Some authorities record that the practice of the height-measure for the knee is [to be calculated] by a twenty-fourth part."
In the *Kapardibhāṣya*:
In a two-thousand-brick altar, there are two layers; in a three-thousand-brick altar, there are three layers. From the fourth addition onwards, the measurement of the bricks is constant. (ĀpŚus 10.9)
And it is known: "Having piled a larger [altar], one should not pile a smaller one. (ĀpŚus 10.10)
This has been explained by the [very] words [of the text].
Regarding the phrase "the fourth": here, the measurement of the bricks is stated to be three thousand;
indeed, it is fixed at exactly three thousand.
It should not be said that there is a return like that of the army, because no other [path] is prescribed.
To demonstrate this very point, he cites the scripture, saying: "It is known."
"Having piled the larger [altar]—either two thousand or three thousand [bricks]—one should not pile the smaller—one thousand; this is the prohibition.
Likewise, having piled [an altar] of seven hundred and fifty or eight hundred and fifty bricks, those ranging from the one-fold up to the half-fold should not be piled.
Thus, in the commentary on the Āpastamba Sūtra by Kapardisvāmin.
The third chapter in the section known as the Śulba-praśna. Karavinda’s Commentary:
He states that an excess in height does not occur when there is multiplicity of the floor-plans (prastāra).
In the Dviṣāhasra fire-altar, there are two layers; the spreading of the loose earth (purīṣa) is performed silently. Regarding those [layers], the rule is:
"He spreads the loose earth upon them"; this applies to the *gaṇḍa*, the *nākṣa*, and other characteristics of the layering (*citi*).
Regarding the four measures to be employed—
in the applications beginning with the fourth application— the three-thousandfold [mantra] mentioned immediately above is constant; the meaning is that it is not less than that, and so forth.

[Objection: Surely, by the very meaning of the preceding rule, it will always be three thousand [bricks] starting from the fourth layer; for what purpose is this stated? [Response: It is said: if this were not stated, then the repetition [of the previous number] as in the case of an army (*anīka*) would result.
Alternatively, since the increase is based on the second and third [layers], it might follow that there would be only one thousand [bricks] in the fourth layer and those following.
Therefore, this is stated: "The measurement of the bricks is constant."
The scripture expands upon this very point:
"O wise one, [know] the greater as having a larger measure and the lesser as having a smaller measure."
Having prepared either a two-thousandfold or a three-thousandfold altar, one should not pile up a thousandfold one;
rather, one should pile up only a three-thousandfold one.

Regarding this, there are verses: "In this context, having laid down a span at the tail" is what is prescribed in the Sūtra; that [prescription] is for the sake of non-differentiation, prohibiting a separate measurement at the tip of the tail.

Since there would be many divisions in the tail because of the difference in the method for the foremost part, the construction does not begin from the tail; rather, it should proceed starting from the tip of the tail.
Likewise, upon that foundation, one should then cover the area that remains in excess of the base with four and a half *prādeśas*.
In the context of dissolution, a contrary statement would thus be meaningful:
"They would not be a span in size at the end, because they possess many divisions."
Where those materials assigned for covering lack the capacity [to perform that function],
there the covering should be provided by other materials available on the spot that possess the necessary capacity.
Since the instruction "cover it" applies to all types of fire-altars,
therefore the *pañcamabhāgīyā* brick is used for the purpose of the hands and arms.
In various instances, the re-performance of both the placement of the pillow and the recitation of the transposed formula is caused solely by the absence of any difference [in the ritual action].
Since the reversal [of the order] is established by worldly convention, he exerts effort toward that end;
therefore, it is understood that even the non-breaking of the bricks was not tolerated by him.
Since this [text] merely restates a number and then prescribes the completion [of the sequence],
we consider that equality applies to the entire scope of the *prastāra*.

If there is a deficiency, one should fill it with those [syllables] prescribed, because equality resides in the locus; for if there is an excess, there would be a lack of sequence, as all expansions are equal on every side.
Thus ends the third chapter in the Śulbadīpikā composed by Karavindasvāmin;
[this is] the commentary by Sundararāja on the two-thousand-brick [altar] with three layers.
At each subsequent layering, the loose earth (purīṣa) is intended for the purpose of joining;
it is piled up with mantras,
beginning from the fourth layer, according to the prescribed measure.

The three-thousandfold [fire-altar] alone is always the superior one; it is understood from the injunction "one should pile it" that in all fires, the two sides— the southern and the northern— must be laid down as exactly equal.
Likewise, [it applies] to the western and eastern sides.
As he says: "There are ten and a half bricks in front, ten behind, eight on each of the two feet, and four *pakṣāgrīyā* bricks on each of the two tips of the wings," and so forth.
Regarding this, Baudhāyana says: "Agni indeed possesses the nature of an animal; just as in an animal, that which is the right rib-bone is the left of the other side," and so forth.
And this applies when such a possibility exists; as it is said: "From either the second or the fourth [set], thirty-six [bricks] are joined together one by one, and one from the fifth.

All the *prastāras* (arrangements) consist of exactly two hundred [bricks]. This is because of the statement regarding the completion of the number for each *prastāra*, because of the mention of only two *prastāras* in the case of the chariot-wheel (*rathacakra*), and because of the statement in the *Śyenaciti*: "This is a two-hundred-fold *prastāra*. Therefore, the *uḍā* bricks and the *nākasad* bricks should be counted together as one.
Bodhāyana, however, says: "The completion of the count occurs on the fifth layer; there are two hundred arrangements (prastāras).
One should understand that the nākasads are equal in number to the five coḍās."
The tenth section;
thus ends the third chapter in the *Śulbapradīpa*, a commentary on the *Āpastamba-Śulbasūtra* by Sundararāja.
The Commentary of Kapardin;

now the fourth chapter. It is known from scripture: "One should pile the fire-altar with square bricks. They are equal squares because the word lacks any qualifying adjunct. (Āpastamba Śulba Sūtra 11.1)

The meaning of this scriptural statement is now deliberated upon: does it refer to squares in general, whether equal or unequal, or only to those that are equal? Why? Because no distinction is mentioned;
no specific qualification is heard in the text.
Therefore, when the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is reached that it refers to squares without distinction, it is replied: only equal squares are to be taken.
Why? Because the word lacks an accompanying term (*upapada*).

Where no such term is heard—such as *dīrgha* (long) or *viṣama* (uneven)—the primary meaning prevails because even squares are primarily "four-sided" (*samacaturaśra*). Therefore, the cognition first arises regarding that which is the primary sense; for that which is thus understood constitutes its meaning. In other cases, the sense is secondary (*gauṇa*).

Therefore, it is established that they should be laid down with pieces that are exactly four finger-breadths square, and not with those measuring one and a half [finger-breadths]. It is known from tradition that they may be a foot in measure, or an elbow in measure, or the size of a thigh-bone, or the size of a small joint. (ĀpŚus 11.2)
There are these four measures;
he explains them as follows:
a four-part [measure] is a *maṇūka*; a fifth-part [measure] is a *aratni*; likewise, it is the size of a thigh-bone.
The word *aṇūka* [denotes] the fourth part of speech;
the *aratni* [denotes] the fifth.
Likewise—in that same manner—the thigh-bone [denotes] the sixth.
"Six-part bricks," according to another Śulba [text]; a quarter-brick is one-quarter of a measure. (ĀpŚus 11.3b)
In that case, one may act according to one's desire, because the meaning of the word is the object [of the injunction]. (ĀpŚus 11.4)

In another treatise, the designation "pāda" is established as meaning "one-fourth. By the word *pāda*, both a fourth part of a measurement and a fourth part of a field are understood. That which has a *pāda* as its measure is called *pādamātrī*.
Since the word *pāda* (quarter) is a relative term, it denotes both a quarter of a *puruṣa* and a quarter of an *aṇūka* and so forth, because of their proximity.

When it is said "with those quarter-bricks" (*pādeṣṭakābhiḥ*), both the quarters of a *puruṣa* and the quarters of an *aṇūka* and so forth are understood. Why? Because the meaning of a word is determined by its context.
And he will say: "The *aṇūka*s are in the place of the fifteen-part bricks. This shows the inclusion of the *aṇūka*s for the purpose of completing the required number.
Some maintain that the two bricks situated in the *ūrū* serve a single purpose.
They complete the count by means of fifteen-part units. If they were seen [in that manner], the arrangements (*prastāra*) would not be appropriate;
furthermore, the statement "the number one thousand is completed for each arrangement" would become meaningless.
If those *prastāras* were two hundred each, the *yajñakratu*s would not be joined;
therefore, the previously stated meaning alone must be accepted,
so that all the statements may possess meaningful significance.
Karavindīyā Vyākhyā:
Now begins the fourth paṭala; it is fourfold.
One piles the fire-altar with bricks that are four-cornered.
To the question of what kind of bricks are to be taken, he says:
"of the word *sanac*."
Those bricks should be taken as neither long nor irregular, but as perfectly square.
Why? Because the word lacks any qualifying adjunct (*upapada*).
For no such adjunct is heard here as "with long bricks" or "with irregular bricks."
Therefore, by the principle that "it should be equal, since there is no scriptural statement to the contrary," they must indeed be equal.
Since long [bricks] also exist in the preceding fire-altar,
there is thus an option between the former fire-altar and this one due to the difference in injunctions.
"Because of the scriptural statement that [the fire] is eternal and without desire;
the mention of one who has mastered the fire-ritual (*agnikalpa*) is for the sake of illustration.
Demonstrating this by means of scripture itself, he says:
These four scriptural passages prescribe the measurement of the bricks;
and because they are possible [to be combined], there is their conjunction.
"Pādamātrayaḥ" means having the measure of a quarter (pāda).
The word "pāda" occurs in the sense of a fourth part, a foot, and so forth;
here, it denotes a fourth part.

That [measurement] consisting of four parts shall be understood as that of the *aṇūka* and so forth, as will be demonstrated in the subsequent sūtra. A *pāda* is one-fourth of a measure; *pādamātrayaḥ* means measuring one *pāda*. An *aratni* is a hand including the little finger.
And that is one-fifth of a man's height;
for it will be stated that "a *puruṣa* is five *aratnis*, and an *aratni* is twenty-four *aṅgulas*. Those [measures] having that dimension are "one *aratni* long."
*Ūrvasthi* means the bone of the thigh. *Aṇūka* refers to the spinal column (*pṛṣṭhavaṃśa*).

These [terms] are included among the bones of the thighs, knees, and so forth, according to the explanation given in the rule: "In the case of those two, [the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] except after *aṇūka*" (Pāṇini 4.1.70).
The fourth part of the person is the thigh-bone;
the fourth part is the ankle.
This he will explain clearly in the subsequent sūtra.
Those [atoms] are the size of a thigh-bone, those the size of a grain of rice, and those the size of a louse-egg;
he speaks thus for the purpose of establishing specific designations according to the measurement of the *ātasoma* and *vadika*.
By the four terms *aṇūka*, *aratni*, *yūpa*, and *asthi*, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are intended as bricks;
for it is seen in the concluding passage that "the brick is one foot in measure."

Furthermore, because of the designation of feminine gender in the case of *saṃjñās* (names/designations), and because usage is observed even with words such as *aṇūka* for bricks—for instance, in passages such as:

"In place of the fifteen-part bricks (*pañcadaśabhāgīyā*), there are four-and-a-quarter five-part bricks (*pañcamabhāgīyā*) in the intervals between the joints; one should lay them around oneself with fourteen parts as appropriate"—the meaning is that a four-part brick (*caturbhāgīyā*) of the measure of an *aṇūka* receives that name (*saṃjñā*).
The *pañcamabhāgīyā* brick—known as the *pañcamabhāgīyā* because it measures one *aratni*.
Likewise, the *urvasthi* brick—known as the *ṣaḍbhāgīyā* because it measures one *urvasthi*. The *pādeṣṭakā* brick—measuring one *pāda*.
Now, how is it obtained that this is "the state of the six-parted"? It is because of the extension of the mode by the word "likewise" (*tathā*).

How is there an extension? Just as the number "one cubit" (*aratnimātrī*)—by virtue of its proximity—is designated as a term for a measurement that is not less than, but immediately following, the previously mentioned measure of one cubit; so too, the number "six parts" (*ṣaḍbhāgīya*)—by virtue of its proximity—is designated as a term for a measurement that is not less than, but immediately following, the previously mentioned measure of one cubit.

Furthermore, it must be stated that [the measurement] is six *caturbhāgīya* bricks; thus, this extension (*atideśa*) serves to indicate the completion of the manner of measuring the parts of the person under discussion.
By this, it is understood that only those ending with the *ūrdhvasthī* have their dimensions measured by the parts, and not those that are merely a foot (*pādamātrī*).
Therefore, because they are situated within its own sentence, [it says]: "In the *upadhāna*, one should place eight *caturbhāgīya* *pādeṣṭaka*s on each of the two tips of the wings."

Furthermore, because of the scriptural observation: "In the interval between the *sandhi*, one should place the *pañcamabhāgīyās* with a quarter added (*sapādāḥ*) upon oneself (the central brick) using fourteen quarters as appropriate.
Here, the "quarters" (*pāda*) of the *aṇūka* and other bricks are taken in the sense of "quarter-units," not as literal feet or limbs.

Moreover, setting aside what is seen in the direct Vedic text (*śruti*), the sequential order of the recitation of the *aṇūka* and others is intended to indicate that the preceding [element] possesses a greater measure.

By this, it is made known that those measuring a *tena* (span) or a *vasti* (cubit) have a measurement smaller than an *aratni* (forearm), and those measuring a *pāda* (quarter-cubit) have a measurement smaller than an *aṇūka*, a *ratna*, or a *cūrnāsthi*. And all of this was stated by the Blessed Bodhāyana, beginning with "One should pile the fire-altar with bricks that are equal squares," and saying, "One should have those bricks made in the fourth, fifth, sixth, and tenth parts of a man."
Therefore, in this context, the *aṇūka* and other units are taken as the measure of a "foot" (*pāda*).
And these are to be understood as half of those [larger measures],
according to the principle that the measure of a foot is prescribed by means of half-measure.
Therefore, there are fifteen *aṅgula* units for the *aṇūka-pāda*, twelve *aṅgula* units for the *aratni-pāda*, and ten *aṅgula* units for the *ūrvāsthi-pāda*.
Thus, there are six types of bricks here;
they are to be made using such measuring instruments.

Now, one might ask: since the knowledge of their dimensions and their practical application are already established through terms such as *aṇūkā* and so forth, for what purpose are these [specific] names like *mahatyaḥ* (the great ones) employed? It is said: this is for the sake of making known that the Vedic terms *aṇūkā* and so on refer specifically to measurements such as a fourth part of a *puruṣa*, so that bricks may be constructed according to the respective fourth-part measurements of each individual *puruṣa*.
For instance, in the world there are two kinds of men: those who are uniform and those who are non-uniform.
Among them, the "uniform" are those of the oceanic type (*sāmudrīya*), endowed with all the auspicious marks.
Those lacking a few [features] are uneven;
those endowed with all the characteristics of the oceanic [type] are even;
those lacking a few [features] are uneven.

The *aṇūka*s and so forth are taken in their primary sense because they possess fixed dimensions relative to that [standard]. For others, however, due to the influence of natural *adṛṣṭa* (unseen force) and other factors existing from the time of conception onwards, there occurs a deviation from the rule of the one-fourth part and so on regarding the *aṇūka*s and others, owing to their having various forms—such as being deficient, excessive, or curved. Consequently, when bricks produced with those measurements are laid down at the time of construction, whether they are laid down in those respective places in numbers equal to that [standard] or fewer to complete the space, the filling of those locations is accomplished by them.

Since great defects such as the clashing of dissimilar materials from various sources would arise there, the terms *aṇūka* and so forth found in the scripture are used to indicate the *puruṣa*, the *caturbhāga*, and so on, in order to avoid such irregularities. To establish this meaning, significant technical names (*mahatyaḥ saṃjñāḥ*) are given according to their etymological significance.
Thus, the meaning established is this: having taken the measurement of a man with uplifted arms, one should have half-bricks made for them by means of the fourth, fifth, or sixth part thereof.
In this regard, some maintain that *varṣaśatya* and *aratnya* have the same meaning.

According to their view, the separate mention of either the word *agni-kalpa* or the word *aratni* in those [passages], as well as their repeated mention and the scriptural evidence (*śruti*), must be regarded as nothing other than the result of the author of the Sūtra’s negligence. This is because [of the aforementioned reasons].
This has been explained.

The meaning is as follows: the "four-part" (caturbhāgīya) and other bricks should be measured by four parts of a man; they should conform to the proportions of a man. Thus, the four-part bricks are thirty finger-breadths (aṅgulas), the five-part bricks are twenty-four finger-breadths, and the six-part bricks are twenty finger-breadths.
Their bases, measured for that purpose, are fifteen and twelve finger-breadths [respectively].
This concludes the fourth chapter according to the commentary of Sundararāja.

Now, he speaks of laying down this very *caturaśva* in another manner: the word *tvāccha* [in the rule] is without an upapada, as there is an absence of qualifiers such as "long" (*dīrgha*) and so forth.
The measure of these, beginning with the quarter (pāda), is understood; he states it: "A quarter-measure consists of four atoms."
A measure of thirty finger-breadths (aṅgula) consisting of four parts of a man is called the *aṇūka*;
a *ratni* consisting of five parts is twenty-four finger-breadths.
The thigh bone should be understood in the same way and by that same method; it consists of six parts and measures twenty finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
Some say that the thigh bone also consists of five parts, but that is incorrect.
This is because they are specified separately as "the size of a *kulmi*," "the span of a cubit (*aratni-prādeśa*)," and "the thigh-bone (*ūrvasthi*).

Furthermore, in the ritual manual (*prayoga-kalpa*), there is a distinct statement: "One makes bricks [of the sizes] one *prādeśa*, one *aratni*, and one *ūrvasthi*," and there is also the mention of "that thigh-bone" and so forth.
Moreover, it is explicitly stated by Baudhāyana: "One should have bricks made for that [altar] in the fourth, fifth, sixth, and tenth parts of a man."
A brick for the foot is one-quarter of a measure;
because there is no distinction [in the rule], this applies to all bricks, including those of the *aṇūka* size and others.
In that case, one may act according to one's desire, since the meaning of the word is subject to such variation.
In common usage, the word *pāda* is well known to denote a fourth part;
in some cases it refers to a mere portion,
as in the expressions “a *pāda* of a *kṛcchra* penance” and “the recitation of a *pāda* of a *ṛc* verse.”

However, it is seen in only one part of the Veda: "The Gāyatrī has three feet; the Paṅkti has five feet; the Śakvarī has six feet. Here, both [meanings] are to be accepted, because the word's meaning applies in both cases.
And here, the definition of the meaning of the word *pāda* is established for the purpose of [determining] the single type and so forth.
In this case, even when there is a statement regarding a fourth part (*caturbhāga*) in relation to this fire-altar, there is no fault in using the term *pāda*;

for those who do not accept the six-part bricks (*ṣaḍbhāgīya*), this is precisely their utility, since the *aṇūka*, *aratni*, and *pāda* are to be understood as measuring ten and eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) respectively.
In the Kapardibhāṣya on the Upadhāna:

one should place eight quarter-bricks (pādeṣṭakās) made from a fourth part of the standard brick at each of the tips of the two wings; and likewise at the two joints, [placing them] so as to leave a gap of six finger-breadths within the body.
At the time of laying the bricks, one should place eight four-part bricks (*caturbhāgīyā*) as foot-bricks (*pādeṣṭakā*) on each of the two tips of the wings.
The repetition "eight and eight" indicates that they are to be placed in every section.
They extend into the body by a measure of six finger-breadths; that is to say, they have entered into and pervaded it.
The two wings are nine finger-breadths wide;
at the hips and the shoulders, there are eight lines running eastward and westward.
There are four on each of the hips and shoulders;
these are the feet. Those on the hips face forward.
On the two shoulders, there are [bricks] facing westward.
Thus, there are forty-eight quarter-fourth (caturbhāgīya) bricks.
In the intermediate spaces between the joints, there are fifth-part (pañcabhāgīya) bricks with one-quarter added. || ĀpŚus_11.6 ||
In the space between the two flanks, there are five parts with an additional quarter;
in the middle, there are quarters;
and ten toward the west.
To their south are twenty-five bricks measuring one-fifth of a span;
to their north are twenty.
Thus, fifty-five bricks are to be laid in the intermediate space between the joints.
Having placed a span-long brick at the tail, one should cover the entire fire-altar with four-part bricks. (ĀpŚus 11.7)

By the word "prādeśa," is a spatial area (*kṣetra*) denoted—as in the phrase "that which is a *prādeśa* at the tail"? Or rather, are the bricks themselves made to be a *prādeśa* in size? If a spatial area were being denoted, then only a row of *prādeśas* would have to be laid down; in that case, the fire-altar (*agni*) would be broken up.
In the other alternative, the *prādeśa*-bricks should be so fashioned that the altar is not broken up.
The term "prādeśa" is used in the singular to denote the class [of bricks].
The *aṇūka* bricks do not lie together with the *prādeśa* bricks;
rather, it is the *pañcabhāgīya* bricks that lie together with them.
Therefore, there are four *pañcamabhāgīyā* bricks in each of the two hips, making eight; thirteen *pañcamabhāgīyās* in the feet;
and eight *aṇūkās* in the fore-part.
Thus, there are twenty-nine bricks in the tail.

Others, however, describe it thus: even in that case where the increase is made by a span (*vitasti*), by the force of the scriptural injunction regarding the square shape, the *prādeśa* alone is to be covered with bricks;
it is for this purpose that the term *prādeśa* is mentioned. Even in that view, the aforementioned sequence of laying down the bricks remains the same.
"Everything" refers to thirty-two [sections].
Twenty-eight are stated for the self; eight are in the front half of the tail.
One should complete the count with foot-bricks. (ĀpŚus 11.8)
One should complete the count with fifteen parts.
In the second row on oneself, there is a central four-part unit; this is the middle two-hundred-fold arrangement.
Karavinda’s Commentary:
At the time of laying down, one should place eight [bricks] measuring fifteen finger-breadths each upon the tips of the two wings during the process of piling.
Likewise, at the joints of the wings and the body, these [lines] are six finger-breadths long within the body;
at the joints of the wings and the body, there are eight [lines], each eight [finger-breadths long].
These six-finger-breadth lines enter the hawk's body at the hips and the shoulders.
By the word "ca" (and), the phrase "in the same way" is drawn forward by implication, [indicating] the absence of a specific object.
On the hips and shoulders, there are four each.
He states the distinction: eight each, facing east and west.
[The lines] run eastward on the two hips and westward on the two shoulders.

Now, one might ask: since the distributive expression "eight and eight" is used, why should there not be eight lines for each of the four locations? It is replied: by the force of the statement "eight eastward and eight westward," it is understood that there are eight eastward and eight westward lines [in total], rather than four in each [direction].
Thus, there are two eastward lines on the hips and two westward lines on the shoulders.

These forty-eight quarter-bricks (*pādāḥ*) are four-part bricks (*caturbhāgīyāḥ*). In the intervals between the joints, one should place five-part bricks (*pañcamabhāgīyāḥ*) with an extra quarter; in the middle of the two wing-joints, within the body of the altar, one should place five-part bricks with an extra quarter, together with their own quarters as required by the context. Here, on the southern side, there are twenty-five five-part bricks to the north of the transverse bricks (*viśayānām*); on the northern side, there are twenty five-part bricks to the south of the transverse bricks.
In the middle, there are ten regions;
thus, there are fifty-five bricks in the intervals between the junctions.

The tail has already been discussed. This effort is made to avoid the consequence of a division that would arise if the tail and the tip of the tail were treated as separate rows in the eastern fire-altar.

In this case, however, it is understood that if the root-region were of a separate measurement, a discrepancy would arise regarding the rule for the fifth-part bricks (*pañcamabhāgīyā*) to be mentioned in the subsequent arrangement; and that must indeed be avoided. Therefore, having covered the remainder of the body and the remainder of the wings with fourth-part bricks (*caturbhāgīyā*), one should place eight fourth-part bricks in the front half of the tail, and then place fifteen fifth-part bricks in the rear half to avoid any deficiency.
And it has been said by the learned: "The absence of obstruction, the filling up in each successive layer of those [fires] whose locations have been established,
and even the state of being distinct— these are the ultimate principles of the fires according to our teachers."
Thus,
the term "fourfold portion" (caturbhāgīyā) refers to the length of the arms.
Regarding the word "covering" (pracchādana), its purpose is also exactly as previously stated.

In this context, it has already been stated that since a division into separate regions would entail the consequence of fragmentation, and because the covering of the entire fire-altar is prescribed, and since four-part bricks (*caturbhāgīyā*) are impossible [in certain areas], and because there is no fragmentation when those mentioned are unavailable, one must perform the covering with other available bricks from that same location whenever the specified ones are unavailable.
In that regard, there are sixteen four-part bricks in the middle of the quarters on the southern wing,
and likewise sixteen on the northern wing.
In the center between the two junctions (saṃdhi) of the body, there are fourteen [lines] in front of each of the feet;
fourteen behind them in the middle of the feet;
and eight in the front half of the tail.
In the second half, there are fifteen fifth-part bricks;
in the interval between the junctions, there are forty-five fifth-part bricks,
wherein there are sixty aṇūka bricks and sixty fifth-part bricks.
There are forty-eight quarter-bricks (pādas) of the size of an aṇūka, and ten quarter-bricks of the fifth part;
these amount to one hundred and eighty-six.
Here, the number fourteen is to be accomplished.
He states its accomplishment:
"When [the breath] has gone to the foot."
In the middle of the body, on the fifth row, having removed the penultimate four-part brick, one should lay down nine six-part bricks as feet.
Having removed one five-part brick from each of the tail and the hips, one should lay down four of their corresponding foot-bricks.
Thus is the two-hundred-fold layout. There are eastward lines in the body, and northward lines in the right and left wings and in the tail.
In the Sundararājīya commentary on the *Upadhāna*: "One should place eight [bricks] each;
the quarter-bricks (*pādeṣṭakā*) of the four-part bricks (*caturbhāgīyā*) are fifteen *aṅgulas*."
At the two junctions (sandhyoḥ)— that is, at the two points where the wings meet— the eight [fingers] are likewise like the tips of the wings.
Those [lines] reach the self [of the bird] at six finger-breadths, and the wings at nine finger-breadths.

Regarding the hips and shoulders—there are four on each, thus sixteen in total, oriented toward the east and west; these are the feet, and the number eight must be understood here as being applied distributively (vīpsā).

Alternatively, by this sūtra, only eight [bricks] are prescribed for the hips and shoulders, while the other eight are to be supplied by means of foot-bricks (pādeṣṭakā), according to the rule: "One should complete the count with foot-bricks."
In every case, sixteen [bricks] are indeed to be laid down.
In the intervals between the junctions— at the interval between the two halves of the foot [pāda], there are forty-five bricks measuring five *bāgīyas* each.
Among these, ten are a span (prādeśa) in measure.
Because of their proximity, the term "pāda" refers to the fifth-parts (pañcamabhāgīyā).
To the south of those pāda-bricks are twenty fifth-parts, and to the north are twenty-five, or vice versa.
Having placed a span-measure at the tail, one should place that area of the span which has increased at the tip of the tail; by implication, this refers to ten spans.
One should protect the entire fire-altar;
thus, when it has been covered, there are one hundred and eighty-nine bricks. Regarding the quarter-bricks...
On the rear half of the tail and on the two sides, one should place four bricks each measuring fifteen aṅgulas.
When this is done, there are one hundred and ninety-five [bricks].
Then, on the front half of the tail, one should place three ṣaḍbhāgīyā bricks each between the two sides.
Thus ends the two-hundred-fold arrangement.
In the other layout, according to the commentary of Kapardin, there are five-part bricks with projections at the junction of the tail.

In the second layer, at the junction of the tail with the body—at the point where the tail meets the body—one should place the *viśaya* bricks, which consist of both [types] and are made of fifth-parts (*pañcamabhāgīya*).
One should arrange them around the body using fourteen quarters (*pāda*) as appropriate. (ĀpŚus 11.9b)
One should lay fourteen of those very same foot-bricks, not touching the interspaces (*viśaya*), upon the self-altar as they fit together;
here, the making of the six-part bricks has been described.

The placement [of the bricks] has not been stated as it was previously for the eastern half; however, those to be placed in front of the tail—three on each side in the eastern half of the tail—are six-part bricks (*ṣaḍbhāgīyā*), with four in the middle.
On the remaining space, there are twelve four-part bricks (*caturbhāgīyā*).
One should cover the entire fire-altar (*agni*) with five-part bricks (*pañcamabhāgīyā*). (ĀpŚus 11.10)
One should complete the count with bricks for the feet. ĀpŚus 11.11a.
In this context, by the term "brick" (*iṣṭakā*) in the verse, the *aṇūkās*—which constitute one-fourth part of the person (*puruṣa*) to be filled—are understood.
It is stated that the fifth-part bricks (*pañcamabhāgīyāḥ*), having been prepared, are to be laid down;
and there are twelve fourth-part bricks (*caturbhāgīyāḥ*) in the body (*ātman*).
The first row consists of bricks measuring five parts;
the second row consists of bricks measuring four parts;
the sixth [row] consists of bricks measuring one span.
The ninth [row] consists of four-part bricks;
in the remainder, there are five-part bricks.
This is the two-hundred-fold *prastāra*.

In this regard, certain ritualists who have not served their gurus and do not understand the intention of the Teacher perform expansions that are either deficient or excessive. However, it is clearly not the intention of this author of the Sūtras when he says, "one should complete the expansion," for had such been his intention, he would have stated everywhere, "one should complete the number in each expansion."
And it has been said: therefore, the expansion (prastāra) should be made from two hundred [units].
Regarding this, there is a verse:
There should be eight [lines] for the hips and the shoulders; these are the feet as declared by the author of the Sūtra. In the middle of those, the fourth lines should be fourteen each.
Within the interval of the *sandhi*, together with the ten quarters of the fifth [line],
ten [lines] are declared to be among them as belonging to the east in the work on the *śulba*.
In the eastern half of the tail, there are four [lines];
however, the remaining ones are indeed the second, the ninth, and the one called the fourth in the body.
The northern [regions] should always consist of five-footed verses;
the middle [regions], however, are made with four-cornered [verses] that are minute, radiant, and [various].
The expansion (prastāra) of this very [meter] has been made with two hundred and twenty-five [syllables].
Thus [it is said].
According to Karavinda’s commentary:
furthermore,
in the second layer, five-five bhāgīya bricks are to be laid down exactly at the junction of the tail.
Because there is no distinction between the self and the tail, they have entered [the body] equally.
One should place those *dhyā* bricks and those *viśaya* bricks, by means of fourteen feet, around— that is, on all sides— of the *pañcamabhāgīyā* bricks as appropriate,
because they are the subject under discussion; ten *viśaya* bricks [should be placed] in front.

On both sides, there are thirty-five-pañcamabhāgīya bricks each; starting from the front and extending toward the self (ātman) while it is being covered, there are nine rows of northward-oriented five-part bricks.
To the south of the fourteen quarter-bricks are two five-part bricks, and to the north are two.

However, when the tail is being covered with the aforementioned [bricks], because it would result in too many divisions, it is not proper for the *ṣaḍbhāgīyā* bricks—even though they have been produced—to be used there; thus, one places three *ṣaḍbhāgīyā*s each on the two sides of the tail, facing westward. Having placed two *caturbhāgīyā*s facing westward on each side of those, one should place three *ṣaḍbhāgīyā*s facing westward in their middle.
And in the rear half, one should place eight *aṇūkā* bricks.

Thus, in the body (ātman), together with the objects (viṣaya), there are ninety-nine fifth-parts (pañcamabhāgīya) and fourteen regional measures (prādeśa); in the two wings (pakṣa), thirty each fifth-part; in the tail (puccha), twelve fourth-parts (caturbhāgīya), nine sixth-parts (ṣaḍbhāgīya).
These total two hundred minus six.
Therein, the number six is to be accomplished.

In this foot, having removed one central *pañcamabhāgīyā* brick from among the rows of nine and five *pañcamabhāgīyā* bricks, one should place twenty *prādeśa*-sized bricks in the middle facing north;
here, the number four is exceeded.

Because it is improper to complete the count by adding bricks of a larger size when there is a surplus, and because it is proper to complete the count by laying down *aṇūka* bricks according to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "the *aṇūkas* take the place of the fifth-part bricks" (*pañcamabhāgīyās*), one should proceed as follows:
having made the previous row so that it is joined together according to the method of the *prādeśa*-row, and having removed the previous internal row, one should lay down eight *aṇūkas* there.
Likewise, having shifted three rows around the *prādeśa*-row and having removed the second row, one should lay down eight *aṇūkas*.
Thus ends the two-hundred-fold layout (*prastāra*).

Regarding this, some authorities— having laid down ten *prādeśas* at the tip of the tail in the first layout and disregarding the *pādeṣṭakās*, complete the count with fifteen-part bricks (*pañcadaśabhāgīyāḥ*)—
and they tolerate even the resulting breakage.
In each of the first two layers, he places the *aṇūka* bricks and their foot-bricks within the intermediate spaces between the joints;
the purpose for placing them in such a manner must be sought.
Some, however, at the time of covering, leave space for those bricks that complete the required number, cover it, and then place the number-completing bricks.
In that regard, however, it must be considered whether there is consistency with the Sūtra or not.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
"The primary scriptural authority (śruti) here, which is connected with the words *ūrva* and *asthi*,
was indeed established by the Teacher himself for the sake of the sixfold division of the Sūtras."

The meaning has been explained by the teachers, and thus it is formulated in the sūtra as "tathorvasthī. Similarly, that which consists of six parts is formulated by others as "tadvadapyanyaiḥ," and likewise in the Śulba of the Hiraṇyakeśins, it is formulated as "tathorvasthī."
The commentators also know this [verse] there as another six-part verse:
"And the venerable Bodhāyana performed the construction on a square altar that was equal [in size], using the fourth,
fifth, and sixth parts plus one-quarter."
By the force of the instruction regarding those [weights] named *ūrvasthin*,
the sublation of those [weights] that are concealed here by these [others] is intended by the author of the Sūtra;
for even *aratni*s and *aṇuka*s would be reversed in their application when there is concealment.
Indeed, there is no possibility [of the fifteen-part bricks] in either the first or the subsequent arrangement;
for in the second [arrangement], the fifteen-part brick is not prescribed,
whereas those [bricks] are prescribed in the first fire-altar, and thus the second is not prior to that.
Because both fires are of the nature of *prakṛti* and because both are eternal,
one must consider how those [qualities] could possibly reach the second fire. However, it is their effect (*kārya*) in that regard which is understood to consist of atoms (*aṇuka*).
Therefore, in a place other than that of the first fire, there should be *aṇūkikā* bricks.

As for those who here perform the completion of the count with fifteen-part bricks (*pañcadaśabhāgīyā*), do they consider this to be obtained through direct instruction (*upadeśa*) or through extended application (*atideśa*)? It is not tenable in either case, because both [the original and the modified forms] are primary (*prakṛti*), and because there is an absence of the relationship between a primary and its modification (*prakṛtivikāra*).
But surely, by the force of the statement that "the minute bricks (aṇūkāḥ) are in the place of the fifteen-part bricks," their inclusion will be established.

If it is argued that this is not so, [we reply]: the statement "in the place of the fifteen-fold parts" (pañcadaśabhāgīyānām) indicates that the small bricks (aṇkus) are to be employed to complete the number for the sake of fulfilling that specific function;
it does not, however, establish them as mere fillers of the number.
Therefore, this point requires further consideration.
What is the meaning of this which has been stated by the Teacher? It is said: [it refers] to the place of the number of the bricks being laid down.

And it was stated by him thinking that, even when the number is achieved through the various arrangements (*prastāra*), if there should be a distinction of parts due to a difference in the bricks, that distinction must be tolerated.
This will be demonstrated in the second *Śyena* sacrifice.
However, some ritualists perform fewer or more *prastāras* in the fire-altar, believing that the required number is fulfilled in the aggregate;
this is incorrect.

When numbers such as a thousand are to be accomplished through *prastāras* starting from fifteen, and no specific distinction is heard in the text, it is only logical—according to the principle that "it should be equal, because nothing is heard to the contrary"—that there be exactly two hundred *prastāras*.

Furthermore, because [the text] states, "by means of the twelfth [finger-breadth] of his hand in the fire of the chariot-wheel," and so forth, there is the production of exactly two hundred [syllables].

Now, one might object: let the completion of the number apply only to those specific arrangements (*prastāra*) where another statement exists saying "one should complete [the number]," but what of those cases where such a statement does not exist? In those instances, the number must be the completion of the total aggregate, otherwise the statement regarding "completion" would result in being purposeless.
It is said: there is no consequence of meaninglessness in that case.
How so? For in that context, the completion of the required number is established by logic, since fifteen *bhāgīya* bricks are prescribed as the means for achieving it.

If all *prastāra*s (spatial arrangements) consist of two hundred [bricks], why is this specifically called a "two-hundred brick *prastāra*"? This is stated merely to introduce what is already established, for the purpose of ensuring that all *prastāra*s consist of exactly two hundred bricks.

Just as one type of *prastāra* consists of two hundred [verses], so too all other *prastāras* must be made to consist of the number two hundred. This effort is undertaken to reinforce, by way of restatement, a meaning already established by logic—even in the absence of an explicit statement regarding completion—that all *prastāras* must be made to consist of two hundred; they should not be fewer or more. Thus it is established that all *prastāras* consist of two hundred.
The sevenfold [altar] has been described as being of its natural form.
Now, the permanent modifications (*vikṛti*) are stated—beginning with the "one-fold" (*ekavidha*).

For the six types of fires starting from the one-fold up to the six-fold, one should have bricks made according to the twelfth or thirteenth part of the *karaṇī* (the diagonal side) of each respective fire.
In this case, the side of the first type is one hundred and twenty fingers (120);
that of the second type is one hundred and sixty-nine fingers and twenty-four *tilas*;
and that of the third type is two hundred and seven fingers and twenty-nine *tilas* (207 29/64).
