4) For the fourfold [altar], there are two hundred and forty finger-breadths (240); for the fivefold, two hundred and sixty finger-breadths plus eleven sesame seeds (260 1/4);
for the sixfold, two hundred and ninety-three finger-breadths plus thirty-one sesame seeds (293 31/32).
Of these *karaṇīs*, one *karaṇa* is formed by taking one-twelfth from each side.
In every direction, one [type of] instrument is made with thirteen [bricks].

Of those two, the instrument for the quarter-bricks (pādeṣṭakā) consists of six or nine types, and by the word "and" (ca), it also includes the half-bricks (ardheṣṭakā). The laying out (upadhāna) is described: on all sides, there are three rows of twelve bricks each.
Then there are five times thirteen;
then one quarter of thirteen;
then one time thirteen.
Then there are thirteen rows (rītis): three on each side and twelve in the middle.
In that arrangement, in the second row—which consists of twelve bricks—one should remove the fourth and eighth bricks and place two half-bricks (ardheṣṭakas) in their stead;
and in that same row, one should also remove the two penultimate bricks and place four half-bricks.
The arrangement consists of exactly two hundred [bricks]. In the second arrangement, there are two rows of thirteen;
then follows one brick consisting of a quarter of a thirteen.
Then there are thirteen quarters on both sides of one [verse]; then four lines of twelve [syllables] each; then thirteen quarters on both sides of one [verse].
Then there are three rows of thirteen; thus, there are thirteen rows.
Here, one should either place the feet after removing six from the middle row. The layout consists of two hundred bricks.

Alternatively, it is stated that in the first layer there are twelve [bricks], and in the second, thirteen. In the case of the complete twelfth [layer], there are long quarter-bricks (*pādeṣṭakā*) and half-bricks (*ardheṣṭakā*) here and there in the first layer; there are seventeen rows (*rīti*) running eastward, and all of them consist of twelve bricks each.
Of all those [rows], the southern one is with half-bricks;
then one with quarter-bricks; then three with twelve-part bricks; then one with quarter-bricks; then one with half-bricks;
then one with quarter-bricks; then three with twelve-part bricks.
In this manner, there are seventeen rows (*rīti*) consisting of the final half-bricks.
Among them, having removed the last three bricks from the fifth, sixth, and seventh rows, one should place a single [brick] in the twelfth row.
Then, having removed the last three bricks from the eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth rows, one should place a single [brick] in the eleventh row.
Thus there are two hundred.

As for the second [set], there are thirteen; the northern rows are fourteen, and by means of the first halves of those twelve and thirteen bricks and the latter halves of them, there are those fourteen rows.
Thus there are one hundred and twelve bricks.
In that case, having extracted thirteen bricks from the eastern half, one should lay down twenty-four quarters (pādas).
In this way, it becomes two hundred.

If all the arrangements (prastāras) are by means of the twelfth [verses], then, having first laid down the first arrangement according to the previously stated method, one should lay down the rows (rītis) facing north from the second arrangement itself.
This is the two-hundred-brick altar.

If all [the bricks] are thirteen-row bricks, then one should follow the method described for the second layer: having laid down the bricks facing east in the first layer, and having removed the thirteen-row bricks from the rear half and laid down the quarter-bricks, one should lay them down facing north in the subsequent layer.
This is the two-hundred-brick altar.

If there are thirteen in one place and twelve elsewhere, then there are thirteen rows of bricks extending eastward toward the north. In the first row and the fifth row, having removed eight [bricks] each, there are twenty-eight quarter-bricks (*pāda*) and two half-bricks (*ardha*) each;
thus, there are two hundred [bricks].
In the second layer, those same longitudinal rows [are used].
There, having removed eight [bricks] from both the south and the north, one should lay down the quarter-bricks and half-bricks as before; thus it becomes two hundred.

In the same way, for the *prauga* and other sections, having laid down the constituent parts with twelve-part or thirteen-part bricks as appropriate, one should complete the count with quarter-bricks and half-bricks.
Enough of this excessive prolixity.
In Sundararāja’s commentary,
it is stated that in both cases [the distance] is one span (prādeśa) without distinction;
from there, ten spans extend forward, and two each on the two sides.

One should fill the entire fire-altar with the *viśayā* bricks together with the self. There are ten rows in the northern part; of these, one should place the second and the ninth with the fourth [bricks], and the sixth with the *prādeśas*.
In the remainder of the self and in the two wings, there are fifth-part bricks.
In the rear half of the tail, nine six-part bricks (ṣaḍbhāgīyās) are placed facing east from the middle of the two sides;
in the remainder of the tail, twelve small bricks (aṇūkās) are placed.
Thus is the two-hundred-brick layering.
One should pile them in reverse order for as many layers (prastāra) as one intends to construct.
This is concluded.
The eleventh section. The Commentary of Kapardin.
It has been established that for those [altars] such as the *ekavidha* (one-celled) which are employed for the sake of the sacrifice, there is the status of having wings and a tail.
Thus, it is stated how the rule for their laying out (*upadhāna*) is performed:
"One should have the bricks made according to the twelfth and thirteenth [parts] of the measuring-strings (*karaṇī*) of those beginning with the *ekavidha*. (ĀpŚus 12.1a)

One should have bricks made from twelve parts and thirteen parts so as to form equal squares: one [type of brick] from twelve parts on all sides, and a second from thirteen parts on all sides. One should lay the quarter-bricks in an alternating manner for as many layers (prastāra) as one intends to construct. (ĀpŚus 12.1b)
According to another *Śulba* [text], the foot-bricks (*pādeṣṭakā*) are of twelve kinds and the half-bricks (*ardheṣṭakā*) are of thirteen kinds;
for us as well, half-bricks must be used in the *prauga* [section].

Even in the case of altars of one kind (*ekavidha*) and so forth, if the first layer consists of twelve [bricks] and the second of thirteen—according to this alternative view—half-bricks must be employed.
Otherwise, the junction would not be fulfilled at all.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
"The measuring cord is of two kinds: [one] with seventy and [the other] with one hundred [units]."
That [measurement] of the fingers should be measured by ten sesame seeds less than the length of a finger.
A *mānikā* consists of three types of cords; by mathematicians, it is calculated as two hundred and eight [units], less six sesame seeds.
The rope for the fourth [altar], the *vidhaspa*, is said to be one *mānikā* in measure,
measured by two hundred and forty [units].
Calulators know that two hundred and sixty-eight mānikās, together with eleven *tilas*, constitute one *vidha* of the fifth kind.
The ritual procedure for the sixfold [mandala] shall measure two hundred and ninety-four,
being deficient by exactly three sesame seeds.
In the foundation (upadhāna), there are three rows of twelve bricks on both sides of the feet;
then five rows of thirteen;
then one row of thirteen.
The foot-pattern (*pādarīti*) is as follows: first, there is one thirteenth [brick]; then three twelfths on both sides of the *rīti*;
in the second [row], there is one fourth and another eighth besides those.
This is the layout (*prastāra*).
In the next arrangement (prastāra), there are two rows (rīti): one of thirteen [bricks], and then one of thirteen with a foot (pāda) added;
then four of twelve.
Now, the six middle bricks are of four types; this is the arrangement of two hundred [bricks].
"Alternately"—this has already been explained.

For those [altars] consisting of one kind and so forth, they should be joined with the first, second, or third layer of food; for all of them, the height measurement is according to the number mentioned in the scripture. ĀpŚus 12.2.

Regarding all [beings] from those of one kind up to those of six kinds, their respective numbers are heard in relation to both the first meal and the second meal. What is meant by this? If the first meal consists of a thousand [beings] and they reach the height of the knees, then these [numbers] are indeed appropriate for the second meal as well.
Those factors (dharmas) possess the nature of seven and a half; and that statement is for the purpose of making known their state as being seven and a half primary natures (prakṛtis).
The commentary by Karavinda has been concluded with the transposition.

But why is there a statement regarding the transposition (*vyatyāsa*) in the modified rites (*vikṛti*)? It is said: because in the archetypal rite (*prakṛti*) there is a disparity between the layers (*citī*) and the spreadings (*prastāra*), someone might have a doubt as to whether this transposition is a property of the spreading or a property of the layer. However, in the modified rite, since there are two layers and two spreadings, when a doubt arises as to whose property this transposition is due to the disparity between the two spreadings, the rule is that one should pile the altar by transposing as many spreadings as there are, in order to avoid a discrepancy. The repetition of the word "transposition" is for the purpose of establishing that transposition is a property of the spreading.
The "single-fold measurement" refers to the first food-intake and the first application among those ranging from one type up to six types; it is that by which one becomes intensely engaged.

The connection is as follows: just as the number—thousands and so forth—is intensely applied according to the manner stated in the scripture (*śruti*), so too should the vertical measurement, such as reaching the knees and so on, be intensely applied.

For all [altar-buildings] ranging from the one-fold up to the six-fold, the numbers such as "one thousand" and the measurements such as "knee-high," which are heard in the scriptural injunctions beginning with "One building the altar for the first time, should build it with one thousand [bricks]," are taught as things to be accomplished within these [buildings] by means of the first, second, and third meals [of bricks]. By this, it is established that when the one-fold is the archetype (*prakṛti*), and the two-fold and others have that as their archetype, they possess the number of one thousand and the measurement of being knee-high, and so forth.
The one-fold [stomas] and so forth are also indeed permanent (*nitya*) because they are not connected with specific desires;
both the archetypes (*prakṛti*) and the modified forms (*vikṛti*) have been stated to be permanent.
Now, the optional (*kāmya*) *prauga* and other [stomas] are being described.
The optional rites are modifications of the constituent qualities, because they are taught as being based on those qualities. ĀpŚus 12.3.
The sevenfold permanent fire-altar undergoes modifications through specific qualities such as the shape of the *prauga* and other forms.
Why? Because it is an instruction regarding a quality (*guṇaśāstra*). It is called an "instruction regarding a quality" because it teaches—that is, enjoins—a quality.

The sentence to be mentioned later, "One should pile the *prauga-cit*," restates the piling of the *prauga* fire-altar and prescribes there a specific accessory—the particular shape of the *prauga* and so forth—for the purpose of the result of removing one's enemies.
Therefore, the *prauga* and other such altars are optional (*kāmya*).
Like the *godohana* vessel and others, they are modifications of the accessories of the obligatory (*nitya*) fire-altar; they are neither obligatory nor are they primary archetypes (*prakṛti*).
In the *Sundararājīyā-vyākhyā* (under the section on transposition):

"An alternative explanation of the statement 'in the interval between the joints, there are five-part [bricks] with a quarter-portion' is as follows: by the word 'quarter' (*pāda*), the very quarter-portions of the *aṇūka* bricks currently under discussion are intended."

Since the feet (pādas) introduced here are eight in number, they are to be understood exactly as such. The arrangement therein is as follows: in the first layer, having left thirty finger-breadths (aṅgulas) on both sides in the space between the joints, there are thirty-five fifth-parts (pañcamabhāgīyās) in the middle; in the remaining thirty finger-breadths at the back and front, there are two each of fifteen finger-breadths oriented northward; in the middle, there are three each of minute bricks (aṇūkās); and because it is impossible to fill the sides of the tail with fifth-parts, there are six each of fifteen finger-breadths at the front on both sides of the tail.

In the remainder of the tail, there are thirteen *aṇūka*s; when this is done, there are one hundred and eight. Having removed one *aṇūka* from the middle of the tail, one should place nine [bricks] measuring ten *aṅgula*s [therein], either in the second part of the body or in the middle, for the sake of facilitating the placement with mantras.

Thus is the two-hundred-fold layout. In the other [layout], excluding the tail, there are ten eastward rows in the body according to the sūtra itself. Therein, having placed the fifth row in the middle of the southern side, one places two [bricks] each, measuring a span (prādeśa), to the east and west of that.

In this manner, on the western half of the tail, there are three *ṣaḍbhāgīyā* bricks each on the two sides and in the middle, all facing east; and on the remainder of the tail, there are twelve *aṇūkā* bricks.
For those who do not accept the *ṣaḍbhāgīyā* bricks, the laying out is exactly the same, with the exception of the tail.
Regarding that, they explain the rule "having laid down a *prādeśa*" as meaning "having laid down a *prādeśa*-brick."
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of a discrepancy.
Since the *prādeśa* measures do not fit together with the four-part bricks (*caturbhāgīyā*), it follows by implication that the five-part bricks (*pañcamabhāgīyā*) are required.
Their placement therein is as follows: in the eastern half of the tail, on the two sides, there are four bricks measuring fifteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
In the middle are six *ṣaḍaṇūkā* bricks.
In the rear half are fifteen fifth-day bricks. At the tip of the tail, having removed two middle bricks on both sides, eight *prādeśa*-bricks are to be laid down.
Thus, there are one hundred and eight [bricks].
Then, as before, having removed one fourth or fifth brick, one should place it at a distance of ten or eight finger-breadths;
this constitutes a two-hundred-brick layout.

In the second layer, there are sixteen *aṇūkas* in the tail; in the body, in the northern row, starting from the fourth [cell], three [cells] eight finger-breadths wide are oriented northward; then one fifth [cell];
then three [cells] eight finger-breadths wide;
then three fifth [cells].
The rule for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is exactly as before.
There is a layer (*prastāra*) of two hundred [bricks].
Thus has the teacher described the laying down of the bricks together with the *aratni* and *prādeśa* measures.
Regarding that which is devoid of those [projections], it is said: there are three *aṇūka*s on each of the two tips of the wings.
Of these, two are fifteen *aṅgula*s long, one behind and one in front.
In this same way, for the two sides as well, the body is joined by a space; thus, there are six *prādeśa*s on each side.
In the remainder of the wing, there are five *pañcamas*.
In the interval between the joints (*sandhi*), there are forty *pañcamabhāgīyas*; the remainder for the body is exactly as previously described.
In the eastern half of the tail, there are eight [units] measuring fifteen *aṅgulas* on the two sides, and six *aṇūkas* in the middle.
In the second half [of the altar], there are three rows extending northward consisting of six-part bricks.
In the first of these rows, there are two [bricks] of ten aṅgulas each on both sides.
In the front half of the tail, there are eighteen six-part bricks.
In the second half, having extracted five bricks from both sides of the *pṛṣṭhya* line, one should lay down eight *pādeṣṭakās*.
In the body (*ātman*), following the previous method, having placed the fifth brick in the middle, one should lay down four *pādeṣṭakās* on both sides.
In this way, the layer (*prastāra*) consists of two hundred bricks.
Now, in this case as well, for those who do not desire the sixfold division, there are six by six fifteen-aṅgula sections on both sides of the tail and at its front;
there are thirteen aṇūkas in the remainder of the tail;
and there are four aṇūkas each at the tips of the two wings.
The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
When this has been done, there are one hundred and eighty-four bricks.
Therein, having removed two fourths and two fifths at the end of the *pṛṣṭhyā* in the *ātman*, one should lay down [bricks] measuring eighteen or eight *aṅgulas*.
The layout consists of two hundred [bricks]. In another layout, at the junction of the tail, there are fifth-part bricks and so forth, according to the Sūtra;
for the body, the previous method is as previously stated.
In the front half of the tail, one should place eight *aṇūkās*; in the rear half, having removed two five-fingerbreadths (*pañcamyaṅgula*) by means of an insertion, one should place eight.
This constitutes a layout of two hundred bricks.
Thus, many varieties of laying down [the bricks] have been described.
Among these, the more logical method should be adopted by the learned.
In all such cases, it should be understood that the bricks are laid down either at the end of the tail or at the end of the wings, whichever is appropriate for each specific instance.
The eleventh section.
For those [altars] beginning with the single-fold [type], there are bricks less than a foot. The two genitive case endings are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*).

One should have bricks made in the shape of a regular square using the twelfth and thirteenth parts of the *karaṇas* (measuring instruments) for those [altars] ranging from one kind up to six kinds; these include both the full bricks and the quarter-bricks (*pādeṣṭakā*).
These are of two types: the four-part bricks (*caturbhāgīyā*) and the ninth-part bricks (*navamya*).
Regarding this, there are the following verses:

There are one hundred and twenty fingers; in the case of a single type of movement, there would be one [unit], while in the case of two types, it should be known as one hundred and seventy minus ten *tilas*.
In three types [of measurements], there are two hundred and eight finger-breadths less by eight barley-corns;
for the fourfold [measurement], the diagonal is two hundred and forty.
In the case of five types [of measurement], there are one hundred and sixty-one and eleven *tilas*;
in the case of six types, three hundred minus six fingers and two *tilas* are to be subtracted.
First, for the single type [of brick], one instrument is made with twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
a second, in the form of a quarter-brick (pādeṣṭakā), is made with half of that, namely five finger-breadths;
and a third is made with three finger-breadths plus eleven sesame-seeds (tilas).
That is called the ninth.
In this manner, by means of nine finger-breadths plus thirteen sesame seeds, one [unit] is formed;
half of that constitutes its quarter-measures.
It is four finger-breadths and twenty-one sesame seeds;
by the third [measure], the ninth is three finger-breadths and three sesame seeds.
In this manner, it should be understood for the two-fold and subsequent [categories].
If one wishes to effect an exchange (*vyatyāsa*) there,
since no specific order for the *prastāras* has been stated, the exchange applies only to the twelve-versed and thirteen-versed [stomas] which possess constituent parts (*sāvayava*).
One *prastāra* is formed with the twelve-versed [stomas] possessing constituent parts, and the other with the thirteen-versed [stomas].
However, there is no "contracted" (saṃkālitopadhāna) arrangement because it has not been so stated, and because it is impossible for this [arrangement] to be extended to the *prauga* and the *citya*.
In that regard, in the first layer (*prastāra*), nine of the twelve bricks are made square in the middle of the fire-altar;
surrounding those are sixty *pādyā* bricks.
Surrounding those are one hundred and twenty-eight *dvādaśī* bricks;
having set aside one on the northern shoulder, four are placed in the *pādyā* positions.
This constitutes a layer (*prastāra*) of two hundred bricks.

When another [space] is covered by thirteen [bricks], there are one hundred and sixty-nine bricks. Having removed the four bricks situated in the middle of the fire-altar, there are four *pādyā* bricks in each corner. On the spine (*pṛṣṭhyā*), having removed one from behind and one from the front, there are nine new [bricks] for each of the nine [sections].
The layout consists of two hundred [bricks].
The vertical measurement is of one type; furthermore, for those [altars] beginning with the one-type [altar], there are also numbers such as a thousand.
And the vertical measurement indeed occurs in seven types, beginning with that which reaches the knees.
The meaning is that even when there is a decrease in the field, there is no decrease in the number or the vertical measurement.
The *Kapardibhāṣya* states: "Optional modifications of qualities [are prescribed] because they are instructions regarding qualities. (Sūtra 3)
The optional *prauga* and other such offerings are modified by means of a quality—what is meant by this? That the accomplishment of the result does not belong to the fire-altar (*agni*).
Why? Because it is a teaching of a quality.
"Śāstra" means that which teaches (*śāsti*).
In this case, it is the quality (guṇa) that is enjoined, not the fire;
therefore, because it is an injunction of a quality, like the *godohana* vessel and others, these are stated as qualities leading to specific results.
"One who has rivals should pile the prauga-citi," so it is known. (ĀpŚus 12.4)
The *prauga* is the front part of a cart.
One who has many rivals should pile it in that shape; he who has many rivals should pile it thus.

Having made a square plot of ground twice the size of the fire-altar including the *aratni* and the span, one should draw a line from the middle of the eastern side toward the two hips (*śroṇi*). That is the standard *prauga*. (ĀpŚus 12.5)
The rites of piling are declared to be of one kind. (ĀpŚus 12.6a)
And this statement is for the purpose of making known that the half-seventh [unit] is the fundamental measure (*prakṛti*).
A cord measuring fifteen *aṅgulas* and nine sesame seeds, when laid out between four persons, makes it twice as large.
Likewise, having spread out the square according to the method stated in the Sūtra, one should delineate the buttocks (*śroṇi*).
And one should have the auxiliary structures built;
with twelve, thirteen, and one and a quarter [parts], it takes the shape of a prauga.
One should have the *prauga* bricks made. ĀpŚus_12.6b.
A cord measured by four *aratnis*, fifteen *aṅgulas*, and twenty-one sesame seeds becomes the *īṣā*-measure; this is the measurement for the two axles (*akṣau*).
One should have the ritual implements made with the twelfth and thirteenth parts of that [cord].
With the twelfth part, the *prauga* is placed at the front in the first layer.
There are sixty-four foot-bricks (pādeṣṭakā), four in each of the two hips;
thus, there are one hundred and twenty-four.
There are also four half-bricks (ardheṣṭakā) in the hips alone.
In another arrangement, there are thirteen bricks in each of the two hips, forty-four in the feet, and two half-bricks; thus, there are one hundred and fifty-eight thirteen-brick units.
This arrangement totals two hundred bricks.
In this manner, one should pile them in alternating fashion.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
"The vimāna at the rear is measured by nineteen aratnis, along with eight finger-breadths and twenty-five sesame seeds."
A single celestial palace (vimānikā) is measured at twenty-one aratnis, fifteen finger-breadths (aṅgulis),
and twenty-one sesame seeds.
These three [lines], having been leveled together, form the *prauga* of the fire-altar;
one should fashion their construction exactly according to the sūtra.
In the commentary of Karavinda: "He measures the prauga; the prauga is the front part of the cart."
One who has rivals, being oppressed by his rivals and kinsmen, should pile the fire-altar in that shape; by means of it,
he truly drives away his rivals.

To whatever extent [the altar] extends—from the extent of the sevenfold [altar] together with the *aratni* and the *prādeśa*—one should make a square ground twice that size. Then, starting from the middle of the eastern side of that square, one should draw a diagonal line toward the two hips (*śroṇi*).
For the seven-and-a-half-fold [altar], the ground is twice that size, namely fifteen *puruṣas*.
Its side-measure (karaṇī) is three puruṣas, one hundred and four aṅgulas, and twenty-five tilas.

With that [measure], having left a passage for the sacrificial post-hole (yūpāvaṭa) at the rear, and having marked out a square of equal sides extending forward, one should draw a line from the midpoint of the eastern side-measure toward the south.
That ground becomes the shape of a Prauga altar, measured according to the sevenfold [altar].
The meaning is as follows: although there are twelve and thirteen *karaṇīs* (measuring squares) here among the *karaṇīs*,
and by means of them the *prastāra* (diagrammatic expansion) is inverted, one should nevertheless grasp it as being of a single kind, beginning with [the first] in this manner.

The distinction, however, is that one should have the *prauga* bricks made; the *karaṇas* (constructive units) should be in the shape of a *prauga*. Those [units] consisting of twelve or thirteen parts—namely the quarters (*pādas*) and the halves (*ardhas*)—should be in the shape of a *prauga*.
Those twelve and thirteen-part bricks, consisting of quarters and halves, are to be taken in the shape of a prauga (forepart of a chariot).
Four *puruṣas*, thirty-nine *aṅgulas*, and twenty-one *tilas*—this is the measure of the prauga. That is the side-measure of the prauga.
One should have the components made by means of the twelfth and the thirteenth [finger-breadths].
The feet and the halves consist of thirty-eight finger-breadths and twenty-five *tilas* of the twelve-part units;
this measure is its face.
The two side-measures are forty-three finger-breadths and ten *tilas*.
One side-measure of the *argha*-bricks is that same [measure];
the other is thirty-eight finger-breadths and twenty-five *tilas*.
The face [of the brick] measures nineteen finger-breadths and twelve and a half sesame seeds;
for the foot-bricks, it is nineteen finger-breadths and twenty-two sesame seeds.
Now, for those bricks consisting of thirteen parts, one face measures thirty-five finger-breadths and twenty-five sesame seeds.
The two side-measures are thirty-nine fingers minus one *tila* each;
for the half-bricks as well, one side-measure is the same,
while the other is thirty-five fingers and twenty-five *tilas*.

The face of the foot-bricks is seventeen finger-breadths, twenty-nine sesame seeds, and one half of a sesame seed; their two side-measures are twenty finger-breadths less half a sesame seed each. The face of the [other] bricks is seventeen finger-breadths, twenty-nine sesame seeds, and one half of a sesame seed.
Their two side-measures are twenty finger-breadths less half a sesame seed each.
In the first layer of the foundation, one should place sixty-four *pādeṣṭakās* at the front of the *prauga*;
at the two hips, one hundred and twenty-four *dvādaśīs*, and four half-bricks (*ardheṣṭakās*).
This constitutes a layer of two hundred bricks.

On the other [side], there are twenty-one and a third bricks on each of the two hips; thus, there are one hundred and fifty-two thirteen-brick [units]. This constitutes the two-hundred-brick arrangement (*prastāra*), and it must be performed with alternation (*vyatyāsa*).
Sundararāja’s Commentary:

The optional [fires]. Because they are taught as possessing specific qualities (*guṇa*), the optional fires beginning with the *Chandaścit* are modifications of the qualities of the permanent (*nitya*) square fire-altar; since that very altar is modified merely by its qualities, they accomplish both the fruit of the quality and their own respective fruits.

Just as the Ukthya and other rites are modifications of the qualities of the Agniṣṭoma; so too, the *praugacit* is not clearly defined: the *prauga* is the front of a cart, which is triangular; that which is piled in that manner is the *praugacit*.
The suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule *karmaṇyagnyākhyāyām*.
He states the measurement of that fire: "as large as one would draw."

The side-measure (*karaṇī*) of a sevenfold [altar] measuring one *aratni* and one *prādeśa* is three hundred and twenty-eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and twelve and a half sesame seeds (*tila*). Its double-measure (*dvikaraṇī*) is four hundred and sixty-four finger-breadths less a quarter; this is the side-measure of a square piece of ground fifteen *puruṣas* long. The side-measure of the *praṇaga* is four *puruṣas*, thirty-nine finger-breadths, and twenty-one sesame seeds.

Since the rule "as large as the fire" (*yāvān agniḥ*) would already suffice, the specific mention of "a cubit and a span" (*sāratniprādeśa*) is because that alternative belongs to another recensional branch (*śākhāntara*) and must therefore be accomplished with effort. It has already been established previously that in the case of altars ranging from one kind up to one hundred kinds—whether consisting solely of [the standard] *aratni* and *prādeśa* measures or otherwise—variations in their dimensions may indeed occur according to one's desire. In that regard, for those altars such as the *prauga-cit* which lack wings and tail, a finger-breadth (*aṅguli*) should be conceived as the two-hundredth part of a man brought forward by the scriptural texts concerning space and so forth (*khākāśa-śruti-veda-ekām ityādi*). A sesame seed (*tila*) is the thirty-fourth part of that [finger-breadth].
That *prauga* is constant by its very nature.
When it is thus performed, that ground becomes the *prauga*.
The methods have been stated as "by twelve," "by thirteen," and so forth.

One should draw the *prauga* lines on both sides of the twelfth [line]: one at thirty-four and a quarter finger-breadths (43 + 1/4) from the [corner], and the other at thirty-nine finger-breadths less ninety (39).
The *pādyā* lines are drawn at half these distances.
From the third [digit] up to the ninth;

for the thirteenth, however, there are forty finger-breadths minus one sesame-seed on one side, and thirty-six finger-breadths minus three-quarters on the other. The subsequent [digits] are half of these.
And with the third [verses] and the ninth [verses].
In the first arrangement regarding the *upādāna*, there are twelve rows of twelve bricks each, made from one hundred and forty-four twelfth [verses].
In the four middle rows, having removed sixteen from the center, sixty-four are to be laid down.
Having removed the two principal *prauga* bricks from the ninth row,

there are two hundred bricks for the first layer (*prastāra*). In the subsequent layer, there are thirteen rows consisting of one hundred and sixty-three bricks each, formed by the thirteen [thirteenth-row] bricks.
Among those, on the tenth [day], having removed seven bricks, twenty *pādyā* bricks are to be laid down,
and eighteen from the ninth;
thus [the total] becomes two hundred.
The Kapardibhāṣya states:
"One who desires, 'May I drive away my born enemies and [ward off] those yet to be born,' should pile the Prauga altar in both ways; so it is known. (ĀpŚus 12.7)

One who desires, "May I strike down both those enemies already arisen and those yet to arise," should pile the altar in the shape of a cart facing both ways, just like a cart with its face turned away. ĀpŚus_12.8 ||

Having laid out a square measuring-altar of that same size, one should mark off from the middle of the eastern and western sides a distance equal to that [side], and drop marks on the southern and northern sides; that is the ever-present *prauga* (fore-part) on both sides. (ĀpŚus 12.9)
Regarding the statements on the *prauga-cit*: one should have bricks made that are shaped like a *prauga* (a chariot-pole) on both sides. ĀpŚus_12.10.
At that very time, the measure for the sevenfold [fire-altar] is doubled.
Here, however, the width is double the length of the long quadrangle.

Having fixed stakes at the center of the transverse measurement—measured by two men, three cubits, sixteen finger-breadths, and twenty-one and a half sesame seeds—and having wound a cord around the stakes, one should discard [the excess] from the outside.
The measurement of the yoke-pole (īṣā) is three hundred and sixty-seven finger-breadths plus fourteen sesame seeds;
one should have the structural components (karaṇas) made with a twelfth part of these.
One should have the bricks for the two fore-ships (prauga) made in the shape of a fore-ship (prauga-cita).
The bricks have the form of *praugha* on both sides; the foot-bricks (*pādāśva*) likewise become *praugha* on both sides.
The procedure for the piling (*cayana*) has been explained regarding the *prauga*.
On this matter, there is a verse:
The wise know that the transverse measuring-line (tiryaṅbhānī) of the northern Prauga fire-altar consists of three hundred and twenty-eight units, together with twenty-one parts of sesamum seeds.
For the square sacrificial fire-altar, which is twice as long as it is wide,
one should drive stakes into the centers of all four sides.
Having joined the cord at the six finger-breadths [from the corners], one should leave it off from the two hips and the two shoulders;
the remainder shall be exactly three and a half [units] in the case of a cart facing away, as appropriate.
Three hundred and sixty-seven [units], increased by fourteen sesame seeds—
this is prescribed as the measurement of the yoke-pins for the northern *prauga* altar.
One should have the side-aisles (prauga) made here with a length of one and a quarter parts on both sides, using a twelfth part of the pole (īṣā) as well as the subsequent part.
Karavinda’s Commentary:
"Both"—
that is, on both sides, it is *prauga*, meaning on both sides it has the shape of a cart-front.
The meaning is: "I shall drive away the enemies already born, and I shall drive away those yet to be born; I shall act in such a way that they are not born.
He explains the scriptural phrase:
"as stated according to the [preceding] rule."

Regarding "vimukhe": the meaning is that one should pile it so that on both sides there is a *prauga* (frontal bulge) having such a form as when two carts with various openings stand joined back-to-back.

At that very time, having spread out the previously mentioned area of one *aratni* and one *prādeśa*—doubling its length for the sevenfold [altar] to form a square—and having driven a peg in the middle of the transverse and side-measures, one should draw a diagonal line from the eastern peg toward the southern peg, then from the south toward the west, from the west toward the north, and from the north toward the east; by drawing thus on both sides, the field takes the shape of a *prauga* (chariot-head).

The length of the long rectangle is twice its width; for the long side, it is five *puruṣas* and seventeen *aṅgulas*, and the crosswise side is two *puruṣas*, sixty-eight *aṅgulas*, and twenty-one *tilas*. This is the measurement of the long square.
Both the ritual implements and the procedure for piling are like those of the *prauga* altar;
the distinction, however, is that the bricks are *prauga*-shaped on both sides.
The measure of these [three persons] is three *puruṣas*, seven *aṅgulas*, and seventeen *tilas*.
Its twelfth part is thirty *aṅgulas* and twenty-five *tilas*.
Its thirteenth part is twenty-eight *aṅgulas* and nine *tilas* less one-third.
The *tiryaṅbhānī* (transverse measuring-line) of the *prauga* (fore-altar), on both sides, is two hundred and twenty-eight finger-breadths and twenty-one sesame seeds.

The measuring-rod (*karaṇa*) should be made such that it is measured by a twelfth part and a thirteenth part of that [line]. The half-bricks (*ardheṣṭakā*) are equal in length to those consisting of twelve parts and thirteen parts, and in width they are half as wide.
The quarter-bricks (pādeṣṭakā) are half [the size] in both length and width. Those quarter-bricks which were laid down in the first layer are to be laid down elsewhere in the second layer.
In the case of the twelve-part division, there are four quarter-bricks; in the case of the thirteen-part division, there are two.
In Sundararāja’s commentary,

it is stated: "In both cases, when it is not a cart— that is, when it is turned away, with its face reversed so that it faces east and west— it becomes such that this fire is like the part of a cart."
One should then lay out a long rectangle twice as wide as the area of the fire-altar;
its crosswise measurement (tiryaṅbhānī) is three hundred and twenty-eight finger-breadths and twenty-two sesame seeds.
The side-measure is double [the length].
Having thus laid it out, one should fix it at the midpoint between the eastern and western *karaṇīs* and at the midpoint between the southern and northern [axes].
One should cut off the *bahis-paṅkti*.
That which is stated as "one-fold" refers to bricks and so forth; it is stated in both ways.
The twelve [sides] have four sides each measuring thirty fingers and twenty-one sesame seeds;
one diagonal measures twenty-seven fingers and thirteen sesame seeds;
the other is double that.
With half of these [units] come the *pādyas*, and with the third parts, the ninth [rows].
For the thirteenth [row], there are four planks measuring thirty-two and a half finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*); this is one diagonal cord (*karṇarajju*).
The laying down [of the bricks] is performed in the same manner as for the widow.
The *rītis*, however, begin from the corners and so forth.
In the second *prastāra*, there are twenty *pādyas* in the middle and eighteen *navamīs*;
these too are to be applied behind and in front of the central *pādas*.
"One who has rivals should pile the chariot-wheel-shaped altar," so it is known; this is the commentary of Kapardin. (ĀpŚus 12.11)
Having made a circular area of ground as large as the fire—measuring one *aratni* and one *prādeśa*—one should place a square [altar] upon it, as far as it can fit. (ĀpŚus 12.12)
In another *Śulba* [text], two chariot wheels are mentioned; by this teacher, however, only one is mentioned. Therefore, that very [wheel] is described here.

Having made a circular area of ground twice the size of the fire-altar—including the *aratni* and the *prādeśa*—one should construct a square-making tool using the transverse cord (*tiryaṅbhānī*) on both sides of the *prauga*. With that, one should have the bricks made.
Having laid down one hundred and forty-four of those [bricks] in the square, one should superimpose a square upon them as far as possible.
Thus ends the twelfth section.
With its diagonal cord, one should have twelve bricks made. (ĀpŚus 13.1)
Having placed six of them upon the foundation, one should divide the remainder into eight parts.
There are four *pradhika* bricks.
Among those *pradhika* bricks, having laid down six bricks made with twelve [units], one should divide the remaining *pradhika* space into eight parts and place them with eight [units].

We shall describe their construction: one [board] is thirty-three finger-breadths minus eight sesame seeds; another is thirty-one finger-breadths minus twelve sesame seeds; one is twenty-eight finger-breadths; and one is twenty-eight finger-breadths plus two sesame seeds. With these four boards, one *karaṇa* is formed; of this, one should plane the fourth board so that it takes the shape of a bow and so that the arrow [fitting within it] is exactly eighteen sesame seeds in measure.

Likewise, one [measure] is thirty-one finger-breadths minus twelve sesame seeds; one is twenty-one finger-breadths minus eleven sesame seeds; one is thirty-eight finger-breadths plus three sesame seeds; and one is thirty-nine finger-breadths plus twelve sesame seeds. With these four, the second *kararaṇa* is formed. One should plane its fourth side as before, so that its length becomes equal to an arrow (*śara*) plus two sesame seeds; one should plane it accordingly.

One [span] is forty *aṅgulas* less ten *tilas*; one is thirty-three *aṅgulas* less ten *tilas*; one is thirty-two *aṅgulas* plus one *tila*; one is thirty-two *aṅgulas* plus twelve *tilas*; one is twenty-eight *aṅgulas* plus eleven *tilas*; and one is forty-five *aṅgulas* less four *tilas*. With these four, the fourth *karaṇa* is formed. One should plane that fourth [side]. And as before, the two measurements are two *aṅgulas* less three *tilas*. Regarding this, there are two verses: [The verses follow.]
A cord made from another [measure], measuring one hundred and eighty-seven finger-breadths, forms the noose;
the dawn (oṣā) makes the circular chariot-wheel mandala.
The cord for making the square measures two hundred and sixty-four [finger-breadths].
Combined with thirteen sesame seeds, [one should worship] upon the sacrificial fire, which is like the wheel of a chariot.
Karavindīyā Vyākhyā: "And the chariot" means the chariot-wheel; it is circular in shape. This is for one who has enemies—that is, one being oppressed by them—in order to conquer them.
It should be as follows:

the diagonal (karaṇī) of a space measuring two *puruṣas* and eighty-eight finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*) plus one span (*aratni*) and one step (*prādeśa*) is twenty-one *tilas* more than half the diameter.
Having divided and drawn a square of the maximum possible size within that [space], [one proceeds].
The side of that square measures two hundred and sixty-four finger-breadths and thirteen sesame seeds;
its twelfth part is twenty-two finger-breadths and one sesame seed.
The side-measure for the twelve-part bricks is four [units].

In the middle of that, there are one hundred and forty-four circular bricks (*iṣṭakā*). Having laid down six of those twelve-part bricks on each rim (*pradhi*) and completed that, one should divide the remainder—the portion left over from the rims—into eight parts.
Among these, in the southern half of the eastern rim, near the side-measure for the square bricks, there are three twelve-part bricks oriented north-south.

Having drawn a line to the north, one should divide the remaining space by one and a half units into four parts. In each part, there is one *karaṇa*; for three of these, there are two parts in front [of the *karaṇa*] and two parts to the south of it. In this division, the transverse measurement (*tiryaṅmānī*) of the four parts at the rear is thirty-three finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
A single sesame seed [unit].
Therein, the construction of the southern portion is performed with three side-beams (*phalaka*);
therein, the cross-beam (*tiryaṅbhānī*) mentioned is equal to four [units], while the side-beam (*pārśvamānī*) is only one.
And that [first side] is forty-six finger-breadths and twelve sesame seeds;
the second [side] should be stated as forty-two finger-breadths and twenty-five and a half sesame seeds.
Having drawn [the shape] with a cord or a compass-measure equal to half its width, one should plane it.

The second south-side measuring line is the same as that which was described as the north side of the southern [section]; and the cross-measuring line is stated to be forty-two finger-breadths and twenty-five sesame seeds. The north-side measuring line is forty-two finger-breadths and twenty-five sesame seeds.
The face [of the chariot] is thirty-four finger-breadths and ten sesame seeds; one should plane that first. The same measurements, but reversed, are the dimensions for the rear half.
This same method of division applies to the northern half; there,
for all [the bricks], that very [line] is subsequently the transverse line and the southern transverse line.
The right side of those on the north becomes the right side;
they are indeed those very same faces.
Here, the fifth is like the fourth.
The sixth is like the third;
the seventh is like the second;
the eighth is like the first.
In this manner, these instruments are positioned with their faces turned toward the south, north, and west upon the southern, northern, and western rims respectively.
In the *Sundararājīyā* commentary,
it is explained that the width of the chariot wheel is already detailed in the procedure for the mandala.
Having fixed a peg in the center, one should draw a circle with a radius of one hundred and eighty-five finger-breadths (aṅgulas) plus fourteen sesame-seeds (tilas).
Its circumference is one thousand one hundred and sixty-five finger-breadths minus one sesame-seed.
In the middle of that, one should lay out a square using a side-measure of two hundred and sixty-two finger-breadths plus seven sesame-seeds, which is twice the half-diameter (viṣkambhārdha).
Outside the square are four protrusions.
Thus ends the twelfth section.
One should construct its square base with sides measuring twenty-two finger-breadths plus five *tilas*.
In the middle of the square, one hundred and forty-four bricks lie.
Of these—one should divide them. Having laid down six squares in the middle of the *pradhi*, one should divide the remainder of that *pradhi* into eight parts.
Of the six [channels] thus established, two each are said to be on the sides and four at the mouth;
of these, there are four functional types,
the first being triangular.
Of that [frame], one horizontal plank is twenty-six finger-breadths long and joined with three sesame-seeds;
the second is thirty-three finger-breadths long, diminished by seven and a half sesame-seeds;
and the third is forty-two finger-breadths long, joined with eleven sesame-seeds.
One should fashion that bow in the shape of an ear,
such that the arrow consists of six *tila* seeds and one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
For the second [bow], there is a single transverse plank measuring twenty-six *aṅgulas* and three *tilas*.
One side measures forty-two finger-breadths and eleven sesame seeds;
another side measures thirty-three finger-breadths less seven sesame seeds;
and the other side measures thirty-six finger-breadths and twenty sesame seeds.
One should fashion it like that bow so that the arrow becomes three *tilas* less than a finger in length;
the third transverse plank is twenty-five and a half fingers.
The second [side] is thirty [units] minus sixteen *tilas*.
One other side is thirty-three [units] minus seven *tilas*; one should plane that so it is like a bow.
Its arrow (diagonal) is twenty-five *tilas*.
These same four *karaṇas* occur in reverse order in another *pradhyardha*;
likewise, there are four *pradhayas*.

In the *kapardibhāṣya* regarding the placement [of bricks]: one should form the corners toward the intermediate directions of the square; in the middle, on the other layer. One should pile them in alternating fashion for as many layers as one intends to construct. (ĀpŚus 13.3)
This has been explained.
This same arrangement applies to the mandala, the cremation ground, and the droṇa.
It is known from scripture: "One who desires food should pile the droṇaciti. (ĀpŚus 13.4)
"For one desiring food, [the altar] is piled in the shape of a droṇa," so says the Śruti.
There are indeed two kinds of droṇas: those that are square and those that are circular. (ĀpŚus 13.5)
In that case, one may act according to one's desire, because the meaning of the word is intended to apply to the object.
The word *droṇa* denotes a water-receptacle that is circular,
made of wood, provided with a handle, and square; it is stated that one or the other of these is to be understood here.
One may build it either square or circular according to one's desire;
since no specific distinction is prescribed, one should build it either square or circular,
as both terms are applicable.
Or it may be square, for its treatise on qualities is fourfold.
And it is square. ĀpŚus_13.8.
"It subsequently becomes a handle because of its conformity," so it is understood. (ĀpŚus 13.9)
The word "vā" (or) serves to exclude the alternative position;
it does not signify an option.
This [altar] should not be strewn in the shape of a circle; it should be strewn as a square alone.
Regarding the scripture concerning its quality, namely, "the food is placed in a *droṇa*," that [measure] is applicable to a square *droṇa*, not to one that is circular in shape. Therefore,
by virtue of this connection with the quality, it must be determined to be specifically square.
Therefore, it should be measured out as a perfect square.
Behind, in the place of the tail, there is a *nitsaru* (a peg or projection), because of the scriptural statement regarding its conformity; this is for the purpose of achieving that specific form.
This is the Karavindīyā commentary.
One should observe closely.
It has been explained.
O Droṇa.
A vessel that has food as its support is called a *droṇa*.
One who desires food should pile it in that shape.
There are two [types].
The word *tu* indicates a distinction:
the wooden troughs (*droṇa*) are not of a single type like the *prauga* and so forth, but rather are of two types—quadrangular and circular.
The word *khalu* denotes well-known fact.
Because it has been stated [that it is] "due to being that," both types are to be understood, since the word *droṇa* is employed in both cases.
The squares must be taken as being indeed square.
Why? Because that for which this teaching of qualities exists is square; having referred to the natural square fire-altar (*agni*), the shape of a *droṇa* vessel is prescribed for one desiring food.
Therefore, the meaning is that this too must be understood as being perfectly square.
"Behind"—
behind the self, there is a noose situated at the tail;
"noose" (tsaru) means the fist.
Just as for a man standing facing the east, a person standing behind him would also have his fist behind [his back], so it is here as well; this is the meaning.
In Sundararāja’s commentary on the section concerning the placement [of the fire-pan]: "Or it may be square.
He states the reason for this:
That which is—namely, the fire—is quadrangular;
it is a "guṇaprāpaka" (attainer of qualities) because it is a perfect square. That which is—namely, the fire.
*Paścāstaru*—it is understood thus:
that which has its sun (*sūrya*) behind it is so described;
or it may be an uncompounded term.
The word *tsaru* possesses both genders;
the lexicographical statement that "*tsaruḥ* is masculine" is an error,
because of the usage in the expression "*daśamaṃtsaru*" (having ten handles).
"Proportionality" means conformity to the *droṇa* measure;
and this is the same for both the circular and square [mandalas].
Thus said Bhāradvāja:
"One desiring food should pile it in the form of a trough (droṇa), either square or circular; its handle is at the back.
Thus Kātyāyana has stated quite clearly.
"A tenth part is turned [toward] the west, or else toward the east; it is exactly the same even on a white [spot].
(Kapardibhāṣya): It is stated that a tenth part of the entire ground constitutes the handle (*tsaru*), and its removal is performed by means of its tail (*puccha*). (ĀpŚus 13.10)
By means of that [measurement], one should have twelve bricks made; [some] one and a half [bricks] and [some] quarter-bricks. ĀpŚus 13.11.
A field of twelve *caturbhāgīyās* is the tenth part of a *saratniprādeśa*.
Its cross-measure (*tiryaṅbhānī*) is six finger-breadths in length, and its side-measure (*pārśvamānī*) is twice that.
When a square is formed by means of a diagonal cord (*kṣṇayā rajju*) upon that [side-measure], it becomes a field of twelve *caturbhāgīyās*.
The measure of a *yaca* is [one unit];
by that same measure multiplied threefold, a *droṇa* is formed. Its extraction by means of the tail has been stated—the path of measurement is explained by the tail itself.

One should have twelve bricks made from its [the *droṇa*'] measure; "its" refers here to the *droṇa* with its handle—that is, by means of its triangular, equilateral portion, which constitutes one-fourth [of the whole]. Regarding the half-bricks (*ardheṣṭakā*) and quarter-bricks (*pādeṣṭakā*), ritualists are divided in opinion: some desire the quarter-brick to be laid crosswise (*akṣṇayā*), while others desire it to be a long-quarter-brick; for they hold that without those [long-quarter-bricks], it is impossible to complete the required number.

It has been stated in the *Śulbāntara*: "Regarding the half-bricks (*ardheṣṭakā*). Here too, because of the word "and" (*ca*), it means "and the half-bricks. And the instruments (*karaṇa*) are as follows: one instrument is thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) less one sesame-seed (*tila*); the second is one and a half [finger-breadths] on one side; the first instrument is fourfold in length on both sides with a diagonal; by that, there is the third instrument for the quarters (*pāda*); and the fourth instrument for the half-bricks is by means of that very same long third instrument.
On the *upadhāna* layer, he places one and a half bricks on the front part of himself facing westward, and two on the hips facing eastward. (ĀpŚus 13.12)
One should cover the entire fire-altar with square bricks. ĀpŚus_13.13 ||
One should complete the count with brick-pieces for the corners (pādeṣṭakās). ĀpŚus 13.14.

In the next layer, he places bricks measuring one and a half [bricks] on the self (the central part), extending northwards from the south and southwards from the north; and on the two sides of the handle, [he places bricks] extending southwards and northwards. ĀpŚus_13.15 ||
One should cover the entire fire-altar with square bricks. ĀpŚus_13.16.
One should complete the count with bricks for the feet. ĀpŚus_13.17.
One should pile them in an alternating manner for as many layers (prastāra) as one intends to construct.
Thus ends the thirteenth section.
Regarding the laying of the bricks: having laid the half-bricks according to the Sūtra, one should cut seventeen bricks diagonally in the eastern half into two halves each.

If the quarters are long, one should not cut the bricks in the northern row; as there are forward quarters, so there are eight [halves] in the southern row, and likewise eighteen in the eastern direction.
In that case, the layout (prastāra) is exactly as before. In another layout, one should cut eighteen bricks from the back part of oneself within the construction frame;
two bricks each by means of simply dividing them in two.
If the feet are long in the eastern row, one should break nine bricks;
or as in the northern [row], two by two behind the spine, and likewise in front, half-bricks and quarter-bricks in the middle of the cords, with the feet oriented toward the north.
In this way, the arrangement consists of two hundred [bricks].
Regarding this, there are these verses:
"Three hundred and ninety-three *tilas* (sesame seeds) constitute the measure of one *āḍhaka*;
that same measure, multiplied by three, is the *droṇa*."
In the case of the fire-altar called Droṇa, which is square and situated in a cremation ground, the divisions are the quarters and the halves, and these are the constituent parts.
Where there are feet in the first layer, there are none in the upper one;
in the first layer there are two halves, and in the upper layer there are four.
And having placed [the foot] on the upper layer, preceded by the state of being one and a half;
wherever there may be one and a half [units], there the feet should be long, provided that they are indeed [so].
They should be oriented toward the east on the first layer and toward the north on the upper layer;
there are seven rows of half-bricks surrounding the middle of the foot on the upper layer.
Thus it is.
Karavindīyā Vyākhyā:
The hilt (tsaru) is one-tenth of the entire area of the fire-altar (agnikṣetra).
The neuter gender designation is according to Vedic usage.
The tenth part of the area of a *saratni* is the field of a *dvādaśabhāgīya*.
Its extraction (*nirhāra*)—that is, its separation from the whole—should be performed by means of the tail, that is, by means of the region of the tail.
This is called the "extraction" (*nirhāra*) for one who wishes to extract a square from a square:
the side-measure (*karaṇī*) of the square self-altar is three hundred and eleven *aṅgulas* and twenty-six *tilas*;
but that of the *tsaru* (handle) is one hundred and three *aṅgulas* and thirty-one *tilas*.
What is the side-measure (*karaṇī*) of that [altar]? And what is the side-measure of that *droṇa*? It is ten and twenty-six finger-breadths less a sesame-seed (*tila*).

The side-measure of the twelve-part bricks is, on one side, twenty-six finger-breadths less a sesame-seed, and on the other side, thirty-nine finger-breadths less one and a half sesame-seeds. The second set of tools consists of quarter-bricks, which belong to the same twelve-part series.

By the use of the word "and" (ca), half-bricks are also included, because it is impossible to complete the required number without them. And it is stated in another Śulba-sūtra: "Foot-bricks and half-bricks"—thus one should break the first mould diagonally.
The side-measuring brick is either with a quarter [of a unit] or twelve parts;
its fourth part is the cross-measuring brick, which is a quarter-brick (pādeṣṭakā).
In the *upadhāna* layer, he places twelve bricks facing west upon himself in the eastern part;
in the *tsarva* section, four [bricks].
There are four in each of the two hips;
thus, there are twenty-four and a half [ribs].

Having covered the entire remaining area of the fire-altar with twelve-part bricks, one should place two rows of four-brick units on the tail; in front of those two, there are one brick of the *viśaya* form and four bricks;
and in the direction in front of that, there is one [additional] brick.
In the center, there are twelve bricks with their long axes oriented northward;
one hundred and twenty-one square bricks;
and twenty-four half-bricks.
On the northern side, having removed nine squares, one should lay down thirty-six long bricks facing west. On the southern side, having likewise removed nine, one should lay down thirty-eight bricks.
In the eastern direction, having removed the two outermost among the twelve-part bricks, one should lay down two half-bricks each.
If there are eighteen square-foot bricks in the eastern half, having removed them diagonally, there are seventy-two foot-bricks; having removed two bricks, there are two pairs of half-bricks.
This layer consists of two hundred [bricks].
On the western side—
twelve [bricks] toward the north on the northern stone, and likewise twelve toward the north on the southern stone.
There are four on each of the two flanks of the tail;
thus, there are thirty-two eastern lines.
In the tail there are four squares; in the body, twelve bricks with their faces oriented toward the east;
that makes one hundred and twelve.
Then, on the self (the central part), having removed ten squares, one should lay down thirty-two bricks as side-steps (*pāda*) diagonally.
And there should be four long bricks facing inward; having removed nine bricks in the eastern row, one should lay down thirty-six bricks as side-steps facing north.

Afterwards, having placed eighteen square bricks of nine padas each extending towards the north upon the self (the central area), one should place before them, on both sides, seven bricks of two padas and half a brick each; before those, one should place eighteen bricks of half a brick each; and before those, one should place nine bricks of a pada each.
This layer consists of two hundred bricks.
This is the Sundararājīya commentary.

The meaning is that one should measure it at the back, as if it were the tail of the whole [altar] protruding from itself. That [tail] is a square *droṇa*-shaped mound, a perfect square measuring twelve hundred and thirty finger-breadths plus eight *tilas*. In its middle part toward the back, one should construct a handle (*atsaru*) which is a perfect square measuring one-third of the side of that [square].
One should cause its side-measure (*karaṇī*) to be made.
By means of the *ātmakaraṇī* (the self-measuring cord) twelve units long, measuring twenty-six finger-breadths and one-third of a *tila*, they are made into equal squares.
The half-bricks (*adhyardhā*) and the quarter-bricks (*pādeṣṭakā*) are likewise; and the ninth bricks are made with the third part, as before.
In the taking up— by means of twelve [verses], the northern course is established.
In the front row—there are four full bricks and four half-bricks; likewise for the two hips, there are four each.
Thus, there are twelve.
One should cover the entire fire-altar with twelve [sets of bricks]; when thus covered, there are one hundred and forty-eight [bricks].
One should fill [the remaining spaces] with quarter-bricks (pādeṣṭakā).
Within the self, there are twelve eastern lines.
Therein, having omitted two from the south, the three preceding ones and the ninth are the northern lines.
From there, there are twelve lines for the feet.
Then there are three [bricks] of the ninth [set].
Then twelve [bricks] starting with the eastern quarter. Then three [bricks] of the ninth [set] facing north.
Then, in the first half of the twelfth [day],
the procedure for the twelfth day is exactly the same.
In this manner, there is a two-hundred-fold arrangement.
In the other [direction]— twelve each toward the north and the south;
"toward the south" (dakṣiṇā) is understood as the accusative plural.
On both sides of the handle, four [lines] toward the south and four toward the north;
one should cover the entire fire-altar,
which results in one hundred and forty-four [units].
One should fill [the space] with foot-bricks; in the self-altar, there are twelve rows toward the north.
Here, in the western part, three ninth [bricks] are placed facing east, starting from the south of the one and a half [brick].
Then there are eight *pādyā* days;
then three *navamī*s;
then the twelfth day; then three *navamī*s.
Then there are eight *pādyā* [verses], then three *navamīs*,
then the twelfth,
and then three more *navamīs*.
Then it is one and a half [units].
Thus is the preceding method;
the arrangement consists of two hundred [bricks].
Having desired to perform the transposition, the method for the circular *droṇaciti* will now be described:
a bamboo rod one hundred and seventy-six *aṅgulas* long, minus three sesame seeds [in length], with holes at both ends.
Having driven a peg into the center and fastened a bamboo tube to it, one should draw a circle with a hole at the other end.
At a distance of one hundred and sixty-eight finger-breadths plus two sesame seeds behind the central peg, another peg should be placed;
behind that is the handle.
One should make a measuring cord (*samacāra*) four hundred finger-breadths long, minus two *tilas*.

Having fixed a peg (*śaṅku*) four hundred finger-breadths behind the central peg of the mandala, minus three *tilas*, one should attach the bamboo rod to that [peg] and, using the other end of the hole, draw from the southwest corner of the handle toward the northwest corner, so that the tip of the handle takes the form of a cross. As the mandala is rotated, as far as the front end of the handle is held, so far it comes back behind.
Then, in the middle of the maṇḍala, one should lay down a square as before, measuring two hundred and forty-nine fingers minus eight tilas.

With its diagonal (karaṇī), twelve bricks—each measuring twenty-one fingers minus nine tilas—are formed; four hundred and forty-four bricks lie within that square. Then there is one long measurement (dīrgha-karaṇa).
Its width is twenty-five and three-quarter finger-breadths (aṅgulas) plus one sesame-seed (tila);
each side is thirty-four finger-breadths plus twenty-two sesame-seeds.

Four of these [tiles] are to be placed at the base and middle of the ridge-pole (pradhi), four in the east and west oriented lengthwise from front to back, and four in the south and north oriented lengthwise from left to right.
In the remaining *pradhi* sections there are seven bricks each;
at the mouths of the four [sections] there are three each;
and on the two sides there are two each. Thus, there are four types of construction for them.
The first [side] is a triangle; its first plank is twenty-eight finger-breadths minus six *tilas*.
The second is thirty-six [finger-breadths] minus seven *tilas*.
The third, which forms the hypotenuse, is forty-six finger-breadths minus one-third; one should carve it like a bow so that the arrow [the perpendicular] becomes one and a half finger-breadths.
For the second [side], one *tilyaka-phalaka* is twenty-eight units less six *tilas*;
the other is forty-three units less three parts;
and one side is thirty-six units plus seven *tilas*.
The distance between the sides is thirty-nine [finger-breadths] plus eighteen sesame seeds;
one should plane it so that it is curved like a bow, such that the arrow (the perpendicular) is four sesame seeds and one finger-breadth.
One transverse plank of the third [section] is nine [finger-breadths] plus one sesame seed.
The other [side] is sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgula) plus one sesame seed (tila).
One side is thirty-five finger-breadths minus twelve sesame seeds, while the other side is thirty-five finger-breadths plus twelve sesame seeds; one should plane it so that it is like a bow.
The arrow (śara) consists of thirty sesame seeds.
For the fourth [altar], the two transverse sides are sixteen *tilas* long, and the two lateral sides are thirty-five *tilas* minus ten *tilas*.
One should plane one lateral side so that it is shaped like a bow;
the arrow (the distance between the ends of the chord) is twenty-nine *tilas*.
This brick is to be placed in the middle of the rim (pradhi), with three bricks each on either side as previously described, arranged in forward and reverse order.
Thus, there are one hundred and eighty-eight bricks in the area of the mandala.
Then, having removed the three bricks from the middle of the other rim, one should place them at the very end.
When only the handles remain, there are twelve long bricks;
this constitutes a layer of two hundred [bricks]. Another layer is exactly the same.
The corners of the square, however, are located in the cardinal directions.
For the handle, there are two other measurements;
therein, one is twenty-six finger-breadths less three sesamum-seeds, and the other is a plank of the size of a sesamum fruit.
On the two sides, at one-third of forty finger-breadths (aṅgula),
there is a diagonal cord (akṣṇayārajju) measuring forty-three finger-breadths plus six sesame seeds;
the other measures fifty-one finger-breadths plus ten sesame seeds.
One side-plate should be carved like a bow;
that arrow is four *tila*-grains wide.
The other side is likewise.
The inner cavity, however, is exactly like the shape of the bricks: these bricks are four each on both the *tsaru* and the sides, extending toward the north.
Then there is another square measuring twenty-six minus six *tilas*; one of its *tilya*-sized faces should be carved like a bow so that the arrow [of the cavity] becomes sixteen *tilas*.
In the same way, the other transverse plank is also treated. The inner cavity, however, is exactly like the shape of the bricks.
Just as these four bricks with handles are placed in the middle, so there are two hundred layers; one should pile them in alternating fashion for as many layers as one intends to pile.

Thus ends the thirteenth section. It is known from the tradition: "One desiring cattle should pile the fire-altar in the Kapardikṣāmya manner, which is to be constructed with a complete set of layers. ĀpŚus 14.1.
He piles the bricks while actually removing them [from the fire-pan]. ĀpŚus_14.2.
The sacrificial pits (cātvāla) are located in the cardinal directions; it is known from scripture that one draws [the earth] from them toward the east. (ĀpŚus 14.3)
"Samūhya" refers to a specific method of piling, not a specific shape. This rule applies only to the archetype (*prakṛti*), not to its modified forms (*vikāra*).
Having placed bricks around the area of the fire-altar, one piles them in such a way that they are gathered together; that is to say, one piles them by taking them from all sides.
This is the very procedure for the foundation: "Catafalques (cātvāla) are to be made outside the altar in every direction;
from those catafalques, he draws up the loose earth (purīṣa), the dust," so says the Śruti.
"One desiring a village should pile the Paricāyya," thus it is known. (ĀpŚus 14.4)
This also is the procedure for the insertion of the wedge.
He encloses the central naturally perforated brick with groups of bricks moving clockwise; that is the *pariyāyya* enclosure.
On the third layer, having laid down the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick, he lays down groups of bricks (*iṣṭakāgaṇa*) around that *svayamātṛṇṇā* in a clockwise direction;
this is the *paricāyya*.
"One desiring a village should pile the *upacāyya*," so it is known from tradition. (ĀpŚus 14.6)
He was addressed by the *paricāyya*: ĀpŚus 14.7.
As before, there is an exchange with the *paricāyya* fire-altar.
[End of] Karavindīya-vyākhyā, Samūha section.
In this context, the quality is the act of piling up (*samūhana*), not a specific form.
"One desiring cattle should pile this very fire"—
here he states the ground for the application of the term *samūhya*:

"Samūhan" means "as if piling up. Having placed the bricks around the fire-site (*agnikṣetra*), one should pile them up—meaning, one should place them in such a way that they are accomplished so as to be higher and higher from the outside toward the inside. This is the meaning: having made the entire fire-site high in the interior and low on the exterior by means of loose earth (*puriṣa*), and having placed the bricks there, one should fill the site with the loose earth together with the bricks.
It is prescribed regarding the directions:
there are *cātvālas* in all four directions.

Due to the abundance of soil (*purīṣa*), there is a multiplicity of *cātvālas*. Having measured out each individual *cātvāla* in the directions with a *śamyā*, one separates [the soil] for the *uttaravedis* at that very time, as in the archetype.
"Having taken clods of earth from all of those [sites], one should pile them upon the altar.
This refers precisely to the measurements and the laying down of bricks already under discussion.
"Practiced"—
the quality here is the act of practicing itself.
He explains the meaning of the Vedic revelation (śruti):
The middle [altar]—[the syllable] *yyaḥ*.

Having laid down the bricks beginning with the *ākramaṇa* and ending with the *svayamātṛṇṇā* on the third layer, one should surround the *svayamātṛṇṇā* clockwise with groups of gold bricks (*hiraṇyeṣṭakā*) moving from left to right.
This surrounding (*paricayana*) sets aside the positions of the original [bricks].
This is two hundred;
"upa-ukta" (consecrated) is also a quality consisting of an accumulation.
Piling up (*upacayana*) is the act of piling (*caya*) near together;
these very [bricks] serve as the materials for constructing the celestial palaces (*vimāna*).
Everything is like the *paricāyya* fire-altar.
This is the distinction: the first begins from the outside and ends near the *svayamātṛṇṇā*;
the second begins near the *svayamātṛṇṇā* and ends on the outside.
This is the commentary of Sundararāja.
Now begins the fourteenth section: Having placed bricks all around the site of the fire-altar, he lays them down as if piling them up in one heap by sweeping them together.
The *cātvāla* pit is to be surrounded by the *paricāyya* mound; having laid down the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick, he lays down all the other bricks around that *svayamātṛṇṇā*.
However, there are no specific requirements such as laying them facing east or west.
Each preceding group [of bricks] is near the *svayamātṛṇṇā* [brick];
each subsequent one is further out from that.
The form of these two, the *samūhya* and the *paricāyya*, is exactly like the archetype (*prakṛti*), and the bricks are the same, as there is no mention of any specific difference.

Alternatively, when the collection [of bricks] is performed by standing around the group, a pile of bricks takes the form of a circle; thus, by implication, the fire itself takes the form of a circle.
Furthermore, since the surrounding of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks is possible only within a fire that is circular in shape, it follows by implication that the fire is circular.
And so says Baudhāyana: "The *samūhya* and *paricāyya* fires are explained by the preceding [section on] the chariot-wheel-pile (*rathacakracit*)."
The meaning is that *upacāra* is simply another technical term for the same [concept] found in other systems;
this is from the *Kapardibhāṣya*.
"One who desires, 'May I prosper in the world of the ancestors,' should pile the Śmaśānacit altar; so it is known. (ĀpŚus 14.8)
He who should desire, "May I prosper in the world of the fathers," he should pile [the fire] in this manner. Indeed, there are two kinds of cemeteries: square and circular. (ĀpŚus 14.9)
In that case, one may act according to one's desire, because the meaning of the word is the object [of the injunction]. (ĀpŚus 14.10)
Or it may be square; for that which has an instruction regarding its specific quality. (ĀpŚus 14.11)
It is square; with the exception of the handle, it is described as being built in the manner of a *droṇa* altar.
Cemeteries exist both in square shapes and in circular shapes;
in this regard, the application of the term [“cemetery”] occurs according to one’s preference, since the term applies to both.
For instance, if it is circular in shape, like a chariot wheel.
"Or square"—this has already been explained.
The scripture concerning whose qualities is connected with the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka) pertains to the square cremation ground, not the circular one;
for there the pits (khālāḥ) are dug,
and the connection with those ancestors for whom the ancestral rites (paitṛmedhika-kriyā) are performed is established through prosperity.

Therefore, it should be built as a square. If it is a square, then, with the exception of the handle (*āt-saru*), it is described as being built like a *droṇa* altar; all of that has already been explained in the section on the *droṇa* altar.
"One who desires cattle should pile the Chandaścit," so it is known. (ĀpŚus 14.13)

He explains the meaning of this scriptural statement—"One desiring cattle should pile the *chandasvat* [altar], wherein the bricks are piled with the *chandases* (metres)"—by means of two scriptural citations:
"One should pile with all the *chandases*" is one; "with the archetypal ones" is the other. (ĀpŚus 14.14)
The fourteenth section:
One scriptural tradition holds that [the fire-altar] should be covered with all the meters of the ten mandalas;
another scriptural tradition holds that it should be covered with the original meters—those meters which exist in the archetype (prakṛti), such as "Agni is the head," and so forth.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the commentary on the Āpastamba Śulba Sūtra, known as the Kapardisvāmī Bhāṣya;
[this is] the Karavindīyā Vyākhyā.
"Śmaśā"—
one who desires growth in the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka) should pile [the fire-altar] like a cemetery (śmaśāna),
because it consists of two parts.
[The section on] the *gata* [is concluded].
In the world, two kinds of cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*) are seen, having the form of fire-altars (*agnyāyatana*) and enclosures (*prakāra*): namely, square and circular.
"Square" (*caturaśra*)—the suffix *-śraḥ*.
Because it is the natural form, one should pile it as a square alone and not as a circle; thus the summary has been stated.
The cremation grounds should be constructed like the *droṇaciti*;
one should avoid the handle (*tsaru*), and all other measurements should be like those of the *droṇa*.

The twelve-part bricks are one and a half [parts], half [a part], and a quarter [of a part]; they are twenty-seven finger-breadths and thirteen sesame seeds. The one-and-a-half [bricks] are similar on one side; on the other side, they are forty-one finger-breadths and three sesame seeds. The half [bricks] are similar to the twelve-part bricks on one side; on the other side, they are half of that. The quarter [bricks] are similar to the twelve-part bricks on one side; on the other side, they are nine finger-breadths and slightly more than four sesame seeds.
In the first layer of the *upadhāna*, one covers the front and back with bricks measuring one and a half [bricks] that have the appearance of squares;
the completion of the count is effected by using quarter-bricks and half-bricks.
In the second layer, on the south and north sides, one covers them with square bricks measuring one and a half [bricks], and so forth, as previously described.
*Chandas*: it is called *chandas* because it is sung (*cīyate*) with those chants (*chandobhiḥ*) and verses (*ṛgbhiḥ*); this alone is the distinction.
Everything else is exactly the same as the original form (*prakṛti*).
One should pour out [the soma] with all the *chandasya* verses found in the ten *maṇḍalas*.
Having divided those into a thousand parts, one should place each brick with one of those parts.
In place of the *yajuṣ* formulas, the *chandas* (metres) should be used.

Therein, having divided the *chandas* according to the number of *iṣṭakās* possessed of *yajuṣ* formulas, one should place each individual *iṣṭakā* possessed of a *yajuṣ* formula with each single division of those [metres]. However, the *lokampṛṇā* bricks are to be placed as before.

Alternatively, one should lay down the bricks belonging to Yājñasenī, beginning from the front, using all the meters found in the ten-fold [Ṛgveda]—namely, the Gāyatrīs, Triṣṭubhs, Jagatīs, Anuṣṭubhs, Bṛhatīs, Uṣṇiks, Paṅktis, Akṣarapaṅktis, Viṣurūpas, and those divided into three parts—as well as the Aticchandas divided into three parts, and all the Dvipadās.

Prākṛta means by those [verses] belonging to the *agnikāṇḍa*, such as the section beginning with "Agnirmūrdhā," which consist of *gāyatrī* meters and so forth; it does not mean by the ten-fold collections (*daśatayī*). This is another point, and it has been established that there is no division beyond this.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
"The fires increase one by one, indeed, in sequence up to one hundred and one;
they are taught in the third chapter, and their divisions [begin] from the fourth."
The nature of the fires is either of one kind or of seven kinds.
If it is of one kind, then for the six [fires] there are no wings or tails.
When they possess sevenfold nature, they also come to have wings and a tail;
