for those beginning with the sevenfold, that very same [nature] exists up until the one-hundred-and-one-fold.
With those twelve parts of the *karaṇī*s, combined with or subtracted from the stated parts, bricks are produced separately according to their forms; thus, the foundation is of three kinds.
The threefold nature of the *ekavidha* and other [altar types] arises from their having a side;
likewise, the threefold nature of the pair of *prauga* altars arises from this, and not otherwise in the absence of a side.

There are two square [altars], two prauga-shaped ones, the chariot-wheel-shaped, the trough-shaped, and the piled-in-mass; the last two are preceded by the term *paryupapūrva*; the *śmaśānacit*, the *chandaściti*, and the *śyena* [are also mentioned]; the *kaṅkacit* and *alajacit*—these are the sevenfold types; the fivefold are as before, and the tenfold are the burners (*dahana*).
The Prauga-cit, the Ubhayaprauga, the Rathacakra, the Droṇa-cit, the Śmaśāna-agni,
and those beginning with the Kūrma-cit— these are said by others to be without wings and tail;
other fires, however, are described as having wings and tails, both those already mentioned and those yet to be described.
I shall explain the fires, headed by Śyena, here in these two subsequent chapters.

Thus ends the fourth section in the Śulbapradīpikā composed by Karavindasvāmin; [this is] the commentary by Sundararāja on the [sections] beginning with "śmaśānasya," "dvayārthatvāt," and "caturviṃśati-uktaḥ."
In this case, for the square shape, the side-measure (karaṇī) is three hundred and twenty-eight finger-breadths and twenty-one sesame-seeds.
With its twelfth part—twenty-seven finger-breadths and thirteen sesame-seeds—the twelve-part bricks (dvādaśabhāgīyāḥ) are formed;
with half of that, the quarter-bricks (pādyāḥ); and with a third of that, the ninth-bricks (navamyaḥ).
The *adhāra* is as before.
In the placing [of the bricks], there are twelve and a half bricks facing west in front,
and twelve facing east behind.
The remainder is like that of Droṇa;
since everything is absent there, sixteen bricks are omitted.
Therefore, having removed two from the middle of the fire-altar, eighteen *navamyaḥ* should be placed.
The layout consists of two hundred [squares].
Another is exactly like this,
but with the reversal of the east and north.
In the maṇḍala, the chariot-wheel of the cremation ground is explained as the *chandaścit* (the piling with meters);
it is called *chandaścit* because it is piled by means of the meters (*chandobhiś cīyate*).

The suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *kṛ* when a Vedic term (*chāndasa*) is the upapada; otherwise, it is applied after the object (*karman*) when the word is not called "fire" (*agni*). Regarding that [the laying of bricks], one opinion is as follows: one should lay all the bricks with Vedic verses (*chandobhiḥ*) brought from the ten maṇḍalas of the Ṛgveda, which consist of all the meters—beginning with the *gāyatrī* and increasing by four syllables each up to the *atidhṛti*, or up to the *utkṛti* making twenty-one varieties—specifically including the *trivṛt*, *kakubh*, and others.

Another opinion holds that [the fire-altar] consists of the *prākṛta* (archetypal) fires, studied in the section beginning with "mūrdhan" and dedicated to Yājñasenī, which have been practiced again and again.
The form of this fire is exactly like that of the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Some, however, because of the eternity of the statement "this is indeed the image of birds," also desire the form of birds.
As Vaudhāyana has said: "Its form is that of the shape of a hawk."

Thus ends the fourth chapter of the *Śulbapradīpikā* composed by the venerable Sundararāja; this is the commentary of Kapardin. It is known from scripture: "One who desires heaven should pile the fire-altar in the shape of a hawk (*śyenacit*). (ĀpŚus 15.1)
The side becomes curved and the tail is turned away. ĀpŚus_15.2a.
It is to be piled like a hawk; one who piles it as a hawk-pile should pile it in that shape. He himself will later state that the fruit of the shape is the accomplishment of that form.
It has crooked wings and a spread tail—that is, a tail that is not contracted.
How is there curvature?
He raises [the grass] from the west towards the east; he raises it from the east towards the west. For it is known that such indeed is the fanning out of the wings among birds. || ĀpŚus_15.2b ||
He raises it from the front, facing westward;
thus, he whose wings are curved is "curved-winged.
The word *hi* indicates well-known fact.
"Even so"—that is to say, even in this very way, among those birds flying upward, there occurs the fanning and bending of the wings; such is the sacred tradition (śruti).

To whatever extent the sevenfold fire-altar, including the *aratni* and the *prādeśa*, is completed, there is one *prādeśa* as the fourth part of the body and eight *caturbhāgīyā*s. Of these, three constitute the head; the remainder one should divide between the two wings. (ĀpŚus 15.3)
The fire-altar, when increased by an *aratni* and a *prādeśa*, becomes as large as the original; the remainder of the instruction is that one should take [the measures] such that it is a *prādeśa*.

In the case of a fire-altar measuring one *aratni* and a *prādeśa*, having taken a *prādeśa* for the tail, four *caturthas* (fourths) of a *puruṣa*-field for the body, and eight *caturbhāgīyās* (quarter-bricks) for the remaining *puruṣa*-field, two of those *caturbhāgīyās* should be placed on the head.
All the rest, having been divided, should be distributed between the two wings.
In the *prādeśa* it is six finger-breadths;
in the *puruṣa* it is sixty finger-breadths;
in five *caturbhāgīyās* it is nine finger-breadths less a quarter.
One should reduce this very [measurement] by one in each case:
a man is five *aratnis* long; a *vyāyāma* is four *aratnis*; twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*) constitute an *aratni*; half of that is a *prādeśa*: such is the established rule. (ĀpŚus 15.4)
"Five"—this is the measurement of the person (*puruṣa*).
"Four"—this is the measurement of the *aratni*.
"Arrangement" (*kḷpti*)—such is the conceptual construction.
The word *iti* indicates a manner; the meaning is that one should construct [the measurement] by this method. Thirty finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) constitute a fourth part (*caturbhāgīya*).
Karavindīya’s Commentary:
"Śyena"— that is, the śyena is a particular species of bird.
"One who desires heaven should pile the fire-altar in that shape.
Since it is said, "This [ordinary fire] is piled in the likeness of birds," the ordinary fire is merely similar to birds;
this [altar], however, is similar to a hawk.
He explains what kind of hawk it is:
"vakra-te.
One whose two wings (pakṣau) are crooked—that is, not straight—is "vakrapakṣaḥ" (one with crooked wings).
"Vyasta" means spread out; that whose tail is spread out from the base upwards and upwards is so described.
"From behind, he raises it towards the east" (paścāt prāṅ udūhati) means raising or lifting up; one should raise the first half of the wing from the base, starting from the rear toward the front.
"From the front, he raises it towards the west" (purastāt pratyaṅ udūhati).
Starting from the middle, one should raise [the wings] toward the west, beginning from the front;
thus, the phrase "evamiva hi" is a conventional expression for the entire group of feet.
"In the midst of birds"—that is, in the middle of the wings of hawks.
*Bending* (*nirṇāma*) means the act of bending, a state of bowing down after having gone forth.
*Is perceived* (*vijñāyate*) means it is heard or seen.
By the force of the expression "bending of the wings" (*pakṣanirṇāma*), the bending is seen between the two wings; that is, it is seen in birds.
One should divide the previously mentioned *prākṛta* fire-altar into its own wings, tail, and head.

To specify which divisions these are, he says: from the tail, a space of one *prādeśa*; and from the self (*ātman*), a space of one *puruṣa* out of four *puruṣas*, which consists of eighteen parts of four *caturbhāgīyā*s. Having taken as much area as those [bricks] are laid down, one should form the head at the front of the self, consisting of three of those *caturbhāgīyā*s.

One should divide the remaining fifteen (or twenty) four-part bricks between the man and the two wings, which are respectively one span and one man plus a span in length—the meaning is that one should add them [to those measures].
Thus, each wing consists of four and a half cubits less one-fourth of a finger;
the body is two and a half men.
The tail is one man's length;
the head consists of three four-part bricks.
The construction of the five-spoked [altar]:
"The man is five cubits in Agni;
as large as a man with arms raised is he"—this is because of the injunction specifying the particular measurement of the man.
Otherwise, it is four *aratnis* long;
twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) constitute one *aratni*,
and half of that is a *prādeśa*.
And that [staff] is twelve finger-breadths long;
this is the established rule—the convention of the teacher.

In the *Sundararājīyā* commentary, it is stated that although this *śyenacit* (falcon-shaped altar) is recited in the section on optional rites (*kāmyaprakaraṇa*) in the *Taittirīyaka*, it is indeed obligatory (*nitya*), because its fruit is heaven; for like the square fire-altar (*caturaśrāgni*), this one also has heaven as its fruit.
"Indeed, this Agni is built for the sake of the heavenly world (*suvarga*)," and the indicative marks (*liṅga*) for this have already been shown previously. It is stated [as follows]:
Immediately following the scriptural statement, this [instruction] is a supplement to the Śyenacit passage;
therein, the curvature is in the middle of the wings,
and the expansion is at the tip of the tail.
The Śruti itself also describes the manner of bending the two wings:
"In the middle of the wing, one bends it forward from the rear;
at the junctions of the tips of the wings, one bends them backward from the front."
For just as there is a bending or curvature in the middle of the wing of birds—that is, a folding-in of the middle of the wing—so too is this seen;
the meaning is that for birds flying upward, such a bending in the middle of the wing is indeed observed.
*Yāvā te*.
This fire-altar, when measured by the *śyena*-cutting, becomes exactly as large as that which results when measured by a cubit (*aratni*) and a span (*prādeśa*).
The purpose for taking the cubit and the span has already been stated.
In that regard—

The remainder is that one should place eight *caturbhāgīyās* on the forepart; on the tail, one should place eight *caturbhāgīyās* from the self itself—namely, a *prādeśa* more than a man, which is the fourth part of the self.
The remainder is the self.
Two and a half puruṣas [in height]; the tail is exactly one puruṣa in measure;
those [parts]—the head.

One should fashion the head from three of those [units] consisting of four parts each; one should extend the other [unit]. Then, having divided the remainder of the body and the tail here into two parts, one should place them upon the two wings.
In each wing, there is a half-prādeśa (six finger-breadths) and a half of the fourth part of the body (sixty finger-breadths).
When five caturbhāgīyas are placed in the middle of the wing with the length of a puruṣa, there are twenty-nine finger-breadths by a quarter;
thus, the natural wing consists of one hundred and forty-four finger-breadths.
Combined with these, it amounts to two hundred and twenty-nine fingers minus one quarter (pādona).
This is what he will state in the passage beginning with "nine and a half aratnis," and so forth.
This is the fifth arrangement.
The length of the wings is nine and a half cubits and four finger-breadths less a quarter. (Āpastamba Śulba Sūtra 15.5)
The length of the wings (*pakṣāyāma*)—that is, the extent of the two wings—is ten *prādeśas* and *aratnis* less a quarter of an *aṅgula*.

In the original measure, there are six *aratnis*; in the half-man (*ardhapuruṣa*) measurement, there are two *aratnis* plus one *prādeśa*, which amounts to eighteen *aṅgulas* less a quarter. In the *prādeśa* itself, there are six *aṅgulas*. Together with those eighteen, the total for one *aratni* is nine *aratnis* and five *aṅgulas* less a quarter. All of this combined results in nine *aratnis* and five *aṅgulas* less a quarter.
This is the extent of the two wings.

He makes a cord of two men's length with loops at both ends and a mark in the middle. Having fixed the two ends against the two rear corners of the wing, he should stretch it eastward along the mark; likewise in front. That is the bend (nirṇāma). || ĀpŚus_15.6 ||
By this, the subsequent position has been explained. ĀpŚus 15.7.
Having made a rope two *puruṣas* in length with loops at both ends, one should make a mark in the middle—this is the ellipsis.
By this very method, the bending of the northern wing is also explained.
This is the curvature of the two wings. // 7 //
The ātman measures two puruṣas in length and one and a half puruṣas in width. ĀpŚus 15.8.
At the tail [of the altar], one should extend a cord one and a half puruṣas wide, measuring one puruṣa toward the west; then another to its south and another to its north. (ĀpŚus 15.9a)
The self (the body) is two puruṣas in length and one and a half puruṣas in width.

Having thus laid out this long rectangle, one should mark it so that at the place of the tail there is a transverse side of half a puruṣa and a lateral side of the measure of one puruṣa; "one should do" is the meaning.
On the right side of that square, one should construct another such square, and likewise another on the left.
In this manner, there are three squares, each with a side-measure of half a man; one should draw them diagonally so that there remains [a space] of half a man at the end. ĀpŚus 15.9b.
Having made a square at the head with half a man's length, one should drop [the cord] from the midpoint of the eastern working-cord toward the two southern corners by that same distance. ĀpŚus 15.10.
Thus ends the fifteenth section.
Those two which are situated on the sides are square;
one should draw them diagonally across the corner so that at the point of junction—the junction of the body and the tail—there is a measure of half a man's height made for the preceding [section].
Just as the southern [side] is like the eastern, so too the northern is like the eastern.
Even when this has been done, there remains a space of half a person's height.

Having made a square at the location of the head with a measurement of half a person's height, one should—beginning from the midpoint of the eastern measuring-line (karaṇī)—project it onto that very same half in the middle—that is, one should draw it.
"He leaves three remaining," he will state later;
here too, it is said, "three heads.
This is the fifteenth section.
Karavinda’s Commentary:

Having measured out the space behind the location of the sacrificial post (yūpāvaṭa), leaving a passage for movement, and so forth, one should drive stakes at the junctions of the wings. Then, having made the length nine cubits, a span, a finger-breadth, and a quarter-part by means of a cord running north-south, one should drive stakes at the tips of the wings.
In this manner, a man is diminished by eleven finger-breadths and one span (*prādeśa*).
Among those, eight and a half finger-breadths constitute one *caturbhāgīyā*.

Having made a cord with loops at both ends measuring one and a half men in length, having marked its middle, and having fastened it to the two pegs at the rear edge of the wing, one should drive in a peg after shifting it eastward along the mark.
In this manner, having fixed a mark at the two previous limits and shifted it westward by that same measure, a peg (śaṅku) is placed there.
When this is done, a mark falls twenty-four finger-breadths and seven and a half barley-corns from the middle of the front wing along the western side-measure; and likewise in front.
This is the *nirṇāma*—the bending outward of the wing.
From "half of ten" (ardhadaśamāḥ) up to "that is the bending" (sa nirṇāmaḥ), one should formulate the opposing position as well.
Vyāsa says: One who hates himself should measure himself as two puruṣas in length from east to west and one and a half puruṣas from north to south along the spine.

Regarding the tail: having laid out three squares, each measuring one *puruṣa* in length and half that in width, extending westward and oriented north-south, one should draw a diagonal line from the southern square toward the southwestern corner;
likewise toward the northwestern corner.

When this has been done, at the base of the tail there is a square measuring half a man's height in width and one man's height in length, and at the tip it measures one and a half man's heights in width.
Regarding the head:

having made a square in the middle of the eastern side-line of the self [the altar], with a length and width equal to half [of the whole] like a tail, one should drop a line from the center of that eastern side-line toward the centers of the southern and northern side-lines—one should discard what lies outside the two lines.
Fifteenth Section. Sundararājīya Commentary: Half a Yāma.
Vyāsa is exactly one puruṣa in measure; now, his [the next's] measurement is two puruṣas.
Just as when the two ends of a cord— the front and the back— are fixed at their respective tips and the portion cut off from behind comes forward,
by this analogy the Self is explained as being "Vyāsa"; in this very manner, three persons reside within the Self.
"In the tail—
the head is in front of the self.
Thus ends the fifteenth section.
According to the commentary of Kapardin,
one should cut off the hips and shoulders from the Apayās.
By the word *apyaya*, the junction of the wings, tail, and head is expressed.
One should cut them toward those [junctions]—one should remove the hips and shoulders.
Starting from the junction of the head, one should proceed toward the junction of the wings.
In the same way, two four-part units (caturbhāgīya) are removed from each of the hips and the shoulders; thus, two by two are discarded. As it will be stated later: "Forty [units] remain."
For thus indeed is the hawk. ĀpŚus_16.1b.
This is well known.
And he will say: "As far as the similarity with the traditional instruction.
One should have the instrument made for the person five *vitastis* long and six *vitastis* wide, bent according to the requirements; that is the first [instrument]. (ĀpŚus 16.2)

It is five puruṣas in length and six puruṣas in width—the side-measure is one aratni, and the cross-measure is six parts, bent in such a way that it fits; by the word "bent" (nata), stretching out (prajambhana) is meant.
One should stretch it out in that manner;
one should make one [side] long diagonally.
"According as it is joined" means according to its application (*yathāyoga*);
that is the first performance.
"First" is its designation.
Those two are joined facing east; that is the second [set]. (ĀpŚus 16.3)
Having approached those two [ends] inverted, the second *karaṇa* is such that they remain joined on the middle plank;
one should increase the sixth part of the first by an eighth part. That which is bent according to its application is the third. (ĀpŚus 16.4)
One should divide the first [side] into six parts and increase it by eight parts; one should make it long.
What is the measure? One should cut it diagonally.
Once cut, the joining is such that the bending and the stretching constitute the union.

Just as an additional half-unit is applied to the bending of the wing, so too the bent or curved third construction unit is an additional half of a four-part unit (*caturbhāgīyā*). One should cut off from it a portion equal to a four-part unit diagonally; that is the fourth [unit]. (ĀpŚus 16.5)
Having drawn one and a half *caturbhāgīyās* on the ground, one should not omit the *caturbhāgīyā*.
The rule by which bricks of such a nature are made is the fourth rule;
for he will state later, "the *ṣoḍaśī* [is made] with four."
This, then, is the instrument.
In Karavinda’s commentary as well: the word "confluence" (apyaya) refers to the junction of the wings, tail, and head of the hawk (śyena).
Starting from the dissolution of the head up to the dissolution of the wings, and starting from the dissolution of the tail up to the dissolution of the wings—
in this very manner it has proceeded.
The hand— first,
for a person, twenty-four finger-breadths on one side and twenty finger-breadths on the other; this is the first instrument (karaṇa).
"It should be bent according to its application"—one should fashion it in whatever way is appropriate for the support (*upadhāna*).
The method of bending will be explained above in the section on the hawk (*śyena*).
The terms "first" and so forth are for the sake of convenience in practical usage.

Regarding these two: that which was previously described as the first construction—where one [cord] is laid southward and one northward—in the *saṃhitā* [construction], the two side-measures (*pārśvamānyau*) are twenty-four finger-breadths long, and the two cross-measures (*tiryaṅnānyau*) are forty finger-breadths long.
By means of the method for bending one of them, [the cord] becomes depressed in the middle and elevated on one side.
That is the second instrument.

One should extend the sixth part of the first instrument—twenty finger-breadths—by an eighth part, namely fifteen finger-breadths, bent according to the requirement; such that the sixth part becomes curved in accordance with the face, while the eighth part becomes straight in accordance with the body—that is the third instrument.

The [brick] called the four-part atom (aṇūkā) consists of four parts; it should be made with one and a half parts. One should cut a portion equal to a fourth part of that [atom] diagonally across its width.

This is what is meant: having made [the rectangle] forty-five *aṅgulas* in length and thirty *aṅgulas* in width, one should cut it diagonally at thirty *aṅgulas*. Thus, one side-measure (*pārśvamānī*) is forty-five *aṅgulas*; one cross-measure (*tiryaṅbhānī*) is thirty *aṅgulas*; and one diagonal measure (*akṣṇayā*) situated [therein] is forty-two *aṅgulas* and fourteen sesame seeds (*tilas*).
This is the fourth instrument.
The commentary of Sundararāja also states: "One should cut [the lines] from the junctions of the wings, tail, and head; one should delimit them from one another by drawing diagonal lines."
In this way, the "half-man" (ardhapuruṣa) of the self is rejected.
It is thus: first, twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgula).
The side plank is twenty finger-breadths in width; it is bent according to its application, being curved as is appropriate for the wing.
One of its diagonal cords is thirty-five [units] long with twenty *tilas* added;
the other is twenty-six [units] long with six *tilas* added.
When it is prepared in this way, the twelfth part of the wing’s length—namely, nineteen finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*) and two *tilas*—becomes the width of the brick.
This is the first method of construction.
In the natural form, which lacks the *aratni* and *prādeśa* measures, there is a reduction of thirty finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) from the length of the wings;
accordingly, the bricks are bent.
There, the two ears are twenty-one and twenty-nine [finger-breadths] respectively, joined with three sesame-seeds (*tila*);
those two are joined so that the second becomes six-cornered (*ṣaḍaśri*).

Now, having drawn on the ground a third [square]— a long rectangle with equal ears (diagonals), fifteen *aṅgulas* in width and one *aratni* in length, extending toward the east— one should join it with the first [square] which extends toward the east;
that third [square] is called "inclined" (*nata*) because it is straightly situated yet inclined relative to the first, as in the expression "inclined according to its connection."
Regarding the fourth part— one side-measure is fifteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas),
while the other is forty-five finger-breadths.
One [measurement] for the horizontal line is thirty finger-breadths;
the other is forty-two finger-breadths plus fourteen sesame seeds.
— *Kapardibhāṣya*
The fifth [portion] is half of one-fourth.
That which is thirty-one finger-breadths on one side and fifteen finger-breadths on the other is the fifth;
its diagonal division is the sixth. (ĀpŚus 16.7)
The sixth [mark] is the division: "One should divide that fifth [mark] by means of a diagonal line across the corner.

One should draw a line westward for a fifth part of the man's length and with a width of one-tenth; another to its south and yet another to its north. One should mark those two diagonally at the two corners of the southern shoulder. That is the seventh. (ĀpŚus 16.8)
One should draw a line one *aratni* in length and one *prādeśa* in width, directed westward and extending toward the west.
On the ground, on the right side, one should likewise draw another such line, and on the left side, yet another such line.
Then, starting from the two corners of the southern and western lines, one should draw a diagonal line across them like the handle of a ladle (*sruc*).
That is the seventh.
The same applies to the others. However, one should draw the northern [line] from the northern limit; that is the eighth. (ĀpŚus 16.9)
Having done so, one should likewise draw the northern square, starting from the northern corner and extending toward the southern corner like a *sruc* ladle; that is the eighth.
The ninth consists of a diagonal division on both sides of the four-part [square]. (ĀpŚus 16.10)
The ninth instrument for that four-part brick (caturbhāgīyā) is a cutting or breaking performed diagonally across both ears;
likewise, a quarter-brick (pādeṣṭakā) consists of three such [parts].
On the foundation layer, one should lay down sixty bricks on each of the two sides, starting with those facing north. ĀpŚus_16.11.
On the two sides of the tail, there are eight and eight; on the sixth [rib], three; at the tip, one; then three; then one. (ĀpŚS 16.12)
When there is a cessation of questioning, two fourths [are used] in case of doubt; but after those two, when the army is drawn up in formation, two fifths [are used]. ĀpŚus 16.12.
At the time of laying down [the bricks], on one side he should lay down sixty first [bricks] extending northward—thirty each, alternating their placement.
The same applies to the other side.
On both sides of the tail there are sixty bricks: eight on one side and eight on the other.
He asks, "How? and says: three [lines] at the tip of the tail, and one in front of them;

in this way, they are made by reversing [the order] on the upper side. They are placed transversely in the tail and in the self (ātman)—that is, behind those two, in the tail, joined in formation like a flock of rams with their faces together.
The sixteenth section: Commentary by Karavinda; the fourth [chapter].
That which is thirty finger-breadths in length and fifteen in width is the fifth instrument.
Of that [sixth], having made a diagonal division of the fifth, the sixth becomes the *karaṇa*; that is the foot-brick (*pādeṣṭakā*).
Of that, one side is thirty-one finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), another is fifteen finger-breadths, and the other diagonal side is thirty-three finger-breadths plus nineteen sesame seeds (*tila*).
This is the sixth instrument.
Puruṣa:
Having made a square measuring twenty-four finger-breadths in length and half that in width, one should likewise make two such squares to its south and north.
Thus, having made three squares, one should draw lines from the southern and western corners toward the northern and southern squares.
Thus, the two side-measures (pārśvamānya) are twenty-six finger-breadths and twenty-eight tilas;
the two cross-measures (tiryaṅbhānya) are twenty-four finger-breadths.
This is the seventh construction.
Thus—the eighth [section]—having made three squares like the seventh, one should draw the southern [square] toward the southern rear corner and the northern [square] toward the northern rear corner.
In this way, those same two side-measures remain: the eastern side is twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) long, while the western side is thirty-six finger-breadths long.
That which was indeed the eighth instrument at that time.
The division of the four-part brick (caturbhāgīyā) into two parts diagonally would constitute this quarter-brick (pādeṣṭakā).
The two side-measures are twenty-one finger-breadths and seven-tenths of a finger-breadth diagonally, and thirty finger-breadths across;
such is the ninth constructional instrument (*karaṇa*).
Now, the placement (*upadhāna*) is described:
Having meditated upon it, at the time of placing the bricks, one should place sixty bricks facing north on the right wing as the first layer,
and sixty on the left wing.
This is a Vedic irregularity regarding case endings (*chāndaso vibhaktivyatyayaḥ*).
From the word *puccha* [with the suffix] *-ṣṭha*, eight [bricks] each are produced by the formation of the sixth [instrumental] case, [to be placed] on the two sides of the tail.
He states the manner of placing [the bricks]:
"three"—on which sides? On the two sides of the tail, thus indeed.

At the tip of the tail, there is one line on the southern hip facing east with its outer end distinct; to the north of that, two lines with their tips pointing in different directions, their outer ends joined;
and in front of those two, one line with its outer end distinct.
[The line] has its tips pointing eastward. In front of that, as before, there are three [lines].
In front of those, as before, there is one [line].
In the same way, it is also on the northern side.
Regarding the inquiry: "In the junction of the tail and the self, there are two fourths in the sphere;
because there is no distinction, the tail and the self are equal."
Three [are used] for the benefit; two of those are for the animal; five are for the purposes of the fifth [altar];
the *anīka* is the front.
When joined by that, it is like a fight between rams.
The sixteenth section:
the commentary by Sundararāja on the fourth [chapter], the fifth [section].
It is thirty finger-breadths in length and fifteen finger-breadths in width;
it is a long rectangle with equal ears.
Of that—[the sixth].
Puruṣa: My [measurement] is such that the front part is one span wide, while the back part is three spans;
for both the seventh and eighth [sections], the side-boards are twenty-seven [units] less six sesame-seeds.
When a square divided into four parts is split diagonally on both sides, four ninth-parts (navamāḥ) arise as triangles;
one of these is the ninth instrument (karaṇa).
One of its planks is thirty finger-breadths long;
the other two are twenty-one [finger-breadths] and seven [finger-breadths] respectively. One should meditate upon this.
The first [lines] are those made by the first makers;
likewise, in the cases of "sixty" and so forth, they extend toward the north, being oriented to the north.
"Ask"— these are sixty [bricks] extending toward the east.
He states the manner of laying them down:
Of the three [lines], two are with their tips pointing eastward;
one has its tip pointing westward.
Question:
Those [lines] which are directed toward the north and those directed toward the south—
these are fifteen finger-breadths each in length for both the body and the tail.
Three [breaths]—
united in the welfare, united in the mouth,
rising upward.
Sixteenth Section: Kapardibhāṣya.
On the remaining [parts], ten lines are drawn from the fourth [corner]; on the hips and shoulders, eight lines are drawn both eastward and westward. (ĀpŚus 17.1)
On the remainder of the tail, there are ten [stitches] extending crosswise;
on the hips and shoulders, there are eight; and on the hip, four extending forward, which have been made by reversing those on the northern and southern sides.
And likewise on the two shoulders;
and in the remainder, there are twenty-six [verses], eight sixties, and four pentads. (ĀpŚus 17.2)
In the self (ātman), which remains as the remainder, there are twenty-six fourths in the region;
eight and four fifthths.
The method for their placement is stated: on the path of the objects of perception (viśaya), there are fourteen fourths across the self.
On their two sides, two each were made by reversing the two eastern ones;
on the northern side, there are fourteen, with two placed crosswise between each pair of sides.
These twenty-six fourths have been laid down.
Four [lines] are situated at the corners, each consisting of four parts;
upon them are four fifth [lines] extending horizontally,
and eight sixth [lines] also extending horizontally.
The two [bricks] marked with the dative case are on the head; and the two preceding them are in the east. ĀpŚus 17.3.
This is the two-hundred-fold arrangement. (ĀpŚus_17.4)
In front of those two objects, the two eastern fourth [fingers] are crossed and placed to the south.
"This" [is said]. Why is this so, given that it is only two hundred [units]? This is a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*).
This arrangement which is defined as "two hundred" fulfills the number when it is stated that "one should fulfill the number";
otherwise, it would not be known which number was to be fulfilled.
If it is argued that there is a fixed number of one thousand, [we reply: no;
for then the injunction "one should complete it by adding further layers" would become meaningless.
Therefore, this is a general technical rule (paribhāṣā).

In the subsequent layout, the second [lines] consist of five [units] each at the two corners; the third [lines] consist of five [units] each at the two points of convergence; these constitute eight parts for the body.
The second [set] consists of those that have become curved. *Nirṇāma* is a curved region;
in that region, there are five of the second [set] for each.
And for the two wings and the tail, there are third [units]: the third units at the wings and the tail occupy eight parts of themselves;
they remain in the self [of the body] as merely a four-part brick. Five by five, having been reversed, they are placed in the northern wing and tail.
In the remainder, there are forty-five first [lines] facing east.
On the right side there are twenty-five;
on the right wing twenty-five, and on the left side twenty-five; on the left wing twenty;
and on the two sides of the tail five bricks each in the seventh layer.
On the northern side, they are made by reversing [the order];
and one each of the second and fourth [sections] is joined on either side.
In the second and fourth rows, there is one seventh [square] on each side;
one has been placed inverted on the right side,
and the other on the left side.
In the remainder, there are thirteen eighth-day offerings.
Thirteen and eight [bricks] lie on the region of the tail;
and on the hips and shoulders, eight fourths, both southern and northern.
In the south, it is extended toward the south; having been made by reversing [the orientation], in the north hip it is extended toward the north;
in the right shoulder it is extended toward the north; having been made by reversing [the orientation].
And in the remainder, there are twenty, thirty, sixty, and one fifth [of the verses]. ĀpŚus 17.7b.
By the word "and" (ca), the four *caturthīs* are drawn forward;
there are thirty *ṣaṣṭhīs* and one *pañcamī*. Their location for insertion is stated: on the right side of the self (*ātman*), there are ten *caturthīs*.
Five lines run eastward and five westward; likewise on the northern side.
In the middle, there are thirty-sixth lines running eastward and one fifth line;
of these, fifteen run eastward.
On the head, there are two [lines] in the fourth [position], and in front of those, four in the ninth.
This is the two-hundred-fold ritual expansion (prastāra). ĀpŚus_17.9 ||
One should pile the layers in reverse order for as many layers as one intends to construct.
The four *navamīs* are at the beginning. "This" — this has already been explained. For what purpose is this? It is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*).
What is being restricted here? It is the uneven arrangement of two hundred bricks that is restricted, not the Śyena altar above it.
It is the Śyena itself that is restricted, not anything else.

How is it understood that it is not anything else? From the statement regarding the completion of the arrangement (*prastāra*); for even there, it is only this that is said—"one should pile it with an interchanging pattern"—and not a statement regarding [the Śyena's] completion.
Therefore, there are two hundred other types of *prastāra* (arrangements),
as they are defined in this very context.
In the preparation of the bricks, one should take forty-five *aṅgulas* with the right hand and have the fourth parts made.
"Those that are inverted are on the left;
one should pile them in reverse order as many times as one intends to make layers.
This has been explained.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
It should be made nineteen finger-breadths across, including two sesame seeds;
it should be fashioned in such a way that it is bent according to its proper application.
Just as in the northern region, there is an increase by one-sixth part in the sixth part;
likewise, the third instrument should be bent according to the appropriate application.
That specific difference of the fourth [digit] will be forty-two finger-breadths (aṅgula) plus fourteen sesame seeds (tila) for the Karaṇa.
The ear-plate of the sixth [face] should be thirty-three finger-breadths, augmented by eighteen sesame-seeds; the others are to be measured according to the lines.
These twenty-seven [units] are situated at the side of the seventh;
and on the plank of the eighth, there are six less eight [tilas].
Having reversed the first and third [verses] again and again,
one should likewise have the bricks made for the sacrifice using the seventh and sixth [verses].
Having reversed [the measurements] thirty-five times, one should also have it made with the fourth [unit];
the experts know that this alone is the method for making bricks.
In the tail [of the altar], ten [bricks] are prescribed to be placed crosswise in the fourth layer;
and between the two [rows], there should be fourteen crosswise bricks in the fourth layer.
From the fourth [row], six on each side of those [central ones] extend transversely;
in the corners, five extend transversely from the fifth, and likewise eight from the sixth. Similarly, up to the end of the tail, thirty are prescribed for the head.
The eastern and the western [rivers], and the fifth among the eastern ones.
From the fourth [row], there are twenty on both sides of those [rows], as well as in the remaining [spaces];
all else is according to the sūtra; thus the layout (prastāra) in the sacrifice consists of two hundred [bricks].
The hips and likewise the shoulders—these six are indeed of that same kind;
the four [other] parts... are not those of the ancestors on the right.
The right [side] should be known as being on the hips, and likewise the left on the shoulders.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the commentary on the Āpastamba Sūtra by Kapardisvāmin, in the section known as the Śulba-praśna.
This is the Karavindīya Vyākhyā (Commentary).
In the remaining [sections]— from the tail [upward]— ten [lines] are produced by the fourth karaṇa, extending crosswise.
And likewise, four [tiles] for the hips (śroṇyaṃsa) were made by reversing them on the upper side of the two hips.
Regarding the remainder— because of the word "and" (*ca*) in the rule *myaḥ śeṣe ca*, the fourth case endings (*caturthī*) are supplied [from the previous rule].
When the self is the remainder, there are twenty-six fourth case endings.
There are eight sixties and four fifties;
these constitute thirty-eight [units].
Their placement is described as follows:
on the head— among those situated at the tail and the middle— there are fourteen eastward lines (rītis) in the transverse self, each being the fourth [from the previous].
On their two sides, there are two behind and two in front, as well as one to the south and one to the north;
thus there are eight. Of these eight, four face east and four face west.
Of these fourteen [deities], there are two each on the right and left sides;
those four together thus constitute twenty-four fourths.
Here, at the corners,
there are four unextended [squares] measuring four parts each;
within them, there are four fifth-parts extending transversely.
There are sixty-eight [channels] directed horizontally.
On the head, there are two eastern [channels] on the right and left respectively; in front of those two [groups of] twenty, there are two further eastern [channels].
Thus it is in the outer particularity.
This is the "two-hundred-fold" arrangement (*prastāra*).

Although the two hundred-fold arrangement is established by virtue of the collection of numbers—such as the location and so forth pertaining to the rules for laying down the bricks—the explicit statement "the two-hundred-fold arrangement" is made in order to ensure that the arrangement is indeed two-hundred-fold.
The *apa-kriyās* are the *nirṇāmas*; it has been stated that they are the curved regions between the two wings.
On those [curves], five each on the southern and northern wings are to be placed in accordance with the *nirṇāmas*.
Moreover, the *vaitas* [beings] of the third instrument— the *vaitas*— have understood themselves as five times five, increased by one-eighth, and the fortnight as six parts.
In the remainder—the southern part of the right wing, twenty-five;
the northern part of the left wing, twenty-five; and on the south [of the body], twenty.
Regarding the tail: on the southern side of the tail there are five rows of seven bricks each;
on the northern side, there are five eastern rows.
The second [verse] states the placement of the other two seventh [bricks]:
the second [brick] is placed in either of the two seventh rows situated at the sides of the tail.
One should place one *pratisaṃhitā* brick upon another as the fourth, and one *caturthīpratisaṃhitā* brick upon another as the seventh.
In this manner, twelve seventh bricks have been laid down.
Regarding the remainder: in the remainder of the tail (*puccha*) of the eighth [section], there are thirteen northern *rītis* produced by the eighth *karaṇa*, and five *rītis*.
Between the two seventh [sections] situated on the sides at the tip of the tail, there are five and eight [tiles].
On the second [lunar day], there are three at the beginning; among the seven seventh days, there are three eighth days;
and on the third [lunar day], there are three.
According to the fourth method, one [line] is among the three seventh lines;
according to the fifth method, one [line] is between two seventh lines.
Thus, thirteen eighth lines should be placed with their tips pointing east or west as appropriate.

From the hips and shoulders, there are four [lines] for the hips and shoulders: two each on the right ones for the right [shoulders and hips], and two each on the left ones for the left [shoulders and hips].
All of these are distinguished by being on the outer side.
In the remainder— namely, when the *ātmanepada* suffixes remain— there are twenty [forms].
By the word "and" (*ca*), in the absence of a specific statement, the fourth case endings are applied to the head [of the compound].
And before those two, there are four ninth-day offerings.
This is the two-hundred-fold arrangement;
the mention of "two hundred" is for the purpose of dispelling any doubt regarding the lack of restriction to two hundred arrangements.
The section on the transposition of vowels and consonants is concluded.

Now, the spreading (*prajambhana*) of the blades (*phalaka*) is described: one should spread the first blade such that its transverse measurement (*tiryaṅmānī*), which is twenty finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), becomes nineteen finger-breadths and two-eighths of a *tila* (two *tilas*) when straightened.
One should spread the second blade in the manner to be described: its wing-measure (*pakṣanamnī*) is twenty-four finger-breadths and seven-and-a-half *tilas*.
One-sixth of that measure is four finger-breadths.
And there is a quarter-tila [measure].

By means of that, due to the length of the second side, one should create a projection at a point twenty-four finger-breadths from the middle of the two planks of forty finger-breadths each; in such a way that its two parts, taken individually, become similar to the previous ears. However, for the third [side], there is a bending at the junction of the sixth and eighth parts.
One should bend the sixth part as before;
however, the bending of the eighth is simply its remaining straight according to its own nature.
That bending occurs in relation to the sixth.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
In the Śyena sacrifice, the first [verse] describes the rending by the primary instrument;
the second and third describe the bending of the fruit-bearing branch.

In this hawk-shaped altar, there is the spreading out of the body-measure; that which is the diagonal of the tail is likewise the diagonal of the wing for the sixth [altar], according to its straightness.
The result of the bending of the second and third sides is the diagonal of the sides; the bending at the beginning of the sixth [side] is from the diagonal of the sides.
The *tiryaṅbhānī* should measure nineteen finger-breadths, one-eighth part, and two sesame seeds; one should extend [the site] with a cord according to that measurement.
The sixth [measurement] is the bending of the wing, measured at four finger-breadths plus one-quarter of a sesame seed; by that, there shall be the downward curvature of the feathers.
In this way, having inferred the *jambhana* according to the path stated by the second hawk,
the bending of the fruit of the instrument must likewise be prescribed.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Śulbapratīpikā* composed by Karavindasvāmin;
[the commentary] of Sundararāja on the remainder is as follows.
The buttocks extend upward;
and from one's own hips and shoulders, two each are on the outer sides.
In the remainder, there are five [lines] from the fifth;
in the self-remainder, there are twenty-six fourths: eastern and western.
Therein, in the middle two rows, there are seven each with their tips pointing north and their tips pointing south.
In the second and fifth rows, five [deities] each are prescribed;
in the middle row, there are others to the south and north, as well as to the east and west.
Between the first and last rows, there is one fourth [deity] each to the south and north, and two sixth [deities] each to the rear and the front.
Those eight are oriented toward the south and north;
in the remaining two rows, there are four fifth [lines] extending toward the north;
and at the head, there are two fourth [lines] in the intermediate direction.
At the point of dissolution, it is like the tail at the point of dissolution;
at their two exits, there are two fourths with external distinctions.
The meaning is that this "stāra" (spreading) must be performed here with effort in order to complete the number;
[one should perform] each one of those others individually.
On either side—on the right or on the left—one should place a single *saptamī* brick between two others, using the second and fourth *saptamī* bricks as a continuous sequence.
In the remaining cases, [the suffixes] ṣṭhan and ṣṭraṇ are applied; in the remaining cases, [the suffixes] śuc and cha are applied; and [the suffixes] śroṇi and aṇac are also applied.
There are two pairs of external particulars;
in the remainder, there is a fifth [category] regarding the self-remainder, which consists of twenty [fingers] extending eastward from the fourth [toe].
In the middle, with thirty-two bricks extending eastward in six rows, there are two courses;
having removed two from the southern one, one should place a single fifth brick [in its stead].
On the head, two [mantras] in the dative case are recited facing north.
Three myas extend northward.
This is the *Stāra* (spreading); "one should spread crosswise"—
thus ends the fifth chapter of the *Śulbapradīpikā* composed by Śrī Sundararāja, [along with] the commentary of Kapardin.
"One desiring heaven should pile the Śyenacit," so it is known. (ĀpŚus 18.1)

The wings are bent and the tail is spread out; he raises it from behind toward the front, and from the front toward the back. For it is known that such indeed is the fanning-out of the wings among birds. (ĀpŚus_18.2)
The re-introduction of this scriptural passage is for the purpose of establishing another path;
or rather, this is a different scriptural passage altogether,
and it is precisely this that constitutes the path of the letter (ākāra-mārgatā).
"Vakra" (crooked)—this has already been explained.

For a person, one hundred and twenty units, together with the *aratni* and the *prādeśa*, result in the sevenfold [altar]. Of these, forty are for the body, three for the head, fifteen for the tail, and thirty-one for the right wing, and likewise for the left. (ĀpŚus 18.3)
The sixteenth part of a man is a *ṣoḍaśī*. When these are counted, one hundred and twenty *ṣoḍaśīs* are contained within seven and a half [mantras].
Setting aside seven, when multiplied by sixteen, it is one hundred and twelve.
In the case of half a puruṣa, there are eight in twelve;
when added, they become twenty.
Thus, one hundred and twenty [deities] are complete.
Regarding the phrase "of these": of those sixteen [energies], forty are to be placed within the self; three are to be placed on the head—the remainder being that they are to be placed everywhere;
and fifteen are in the tail.
There are thirty-one on the right wing and likewise thirty-one on the left; how these are to be placed is now explained:

Having laid out a long square measuring one and a half puruṣas across and two puruṣas in length, one should remove two ṣoḍaśī bricks from each of the hips and shoulders; forty remain, and that constitutes the body (ātman).
The cross-measure (tiryaṅbhānī) is one and a half puruṣas, and the side-measure (pārśvamānī) is two puruṣas.
Having thus laid out the long square, one should discard—meaning, set aside—two sixteen-part units each from the two hips and the two shoulders.
Diagonally... so that, having made four squares of the measure of half a puruṣa at the hips and shoulders, one should discard the other halves diagonally.
The remainder is forty;
that is the self.
Having made a square on the head with a side of half a man's length, one should mark it at the midpoint of the eastern cord and project that distance toward the south and north.
This has been explained—the three [verses] remain; that is the head. (ĀpŚus 18.5b)
Three remain.
That is the head.
The person is two units wide and sixteen parts long; the right wing is likewise, as is the left. (ĀpŚus 18.6)
The transverse measurement is one *puruṣa*;
the lateral measurement is two *puruṣas*.
On the right wing, there is an addition of sixteen-sixteenths of a *puruṣa* (one-eighth) and four finger-breadths (*aṣṭāṅgula*). The same applies to the left wing.
The rejoinder is exactly like that.
At each wing-tip, having made four squares with a man as the fourth [unit], one should draw diagonals across them and discard the halves; thirty-one remain.

At the tips of the two wings, having made four squares each measuring one *puruṣa* and one-fourth [of a *puruṣa*], and having drawn diagonal lines across them from corner to corner, one should discard the halves.
One should discard the portions of the tips of the southern wing that have protruded outside by means of the needle.
In a length of two *puruṣas*, there are thirty-two *ṣoḍaśīs*.
And one [unit] consists of a sixteenth part;
when two of those are subtracted, thirty-one remain.
Having left a space at the tip of the wing, one should draw an eastward line in the middle of the wing.
"By the tip of the wing" refers to squares made with a side of one-fourth of a *puruṣa*;
the meaning is that one should leave out half of one-fourth of a *puruṣa* from the length of the wing.
One should draw a line extending forward from the middle of the wing.

At the end of the wing, having fixed the person-line, one should make a mark at the end of the person. To the east of that mark, one should make another mark at the end of the person; between these two marks, one should draw the two ends separately. This is the bending of the wing. By this, the northern wing is explained.
Having fixed a bamboo pole of one man's length at the junction of the side for the self, one should make a mark at the end of the man [the width] and at the end of the bamboo along the line itself.
From that peg, having placed the bamboo pole extending eastward along the line, one should drive a stake or make a mark in the final hole and draw the two ends of the two pegs apart.
Starting from the other peg, one should draw [the line] to the other end.
Starting from the previous *nitoda* (peg) up to the front edge—
this is the bending of the wing;
by this [method], one should likewise perform the bending of the rear wing.

The eighteenth section: Two puruṣas in the rear, half a puruṣa in the front, and a puruṣa less a fourth part in length; there are eighteen karaṇīs on the two sides, which they take up fifteen times—that is the tail. (ĀpŚus_19.1)
At the back, it is two puruṣas wide;
at the front, it is half a puruṣa wide;
its length is three-quarters of a puruṣa.
He makes eighteen and sixteen [bricks] on the two sides;
the eighteen-making line is for the two sides.
These fifteen and sixteen [bricks] encompass them.

How does one construct [the altar] that is half a man wide and three-quarters of a man long, consisting of six parts? Its two sides are equal squares, each measuring three-quarters of a man on all sides.
One should draw diagonal lines across them and discard one half of each.
He makes each of the remaining [fingers] four and a half;
four and a half plus four and a half is nine.
When six are added to the nine, there are fifteen.
That is its tail.
In the Karavindīyā commentary,
that same scriptural passage is read once again in order to instruct on the second Śyena altar for one who desires to perform it.
Regarding this, he states the distinction:
"Of the person—
on the other [side], the sixteen parts"— meaning they are measured as sixteen portions.
By means of those sixteenfold units, the sevenfold fire-altar, including the *aratni* and the *prādeśa*, amounts to one hundred and twenty.
For instance: having set aside seven, when multiplied by the sixteenfold units, it becomes one hundred and twelve.
When half [of the stoma] is multiplied by sixteen, there are eight;
when those eight are added to it, there are one hundred and twenty ṣoḍaśīs.
Of these, forty are in the self (*ātman*), meaning that the self consists of forty fields of ṣoḍaśīs.
There should be three sixteen-part bricks on the head; fifteen in the tail;
the area of the tail consists of fifteen sixteen-part bricks.
There are thirty-one [units] on the southern wing,
and likewise on the northern wing; the southern and northern wings consist of thirty-one sixteenfold fields each.
Having analyzed it in this way, he stated the measurement of the vimāna:
the internal length along the spine is two hundred and forty finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
The width is one hundred and eighty finger-breadths.

Having thus laid out a long square, one should construct four squares measuring half a man's length at the hips and shoulders; then, from the terminal corner along the side-measure of oneself toward the terminal corner along the cross-measure, one should draw diagonal lines.
One should discard what lies outside the lines.
Forty remain;
that constitutes the self.
How so? Eight sixteenths in length.
Transversely there are six;
eight multiplied by six is forty-eight.
Therein, having removed two from each of the hips and shoulders, eight are removed.
There are [these];
the remaining forty-four reside within the self.

Regarding the head (*śiras*): having made a square measuring half a *puruṣa* on the back line, in front of the two shoulders at the region of the head, and having performed [the construction] starting from the eastern diagonal line (*karaṇī*), three [lines] remain;
that becomes the head.
"Puru-tara" means a man's height;
it is two men's height plus seven and a half finger-breadths.
In this manner, having made a long quadrangle on the right side,
one should do likewise on the left as well.

At the tip of the wing— having made four squares of thirty finger-breadths each with a man as the fourth part— one should draw lines across each of them from south to west and discard their eastern halves.
In this way, thirty-one *ṣoḍaśī* bricks remain.
That is the right wing.
How so? In the wing there are thirty-two sixteen-part [stotras] and one sixteenth part.
Those are thirty-three.
When four halves have been excluded by those two, thirty-one remain. The same applies to the subsequent side.
There, having drawn four eyes diagonally from north to south, one should discard the eastern halves.

Having left a space of thirty finger-breadths at the tip of the wing— that is, having set aside thirty finger-breadths at the tip of the wing— one should draw an eastward line in the middle of the wing.
When the tip of the wing has been set aside, the remaining wing measures two hundred and nineteen finger-breadths less three half-finger-breadths.

In the middle of that [space], starting from the west and extending eastward, one should draw a line exceeding one hundred and nine and three-quarter finger-breadths (109 3/4 aṅgulas), passing beyond the wing-line.
Having placed a bamboo-measure (veṇu) of one puruṣa at the western end of the wing and fixed it, one should drop the other end of the bamboo onto the line running southeast.
That [point] falls fifty-five finger-breadths and twenty-five sesame-seeds (tilas) to the east of the western edge of the wing.
There, one should make a mark (nitoda)—that is, a dot.
And from that, at a distance of one man's height along the same eastern line, one should make a second mark.
One should draw lines connecting the two marks to their respective ends.
Starting from the two *nitoda*s (piercing-points), one should draw [the lines] separately and distinctly up to the ends of the wings.

Starting from the western *nitoda*, one should draw westward to the tip of the western wing and to the junction of the wing (*pakṣāpyaya*). That is the bending of the wing; this indeed constitutes the bending of the wing.
Starting from the previous *nitoda*, one should draw the previous tip of the wing (*pakṣāgra*) and the end of the wing (*pakṣāpyaya*) toward the west.
That is the bending of the wing (*pakṣanamana*); thus, the bending of the wing occurs.
These—those.
Straightforward.
The tip of the tail is two cubits in length;
its base is one and a half cubits in length.
The length is one man minus a quarter;
there are eighteen karaṇīs on each side.
It is called "eighteen-karaṇī" because it makes eighteen.
Since the sixteenfold altars (*ṣoḍaśī*) are the subject under discussion, the *karaṇī* for those eighteen [altars] is as follows:
they are indeed the diagonal lines of a square measuring ninety finger-breadths (aṅgula) and equal to three times the measure of a sixteenfold altar.

To explain: from the base of the tail, both to the south and to the north, the side-measure and the cross-measure are each endowed with a dimension equal to one-fourth of a person’s height (*puruṣa*).
"By three [and] nine" refers to the diagonal cords of a field of sixteen *iṣṭakas*.
In this case, the diagonal cord of a square produces an area twice its own size; thus, those two [cords] of eighteen units are the *karaṇīs* for the sixteen-unit squares.
These are the four *karaṇīs*.
In the case of the two [altars] measuring sixteen and eight *ṣoḍaśīs*, they take up eighteen *karaṇīs* as the transverse sides and fifteen *ṣoḍaśīs* as the side-measures.
How so? One constructs six [squares] with a width of half a man and a length of three-quarters of a man;
on both sides of that, there are two equal squares, each measuring three-quarters of a man on all sides.
One should draw those diagonally.
Of the remainder, each makes four and a half;
thus, four and a half plus four and a half makes nine.
When six are subtracted from nine, fifteen remain;
that is the tail—known by the name "tail.
Now the instruments (karaṇas) are described.
The commentary of Sundararāja:

Now, in order to explain the *śyena-cit* (the hawk-altar) already mentioned by means of another method, he introduces the Brāhmaṇa passage once again: "It is said regarding the hawk... (*śyena ucyate*).
Of the person— [it is] divided into sixteen parts, that is, sixteen portions.
Those bricks, which consist of four parts each, are one hundred and twenty in number.
By the rule "śadantaviṃśateśca," the suffix *ḍa* is applied.
Thus, the fire-altar consisting of seven layers (*saptavidha*), measured by the *aratni* and *prādeśa*, results in one hundred and twenty units of sixteen parts of a man’s body (*puruṣakṣetra*).
Of these, within the self, there are forty sixteenfold units.
Three [are] on the other side;
then he speaks of the measure of the self: "one and a half selves."
The method for laying out the sixteen parts (*ṣoḍaśī*) should be understood as follows: it is stated that the hips and shoulders [are laid out] toward the center;
the head is one-sixteenth part [of the total], which is four and a half finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
In the natural form, however, which is devoid of the *aratni* and *prādeśa*, a reduction of thirty finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) from its previous extent must be observed.
In a length of two *puruṣas*, there are thirty-two *ṣoḍaśī*-parts,
and one [additional part] by way of a sixteenth portion.
Thus [there are] thirty-three;
from that,
the other fortnights.

One should remove the southern half-parts of those [bricks] on the south, and the northern half-parts of those on the north. Regarding the bending of the wings: having set aside a square measuring thirty finger-breadths at the tip of the wing, one should draw a line through the middle of the head of the wing, which measures two hundred and seventeen and a half finger-breadths. Then, having fixed a bamboo rod of one *puruṣa* length at the western end of the junction of the wing, one should drop it onto that line.
Wherever that line falls, one should make a mark there and drive a peg into it.
Having fixed a man there, and having made a mark at the end of the man's length to the east, one should draw the eastern and western limits following that [mark].
Regarding the eastern arrow, it was already stated that "the cord is two men long"; here, the bending [of the cord] should be understood as described by this different method.

These—the two well-known [diagonals]—are the diagonals of the tail of the eighteen [finger-altars] and the sixteen [finger-altars]; they consist of nine [fingers] plus a quarter-tila each, and they form the diagonal sides of the 270-finger [altar].
The number of the sixteen [finger-altars] for the tail, self, and head should be visualized by drawing them on the ground.
According to the commentary of Kapardin, one should take up the *ṣoḍaśī* cup with four [verses].
That which stands in the sixteenth part of the man is the *ṣoḍaśī*.
One should encompass it with four [parts]—meaning one should cause it to be made—with the fruits to be described:
by the eighth [part] with three eighths, and by the fourth with a specific fourth. (ĀpŚus 19.2b)
The half-brick [is laid] with three, two, and four [fingers], and with a fourth plus a fraction. (ĀpŚus 19.3)
One foot-brick is laid with three [units], one with a fourth part plus a specific quarter, and two with half-units plus a specific quarter. ĀpŚus 19.4.
The wing-brick is laid with four [units], two fourths, and two sevenths. ĀpŚus 19.5.
In the middle of the fortnight, [he should recite] with four [verses], with two, with two [verses] of the fourth [chapter], and with two [verses] of the seventh [chapter]. ĀpŚus 19.6.

One [brick] on the tip of the wing with three [formulas], one with the fourth alone, one with the fourth and the seventh, and one with the fourth and the seventh together with a specific addition. ĀpŚus 19.7.
By the eighth part of a man, which is fifteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
by three eighths—that is, by that same measure tripled, which is forty-five finger-breadths;
and by the fourth with a slight excess—that is, by the fourth part with a slight excess.
"By the phrase 'one should increase the measure by a third,' and so forth, [it means] by the increased measure of forty-two finger-breadths (aṅgulas) plus fourteen sesame seeds (tilas).
In this way, the sixteenfold brick (ṣoḍaśī) is made by these four [measures].
'One should encompass the half-brick with three [measures]'—this is the remainder to be supplied everywhere."
"By two" means by those measuring thirty finger-breadths; "with distinction" means according to the stated measurement. One should have it made with these three.
"By the foot"—this has already been explained. "The fourth"—one [syllable] by means of the fourth;
it is the qualified form of the fourth.
The fourth [section] is with distinction. By its two halves: "pakṣa" means for the sake of the wing—[thus] *pakṣeṣṭakā* (wing-bricks).
One should grasp that [line] with four [syllables],
and with two— namely, with the two fourth syllables and the seventh syllable of the word *puruṣa*. Its bending will be described below.

Regarding "in the middle of the fortnight" (*pakṣamadhya*): by means of these four—the fourth, the two seventh [notes] which have become curved, and so on—one performs the *pakṣamadhya* [melody]. "In the fortnight" (*pakṣa*) is understood. Regarding "by the fourth": one [measure] is with the fourth of the *puruṣa*; one is with the fourth and the seventh which have become curved; and one is precisely with the fourth and the seventh along with its specific quality (*saviśeṣa*).
Karavindīya Vyākhyā:
"Ṣoḍaśī" refers to that which remains when the person is divided into sixteen parts; it is the sixteenth part.
One should encompass— that is, construct— the *ṣoḍaśī* with four types of panels;
[specifically] with the eighth, which, by virtue of the context, refers to the person (*puruṣa*),
meaning fifteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
By three [sides] of eight [units each], making forty-five finger-breadths;
by the fourth, thirty finger-breadths;
and by the fourth plus a distinction, forty-two finger-breadths with an addition of four and a half sesame seeds, situated diagonally.
The word *iti* has the sense of "and" (*ca*).
By this and by that—that is, the eighth and the three eighths are the two lateral lines (*pārśvamānyau*);
the fourth and its specific [multiple] are the two transverse lines (*tiryaṅmānyau*).
The word "fourth" is used specifically for the sake of attaining a further distinction within that very fourth [dhyāna].
In this manner, one should have the *ṣoḍaśī* constructed with these four planks.
The word "ardhe" (in the half) implies that one should enclose it;
one should enclose the half-brick with three wooden planks.
It consists of three panels, measuring thirty finger-breadths each by forty-two finger-breadths and fourteen sesame seeds.
Regarding the feet—it consists of three parts: two measuring twenty-one fingers and seventy *lā*s each, and one measuring thirty fingers.

The two wings [are formed] by two bricks measuring thirty finger-breadths and two measuring seventeen finger-breadths plus five sesame seeds; one should have the wing-bricks made from these two pairs of equal fourth-parts.
And its naming will be explained later on.
"Intermediate side" (*pakṣamadhyīyā*) refers to that which is suitable for the middle of the side;
it [is made] with four [sides], namely two of thirty *aṅgulas*, two of thirty-four *aṅgulas*, and two of seventeen *aṅgulas* plus ten *tilas*.
"Of the wings"—meaning that which is suitable for the tips of the wings (*pakṣāgrīyā*).

One should enclose it with three planks: one measuring thirty finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), one measuring forty-seven finger-breadths plus five sesame seeds (*tila*), and one measuring fifty-nine finger-breadths plus nineteen sesame seeds.
Thus, the six types of bricks have been described.

Regarding the three types— the *pakṣeṣṭakās*, *pakṣamadhyīyās*, and *pakṣāgrīyās*— the commentary of Sundararāja explains that they are intended for their fitness to be placed in their respective positions and for the leveling of the field.
Now, regarding the [auxiliary] rites: the *ṣoḍaśī*— the particle *ṇa* here refers back to the aforementioned fourth *śyena*.
One should enclose this with four wooden planks;
therein, the side planks consist of one eighth and three eighths [of the total width],
while the upper planks are laid crosswise.
The fourth [altar] with its specific dimensions has a side of forty-two finger-breadths and fourteen sesame seeds as its double-measure;
it is described as being "half" and "one-quarter."
The eastern hawk [is] different from the others;
on the fourth side-board, it is thirty finger-breadths;
on the seventh cross-board, it is seventeen finger-breadths plus five *vr̥ttilas*.
The two brick-pakṣas, namely the pakṣamadhyī and the other,
constitute this entire wing.
In the Pūrvāśyena, the form is like that of the second [altar];
and "wings" refers to the wing-bricks— the half-bricks.
In the whole [altar], there is one [span];

according to the *Kapardibhāṣya*, the seventh [measurement] of the side-constructing cord is the transverse-measuring cord; and the fourth part of a man is the side-measuring cord. One should expand the construction by means of its diagonal cord. ĀpŚus_19.8a ||
One should lengthen it.
By this [it is meant] "the measuring-line" (*karaṇī*).
"The measuring-line of the wing" (*pakṣakaraṇī*)—that is, the brick which is the measuring-line of the wing.
The method for that has been stated: "With the man as the seventh, the *tiryaṅbhānī* with the man as the fourth, and the *pārśvamānī*";
[and] "the wing-brick by four. One should expand—that is, lengthen—that very same construction which has become elongated.
How may one lengthen the construction with a single straight cord?
One should bend the side-boards by means of the seventh plank.
The space between the root of the *nitoda* (the central point) and the *lekhā* (the line) is the *pakṣa-namanī* (the wing-bending line).
Having divided that into seven parts, [one proceeds] with one part.
What is meant by this? One should bend it so that its seventh [part] becomes horizontal through that amount of bending.
In this manner, one should bend the ribs as they ought to be bent;
one should perform the bending of what is already bent. This same method applies to the tips of the wings as well.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"It should be sixteen finger-breadths across, less sixteen sesame seeds;
likewise, one should bend it by four and by seven [units]."

On the *upadhāna* layer, there are four *pādeṣṭakā*s on the head in front; five behind the head; eleven on each side at the junction of the wings; eleven behind them; five at the junction of the tail in front; five behind them; and fifteen at the tip of the tail. (ĀpŚus 19.9)
The word "should place" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
One [tile] is at the front on the forehead, in the shape of a nose;
behind that, three.

"By another"—as with the ear-ornament—refers to the very bricks of the feet. "In front"—meaning, eleven bricks are placed in front of the junctions of the wings on the self (the body); "behind"—meaning, there are eleven at the junctions of the wings; these are the same.
"Before"—meaning five before and five after the point where the tail terminates.
"Fifteen"—meaning fifteen at the tip of the tail.
These are the fifty-six bricks for the feet.

Pakṣaka—nevertheless, because it is primary and by virtue of its functional capacity, this refers to the side-measure (*pakṣeṣṭakākaraṇī*) of the wing; the side-measure of the half-wing divided by the length is the "wing-measure" (*pakṣakaraṇī*).
It is nine hundred and seventy-five finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).

Its seventh [side] is fifteen *aṅgulas* long, with eighteen sesame seeds (*tilas*) added; it should be straight. One should bend that *karaṇa* straight across—meaning one should bend it thoroughly—in such a way that its transverse side becomes the diagonal of the *karaṇa* being bent.
However, even while the *karaṇa* is being bent, the lateral side remains exactly one-fourth of a *puruṣa*. Here too, "bending" (*prajambhati*) has the sense of measuring.
This is what is meant: having tied a cord to one end of the measuring instrument (karaṇa), one should pull it with force diagonally toward the opposite end until that end reaches its measure.

When this pulling is done such that the two ends are brought close together, the space between the two side-measures (pārśvamānī) becomes straight; thus one should extend the diagonal (pakṣakaraṇī) so that it becomes exactly one-seventh [of the total], neither less nor more.
Even though the space between the two cross-measures (tiryaṅmānī) remains straight, it is exactly one-fourth of a man's height.
By this, a reduction of the transverse measure (*tiryaṅmānī*) is made for the sake of curvature and for the leveling of the area.

Alternatively, having made the transverse measure fifteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) plus eighteen sesame seeds (*tila*), and having made the side-measure (*pārśvamānī*) thirty finger-breadths, one should divide [the area] into a square by means of those two; then, by means of a diagonal cord (*akṣṇayārajju*) of that [square], one should stretch out the construction of the wing-bricks (*pakṣeṣṭakā*).

This is what is meant: having stretched a cord longer than the aforementioned diagonal cord, and having fixed one end of it for the construction of the wing-brick, one should "stretch" (or "align") that end toward the other end diagonally—that is, one should measure it.

The meaning is that one should bend it so that the diagonal cord (akṣṇayā-rajju) occurs between those two ends. When this is done, the single diagonal cord of this instrument becomes longer by one and a half finger-breadths (ardha-dvaya-aṅgula), while the other [cord] becomes shorter by that same amount.
The second explanation, which has been proposed by certain individuals, does not possess the quality of being straightforward.

Having explained the rule for bending by means of the *prajambhana* (stretching) of the bricks forming the wings (*pakṣa*), the curvature of their surfaces is now stated for the purpose of achieving the bending of the bricks located in the middle of the wings (*pakṣamadhyīya*) and at the tips of the wings (*pakṣāgrīya*). Regarding the "wing-bending measure" (*pakṣanamanī*): that measure by which the wing is bent is the *pakṣanamanī*.
It is the western measure from the first indentation (*nitoda*) on the line marking the middle of the wing.
And it has been stated to be fifty fingers (*aṅgula*) plus twenty-five sesame seeds (*tila*).
Its seventh part is eight and a half *tilas* and seven *aṅgulas*.
By that [measure], one should bend—i.e., curve—the planks (*phalaka*) which are long for the two middle sections of the wings and for the two end sections of the wings.

This is the meaning: by bending it at the center in such a way, the two parts of the middle section of the wing become as previously described, with their transverse measurement being a seventh [of the span] and their lateral measurement being a fourth of a *puruṣa* according to the measure of the wing-span (*pakṣakaranyā*).
Likewise, between two planks of twice-seven [i.e., fourteen] units, at the seventh unit alone, one should effect a downward bend with the seventh [unit] on one plank and an upward bend on the other.
Regarding this, there are verses:
"The construction of the wing-brick is as follows: one should stretch it out with a cord so that its transverse measurement becomes one-seventh of the wing-measuring cord."
In the middle of the fortnight, when the two long fruit-ends are not made,
there would be a bending by means of the seventh bending-stick at a distance of seven mātrās.
This same act of bending applies even to the formation of the wing-tip;
its inclination occurs at the seventh part, while another part of it becomes straight.
The measurement for the bricks and their divisions should be such that they are fifteen finger-breadths in length and eighteen sesame seeds in width.
In the first Śyena sacrifice, the tearing apart of the initial instrument is the fruit;
the sixth side-constructing line is such that it becomes the sixth width.
The result of the second, third, and sixth [squares] is the natī;
the square-root of the side of Vyāsa is the sixth, and there is no natī in the eighth.
These two verses concern the initial hawk.
In this case, there are four side-bricks (pakṣeṣṭakā) and six foot-bricks (pādeṣṭakā);
furthermore, the half-jānu and daśama bricks are used for the coḍāna and ākasada sections.
At the time of laying the foundation bricks (*upadhāna*), one should place four foot-bricks (*pādeṣṭakā*) belonging to the head in the eastern part, in front [of the body].
Of those four, one in the front has its point directed eastward because of its outward-facing characteristic.
After that, there are three;
among them, the middle one has its tip pointing westward.
Five [lines] are for the dissolution of the head; beyond that, five [more];
and two with their tips pointing westward.
It is simply [the rule] "after *ap* and *pṛcch*, when there is a replacement by *āt*."
Ten in the east, ten in the west, in front of the two ends of the wings,
and eleven with oneself.
Five [blades] with their points directed inward.
Apaśa—
after the western wing-junctions, eleven [lines] to the west,
with their tips pointing westward.
And to the east,
there are five lines in front of the junction with the tail;
among them, three have their tips pointing westward.
Furthermore, there are five [lines] in front of the point where the tail merges;
among them, two have their tips pointing westward.
Five—
fifteen [bricks] are to be placed at the tip of the tail;
among them, seven have their tips pointing westward.
These are the fifty-six bricks in the quarters.
According to the commentary of Sundararāja:
"The side-measure (pakṣakaraṇī)— that is, the transverse measure of half the wing— is eight hundred and seventy-five finger-breadths."
Half of that [square] is seven [units], fifteen finger-breadths (aṅgula) and eighteen sesamum seeds (tila).
One should stretch out—that is, bend—the frame by means of a diagonal cord (akṣṇayā rajju) so that its transverse side becomes exactly thirty finger-breadths;
one diagonal (karṇa) is forty finger-breadths and twelve sesamum seeds.
Another [measurement] is twenty-seven [aṅgulas] with twenty *tilas*.

When the *aratnis* (or *prādeśas*) are excluded, one ear is twenty-three and a half [aṅgulas], while the other is forty-three [aṅgulas] minus five *tilas*. And the width of the brick is thirteen [aṅgulas] with thirteen *tilas*.
Now, he describes the bending of the tips of the wings and the middle of the wings:
"The wing-bending [rope] should be one man's length."
Of that [wing], one should bend the horizontal planks of the wing-tiles (*pakṣeṣṭakā*)—which constitute a portion of the wing situated between the tip and the middle—at the seventh [unit].
