One should plane those horizontal planks of the wing-portion, which has a diameter of fifteen *aṅgulas* and eighteen *tilas*, in such a way that they become seventeen *aṅgulas* and five *tilas*.

There are two wing-iṣṭakas joined along their sides, and one for the middle of the wing, which is six-cornered. Having drawn on the ground a wing-iṣṭaka with a long ear in the northeast, one should make a square of thirty aṅgulas to its south and then cut off its southeastern half diagonally. That is the five-cornered iṣṭaka for the tip of the wing.
Since it will be stated later that "here the aṇūka bricks occupy the place of the fifteen-part bricks," two making-tools named *aṇūka* must be prepared.
Having drawn two squares of thirty finger-breadths each, one to the south and one to the north, one should remove the southeastern half of the southern square by means of a diagonal line,
and the northwestern half of the northern square;
this constitutes one *aṇūka*.
The second is a triangle;
one of its sides is sixty finger-breadths, and the other two are each four finger-breadths more than that.
Then the supporting brick (upadhāna): one [brick] with its front toward the west, on the head.
Behind it are three;
[then] five *pādeṣṭakās*.
The northern method.
The former— eleven [methods]—
are indeed the northern method, within the Self alone.
These fifty-six [verses] also were recited facing north.
Nineteenth Section: The Commentary of Kapardin. Four [bricks] each are placed at the tips of the wings and four at the junctions of the wings and the body. Āpastamba Śulba Sūtra 20.1.
He should place those [bricks] around the self [altar] with four sets of sixteen [bricks] each, as appropriate. ĀpŚus_20.2.
In the northern wing, they are placed inverted;
there are four objects [of measurement] for each of the four sides.
At the junction of the wings, upon the completion of the southern wing, the bricks are placed inverted in the northern wing, measuring only one brick.
On the two wings, there are [bricks] measuring half an iṣṭakā in the middle;
by the word "those" (tāḥ), the viśayā bricks are referred to.
In the middle (ātman), they are placed by four ṣoḍaśī bricks each, arranged in reverse order.
Just as one should lay down those four bricks situated at the convergence of the right wing, so too should one lay down the four situated at the convergence of the left wing;
in this sense, the word "pari" (around) is used.
Four [verses] each are to be recited during the two middle parts of the fortnight.
One should cover the two wings with bricks facing eastward. ĀpŚus 20.4.
There are four bricks that are curved and located in the middle of the wings; there are likewise four in the middle of the right wing and four in the middle of the left wing.
These are the wing-bricks (pakṣeṣṭakā) whose characteristics have been described.
With these, aligned toward the east, one should cover the two wings.
One should place them on the two wings;
having reversed them, there are forty-four made of *kāritā* wood.
One should cover the remainder with *ṣoḍaśī* bricks.
One should lay down the remaining fire-altar site with sixteen *ṣoḍaśī* bricks.
The final external particulars, with the exception of the head.
In the subsequent layer, one should place two *ṣoḍaśī* bricks with their heads toward the east and their distinctive parts facing outward.
The "final existences" (*antyā bhavāḥ*) are those situated at the end of the fire-altar;
they are the external particulars, being distinguished from the outside—excluding the head.
Within the self, in the center, there are six facing east and six facing west.
There are two rows in the body and the remainder in the tail.
If the sixteen-fold bricks alone are laid down in them, the number is fulfilled, yet there remains a discrepancy.
In all four types of layouts (*rīti*), the [excess] difference must be avoided;
therefore, half-bricks (*ardheṣṭakā*) should be laid down.

How are they laid down without being explicitly mentioned? They are indeed already mentioned by the author who says: "Whatever becomes square or triangular, one should cover it with half-bricks or quarter-bricks (*pādeṣṭakā*)."

Now, if half-bricks are laid down, does not the number exceed [the prescribed total]? This is not a fault; for it was stated in the previous chapter that the arrangement may have fewer or more [bricks]. There are two rows in the tail.
Having laid down three half-bricks in each [row], there are sixteen [whole bricks]; furthermore, on the northern side, there is one half-brick in each [row].
Thus, in the self [of the altar], there are three ardhēṣṭakās to the south of the two rows;
then two ṣoḍaśīs, each one above the other;
and on the head, two ṣoḍaśīs laid crosswise.
Thus there are two hundred and eight [bricks].
Regarding the phrase "in the other"—one should place two *ṣoḍaśī* bricks on the eastern part, externally distinguished and shaped like a nose;
having reversed their position, they are placed on the south.
Those two other objects are internal distinctions.
One should place two half-bricks around [the space] as appropriate. (ĀpŚus 20.7a)
To the west of those two, one should place on the body a space measuring half a brick; the remainder is on the head.
One should lay them down in such a way that they are joined on both sides. These four are the *viśayas*.
According to Karavinda’s commentary: there are four [lines] for each of the two.
The *pakṣās*— by which the *pakṣāgrīyās* are drawn along by the word "and" (*ca*)—
should consist of four *viśayas* each at the two ends of the wings (*pakṣāpyaya*). These are the *pakṣāgrīyās*.
They lie on the two wings with the seventh [syllable],
and on the self with the remaining fourth.
Having meditated upon them,
one should lay them down in such a way that they are joined by the four *ṣoḍaśī* bricks on all sides around the foremost bricks at the tips of the wings;
and one should lay them down so that the specific variations (*viśeṣāḥ*) of the foremost bricks at the tips of the wings remain contiguous— this is the meaning.
The two [terms] "cata" and "yoḥ" are to be understood according to their respective application.
This has been explained.
One should cover the two wings according to the requirements; that is to say, one should cover the two wings with forty by forty wing-bricks (pakṣeṣṭakā) extending towards the east.
Now, one should cover the remaining unenclosed fire-area— the portion of the tail that remains— with sixteen *ṣoḍaśī* bricks. There are two rows in the middle of the tail.
There are four bricks in the east and six bricks in the west;
two by two, they are accompanied by specific distinctions.
These ten [lines] are within the self;
in the middle of the self are three rows.
The four eastern groups of eight bricks are within the self alone;
behind and in front, there are two northern rows of four bricks each.
These total twenty.
On the head are two sixteen-year-old girls.
The final [bricks]—
those to be placed at the end are the final ones;
four in the tail and four in the body.

"External particulars" (*bāhyaviśeṣāḥ*) means particulars situated outside. Furthermore, there is no completion of a numerical total here, because the numbers are employed in groups of two hundred at their respective places. For instance: fifty-six brick-pieces for the feet—eight each for the *pakṣāgrīyā*s—and forty each for the wing-bricks (*pakṣeṣṭakā*).
There are eight;
in the middle of each fortnight there are forty-four sixteen-day periods;
thus, there are two hundred.
Having omitted [the previous ones], in the second layer, one should place two sixteen-brick units with their points directed eastward on the eastern part of the head, at the outer edge.
Those two— behind those two *ṣoḍaśī* bricks, on the head [of the altar], in the space measuring half a brick and a quarter brick, specifically within the self; thus,
there are two *ṣoḍaśī* bricks within that specific space.
With two [verses]— namely, "dhyāt" and "te"—
one should enclose those two *viśaya* bricks with two half-bricks (*ardheṣṭakā*) that are themselves *viśaya*, as appropriate.
The meaning is that one should lay down the sixteen half-bricks and the [other] bricks in such a way that their joints become continuous.
The commentary of Sundararāja states: "Of those two [lines],
there are [spaces] in the self equal to half-bricks."
Having meditated upon those [lines],
one should draw the southern ones with their tips pointing south, meeting at the south, and the others pointing north.
One should draw four lines for the meditative squares, extending eastward by eighty [units] on each side.

One should cover [the area] with *aṇūka* bricks; for it will be stated that they occupy the place of the fifteen-part bricks (*pañcadaśabhāgīyā*). In order to avoid a discrepancy in the covering together with the *aṇūka*s, there are sixteen northward rows (*rīti*) there, including those previously placed at the tail, the body, and the head. A row of foot-bricks (*pādarīti*) has been mentioned at the tip of the tail.

On the second [row], there are four sixteen-bricks (ṣoḍaśī) in the middle of the two side-extensions (aṇūka). Likewise, on the third, sixth, and thirteenth [rows], there are twelve sixteen-bricks extending forward in the intervals between the joints by means of two kinds of aṇūkas. On the rear half of the head, there are two sixteen-bricks; this constitutes the two-hundred-brick layering (prastāra).
"Last"— the word "and" (*ca*) should be supplied here after "head.
There are distinctions between the two.
Those [bricks] which are to be placed at the ends should be external special bricks (bāhyaviśeṣāḥ) consisting of sixteen parts;
and this [is to be done] within the body itself,
because it is impossible on the two wings and because of the possibility of a division in the tail.

Therefore, one should place eight *ṣoḍaśī* bricks upon the hips and shoulders of the altar— four on the right side with their points facing south and four on the left side with their points facing north—
two on each part. In this case,
the required number is completed by the *pādyā* bricks to be mentioned later, which are described as being either square or triangular.
In that [diagram], there are two half-bricks in front of the dissolution of the tail and two half-bricks behind the dissolution of the head;
in their midst are twenty-four quarter-bricks (pādyāḥ),
and on the two sides are six sixteen-part bricks (ṣoḍaśyaḥ) each.
Alternatively, having set aside thirty-six of these sixteenfold bricks which serve as foot-bricks, thirty-six half-bricks are to be placed;
among them, those situated on the right side have the north-eastern orientation, while those on the left are the reverse.
In the middle of the tail, six *ṣoḍaśī* bricks are laid extending toward the east; then, on both sides of that, four half-*iṣṭakās*;
the remainder is exactly as before.
In this regard, there are five methods of the Easterners or eight of the Northerners concerning the self (ātman).
Furthermore—
one should place these two as well on the western side with their tips pointing eastward.
By two [verses]—one should place two half-bricks at the end of the head between those two sixteen-brick [sections]; this is the meaning. (Kapardibhāṣya)
One should take hold [of it] by means of two external characteristics. ĀpŚus 20.7b.
Since the third case ending (*tṛtīyāpada*) is heard in both instances, this is a separate injunction and not a qualification of the two preceding ones.
The word "and" (*ca*) must be supplied [after *bāhyaviśeṣābhyām*], as in:
"And one should enclose [the altar] with the two external special bricks (*bāhyaviśeṣābhyām*) and with half-bricks (*ardheṣṭakābhyām*)."
Because there is no space on the head, he should place them upon himself alone; he should place the sixteenfold external particulars at the joints of his own limbs. ĀpŚus 20.8.
The parts of the self are its instruments; at their joints—in the hips and the shoulders—there are four external particulars and sixteen internal particulars.
On the two tips of the wings, there are four half-bricks each.
In the parts shaped like nails, four bricks each should be laid in the form of horses.
One should cover the two wings with bricks for the wings laid out facing north.
One should lay down the wings with bricks having their lengths oriented upwards.
Having reversed fifty-six [bricks], they are made to function [as such].
Three half-bricks each are to be placed on the two sides of the tail. (ĀpŚus 20.10)
On the two sides of the tail, there are three sets of three half-bricks each, with their specific features facing outward.
One should cover the remainder with *ṣoḍaśī* bricks. (ĀpŚus 20.11a)
One should cover the remaining area of the fire-altar with sixteen-particle bricks.
The last [parts] are the external particulars, except for the tail.
This [section] is concluded,
excluding the tail.
This is the Karavindīya commentary.
Regarding the "external"—
it is simply "those two.
One should encompass those same two *ṣoḍaśī* bricks with two other external, specific half-bricks.
These two halves exist within the self because there is no space [for them] in the head.

This is what is meant: before the two external distinctions of the object and the sixteenfold [set], there are two halves within the self; likewise, to the south and north of the object and the sixteenfold [set], there are the other two halves in the external distinctions.
From the self,
[arise] the instruments of the self;
at their joints— the hips and the shoulders— are sixteen, four in each.
In all instances, there is a Vedic (chāndasa) transposition of case endings.
One should place four *ṣoḍaśī* bricks near the wings and the tail of the self;
although it will be stated later that "the last ones are the outer special bricks," the explicit mention of "outer special bricks" here is for the purpose of completing the required number.

This is for the purpose of ensuring that when the extraction of the sixteen [bricks] is required for the sake of providing supports for the feet and the half-footed bricks, the extraction of these [other bricks] does not occur.
For each of the four [sides], there are four half-bricks as counter-parts, specifically on the outside.
In the case of the *pakṣa* [arrangement]: there are seven rows (*rītayaḥ*) consisting of six *pakṣeṣṭakas*, with the northern one being the *pakṣa*.
The three nights are merely external distinctions.
Ava—
yet what remains within the self is the thirty-threefold station of the *ṣoḍaśī*, the twelvefold tail-station of the *ṣoḍaśī*.
Except for the tail, all the outer segments (bāhyaviśeṣāḥ) would be the last ones from the end;
however, in the tail, the sixteen parts (ṣoḍaśyaḥ) are the last ones and are indeed inner segments (abhyantaraviśeṣāḥ).
According to the commentary of Sundararāja:
"He should take those two outer [bricks]";
he should enclose them on the south and north within the self (ātman) by means of two half-bricks characterized as being external.
One should apply [the measurements] to the self: from the eight-sided self, there are eight radii.
Therein, the four joints formed by the right and left lateral radii together with the pelvic and shoulder radii [are established].
Therein, at the two hip joints, there are two sixteen-finger-breadths [of sutures] with their tips directed westward;
at the two shoulder joints, there are two with their tips directed eastward.
Thus, there are four sixteen-finger-breadths.
Regarding the four joints at the front and back of the two *karaṇī*s: first, concerning the two front ones, it is stated that one should enclose them with two external special bricks;

since half-bricks have been mentioned, for the two rear ones as well, in order to achieve similarity with the front and to avoid a break in the alignment, only full bricks (*adhyardha*) should be laid.
As for the four [joints]...
In one case— [one should] bestow each [deity] with fifty-six; in the other two cases— three.
Regarding external particulars:
*Kapardibhāṣya*—Whatever [space] may result that is square or triangular, one should cover it with half-bricks or quarter-bricks. (ĀpŚus 20.12)
In all cases, the sixteen [finger-breadths] alone lie [therein].
If they were projected in that manner, there would be a discrepancy everywhere;
therefore, when an effort is made to avoid such a discrepancy, two types result: either a triangle or a square.
In the previous layout, both a square and a triangle were produced;
here, however, there is only a triangle.
There, one should cover or lay down the area using either half-bricks or quarter-bricks.
At the end of the *pucchāpyaya*, there are four sixteen-brick layers as the objects of placement:
two facing east and two facing west;
behind them are ten sixteen-brick layers.
The same applies to the tail on the side.
On both sides, there are two parts of the *viśayā* measure and two of the *ātmi* measure.
In front of those, four *ṣoḍaśī* measures are attached, extending eastward as the fourth [set].
In front of those, six reversed bricks are placed on the northern side;
in front of those, four half-iṣṭakas;
and in front of those, four sixteen-part bricks facing west, which are joined with them.
In front of them are two sixteen-brick [units] with their tips facing different directions and pointing eastward;
between those two are two half-bricks; and in the middle of the body is a brick measuring one-quarter of a half-brick.
Within the self, there are two halves as objects on both sides;
these two sixteen-part halves joined together thus constitute one hundred and twenty-eight.
In this regard, some long-lived ones, disregarding this Sūtra, have produced other methods according to their own whims and merely carry out the completion of the count.
What indeed is impossible for them? We, however, accept what has been stated in accordance with the intention of the author of the Sūtra.
(Karavindīyā Vyākhyā)

Having thus completed the filling of the area (*kṣetrapūraṇa*), he states that the filling of the number (*saṃkhyāpūraṇa*) obtained by nature should be performed in this manner: "And whatever..."—that is to say, when the area is being covered with *ṣoḍaśī* bricks, whatever quadrangular or triangular space may remain after some [bricks] have been removed for the sake of completing the number, that area should be covered with half-bricks (*ardheṣṭakā*) or quarter-bricks (*pādeṣṭakā*). The meaning is that one should complete the count with those. Now, it may be asked: how does the verbal injunction "one should cover" imply the completion of the number? It is said in reply:
This is because, following the rule for covering [the altar] with various bricks in the original fire-altar (*agni*), there is an injunction stating, "one should complete the number.

In this case, since the number is not completed when covered by the *ṣoḍaśī* bricks alone, it is understood that the mention of a second covering is intended solely for the purpose of completing that number.
Furthermore, the original fire-altar is of two kinds: one consisting of square bricks of equal size, and one consisting of square bricks of unequal size.
In the first [section], on the square fire-altar, the count is completed with half-iṣṭakās consisting of fifteen parts;
in the second [section], it is completed with quarter-iṣṭakās and those consisting of six parts.

Therefore, here too, there are quarters (pāda), halves (ardha), and small bricks (aṇūkā) prescribed; since these exist, it is understood that the completion of the count is appropriately achieved by filling with quarter-bricks (pādeṣṭakā) and half-bricks (ardheṣṭakā), and in the second [layer], by sixteen-bricks (ṣoḍaśī) as required.

Furthermore, since it is logical that the required number must be completed, and because it is impossible to complete the number with bricks other than those prescribed here, whereas it is easily accomplished by means of quarter-bricks (*pādā*) and half-bricks (*ardhā*), it is more appropriate to complete the number with those very bricks. Therefore, having removed some of the covered bricks, one should place as many quarter-bricks, half-bricks, and sixteen-part bricks (*ṣoḍaśī*) as are necessary, according to the requirements.
In Sundararāja’s commentary:

regarding the statement "one should lay down that which is square or triangular," the completion of the count is by means of the *pādyā* and *ardha* bricks; in that case, according to the view of completing [the count] with the *ardha* bricks, there are six rows (*ṛti*) oriented eastward in the body [of the altar].
There, between the south and the north, there are six half-aras.
On the second [line], two half-aras are stated at the back and at the front;
near those two are two sixteen-part [units] extending toward the east.
Between those two, there are eight half-bricks.
In this very manner is the fifth row.
With twelve sixteen-bricks extending eastward, there are two middle rows.
At the tip of the tail there are two sixteen-finger-breadth bricks;
at the end of the tail, with its point directed westward, there are four sixteen-finger-breadth bricks extending northward from the east.
At the tip of the tail, on the southern half, the brick previously mentioned [is placed].
To its north is a sixteen-part [brick] with its tip pointing north; to its north are two half-[bricks]; then two sixteen-part [bricks]; then two half-[bricks]; then a sixteen-part [brick];
then a half-[brick], as previously described. In this way, the layout consists of two hundred [bricks].
In the case of filling [the grid] with *pādyā* bricks, twelve *ardhyā* bricks should be extracted on the right side of the self and placed; or else, eight *catasraḥ ṣoḍaśyaḥ* should be placed.
The same applies to the left side.
Regarding this layout as well, he states another method:
The word "or" (*vā*) should also be supplied here from the end [of the previous rule].

Just as in the preceding arrangement (*prastāra*), the sixteen-brick units (*ṣoḍaśī*) were prescribed as being at the ends with their specific outer parts facing outward, so too here, two sixteen-brick units each— both with their tips pointing eastward and westward— are to be placed upon the hips and shoulders, making eight in total.
This [arrangement] also does not hold because it is impossible;
for in this case, two half-bricks would have to be placed at the end of the head,
and two half-bricks would also have to be placed at the end of the tail.
The four side-rows are to be filled with half-iṣṭakas;
in the two middle rows there are sixteen iṣṭakas each; in the middle of the tip of the tail there are six iṣṭakas;
then, in the middle of the eastern row, there are two iṣṭakas.
The remaining [bricks] are to be worshipped.
Then, in the east, in the middle, there are two eastern *ṣoḍaśī* bricks.
The rest is exactly as before.
This constitutes two hundred [bricks].

Even in the view that they are to be filled by the *pādyā* bricks, since there is no distinction in all cases as before, although it is possible to use the *pādāyā* bricks, the "reversed" (*viparīta*) distinctions must be applied.
However, some have previously stated that the final ones are the "external" (*bāhya*) distinctions.
Regarding those two *prastāra*s, they state the remainder [of the rule].
That is untenable, because there is an absence of final *ṣoḍaśī*s that lack a fixed specific designation.
In both *prastāra*s, when they say "the final ones," not only the *ṣoḍaśī*s are understood.
Furthermore, whatever final bricks are to be laid down, they should be made as *bāhyaviśeṣas*.
On their heads, one should place two *ṣoḍaśīs* and enclose them with *bāhyaviśeṣas*.
If [the rule] were "at the joints of the *ātmakaraṇīs*, the *ṣoḍaśīs* are *bāhyaviśeṣas*," then the word *bāhyaviśeṣa* would be redundant.
Furthermore, [the scriptural injunctions] "other than the head" and "other than the tail" would be contradicted,
because it is precisely the external parts— the feet on the head and the arghya-offerings on the sides of the tail— that are intended.
As for what was said— that this applies commonly to both types of diagrams—
even if it is impossible to complete [the diagram] with sixteen *ṣoḍaśī* bricks, as many half-bricks (*ardhapādya*) should be laid down until the completion of two hundred.

In that case, since it is impossible to complete the required number with water for washing the feet (pādya) alone— lacking the water for honoring (arghya)— the completion must be done with pādya water mixed with arghya water. The method for doing so has already been stated previously.
The *kapardibhāṣya* states: "The *aṇūka*s are in the place of the fifteen-part bricks. (ĀpŚus 20.13)
One should pile them in reverse order for as many layers as one intends to construct.
The word *sthāna* signifies "application.

This means that the *aṇūkās*, which consist of four parts (*caturbhāgīyās*), are prescribed for the completion of the number, and the fifteen-part bricks (*pañcadaśabhāgīyās*) are also prescribed for the completion of the number;
however, in this particular arrangement (*prastāra*), the number has not been completed by the author of the Sūtra.
In that case, the number should be completed by them if it can be completed by them;
however, in this fire-altar (*agni*), the number cannot be completed by those minute particles (*aṇūkābhiḥ*),
whereas it can be completed in the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Therefore, the application [of the bricks] serves the purpose of the original nature [of the altar].
In that regard, it is possible to complete [the altar] with those [bricks] during the second layer;
therein, the completion of the two hundred [bricks] must necessarily be performed.
Because of the statement, "one should complete [the count] by successive addition," it was stated in the previous chapter that here, however, the number one thousand itself must be completed;
therefore, this is the yoga under discussion.
Regarding this, there are verses:
"The making of the bricks for the wings shall be performed by reversing [the orientation];
likewise, one should have the wing-tips made by reversing them by half."
The sixteenfold [mantras] should indeed be reversed, and there are two sixteenfold ones;
in the thousand-fold and two-thousand-fold [arrangements], the wise know there to be sixty-five.
The wise know that the sixteen [bricks] are placed according to the sūtra, as they are on oneself, on the two wings, on the tail, on the head, and on the remainder.
One should place six in the east and six in the west within the self, making twelve;
one should place two across the head, which are said to be fourteen.
The remaining two rows are in the tail, and likewise two in the body;
one should then insert sixteen half-bricks into those three rows.
There should be one on each northern side and three on each southern side;
in the remaining [spaces], there should be ten transversely, making two hundred and eight in total.
At the conclusion of the Puccha, one should cast four sixteen-finger squares;
at the conclusion of the two Śoḍaśīs, one should cast the two preceding ones in front and on the head.
In the middle of those two, one should place two halves and four squares;
in the remainder for oneself, one should place two halves and two sixteen-squares on the head.
Everything else is as described in the sūtra: two hundred minus twelve [fingers].
On the right side of oneself, there are four [lines] extending toward the south.
On the second and the northern sides there are six; two each on the hips and the shoulders;
one at the junction of the head, and one on the right side of the head.
These sixteen [deities] are to be deposited; they are inverted in the two layers.
This is the explanation of the *Aṇunirṇaya*.
This is a general rule:
those [bricks] described as having fifteen parts in the first square should,
in their place, be replaced by *aṇūka* bricks for the purpose of completing the required number of actions.

How is that technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) taught here? It is for the purpose that even those [bricks] taught here as *ṣoḍaśīs* might be understood by the term *aṇūkās*, due to their similarity in size.
Consequently, the completion of the number in the square fire-altar (*agni*) is achieved with *aṇūkās*;
however, it is established here that it is also accomplished with *ṣoḍaśīs*.
Some maintain that this is also a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) stating that whatever results in a quadrangular or triangular shape [is included];
therefore, they believe that in various fire-altars (*agni*), those [bricks] should also be used to complete the required number with respect to that [shape].
Here, however, the statement "one should cover" is for the purpose of ensuring that these [bricks] are also employed in the act of covering.

Therefore, wherever there is fire available and where there is a need, there should be covering with both those [bricks] and these [others]. As for the order of placement: on the second citi, one should place two *ṣoḍaśī* bricks on the head, facing east and having their outer sides distinguished; behind those two, one should place two *ardha* bricks, facing east and having their outer sides distinguished.
Behind those two, there are two sixteen-finger-breadth squares in the intermediate directions, each adhering to its respective specific feature within the central area.
To the south of the southern one, there is one outer specific feature measuring half a square;
and to the north of the northern one, there is likewise one outer specific feature measuring half a square.
To the south and north of those two, by way of the external distinction, there is one half each.
Then, behind them, within oneself, there are six eastward lines.
There, in the southern line, at the front, from the external distinction, there is one *ṣoḍaśī* brick with its tip pointing east.
And outside of that, there is one brick with its tip pointing inward; between those two, there are six half-bricks (ṣaḍardheṣṭakāḥ).
Of these, three are facing west and three are facing north.
In the second row, behind [the previous], there are two *ardhas* facing south with an external *viśeṣa*;
in front of that, there is one *ṣoḍaśī* facing west, distinguished by an *ardha-viśeṣa*. Of that...
In front are six half-bricks;
of these, three each are oriented toward the east and the west. To the north of those, in front, is a special brick, the *ṣoḍaśī*, with its tip pointing eastward.
In front of that is one half-brick (*ardha*) joined with a specific [brick] of that same kind;
since there is indeed another half-brick placed in front of that, this row consists of twelve bricks.
In the third row, eight *ṣoḍaśī* bricks are to be laid down, beginning from behind the junction of the head and extending to the junction of the tail.
Of these, four run eastward and four run westward;
likewise, there are three rows toward the north,
where the fourth is equal to the third.
The fifth [row] is like the second;
the sixth is like the first.
Therein, for the three southern rows, it is the right side; for the northern rows, it is the left side.
Of the southern and northern [rows], the southern one proceeds along the two sides;
here, those facing west consist of buds,
while those facing east are the opposite of that.

In this way, they spread out the beauty. At the tail, at the ends of the middle row and the sixteen-petaled [lotus], there are two half-[petals] on the south and north, which are external particulars.
After that, in the center, there are two sixteen-petaled [lotuses].
On both sides [of the body], there are three half-bricks each, making eight bricks in total.
Then, at the tip of the tail, there are eight bricks: six sixteen-part bricks (*ṣoḍaśī*) and two half-bricks on either side.
At the tips of the wings, there are four half-bricks on each side.
On each of the two sides, there are seven rows of half-bricks;
these amount to one thousand two hundred bricks.
And in the case of filling with quarter-bricks, the rows remain exactly these same [seven].
In that regard, the specific detail is as follows: on the outer half-bricks at the edge of the tail, one should divide them into two.
On the first, second, fifth, and sixth [sections] of the body, one should place two half-bricks each from the westward in the middle of those [sections].
In the remaining positions for half-bricks, one should lay down pairs of *ṣoḍaśī* bricks.
One should divide the second and fifth [lines] into two parts by means of a half-measure.
Now, it may be argued that since division is to be avoided, it has been carefully eschewed in each of those fires; yet now, it seeks to manifest itself in the tail? This is not sound.

When the number has been completed by means of bricks that are fixed in their positions and arranged without crowding, if a breakage occurs in one part of the bricks, that breakage must indeed be tolerated; for a breakage in one part is unavoidable.
For this very reason, the Teacher himself explicitly stated, "This [altar] consists of two hundred [bricks]," thereby acknowledging the necessity of avoiding such breakage.
The pervasion has been established.
In the *Sundararājīyā* commentary,
regarding the atoms and the square fire-altar (*caturaśrāgni*), the task is to fulfill the required number of fifteen-part bricks (*pañcadaśabhāgīyā*) by avoiding their division.
But here, however, the *aṇūkas* are to be laid down as its effect.
In that case, it is not possible to make two hundred [bricks] by laying down *aṇūkas* that are regular squares;
therefore, the term refers to the areas of the *aṇūkas*.
In that case as well, the *ṣoḍaśī* bricks are not taken;
for it is already established that the remainder [is covered] by the *ṣoḍaśīs*, and because a distinction [in size] would otherwise be possible.
Therefore, bricks of two types—small and large, or of other varieties such as those from the *kṣetra*—must be made.
And since their instruments were already shown [previously],
the Teacher did not instruct them in the instruments; for, according to the view that "the final [atoms] are external particulars," the *aṇūka*s would be of no use.
The method of insertion has been stated;
however, in that alternative view, the use of the *aṇūka* bricks must be performed in the very first layer (*prastāra*) alone, even without [the usual] *aṇūka*s.
The *kapardibhāṣya* explains that the terms *kaṅkacit* and *alajacit* are explained by [the rules for] the *śyenacit*. (ĀpŚS 21.1)
*Kaṅka* is a specific kind of bird, as is *alaja*. One who is to be piled like a *kaṅka* is a *kaṅkacit*; one who is to be piled like an *alaja* is an *alajacit*.
These two are explained by the Śyena-altar—they are explained by the very same Śyena previously mentioned.

Because of its primacy and because it has a span of two hundred [bricks], its shape alone is adopted; the same are the constituent parts (karaṇas), and the same is the method of laying them down (upadhāna-mārga).
The only difference lies in the intention (saṃkalpa): [the altars are named] Śyena, Alaja, and Kaṅka.

For indeed, in this way, the wings of a hawk are larger than the tail and curved, the tail is bent, the body is long, and the head is circular; therefore, it is by the force of the scriptural statement.
The word *hi* indicates what is well-known.
The hawk (*śyena*) is also exactly like this.
*Varṣīyāṃsau* means "larger" or "greater."
The two wings.
Why are they longer than the tail? Not only are they broad, but they are also curved.
"Sannatam" means properly bent; it is said that in a hawk, what is narrow near the body and broad at the tip is called "sannatam."
The self is not long, nor is it a perfect square, nor is it circular, nor is it a long rectangle;
rather, the head is like something that is neither circular nor a long rectangle.
Such is the hawk in the world.
In the same way, the two born from the skeleton exist in the world; therefore, those two born from the skeleton, having that very form,
are explained by that [same principle] due to the power of the Vedic revelation.
Capability is the power of denotation;
only this much is expressed by the direct statement (*śruti*),
because it is impossible to bring about complete equality.
For the Veda does not enjoin a matter that is beyond suspicion.
Or rather, it is without the head-verse, because it is not so prescribed. ĀpŚus 21.2b.
The word "vā" (or) serves to exclude the alternative position.
It should be piled up entirely without a head.
Why? He says: because it is not so prescribed in the sacred texts.

For the head is not prescribed [in the ritual texts]. To the question, "How is it that it is not prescribed? he replies: "And it is known [from scripture]: 'He who desires, "May I be born with my head in that world," should pile the fire-altar with a head (the *kaṅkacita*); for if it were already present [in the ritual], how could one say this? (ĀpŚus 21.3)
If there were a scriptural mention of a head—as in the injunction "one should pile [the fire-altar] with a head"—then how could one say "only thus"? That is the meaning.
If there is no scriptural mention of a head, then this qualification is indeed appropriate;
otherwise, the qualification would be entirely meaningless.
Therefore, it should indeed be built without a head.
If one asks, "What is the form of that which is headless? he says:
"The two wings are naturally curved and the tail is bent, because of the mention of a modification. (ĀpŚus 21.4a)
The two that exist in the *prakṛti* are the *prākṛta* ones;
those very two wings are to be bent.
Why? Because of the scriptural mention of modification (*vikāra*).
"The tail is bent"—the tail must be made bent;

for a modification is heard in the scripture stating, "The wings are spread out and the tail is extended. However, neither the spreading out nor the extension of the wings and tail exists in the original archetype (*prakṛti*).
Therefore, the wings and tail are modifications.
Because the self remains unchanged according to its original nature. ĀpŚus_21.4b.
The self is according to its original nature. Why? Because it is changeless;
for no modification is heard of in that regard.

Therefore, the altar (ātman) is exactly like the model: four men long and square. One should extend the two wings by one cubit or half a span, using a cord of two men's length and so forth, as in the case of the Śyena altar.

But has it not been stated regarding the original form that "one should increase by one *aratni*"? Why is it now said, "by one *aratni* or by half a *prādeśa*"? The statement "by one *aratni*" is intended to demonstrate that it is a modification of half [the size]; it is not meant to bring the length of the wings and tail to exactly that measure. Rather, eight *caturbhāgīyās* should be laid down as the fourth part of the body (*ātman*).
That which is established by the Śyena [sacrifice] should not be performed;

rather, the self (the fire-altar) must be constructed exactly according to its original form (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, because of the statement "the tail is the original," the injunction for the placement (*upadhāna*) is also not applicable.
"If it is to be piled like a hawk," when this is performed, there is a modification only of the first and second layers, not of the others.
Otherwise, even the fourth and subsequent layers would become modified; and if they were so, they would have to be performed as such.
And for that reason, it has been stated that [the body] must be conceived by entering into the instruments (karaṇa).
The tail is just like the eagle itself.
The instruments are now described: that which is bent according to its application in the fourth and sixth [sections] is the first.
The two [bricks] are joined as before; "the second," and so forth.
Now follows the rule for the placement: there are forty-eight first [bricks] pointing northward on the two wings;
the tail is like that of a hawk.
On the two hips of the self [altar], there are three lines each, oriented toward the north, consisting of five finger-breadths (*pañcamī*).

Then, within seven rows, there are fifty-six lines of four finger-breadths each, extending both southward and northward. To the east of those, there are eight lines of five finger-breadths, extending toward the north.
One should divide the two hips with four fifth-lines diagonally;
thus eight sixth-lines are produced.
This is the two-hundred-fold layout.
In the subsequent arrangement, four second bricks are laid at each of the two corners and at the two junctions;
the third bricks are likewise four by four, as before, these being one-eighth parts.
One should cover the two wings with wing-bricks (*pakṣeṣṭakā*).
There are seventy-two [bricks] in the tail, like those of a hawk.
With seven and eight bricks, there are two by two on the hips and shoulders; five each are oriented eastward and westward.
There are seven rows oriented eastward.
Between the third and fifth *rītis*, there are thirty sixth-notes (*ṣaḍjas*) and one fifth-note (*pañcamī*);
in one case there are sixteen and in the other fourteen. Thus, the *prastāra* consists of two hundred [notes].
Alternatively, one should stretch out that same [space] along the spine, measuring half a man's width and one *prādeśa* [in height], extending one man's length toward the west.

To its south, another [span], and so forth; in this manner, one should fashion the tail like that of a hawk (*śyena*). The two wings are as in the original model, measuring two men's lengths in extent.
We shall now describe the instruments: they should be twelve finger-breadths long; once stretched out, one should bend them transversely at the fourth and sixth [sections].
One should have them made so that, when joined together, they remain as they were initially.

Regarding the second and third [sections], one should increase them by a sixth or an eighth part; or those same [dimensions] may apply to the tail. The fourth [section] has a width of thirty-three *aṅgulas* and a length of forty-five *aṅgulas* less fourteen *tilas*, with a slight variation. The fifth has a breadth of six and a half *aṅgulas* and six sides, with a length of twenty-nine *aṅgulas* plus thirty-six *aṅgulas* and fourteen *tilas* at the junction of the tail. At the two joints of the tail, it is eighteen *aṅgulas*; in the tail itself, it is exactly fifteen *aṅgulas*. The fourth and subsequent sections in the body (*ātman*) are modified (*vaikṛta*), whereas in the tail (*puccha*), they remain in their original form (*prākṛta*).
That very same is the rule for placing the fire within oneself.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
"The sacrificial fire, which has no head, has a width of thirteen [units] and a height of twelve."
Likewise, one should bend the first [finger] with the fourth and sixth.
Those two [lines] joined together point eastward; this shall be the second construction.
The third [line] is also increased by one-eighth of a sixth part.
The bricks in the wings should be fourth-parts; the tail is described as being like the tail [of the altar].
There should be fifty-six fourth-parts extending transversely from south to north.
One should place eight [lines] in front and across the two hips;
six and five [lines] for each hip, and four fifth-parts for the hip, thus making two hundred [squares] with their divisions.
Having placed [the measures] on the wings and tail like a hawk, one should also cast them upon oneself;
in the east and in the west, there are thirty-one and five [units] respectively.
On their northern side, there are four [lines] of two sets of sixteen each;
likewise, there are sixteen on the east and sixteen on the west, as well as sixteen on the south.
One should add the fifth vowel to both the first and the last vowels;
however, a transposition of the fourth vowel is not permitted.
Or, even when the tail is one prādeśa long, its width should be twelve [aṅgulas];
likewise, one should bend that first [part] by means of the fourth and sixth [sections].
Those two joined together face eastward, for that is indeed the second constituent;
the third also consists of six parts increased by one-eighth.
Twenty-two [units] doubled, and twenty of sesame seeds;
for the fourth, there is a specific distinction, and it becomes exceeding the horizontal truth.
One should know that the fifth [section] is the original (prākṛta); for the sixth, there are three modified [sections].
The side of the sixth is increased by three, while the corner is thirty-six [units] plus eight.
In this case, the width of the seventh and eighth [sections] is held to be twenty-nine [units],
while the length is thirty-six together with fourteen *tilas*.
One should place the deformed [sections] beginning with the fourth in the tail and in the self;
eighteen finger-breadths in the tail, and the other two in the self.
Karavindīyā Vyākhyā: Kaṅka— these two are specific types of birds born from skeletons.
"Built like a *kaṅka* bird, built like an *alaja* bird"—thus are the *kaṅkacit* and *alajacit* explained by means of the *śyenacit*.
The meaning is that their measurements, the making of the bricks, and the manner of laying them down must be performed exactly as for the *śyena*.
Some maintain that it is the first *śyena* [that serves as the model], because of its primacy.
Others say that because it follows immediately after, it belongs to the second Śyena;
others say it belongs to both because there is no distinction.
Having stated the nature of the Śyena, he restates it here precisely for the purpose of establishing the existence of its "head."
Thus, because it is like this, it is understood as "it is indeed so.

The two wings of the hawk are broader—that is, longer—and curved compared to the tail; the tail is bent near the body and tapers toward the tip; the body is long and not a regular square; it is not circular—that is, not in the shape of a circle—though it is slightly oval.
Nor does a head exist;
that [body] is neither circular nor even quadrangular.
Thus is the hawk seen in the world.
The similarity of the fire to the hawk is only this much.
Why? Because of the power of the scriptural statement—power being the capacity for denotation.
Only this much is enjoined by the scriptural term "hawk."

The meaning is that because this [body] possesses curved sides, a tail set askew, a long body, a circular shape, and a head, one should likewise perceive those two [the Kaṅkāla and Jāta] as having those same forms.

Or rather, it is headless; for the hawk is not [described] as having a head, because there is no scriptural mention of a head. Indeed, there is no mention of a head as there is of the curvature of the wings, tail, and body.
Some maintain that the prescription of the head is understood from the force of the prescription for the hawk;

however, [if this were so], then even in the archetype (prakṛti), the prescription of the head would follow as a consequence, just like the wings and other parts, based on the statement, "This is built in the likeness of birds.
This is not a fault.

For in that case, the prescription of the wings and tail is for the purpose of exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*). Therefore, here too, that [prescription] comes by force of the general injunction (*codaka*); thus, the *śyena* altar is complete with its head.
Furthermore, it is known from scripture: "One should pile the *kaṅka*-piled altar as having a head."

If the head were already present in the *kaṅka* bird by virtue of being obtained through the general rule (*codaka*), then why would it say, "One should pile the *brāhmaṇa*-altar as a *kaṅka*, provided with a head"? The meaning is that it would not have said so at all. Therefore, the *śyena* altar is headless, because the head is specifically prescribed for the *kaṅka*.

Thus, when the similarity consisting merely of the [shape of] space (*vayomātra*) has been established as the subject under discussion, it is understood that the hawk also possesses a head precisely by virtue of the injunction prescribing the attainment of the hawk-form;
this is because of the observation of the placement [of bricks] upon the head in the passage beginning with, "The threefold is your head, O Agni.
Therefore, considering that there is an option (*vikalpa*) between those two, he employs the word "or" (*vā*).
In this regard, the *kaṅka*, *śyena*, and *alaja* differ only in their conventional designations (*saṃkalpa*), not in their form;
like the *Dākṣāyaṇa-yajña* and other such rites, it is called a "hawk" (*śyena*) even when it is headless.

Prior to this, as in the original model, the two wings are curved and the tail is bent; for it is heard in the scripture regarding the modification that "the wings are curved and the tail is spread out.
But the body remains as it was in the original model.
Alternatively, "according to its original form" means that it is unmodified and perfectly square, consisting of four *puruṣas*;
for no modification is heard [in the scripture].
The inclusion of modifications applies to the wings and tail, not to the body (*ātman*).
Therefore, the self (ātman) is indeed natural (prākṛta).
One should increase each wing by one cubit (aratni), half a span (ardha-prādeśa), and a span (prādeśa).
Although it is stated that the two wings are natural, nevertheless, because the tail is heard to be non-natural, the aforementioned measure of being merely a man's height (puruṣamātra) is understood.
Therefore, some think that one should add a span (prādeśa) to the tail and then divide [the space] between the two wings;
others, because the wings are prescribed as being of their original size and because the body is not subject to modification, consider the tail to already include the span.
The Teacher considers that in both cases, the measurements should be inferred according to the method already described.
In this context, according to the view that the tail is not the original model (*aprakṛti*), there is a modification of the first and second ritual instruments (*karaṇa*).
Otherwise, the instruments for those [other parts] are also stated.
By means of the fourth and sixth [instruments], one should stretch out the first instrument so that it becomes thirteen and a half units in width.
Those two are joined facing east.

Of that, the second [row] is one-sixth of the first, which is one finger-breadth (aṅgula); the third is likewise. The laying down [of the bricks] is described as follows: on the right wing, there are forty-eight of the first [type].
Likewise, there are thirty in the north, thirty in the south, and thirty in the body; the same as was stated for the tail applies to the headless wings.
On the two hips, there are three rows each of fifth bricks, oriented both northward and southward.
In front of those, there are seven rows of half-bricks of the fourths;
these amount to fifty-six.
In front of them, there are eight fifth [lines];
on the hips and shoulders, there are four;
one should pierce the fifth line transversely.
This is the two-hundred-brick layout.
In the second layout, there are four of each type of second brick; these [bricks] constitute eight parts of the body.
One should cover the two wings with wing-bricks laid facing eastward.
In each wing there are thirty-six; in the tail, however, as before, there are twelve seventh-day offerings and thirteen eighth-day offerings.
In the hips and shoulders, there are two eastern fifth-day offerings in each.
When there is a remainder of the *ātma* section, one should place thirty-four bricks in the fourth row; seven rows run eastward.
Having removed four fourth-row bricks from between the third and fifth rows, one should lay down thirty, sixty, and one fifth-row brick.
Among those, sixteen and sixty are on one side.
Therein, fourteen [units] are on one side and five [units] are the fifth;
this is the two-hundred-fold layout (*prastāra*).
In the view that includes the *prādeśa*, one should extend a width of one *puruṣa* and a length of one *prādeśa* and one *puruṣa* westward at the tail.
One should fashion the tail with the words "to its south another" and "to its north [another]," and so forth; the two wings remain as they were in the original form.
As for the specific method of construction: one should stretch out the first measuring-rod in such a way that, by being both transverse and straight, it becomes twelve finger-breadths long.
The second [section] is by means of the phrase "having increased those two" and so forth;
for the third as well, it is increased by one-eighth of six parts.
The fourth and subsequent sections are of two kinds: in the fourth [section] of the tail, the width is thirty-three finger-breadths.
Its specific measurement is forty-four finger-breadths plus twenty sesame seeds;
the fifth has a diameter of sixteen and a half finger-breadths;
and the side of the sixth is thirty-three finger-breadths.
These [sides] are thirty-six finger-breadths (aṅgula) each; the width of the two eighth-parts is the same;
the two side-measures are situated obliquely and are twenty-nine finger-breadths each.
The length is thirty-six finger-breadths and fourteen sesame seeds.
The distance between the base of the tail and the edge [of the body] is eighteen finger-breadths.
On the tail, fifteen finger-breadths [are measured], and the fourth part of a sesame seed of the self [the body] and so forth, being modified, are to be placed upon the tail.
The rule for the placement of the bricks applies to the natural self alone;
this is the second Śyena.
Having inferred and performed the aforementioned rites in that modified form, one should build the altar.
In the commentary of Sundararāja,
there is a transposition: "one should desire to perform" [is placed] after the word "known as Kaṅka."
"One who desires, 'May I be possessed of a head in that world,' should pile the *kaṅkacita* with a head-piece.
One desiring stability should pile the *alajacita* with four furrows"—thus the two fires have been explained by the preceding and following [sections] regarding the *śyenacit*.

Now, wishing to prescribe another method for that very same *śyenacit* which has already been mentioned, he says [the following] to show that those two previously mentioned methods are more appropriate:

It is exactly as we have stated, because it is so observed in reality: for the wings of a swooping hawk are indeed broader than its tail and curved in the middle, while the tail is bent at the point of attachment, the body is slightly circular in form, and the head is likewise shaped.
Therefore—since the word *tat* (it) is heard, the word *yat* (which) must be supplied.
The word *hi* is used in the sense of "because.

Because such parts as the wings and tail of the hawk are perceived by direct observation, therefore, by the force of the scriptural injunction (*śruti*) that "one should pile the hawk-shaped altar," it is stated that the hawk-pile consists of such a body having the nature of wings, tail, and head. This is the meaning.
Because it is not mentioned [in the scripture], either the altar should be headless, or it ought to be built in the shape of a hawk (śyenacit);
for it is not mentioned, as the head is not recorded in the section concerning the śyenacit.
This is also an illustration of the unchanging nature of the Self.
He states that there is another authority for the case where [the head] is absent:
"Vijñā—should say."
If the possession of a head were to occur merely by the injunction of the shape of a hawk, then even the *kaṅkacita* [altar] would necessarily possess one;
and in that case, the qualification "possessing a head" (*śīrṣaṇvantam*) would not need to be stated there. This is the meaning.
If it is headless, then what is its form? He says:
"The two wings and the tail are natural"—meaning they are indeed natural, being six cubits or five cubits in length from the ears.
Those two [sides] are to be bent in the manner described as "a rope of two *puruṣas* with loops at both ends.
However, some desire the bending by means of a rope of one hundred and sixty finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*) along the path [of the previously mentioned length].
And the tail remains in its natural state, bent, with a width of half a *puruṣa*.
One should stretch out a man [as a measuring rod] exceeding a span (prādeśa) in length, facing west.
To its south, another [man], and so forth, as described previously.
In the absence of an increase of a span, it is exactly as before.
"Because of the hearing of a modification" means because of the statement, "The wings are curved and the tail is spread out.
For example, from the model (kārāt), the four men [forming the altar] are indeed a perfect square, because no modification is heard regarding the nature of the Śyena-heap.
Regarding this statement from the *Kapardibhāṣya*, "One should pile it in the manner of a Śyenacit," that which corresponds to the traditional scriptural injunction has been explained. (ĀpŚus 21.5)
In this regard, only that similarity which is traditionally established should be accepted as the basis for apprehension.
For words denoting a genus (*jāti*), some form of universal (*sāmānya*) alone is observed to be the ground for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*).
For example, [the term] "Gaur" [is applied to] a "Vāhīka."
In this case as well, the word *śyena* functions by grasping a similarity based solely on what is traditionally handed down;
that similarity has been explained by the passage beginning with "having curved wings" (*vakrapakṣa*).
"It is known in the Aśvamedha that Agni becomes the Tristubh-stoma. (ĀpŚus 21.6)
In that case, all [the mantras] are to be recited, because there is no distinction. (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 21.7)
In that case, there is no repetition of the sevenfold measurement consisting of the cubit and the span.
Why? Because there is no distinction; for no specific distinction is recorded here in the sacred tradition.
Therefore, there is repetition of the whole.
The summary of the long quadrangular [altars] with wings and tails has been stated in brief. ĀpŚus 21.8.

The method for the combination of long quadrilaterals having wings and tails has been stated either by the rule beginning with "whatever is other than the seven" (*yadanyatsaptabhyaḥ*), etc., or by the rule beginning with "the seventh part of the dimension" (*vidhāsaptamakaraṇīm*), etc.; or else, one should proceed by means of the triple-dimension of the bamboo-stick (*veṇu*). This is the meaning.
"It is known in the Aśvamedha that there are twenty-one fires. (ĀpŚus 21.9)

This has been explained. In that regard, the practice for the person [is performed] not by means of the conjunction of numbers of cubits and spans, nor by the conjunction of numbers of cubits and spans. ĀpŚus 21.10.
The section on cord-measurement (Śulbapraśna) is completed.
In that context, the multiplication is by the *puruṣa* (man’s length), not by *aratni* (cubits) or *prādeśa* (spans).
Why? Because of the connection with a specific number—namely, "twenty-one."
In the phrase "not sevenfold," the number is also being enjoined; however, in that case, the *aratni* and *prādeśa* measures are included by means of another sentence,
and they are not included within that number seven.
Therefore, because of that numerical conjunction, it is indeed the repetition of the *puruṣa* [measure] that is intended, and not the *aratni* or *prādeśa*.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"Man has been declared to be of three kinds; he is to be contemplated as being three times that size."
In the twenty-first [type], it is diminished by seven [units] of sesame seeds.
The repetition is for the sake of auspiciousness.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Śulba section of the *Āpastamba-sūtra-vivaraṇa*, the commentary by Kapardisvāmin.

Karavindīyā Vyākhyā: "Thus explained"— that which was prescribed as the "falcon-built" (śyenacit), its manner of construction and its conformity to the scriptural tradition, as well as its entire conformity to the falcon as ordained by Manu— all that has been explained.

In this context, the similarity of the Śyena [fire-altar] that was described through its qualities such as curved wings and so forth, and the method of construction described by the passage beginning with "the Śyena fire-altar has nine and a half cubits" and so on—by means of that [method], the two [altars] born from the Kaṅka and Alaja should be constructed; this is the meaning.

Because of the mention of "threefold" (*triṣyā-ṣāt*), in the rule for the threefold chanting (*tristāva*) of the horse-sacrifice fire (*āśvamedhika-agni*), there is the repetition [of measurement] by the *aratni* and *prādeśa*, not by the *puruṣa*; this is because there is no specific qualification [to the contrary].
The meaning is that, in the absence of a specific qualification, the triple nature (*traiguṇya*) of the archetypal fire (*prākṛta-agni*) is prescribed.
Regarding "long"—it has been stated that this is a compound of long rectangles.
Thus, two long rectangles are combined; the resulting reduction or increase is caused by that [combination].
As far as one desires, he combines long rectangles;
by that, the combination is stated for the first laying out of the fire-altar in the *triṣṭava* configuration.
In the Aśvamedha sacrifice, regarding the scriptural injunction for the twenty-one fires, there is a repetition of persons alone, not of cubits or spans.
As it is said, "The natural fire is indeed sevenfold," the number seven is to be established as distinct units.
It is joined only with men of the same class, not with things such as cubits (*aratni*) and the like.
For the rule "the cubits and spans [should be] to the south by means of a cubit" prescribes them merely in their own form, not by way of a numerical half.

Therefore, since in the archetype (*prakṛti*) the number is connected only with men, it is logical that even in the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), where there is a fire of twenty-one parts, the connection with the number should apply only to men; thus, the cubits and spans would not be repeated.
The meaning is that immediately after the *puruṣa* [measurement], one should perform [the rite] with the *aratni* on the right side.

This is what is being said: because of the Brāhmaṇa’s vision [of the text], since two expansions (*prastāra*) of twenty-one are prescribed for the three-fold stoma (*tristāva*), the fire-altar (*agni*) itself is indeed twenty-one-fold;
it may consist of twelve or ten [verses].
The repetition is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the inquiry.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Śulbapradīpikā* composed by the venerable Karavindasvāmin. Regarding the commentary by Sundararāja:

Now, one might object that in the absence of a head, since the form of the hawk would be unprecedented, there would arise a contradiction with the injunctive statement, "One should pile the Śyenacit. To this, he says:

Furthermore, regarding what is well-known—that "one should pile the Śyenacit"—the fact that it is described as having "curved wings and a spread-out tail" indicates that its form has been stated according to what was prescribed [in the archetype]; for otherwise, there would be the consequence of the injunctions for the modification of the wings and tail being purposeless. This is the sense.

In this view, the measurements for making the bricks are as follows: for the bending of the wings with a cord of two *puruṣas*, the first [brick] has a length of one *puruṣa* and a width of one-fifth [of a *puruṣa*], bent as appropriate. Its one corner is eighteen *aṅgulas*, and the other is fifteen and a quarter *aṅgulas*.
Two by two, joined as before, that is the second.
The first and fifth are joined in the *karaṇa*; this is the third. The fourth, fifth, and sixth are exactly as in the previously described *śyena*.
Regarding those which are to be placed on the tail—the sixth and fourths—there are other *karaṇas* for them.
There, on the fourth side, as before, there is one horizontal plank measuring thirty-three finger-breadths (aṅgulas) and another measuring forty-four and a half finger-breadths;

for the sixth [side], however, there is one board measuring fifteen [finger-breadths], a second measuring thirty-three [finger-breadths], and a third measuring thirty-six [finger-breadths] plus eight sesame seeds (tilas).
On the seventh [side], the two horizontal planks are each the measure of an aratni.
The side is twenty-nine finger-breadths; one ear is [the same],
while the other ear is forty-five finger-breadths less eleven *tilas*.

In the twenty-ninth [construction] of the eight-prastha [altar], there are twelve [bricks] on the side and thirty-six transversely; because there is no head, the ninth *karaṇa* does not exist. In the absence of the *aratni* and *prādeśa*, the tail bricks are exactly as in the previous *śyena*.
And there is a bending of those situated on the wings in accordance with that [bending].
In the two pads (upadhāna), the first eighty [bricks] are directed northward; the tail is exactly as in the previous Śyena.
The distance between the two fourth [bricks] situated at the junction of the tail is eighteen finger-breadths.
In the tail, it is exactly as in the previous Śyena; in the tail, there are fifteen finger-breadths in the body;
in the body, there are nine rows toward the north.
With the bricks facing north;
of these, there are seven middle ones.
With eight fourth [bricks], in the fourth row on the southern row; then sixty-four [bricks], two of which are fourths.
In the same way, there is the sixth style (*rīti*).
There are four *ṣaṣṭhīs* on each of the hips and shoulders;
in the remaining parts, there are six *pañcamīs*.
This is the two-hundred-brick layout. (In that layout, for the headless Śyenacit, there are thirty bricks each in the wings, arranged in rows running northward.)
In the tail, however, it is as before.
In the self, there should be nine rows in the north.
Among those, the first four syllables belonging to the first row should indeed be the sixth vowels (ṛ).
Thus are the final bricks. One fifth brick each is placed to the south and north; those situated at the junction of the tail are said to be in the middle of that.
In this manner, the ten bricks of the final rows should also be arranged;
the fifth rows have two additional [bricks] in the middle, and the fourth rows [are placed] within the *turayī* row.
Two [bricks] are *catasraḥ-ṣaṣṭhikāḥ*;
then two more *caturthī*s as before, followed by six *ṣaṣṭhī*s;
then two more *caturthī*s, two *doṣṭakā*s, and so on—one should fill the remainder of the fire-altar (*agni*) with *caturthī* bricks.
Thus, ninety bricks situated within the self are placed in the first layer;
in the second [layer], four each at the corners;
and in the third, four each at the points of convergence.
In the remainder of the two wings, there are fifty-six first [sets] facing east;
in the tail, as before, there are seventh and eighth [sets]. In the body, there are nine rows; those facing east are with bricks facing east.
In that [arrangement], for those situated at the points where the wings meet, there are five pentads and six hexads both behind and in front.
These are in the middle of the seven rows following the southern and northern directions (as in the previous layout).
In the middle of the second and sixth (or second and eighth) rows, there are sixteen hexads each.
[One should place] those [bricks] in the middle of the southern and northern rows, as in the previous arrangement;
in the middle of the second and eighth rows, sixteen bricks of the sixth [type] each;
thus the arrangement consists of two hundred [bricks].
In that regard, in the other arrangement, the second [syllables] are in the two wings;
the second [syllables] are from the middle of the wings;
and the first [syllables] are at the end, in the remainder.
Thus, in the northern section, there are the eastern ones;
these are all seventy-two.
Now, within the self, there should be nine eastern lines.
In the first [quarter], there is the second letter of the fifth [varga].
The two sixths go toward the setting of the solar fortnight, as does the fifth;
according to the method of the single final [sixth], there are then two sixths, and the setting occurs before them.
In the first [section], there should be one fifth [note] and sixty-sixths; in the second, there is no [fifth note].
In the middle, there should be sixteen sixths; thus they follow the eighth method.
In the fourth and sixth methods, however, it is likewise with the first and the subsequent;
the remainder for the self is by means of the fourths, [and] they have the tail as their domain.
"The seventh, twelfth, and eighth [bricks] are thirteen each, as before;
thus is the second arrangement intended for the second set of eight.
However, some maintain that because of the statement "as in the original form," the bricks [themselves] also [are so arranged].
They say that it is like the *prakṛti* with respect to the self.
Thus, on the side of the first *karaṇa*, there are forty finger-breadths;
the two *aratnis* are indeed transverse (*tiryaṅbhānyau*), and one ear-measure (*karṇa*) is twenty-five [finger-breadths] and seventeen *tilas*.
The other [altar] is fifty-nine and three-eighths *aṅgulas*.
Two [units] combined constitute the second [section], which is one *aratni* in length; one should increase it by the *aratni*-measure of the first [section], bending it as appropriate.

The third, the ninth from the tail, and the fourth, sixth, seventh, and eighth [sections] are as before; the bricks for the body are the fifth-part bricks (*pañcama-bhāgīyā*) according to the original model.

In that case, the *prādeśas* should be made with a width of six *aṅgulas*. On the *ātman*, ten lines (*rītis*) extending northward should be drawn from south to north, each measuring one and a half [units]. In the remainder of the *ātman*, there should be ten northern lines consisting of five [units] each.

Having removed two [bricks] from the middle, there are two fourth [size bricks] at the junction of the tail, measuring eighteen finger-breadths; one measures an aratni in length, and there are two on either side. There are four [bricks] with a width of six finger-breadths. Behind the two situated at the junction of the tail, there are five ardhyā bricks facing east. These are the specific features of the tail; the rest is as before.
On the two wings, there are thirty *prathamā*s each, facing north;
this constitutes the two-hundred-brick layout (*prastāra*).
On the other [altar], however, there are three *nirṇāmayo*s on each side.
In the remainder of the second fortnight, there are forty-two first [bricks] facing east; the tail is as before.
In the body, there are nine rows facing north.
Their beginnings and ends [are determined by] the eastern half-measures;

the final ones [of the middle rows] are by the fifth measures. Of the five middle rows, the first and the others are the eastern half-measures. Having removed the final one of the second [row], one should place there eight [bricks] six *aṅgulas* wide, two each extending northward from the front and from behind;
in the middle, four extend eastward.

According to the eighth method, having extracted the second from the beginning and the last from the end, there are nine, nine, and eight finger-breadths; this is the two-hundred-fold arrangement (*prastāra*).
When, however, they are laid down as equal squares, the two wings are exactly the same; the tail, however, is just as before.

At the two ends of the wings, there are two *aṇūka*s; when the body has been reached by a *prādeśa* on both sides, one should enclose these with six parts of six *aṅgula*s each, making six [parts] with ten *prādeśas*.
In the remainder of the body, there are *aratnis*.
This is the two-hundred-fold layout (*prastāra*).
In the other intermediate junction, however, there are forty-five *aratnis*;
on the hips and shoulders, there are twelve *aṇūkas* each;
and in the remaining part of the feet, there are twenty *aṇūkas*.
Having extracted the [measurement] situated in the middle of the self, there are nine and eight finger-breadths [for the two sides]. (This is the layout for two hundred [finger-breadths]).
When, however, the bending of the wings is performed with a cord of six hundred finger-breadths, then one of the first *karaṇas* has a length of five *puruṣas* and a width of six;
it is bent according to the requirement, and its diagonal (*karṇa*) is twenty-three finger-breadths and twenty-one *tilas*.
Another [measure] is thirty-seven [aṅgulas] with eleven *tilas*.

Having drawn on the ground an eastern square measuring twenty *aṅgulas* in length, thirteen *tilas*, and fourteen *aṅgulas* in width, one should bend it like a wing using a sixteen-*aṅgula* cord with loops at both ends.
One-third of that [length] for the first deity should be increased by one-eighth part.
The third [section] therein is according to the appropriate application;
the others are as before.
In the first layer of the foundation, there are six second [units] on each of the two sides of the central projection.
In the remainder of the wing, there are seventy-two first [bricks] facing north; the tail and the body are as before;
and on the hips and shoulders, there are two sixth [bricks] each.
The layout consists of two hundred bricks;
however, in this case, there are seventy first bricks on each wing,
and five facing east at each of the two junctions.
The third [set] is as before for the tail and the self;
however, in the self, having extracted sixteen sixth [syllables], one should insert eight fifth [syllables].
This is the two-hundred-fold arrangement.
Even in the view that the bricks are like the nature of the self, the bricks should be understood as being concordant with that [nature].

It is stated [in the scripture]: "The altar is twice as large, or thrice as large. In this case, because the gender is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣitatva*), while both Agni and the altar (*vedi*) are intended to be specified (*vihitatva*), the compound-ending suffix is applied. Here, the threefold nature belongs specifically to the original sevenfold Agni.

But there is no distinction based on the repetition of every [measure] performed for the sake of the subsequent quality (*guṇa*); rather, the repetition applies only to the entire *saratni-prādeśa*. This is because, in the injunction regarding the *tristāva*, there is no mention of a specific distinction such as "of men" as there is in the case of the repetition of the *vidhā*s.

Thus, the fire-altar consists of twenty-three and a half men (*puruṣa*s). A bamboo rod (*veṇu*) made of three parts of a man consists of thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*s) less five sesame seeds (*tila*s); these constitute the units corresponding to a man.
The "long fourfold" has been described; the method for two equal squares was stated in that very same place.
Furthermore, the transverse side-measure and the lateral side-measure are each three times the length of the lateral side-measure.

In another Vedic recension (śākhāntara), it is stated: "The person has twenty-one as its measure"; thus, the *ekaviṃśa-stoma* is to be applied here [in the context of] "the *sattra* has twenty-one stomas" and "fifty and a half [bricks]" as the object to be laid down (*upadheya*), because this is the general rule even when there is no specific *stoma*.
In this regard, because there is no conjunction, a number indeed excludes only another number of the same kind; such is the sense, as in the case of the repetitions of the *vidhā* measures.

According to this view, there are twenty-two and a half *puruṣas*; therein, the bamboo representing the *puruṣa* consists of two hundred and three finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and six sesame seeds (*tila*).
In this case, the fourth, fifth, sixth, and tenth [units] should be understood as being equal to one-eighth of an *aratni* (a cubit) each;
even though there is no full *aratni* or *prādeśa*, there are exactly twenty-one *puruṣas* in both wings.
However, in the glorious Rāmāyaṇa, the sacrificial fire of the Aśvamedha is seen to consist of eighteen *puruṣas*.
That funeral pyre for the lion among kings was constructed by virtuous brahmins;
it was like a golden-winged garuḍa, threefold and consisting of eighteen parts.
Thus it is said;
however, since all six types [of stoma] are seen to function as the *kṛti* in other Vedic branches (*śākhā*),
they should be understood as having three chants (*tristāva*).

For the Bodhāyana has stated that even the sixfold altar possesses the nature of the *prakṛti*: "Whether one intends to pile it in a sixfold, sevenfold, twelvefold, or however manyfold manner," and so on.
Here, having piled the altars up to thirteen types, one begins the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Piling an altar beyond that, one should pile it in twenty-two types or more.
But not the former kind. [The rule states:
"Having piled a larger altar, one should not pile a smaller one.

Now, if someone practices a form beyond the twenty-two-fold altar and thereafter begins the Aśvamedha, as at the end of the thirty-fold altar—for instance—his Aśvamedha fire-altar consists of three *stomas* or twenty-one-fold, because there is no other alternative for it.

Thereafter, however, one should perform only the thirty-onefold and subsequent rites, beginning from those previously performed, since the former have already been accomplished. All of this has been made clear by Baudhāyana: "If the Aśvamedha is reached, one should bring it forward and perform the subsequent rite; one need not attend to the others. If it has passed, one should bring it forward, and having brought it forward, one should take up the original form at the conclusion of what was performed."
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Śulbapradīpa* by Śrī Sundararāja. Thus the *Sundararājīya*, the *Āpastambīya-śulba-praśna* together with its commentary, is complete and finished.
